[p. v]

## Vorwort des Herausgebers. — Editor’s Preface

One half of this volume contains the last writings from the period in which Schelling was still predominantly occupied with the philosophy of nature. Beginning and end are here in a certain way joined, inasmuch as the writing against Fichte in part leads back again to the first motives of the philosophy of nature, while the *Yearbooks of Medicine as Science* were based on the endeavor to develop further the science of the organism, the highest point of the philosophy of nature (in the narrower sense), and if possible to bring it to an actual construction of medical science through it. This last undertaking of the philosophy of nature was, however, not carried further by its originator. During the publication of the *Yearbooks* Schelling left Würzburg in the year 1806 and entered upon a different sphere of activity, to which we first of all owe the address on the relation of the formative arts to nature. In the year 1809, however, the treatise on freedom appeared. With this Schelling had advanced to a philosophy which, although materially (as the “presentation of the ideal part of philosophy”) it bordered on the philosophy of nature, yet formally, namely through the further development of the principles as well as through the whole direction it took, went beyond the philosophy of nature and the system of identity; the principles of the latter were indeed not expressly abandoned, but they were already placed in a relation to a personality, to a [p. vi] *will*, and the world was explained not from them alone, but at the same time from their relation to the divine and, in the second place, to the human will, etc. A decisive turn toward what Schelling afterward called historical philosophy had now already taken place. The *Stuttgart Private Lectures* make this still more clearly recognizable. In the development of the principles these still lean wholly upon the concepts of the system of identity, which they so turn, directly and without adding a further principle to the given duality of principles, that they serve as the foundation of a system resting on the individuality of God. In their execution, on the other hand, they appear as an anticipation of much later developments, and show how, as soon as he had crossed over into this new domain, a manifold of Ideas presented itself to Schelling, some of which he held fast permanently, but others he afterward abandoned or at least, as is the case with the *psychological* ones that are especially important here, pushed into the background.

The external occasion for these lectures delivered in Stuttgart is as follows. Schelling spent the winter of 1809— 1810 in the city named (for what reasons, does not belong here). His friends, at their head the then Oberjustizrath Georgii, expressed the wish to hear explanations of his system. Schelling agreed; what he wrote down for this purpose has here been printed, with the use of a transcript by Georgii revised by Schelling himself. Since the communications on each occasion formed the thesis for a conversation following the lecture, the brevity and sketchlike character of the presentation is explained thereby.

Among the reviews at the end of the volume, the one on A. W. Schlegel’s *Ehrenpforte* etc. has been included here belatedly.

Esslingen, in August 1860.

K. F. A. Schelling.

[p. 1]

## Darlegung des wahren Verhältnisses der Naturphilosophie zu der verbesserten Fichteschen Lehre — Statement on the True Relation of the Philosophy of Nature to the Revised Fichtean Doctrine

An Explanatory Writing on the First. — 1806.

[p. 2]

[p. 3]

#### Vorbericht. — Preliminary Remarks

Of the philosophical part of Fichte’s lectures on the essence of the scholar, the author wrote an appraising account, printed in nos. 150 and 151 of the Jena *Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung*,<sup>1</sup> before the existence of the two other Fichtean writings, which had appeared almost at the same time, had become known to him even through the book-fair catalogue, which by chance he had not come across. After he had also read the *Characteristics* *of the Present Age* and the *Guide to the Blessed Life*, he recognized that his work might indeed stand in its worth or worthlessness with regard to the book it appraised there, but that it did not take in the present standpoint of Fichtean speculation, since this had itself advanced from one writing to the next, and there now emerged distinctly a not merely simple but double and triple duplicity in the spirit of its originator — a difference of the author of the *Guide* etc. from himself, not only in his first shape, but also from himself as the author of the *Erlangen Lectures* and still more from the author of the *Characteristics*. This observation, and the position in which he saw himself placed by the quite peculiar Fichtean syncretism with regard to Fichtean philosophy in general, moved the author to draft a more detailed statement of this relation. [p. 4] From this there results of itself the limited significance of that first appraisal, which of course did not foresee what Mr. Fichte would yet work himself up to in the blessed life, and from which only so much has been taken into the present account as could not be passed over, in order to complete the picture of the whole of his way of thinking, scattered through the Fichtean trilogy.

<sup>1</sup> This review has been appended here to the Preliminary Remarks. Ed.

It is possible that another writing will follow this one, containing some lectures delivered in Würzburg on the very same subjects that are treated in the *Guide to the Blessed Life* — for a complete survey of the whole relation between Mr. Fichte’s present view and that which, as Mr. Fichte says, itself bestows upon itself the name of the philosophy of nature.

#### Ueber das Wesen des Gelehrten etc. In Vorlesungen von Johann Gottlieb Fichte. Berlin 1806. — On the Essence of the Scholar etc. In Lectures by Johann Gottlieb Fichte. Berlin 1806.

A second word on the writing at hand in this *Literatur-Zeitung* cannot be surprising. For where would such an exception, as is after all sometimes made, be more in place than there, where a single part or a particular side of the work also admits of, indeed calls for, a particular consideration; and this seems to be the case here. The present writing has, besides its general interest, the particular interest of the speculative utterances by which *Fichte* breaks a silence of several years about his philosophical views. The ingenious appraisal, kept in a fine balance of insight and fairness, which this writing received in nos. 91 and 92 of these pages, has, as is natural, subordinated this side of it to the consideration of the whole. To us, however, this side alone seems worthy of a particular statement, on account of the clear light in which it lets the abiding and essential element of the philosophy of its originator appear again, even under an altered expression. — [p. 5] Another scruple might be raised. Why, namely, achieve that scientific purpose on a work of, after all, always only subordinate significance? Why not await the full and sufficient disclosure of the new presentation of the Wissenschaftslehre? But does he who asks so know whether he or I shall live to see its appearance? Has he forgotten what the author announces at the end of the preface, his ever greater reluctance to converse with the reading public? Besides, nothing in the work of a philosopher is accidental; and in the present work, at any rate, the speculative utterances certainly are not, and whoever does not already here, in the first and second lectures, recognize the essence and the spirit of the Fichtean philosophy now emerging again, to him the elaborated presentation too would hardly afford more insight. — There occur in the writing sidelong glances at a philosophy of which we must, sadly, confess that it is closely related to the author of this statement. What can follow from this for him? Nothing other than the obligation not to conceal his name, that is, not to do what, in relation to Fichte, he would not wish to do in any case. Men such as this have the prerogative that, even in public opinion, only reasons can do them any harm. In this respect the signed review is to him the same as the anonymous one. That one is resolved to stand against him with reasons alone, even in the former, is shown precisely by this free stepping forward. If Fichte has acted aloof and haughty toward a manner of philosophizing that concerns us more closely: we do not wish to act likewise; if he, although without knowing it, has adopted and sought to spread an absurd and plainly false concept of that manner: he is not like others who do this too, and of whom no one speaks; to him we want to show it, and if we are so fortunate as to be able to do so, why should the true judgment be omitted, merely because the true name would also have to be named for it?

The struggle for true philosophy, which distinguishes our age, is not being waged over the being or non-being of an Absolute. An Absolute, whether there is such a thing or not, [p. 6] concerns most people not at all; they only wish to ward it off from themselves, it is merely not to come into their sphere, and as the surest means against it they have chosen the quite simple reflection that all knowing must after all proceed first of all from ourselves, and that whoever only holds fast to this properly is already prevented of himself from ever arriving at an unconditioned. As the chief witness and confirmer of this truth, Fichte has been regarded by its adherents, and on him and his fruitful silence the hope of most was founded, precisely in this respect. It must strike them in a peculiar way when Fichte too declares: all that man does of himself (thus, since knowing is a doing, also all that he knows through himself) is null; it is not man who loves the divine Idea, but this loves and embraces itself in him; in general it is not the subject, not the I that is the ground of philosophy, but precisely the divine Idea. We, on the contrary, wish to accept with sincere joy the first principles which Fichte sets forth in the second lecture. “All being is living and active in itself, and there is no other being than life. 2) The Absolute or God is life itself, and conversely, life itself is the Absolute. 3) This divine life is in and for itself purely concealed in itself, it has its seat in itself and remains in itself, purely arising in itself, accessible only to itself. It is all being, and outside it there is no being.” Who should not rejoice at the vanished opposition in which being was conceived only as the pure negation of activity, but not as that which is activity in itself, while the latter in turn was conceived as the necessary opposite and the denial of all being; who should not rejoice at the happily overcome dread of this word, which was otherwise banished from God and divine things, expelled from the realm of truth, and is now so far transfigured that God is called all being, and that outside of which there is no being.

But these principles do not suffice by themselves, it will be [p. 7] said; what matters, moreover, is how, in or from this divine life and all-being at once, particular being is cognized. As is well known, the philosophy of all times has endeavored either to comprehend a stepping-forth, an externalization of God, in order thereby to explain the world (a vain undertaking!), or to convince the understanding, which can think the world only as something stepped forth, of the nullity of this representation. What does Fichte now do? According to him, “this divine life *externalizes* itself (since according to 3) it surely arises purely in itself), steps forth (since according to this very proposition it remains purely in itself), it appears and presents itself as such, as divine life, and this its presentation or its existence and outer existence is the world.” One sees that Fichte is quite light and unconcerned about this stepping-forth and externalization of God, as about a matter that goes without saying. One can, however, assert with confidence that in the passage above he speaks nothing but words, and that in a stepping-forth of the Absolute out of itself he in fact thought nothing, because nothing can be thought in it. One can be just as certain that he can never have considered this view of the genesis of the world as a whole and in all directions. For, to cite only one point, the world, as that *wherein* God presents himself, is, as he says, “conditioned by the two members, God’s essence in itself and the unalterable laws of an external presentation in general.” Is it now essential to God that he present himself externally, or is it not essential to him? Fichte has not explained himself definitely on this question; by an indirect utterance he would probably have to decide for the former. But then God too in his presentation, that is, he is, in that which is essential to him, *conditioned*, namely through the unalterable laws of an external presentation in general, which as such are independent of him. This is only one of the countless difficulties that lie on the road he has taken, which, if it were as smooth as it here seems, would surely long since have become a highway. How, further, can we still wonder if Fichte, to whom everything seems so easy, [p. 8] cannot grasp that we others do not also grasp, and if he cannot, for sheer clarity, think that it is equally clear to us what he wants, although we do not consider it sufficient?

If we see a man whose spirit awakened our esteem, and to whom we could not deny a distinct consciousness of the highest task of speculation, set up in the course of his work assertions which we must recognize as erroneous, with free courage, in strict sequence, and with bold contempt of the commonplace: we shall not be able to cease to esteem him and to feel strengthened by his appearance. But if we see him trace his true and proper principles back to such as those from which they can in no way any longer follow, and from which he nevertheless wants to have them either deduced or even already deduced; if we see him thus, pressed by the times, lose his own standpoint without winning a new one, and condescend to popularities which by his own way of thinking he would otherwise have scorned: then this must bring a dejecting feeling upon us. What does it mean, with regard to Fichte’s earlier insights, other than to lose oneself, when he lets the divine life in presentation become a life developing into the infinite — in a flux of time *that has no end*? Of all that *Kant* and *Fichte* have asserted, the truest without doubt is that time is a thoroughly merely subjective mode of representation, to which nothing actually occurring, not even in things, can correspond. Here, however, the presentation of the divine life itself is posited as directly afflicted with the *ens imaginationis* of an endless time. The magic of the first three principles is wholly dissolved with the fourth, and we hasten with Fichte, to whom it does not seem quite canny even here, past this region, noting briefly how he soon afterward seeks, in as few steps as possible, to turn back into the customary track and to return to himself. “The divine life remains, namely, life also in presentation. This living existence in appearance we call the human race. Thus the human race alone is there.” The readers will doubtless excuse us from illuminating these propositions [p. 9] in earnest, especially since the earlier review has already said what is to the point about them. We content ourselves with the remark: had the divine Idea become living in Fichte himself, he would behold only the positive and nothing besides, hence would also exclude nothing, and would hardly have attempted this evasion, which only brings the old arrogance before our eyes again, and the unconditional opinion of the infinite sublimity of this species, thus only the worse of the previous view without the better, namely consistency.

So far goes the positive side of Fichtean speculation, which deals with what is there; we turn to the other, which deals with what is not there but nevertheless must be there, with nature; for so contradictory must we render Fichte’s concept of it, as will at once be evident. After all existence and life had already been indirectly denied to it (for man does not belong to nature), a peculiar art will now be needed to restore it so far as is necessary in order merely to be able to explain it. It happens in the following way. The divine life in its presentation is an infinitely self-developing one. *In order that* (p. 30) a progress be possible, however, there must be a check; otherwise the whole completed life would break forth in a single stroke; a halting is therefore necessary, and the life in presentation is limited in all moments of time of its existence (as if limitation were still needed, where moments of time already are?), that is, it is in part not living and not yet pressed through to life. First of all, all scientific rigor is here at an end. Fichte has no other connecting concept at his command than the human one of end and means; the limits are *in order that* development be possible, a concept that is here quite inapplicable, since the concept of limits involves nothing positive at all. But note, moreover, the facility of this philosophizing. To say quite straight out: finitude is, in order that it be, would of course seem to say nothing. I must therefore put forward another expression of finitude, a circumlocution, say that of [p. 10] an infinite, that is, endless further development. That this is already precisely finitude itself in its most meager shape, the listeners will not at once notice, or rather I myself do not notice it, and say now boldly: in order that endless development may take place, there must be a check. This means as much as: worms have no eyes, in order that they may be blind. — Were Fichte now to proceed from here and to say: since, then, the life in presentation is limited in all moments of its existence, nature too is in part not living: this would at least cohere, and would leave something yet to be considered and explained in nature. But no, it is no life at all; rather, from the concept of limits just set up, and merely from this, they (the listeners) have the concept of the objective and material world, or of the *so-called* nature (Fichte does not grant the poor thing even this, so little is it, in his opinion, namely to be called nature). This so-called nature is not living, like reason and the human race, not capable of infinite further development (the endlessness of development is thus only a prerogative of reason), but dead and a rigid existence enclosed in itself. But not even this can it be. Is not a dead existence in itself, and also according to the first of the principles above, the most perfect contradiction? Further, the limits are only limits of further development, that is, of the self-presenting divine life: but from this divine life, the self-presenting, we are here to abstract wholly; nature is not that, the divine life, and the limit, but it is the limit quite alone and nothing but this, and the concept of this exhausts completely the concept of that as well. What, then, is a limit without anything real that grasps itself in it? In fact a complete nothing, not a half, but a perfect non-ens. — The limit, says Fichte, or so-called nature, is absolutely dead, but the dead, it says on p. 28, *neither is*, nor is it in the proper sense of the word *there*; how, then, can the limit, as such, give the concept of an objective world? it is as little the concept of something objective as of [p. 11] something subjective, but precisely the concept of nothing at all; what is completely nothing can also not “be *animated* by the rational life in its development”, not be “the object of the exertion of force by the same.” Let the author solve for us the problem how something that is mere limit without anything real can be acted upon. We hold this to be just as possible as that one should bump one’s head on the angles of a geometrical figure: let us not deny, to be sure, that, if these principles are perhaps meant personally, Fichte did find in nature *his* limit, which at first, quite transparent, did not appear to him, and with which, now that it has gained more consistency for him, he evidently does not know what to do.

We wish briefly to uncover the ground of this confusion. That nature is an objective world, Fichte thinks, it has occurred to no one to doubt, and this stands as firm as ever, and can therefore be presupposed as universally accepted. Yet it is precisely the essential point of conscious philosophy not to see nature as an objective world, indeed to hold the objective world *as* objective in general to be a mere creature of reflection. *This* objective world, which Fichte has in mind, is therefore not even a dead one; it is nothing at all, an empty specter. Fichte would like to annihilate it, and yet at the same time also preserve it, for the sake of moral utility. It is only to be dead, so that it can be acted upon; that it should vanish entirely was by no means the intention.

After the holy zeal and the resistance against nature have now carried the author somewhat too far for his own purposes, its *ground* is nevertheless even given in God. Namely, by virtue of the self-presentation of God, the infinite further development must be; but in order that this can be, the finitude of human life must at the same time be, hence this too proceeds from that self-presentation of the Absolute, and nature has, to be sure! its ground too in God. We admire, indeed, the exact and thorough insight into the course of the matter, but still cannot grasp how something in whose concept nothing positive at all is contained can proceed from [p. 12] God, or how something to which the concept of being is not at all applicable can have a ground, and indeed in God. Yes, Fichte goes still further: existence is now already conceded to nature, only not “an absolute one, that is, one that is for its own sake, but merely one that is the means, the condition of another, and is to be more and more canceled.” — “Do not, therefore (on account of these exceptionally thorough and proven assertions), let yourselves be dazzled,” the address to the listeners continues, “or misled by a philosophy which bestows upon itself the name of the philosophy of nature” (a worse one the worst enemy could not give it), “and which believes it surpasses all previous philosophy by making nature the Absolute, by striving to deify it.” Whom, who has ever been pervaded by the seriousness and depth of philosophy, could such vain thoughts of surpassing others occur, either to cherish them himself or to ascribe them to others? What in philosophy merely surpasses is to that extent no better than that which is surpassed, and is necessarily itself surpassed. Who would want to expend time and effort in order to contribute his share to this constant alternation of surpassing and being surpassed? There are not better and worse philosophies; there is only one true one, and there are untrue ones, which are not surpassed by the former, for they do not stand on the same line with it; and here applies what Spinoza says: “Non dico, me optimam invenisse philosophiam, sed veram me intelligere scio.” As to the deification of nature, however, this favored phrase is itself only a flat petitio principii, in that it presupposes that we others have precisely the popular concept of nature, according to which it is a limit of our life, an object of our activity. — Without something un-divine there is surely no deification. Let Fichte first give us out of his stock something that we could deify; until now, however, we hold more firmly than he to the principle he has set up in words but not comprehended in his own sense: God is all being, and outside him there is no being. According to this principle everything [p. 13] that in nature is being, and so far as it is only being, everything positive in a word, is also equal to the life of God. Of the non-being in it, however, which Fichte alone knows, there can be no question at all, precisely because it is a complete non-being; least of all can it be spoken of as of something that is *animated*, and accordingly, since all life is equal to the divine life, is quite actually to be deified. There follows upon the passage above an almost devout maxim which we must suppose the author himself could not have brought forth without a pleasant blush, but which we pass over, since the first review has already excerpted it. More interesting to us is to touch on an utterance of the latter, since it gives us occasion to express ourselves more distinctly on a main point. The reviewer too “does not hold the cause of the philosophy of nature to be the best, he holds it rather to be an anticipation of a higher sphere of life, which however had necessarily to fail.” In other words, namely *Shakespeare’s* words, this means: In a better world than this I would desire more of your worthy company. Who may now say, however, that there is an anticipation of this kind, who say that something is not philosophy but rather something better than philosophy? Is anything too good for philosophy, and does not the poverty of philosophizing hitherto have its ground precisely in the opinion that philosophy is to be sought in something lesser than that better thing, and ought it not to be sought in this, supposing that the first attempt to find it there had really failed? What if the long-yearned-for and prophesied consummation had to consist precisely in presenting in actuality what was otherwise held inaccessible and, by every view other than that of a philosophy of nature, in fact transcendent? All that reason cognizes of the essence of God fills the sphere of the actual world and is the positive in it: for whoever beholds this positive, the other does not remain even as a limit. This presentation of the life of God not outside and above nature, but in nature, as an actual and present but always divine life, is [p. 14] without doubt the last synthesis of the ideal with the real, of cognizing with being, and hence also the last synthesis of science itself. What good is it, for example, to Fichte, the semblance of the first propositions about the divine Idea and the divine life, which all become transcendent for him through the consequence, since for him God is once again a being outside and above nature, to which he first gives an existence, *in* *that* he thinks to take it away from it? Criticism and his own earlier and better system cry out against him. What the reviewer, moreover, adds as the ground of the necessary failure of that anticipation, “because namely that which exists within *this* mode of existence cannot repeat or reconstruct its genesis,” in this, if we have otherwise grasped his sense, we would rather believe we hear Fichte than him. For it is not that which exists that is to or can comprehend existence; rather, eternal existence itself has itself in reason and in true cognition.

According to Fichte, man can, to be sure, have insight into the excellences set out above with regard to the *that*, but not with regard to the *how* (p. 33). Yet according to an earlier passage, “philosophical cognition is not satisfied by the *that*; philosophy asks not merely further after the how, but, strictly speaking, asks solely after the how” (p. 13). So then this first cognition, too, of God’s coming forth out of himself and of his exhibition in the world is not a philosophical one, and Fichte should not boast of it as a philosophical one, but should confess his not-knowing. — Here, as repeatedly, the reader may come to doubt whether it is possible that such incoherence, such indistinct and self-contradictory talking back and forth should be met with in a work of Fichte’s. We declare expressly that it is so, and that every reader may convince himself, by his own inspection, of the correctness and the literal fidelity of our presentation. For insight into the *how*, Fichte demands the comprehension of *all* the parts of temporal life in a perfected apprehension (hence, presumably, insights of the kind that were otherwise demanded of him, [p. 15] e.g. that a great orator Cicero, or a great king Cyrus, must have existed); in conclusion it is also asserted that the philosophy in question gives itself the semblance of possessing just such insights, “of being able to dissolve the whole of human life into the concept and to replace experience.” It must strike one as odd to see Fichte of all people set himself up as the patron of experience and seek the connection he otherwise scorned, now — against the philosophy of nature; all the more so since this work, too, attests the same lack of intuition and poverty of actual experience as the author’s earlier writings — since, however, he is wholly without any idea of the significance that religion and revelation have for that philosophy, we must regard this unintelligent utterance, too, like the earlier one, as pardonable.

From here on, after nature and the philosophy of nature have been happily disposed of, the discourse then flows on unhindered and unchecked into its accustomed bed, and pours itself out over ethical life and duty in the manner known to all.

What, then, is one to think of the whole, and what is one to say about it with the utmost fairness? It is, to be sure, hard, amid the turns and twists which the inner discord and the concern for one’s own I produce in the struggle against the truth pressing in upon it, to seize the determinate shape and set it plainly before us; yet it can be grasped all the same and cannot conceal itself, however much it would like to. — No one can well hesitate to regard the first principles as a foreign wreath, sought elsewhere and set upon a building already standing, as if someone wished to wreathe the head of an old Doric column-shaft with acanthus leaves of the Corinthian order, ut nec pes nec caput uni reddatur formae. Fichte has taken up the subject-object-ification of the Absolute as selfexhibition, immediately burdened with the misunderstanding of a coming forth out of itself. Withal one cannot fail to recognize a feeling of the nullity in his earlier doing. Proof of this lies especially in his utterances about morality, namely that, as commanding, it is possible only from a lower standpoint of [p. 16] insight , that it has hitherto taught nothing positive, but only what is to be left undone. Other such indications are the already mentioned declarations, repeated several times in the work itself, that what man does for himself is null (though the divine appears to him only as an alien power), and the like.

What is it, then, that in spite of this irresistibly draws him back into death — into the most monotonous and lifeless moralizing, in which the ruler and the student, together with the academic teacher and the writer, receive the same general verdict, indeed in which the divine Idea itself, through the immoderate use made of it in the joy of the newly won expression, is degraded to a true moral panacea and finally even to a household remedy, whereby the student is to be encouraged to diligence and all the other virtues of academic life? What is the ground that the divine Idea, in the course of the exposition, evidently becomes for him a mere figure of speech, that even now he needs God only at the end of his philosophizing, as can be plainly read on p. 169: “that there is a God, is evident without difficulty to any reflection on the world of sense that is but a *little* serious; one must (*must*) in the end after all (!) conclude by laying at the foundation of that existence which is always grounded only in another existence an existence which has the ground of its existence in itself.” Does this passage not prove that Fichte can appropriate the divine only in a dogmatic way, and that it is only cowardice which drives him to disown the previous nature and yet to appropriate that for himself? What is the ultimate ground of all this, as of his decided incapacity to grasp the Idea of the philosophy of nature? For we are firmly convinced that he ascribes to it no other sense than the one that is really accessible to him alone; we do not credit him with the vigorous self-conceit to opine to himself: if only I, Fichte, say that it deifies the dead, my word is enough; nor do we wish to apply to him what he says of men of a certain kind, that they [p. 17] revile the true and first birthplace of a scientific truth, so that the unprejudiced may by no means come upon the thought of looking for it there; rather we believe we assume, with the greatest probability, that he lives really in the blessed opinion that the philosophy of nature has no other and no more than this easy state of affairs, and that its error can be made comprehensible to any child.

What, then, is the ground of this, as of the rest? — It is the absolute need of a finite world, which still holds him ensnared, the necessity in which he even now still stands, of having an *object*, of being, not one with the whole, but for himself. We must declare it empty semblance when he claims to have comprehended the livingness of being: empty talk when he pretends to annihilate nature. He merely does not want to have it as living, but as dead he certainly wants to have it, as something on which he can act, which he can work upon and trample underfoot. Were the objective world to vanish for him as objective, he would vanish for himself as subject; and if that world is not dead, then in his opinion he is not alive. He will sooner fall into the crassest dogmatism than let go of this opposition. When one hears him talk, one does not know whether *he* has more to complain of the hardness of nature, or nature more of his. It oppresses him, jostles him, gnaws at him on all sides, threatens and restricts his life without cease (p. 44); but he repays it for this amply; for what, in the end, is the essence of his whole opinion of nature? It is this: that nature is to be used, to be turned to account, and that it exists for nothing further than to be used; his principle, according to which he regards nature, is the economicteleological principle. “It had to be so, he says (namely, nature had to confine us so), *in order that* human life might win freedom through its own freedom. For this it is now necessary that one subject the forces of nature to human purposes.” Unfortunately this has so far succeeded only with the mechanically acting ones; no man has yet put bit and bridle on the living force of nature, and if Fichte says in another [p. 18] place (p. 29) that nature is to be animated by rational life in its development, then here too the very opposite is the case, for in so far as nature ever serves human purposes, it is killed. When Mr. Fichte has 6 horses harnessed to his carriage and “drives off as if he had 24 legs,” has *he* perhaps animated these 24 legs by his rational resolve, has he not rather restricted their natural livingness? and when he has a table or chair made for him, or cuts a pen, then this, though he writes with it and upon it his nature-animating works, is always only a killing, but by no means an animation. One is more and more led to the conjecture that he lacks, in regard to everything else in nature than the merely mechanical, even knowledge and intuition. — In order, however, that one may be able to do that, that is, for the sake of this excellent purpose of human utility, not perhaps because even in nature “the majesty of God reveals itself most imposingly” (which in a Fichtean work is evidently only a rhetorical flower that has strayed there); for the sake of this purpose — hear it, investigators and priests of nature! — “one must know the laws according to which these forces act, and must be in a position to calculate in advance their manifestations of force.” — But “moreover, nature is to be not *merely* useful and serviceable to man” (the economic view); “it is at the same time to surround him becomingly,” i.e. it is to be (how can one construe it otherwise?) refashioned into fine gardens and dwellings, becoming furniture and other ornament (Fichte’s aesthetic view of nature). The philosophical Nestor reminds us here quite involuntarily of another Nestor, the one in Prince Zerbino. The latter, when he returns in a most ill-humored mood from the grove of poetry, where the forest, the flowers, the breezes had spoken, and his head had been quite muddled by the strange nature, is beside himself with joy when he hears the table, the chair, and the other furniture speak, for these are, after all, no trees and flowers, but natural things animated by rational life itself, which rejoice to be useful conveniences, no longer to [p. 19] stand outside as wretched green trees and to rustle in the wind, *which indeed would not befit any rational being*.

We must say it: the ground of spiritual commonness of every kind is itself the lack of that intuition through which nature appears to us as self-living; indeed this lack sooner or later brings about the complete death of the spirit, which no arts can any longer cloak. There is something incurable in it (we gladly acknowledge it); for all healing power is only in nature. This alone is the true antidote to abstraction. It is the ever-fresh spring of inspiration and of a rejuvenation ever recurring. — In natures without other prominent qualities this lack produces that dullness and lifelessness of the whole heart and spirit which is the inheritance of the socially corrupted, and, where the moral feeling at the same time ails, that discomfort whenever they are to be forced to contemplate an object of nature as it is. What can it produce in natures that at least with force fall back upon their own individuality and are turned inward? In truth nothing other than a moralizing of the whole world that undermines and hollows out life, a true abhorrence of all nature and livingness outside the subject, a crude extolling of ethical life and of the doctrine of morals as the only real thing in life and in science. A crude one; for where should it find measure and cultivation, since for thoughts that delight solely in arbitrary choice the mildness, the creating from within, the quiet course and the eternally uniform order of nature is an abomination? — Whoever seriously attempts on the scientific path this carrying-through of morality without any unity with nature will sooner and more easily become aware how little it affords him, and even in Fichte this becoming-aware is not wholly to be mistaken. It is clear, and he himself sees it, that that doctrine of morals leaves an infinite gulf between thought and life, that it teaches the one to be educated only non-acting, while nature and world urge him to act, and demands that, as [p. 20] they themselves always act in concreto, so too he in every single case should do the true, the apt, the unique thing. But what can be expected of a doctrine of morals in which, as hitherto in all, be it under other names, collisions of duties occur? — To use, finally, such a moral view as an instrument of polemic against the higher has long been recognized in poetry and art for what it is; in science alone is it still to hold? To be sure, it admirably pleases the people, who must always have morality before their eyes, precisely because they are the people, and it serves admirably to create an evil repute for the hated doctrine among this same people. It is with ethical life, in the sense in which it is actually understood in those eulogies, as with the correctness of style; one demands this, indeed one presupposes it as the conditio sine qua non of an excellent work, but as this does not suffice even to produce the semblance of a work of art, so that does not suffice for a truly beautiful and divine life. Who will, says Plato, want to give beautiful and good men laws to speak the truth, to keep contracts sacred, not to overreach others? — There lies infinitely much outside and above the bounds of this morality, not only all that is free life in nature and art, but equally the divinity of disposition itself, which is our redemption from the law and the reconciliation with the divine, since before we were subject to it. — Not all, without doubt, are capable of this view, which may eternally belong to the mysteries of higher humanity. But to these same belong also science, poetry and art. Into these, then, the Malvolios are not to break in, who suppose that because they are virtuous there is to be no more beauty in the world, no excellence of nature, no livingness outside themselves and their like; and when even an otherwise scientific man is made like them by an ineradicably common keynote of his nature, one cannot but lament it.

F. W. J. S.

[p. 21] The aim of this work, as the title already indicates, is by no means a comparative juxtaposition of the philosophy of nature with the original Wissenschaftslehre. If any relation obtains between the two, then this has for some time been clear and decided for everyone who can read German books and understand philosophical ones, and it is not the way of the author to go back upon his path and to do once more what has already been done.

The present purpose requires only the mention that the judgment in this matter rested solely on the fact that Mr. Fichte had taught and asserted: *that a cognition of the in-itself or* *Absolute is eternally impossible for man; that we can know only of* *our knowing, can proceed only from this as our own, and likewise* *remain only within it; that nature is an empty objectivity, a mere* *world of sense; that it consists solely in affections of our I, rests on* *incomprehensible limits within which the I feels itself enclosed, that* *it is essentially devoid of reason, unholy, ungodly; everywhere,* *finally, and throughout dead; that the basis of all reality, of all cognition is the personal freedom of man; that the divine can only be* *believed, not cognized; that this faith too is of a merely moral kind,* *and in so far as it contains more than can be inferred from the* *moral concept, it is absurd, idolatrous*: the remaining propositions that follow of themselves from these we may well spare ourselves from singling out.

[p. 22] It was not within Mr. Fichte’s choice to acknowledge these propositions as his own or to disown them. Partly they could be documented from all his writings and verified in them word for word; partly he had asserted them only just now with such confidence and had been so certain of them in his knowing, that he could hardly think of renouncing them at once.

Had he wished to speak further, he was in the position either of admitting their error as such, or of defending it honestly and bravely against all and sundry. The latter he could, the former he would not. — So there remained only silence.

Otherwise Mr. Fichte had, and, as one may well concede, for the most part with good right and title, the answer in readiness that one had not understood him, had merely failed to penetrate his spirit. Against people whose power of thought stood in an obvious disproportion to that of Mr. Fichte, and to whom not seldom even the first idea of philosophy was lacking, the mere assurance might suffice. Toward the author of the Characterization given of the Fichtean system in the Critical Journal of Philosophy, vol. II, no. I, this rejoinder, unless supported by a determinate and convincing demonstration of the failure to understand, was to be regarded as a poor evasion, and deserved, according to the degree of earnestness with which it was put forward, to be received with a smile or with scorn, but in any case to be rejected without more ado. That his former opponents did not understand him was credible, for they all found that Mr. Fichte was transcendent and too metaphysical, whereas he was zealously endeavoring to convince them of the contrary and to make the plainness of his philosophy comprehensible to them. We conceded the latter to him, and the dispute (if there was one) now took the opposite turn. Since Mr. Fichte, moreover, hoped by his Sonnenklarer Bericht to compel the whole public, that is, the clever and the stupid without distinction, to understand, we could assume that this instruction [p. 23] would not just have been lost upon us. Nor is it to be seen what particular spirit can still lie hidden in propositions such as those singled out above, or how one is supposed to be able to misconstrue them.

Whether one has understood a philosophical writer or not, on this every one must, under the given conditions, be able to come to full clarity with himself. There is in this matter a certainty that may strike down all doubt, and which I, with the readers’ permission, will illustrate by the present case. There was, namely, indeed a time in which I myself believed that I did not wholly understand Mr. Fichte, although he himself thought so and in every way boasted of it; it was the time when I sought something higher and deeper in his doctrine than I could in fact find. Indeed it took no less than the whole series of his latest writings, those on the alleged atheism, the Vocation of Man, the Sonnenklare Bericht, to produce in me the conviction that I had understood him perfectly, and that this self-sufficiency concealed no more than it displayed. Now that I had made the emptiness clear to myself, the not-understanding began on Mr. Fichte’s side and continues to this hour. I must surely have understood him, and far better than he himself thought, since I understood even beyond him, and he first in the year 1806 brought forth singly propositions which the philosophy of nature had already set up in 1801 in scientific connection. On the other hand he has so far remained in debt of the proof that he was not understood by us, and will probably remain in debt of it. The small shame of contradicting earlier utterances by doing so, we were gladly willing to spare him, after what has been said above.

So the silence had its way, which at the same time afforded several advantages. It spared the trouble of setting against the allegedly misunderstood one the now rightly understood system, which cancels all misconstructions, with which one at that time ran the risk of only entangling oneself the further and talking oneself the deeper in. There might still be here and there a good-natured person who interpreted the silence [p. 24] as noble contempt (although otherwise to Mr. Fichte the worst opponent never seemed too lowly to instruct him); or as a fruitful and fearful calm before the storm, of which one could not possibly foresee that it would dissolve into so gentle a rain, as now in the blessed life. Chiefly, however, it was to be expected that, while a higher view of philosophy as a science of the divine and a contemplation of the world from the standpoint of this divine was being developed ever further, the earlier state of things would sink into a happy oblivion, so that one would have trouble bringing the public to a recollection of what Mr. Fichte had formerly taught and asserted. In fact many livelier Ideas had already become a kind of common property, which anyone who bore strength and livingness enough in himself might make his own.

Now, after this has progressed so far, and that fundamental idea of philosophy has been carried through, against the great mass of the age and the cultivation of Fichtean hardening in its spirits and hearts, so far that at least from the scientific side nothing considerable remains to be brought against it, now Mr. Fichte comes, tanquam re bene gesta, and as if nothing had happened, to take quiet possession of a part of the new realm of truth, to be the first to greet this rising light of religion and to surprise the mixed public with the proclamation of it: with the best will, magnanimously to reap what he has not sown, and to work up what he has not planted. Whatever of the religious and ethical Ideas was capable of the higher view of being appropriated by himself and communicated in a popular manner, he artfully picks out and weaves it into a fragrant wreath to crown his own brow with it, and, in order that no one may doubt the originality of the adornment, the philosophers of nature are degraded to the lowest depth and most vigorously reviled.<sup>2</sup>

<sup>2</sup> It hardly needs recalling that we here have in view the three writings: Grundzüge des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters, Vorlesungen über das Wesen des Gelehrten, and Die Anweisung zum seligen Leben. The order given is at the same time that of the composition of these writings; in what follows we shall designate the first of them, for brevity, by Gr., the second by E. V., the third by s. L.

[p. 25] A chief proposition of the Fichtean doctrine, not merely a thought thrown out in passing but, as is well known, a fundamental teaching, was this: that the concept of being is a merely negative one, inasmuch as it expresses only the absolute negation of activity; likewise, that it must be wholly banished from God and from divine things. Now Mr. Fichte steps forward boldly and declares: All being is living, and there is no other being than life. The Absolute, or God, is itself life. God is all being, and outside him there is no being (E., 2nd Lect.). Formerly he taught: With regard to the Absolute, or the in-itself, there subsists an eternal contradiction, for something is supposed to be for the I, and consequently *in* it, and yet at the same time not in the I but outside it; otherwise it would not be an in-itself. This is the circle never to be broken through, the discovery of which is the merit of the Wissenschaftslehre, and in which all finite natures are irretrievably entangled and eternally enclosed. (Grundlage der Wissenschaftslehre, practical part, p. 270). Now, however, we hear: “Between the Absolute, or God, and knowing, in its deepest root of life, there is no separation, but both merge into one another” (cf. L., p. 88). Mr. Fichte had brought his whole philosophy to completion and presented it in many ways without finding it necessary to make the slightest mention of God or divine things, until in the year 1798 he communicated the *results* of his philosophizing on this subject, and even then only because it was to be feared that a forward writer might anticipate a part of the discovery. (Ueber den Grund unsres Glaubens an eine göttliche Weltregierung, Philos. J. 1798, no. 1, pp. 1, 2). Henceforth, however, all philosophizing is to begin from the divine Idea, and the love with which this Idea embraces itself in the individual is to be the ground and beginning of all science. Formerly (see the same place) the philosopher knew too well that only a misguided [p. 26] philosophy, in its embarrassment at having to explain something whose existence it cannot deny, infers a God from the world of the senses: this inference, however, is superstition and yields as its product idolatry, etc. Now this inference has become quite handy and innocuous. For “that a God is, becomes evident without difficulty to the *merely slightly* serious reflection on the world of the senses”; one must (*must*) *finally* after all! end by laying at the foundation of that existence which is always grounded only in another existence an existence which (*existence*?) has the ground of its existence in itself (E. V., p. 169).

It is not that Mr. Fichte sets forth these or those propositions, but that *He* is encountered at all in this region, that is the matter for wonder. We had shown him that he had made the proper principle of sin, I-hood, the principle of philosophy (Philosophie und Religion, p. 42 [VI, p. 43] ff.); now *he* declares this very age to be the age of consummate sinfulness. It had been shown that the whole Fichtean philosophy was an understanding hardened in reflective superstition and rigidified in formal science (Krit. J. loc. cit.). Now he speaks of love and of the apostle John, and the reflection that annihilates itself in God is the highest. The most striking opposition is formed by the morality that once swallowed up all religion, and the ethics that is now deeply abased by this very religion. Every belief in something divine that contained more than the concept of the moral world-order was to him an abomination, most unworthy and most suspect for a rational being (words of the Philos. Journal of 1798, no. 8, p. 379). Likewise all excellence, beauty, and blessedness of human nature was wholly exhausted in dutifulness and ethical life; indeed this was the one thing real in the world and in man. Now how differently! “Only after faith, that is, clear and living thinking, had vanished from the world, did people place the condition of the blessed life in virtue, and so sought noble fruits on wild wood” (s. L., p. 23). But who has more zealously sought to graft upon this wild wood — truly not of virtue, which is [p. 27] excellence itself, but of mere dutifulness — all blessedness and beauty of human nature than Mr. Fichte himself? Can one also gather figs from thorns and grapes from thistles? is the question that presses itself upon every informed reader of the newest of the three writings.<sup>3</sup>

<sup>3</sup> Whoever wishes to be convinced of the nature of this philanthropic utterance — that enthusiasm (of which it is then proved that it goes hand in hand with the philosophy of nature and is one and the same with it) cordially hates both morality and religion *in their true shape* (Gr., p. 221), to him we recommend in the meantime a writing that appeared in the autumn of the year 1805: Beiträge zum Studium der Philosophie als Wissenschaft des All. Nebst einer vollständigen und faßlichen Darlegung ihrer Hauptmomente von G. M. *Klein* (Würzburg, in der Baumgärtnerischen Buchhandlung), where § 50, but especially 51 and 52, present the above religious ideas in condensed brevity, as well as the view of the philosophy of nature on this point generally.

Can the distinction between letter and spirit settle even this bitter quarrel? Well, that would have to be a strange, obstinate, indeed foolish body which weeps when the soul enjoys heavenly serenity, and laughs when it is troubled to death.

Be that as it may, Mr. Fichte has now once and for all acquired all this (his own expression): the divine Idea, the immediate cognition of the Absolute, the blessed life and love itself, and we at least have no intention of begrudging him this acquisition. Rather we rejoice heartily and sincerely that it has gone so well with him as to recognize all this to such an extent; we rejoice that he has put to shame the hope of the faint-hearted, who supposed that he would go on denying, as they do, the cognition of the divine, that he would again raise upon the throne, in place of the serene and blessed God, the gloomy idol of subjectivity and of a base morality; we rejoice in every more living Idea, in every single sound of genuine science in him, and regard them as an indirect, external testimony to the truth. That he also abuses us grossly and even slanders us, and so cuts the last bond that is still preserved between men of opposed modes of thought by inner measure and outward decorum, we would gladly forget, for the sake of the former.

[p. 28] What moves us to undertake the present work is not this, but the observation that he himself, through the principles he has acquired, has brought the matter to a point where it can come to the final decision. He has conceded truths which he formerly rejected; but he has at the same time shown so glaring an inconsistency, so incomplete a consciousness of the content and the penetrating force of those truths, that one need only turn these against him to demonstrate palpably the nullity of the part of his system that still remains, or at least to compel him himself to give up the former truths again as well. That is precisely the most reprehensible thing in the matter, that he wants to unite Christ and Belial, the apostle John and himself; that he does not reject the earlier principles outright (unless an unconscious irony against himself leads him to it), and that he wishes to pass off those higher views only as the crown which he has yet to set upon his doctrine. This doctrine, namely, has indeed had to withdraw into a subordinate sphere and to be beaten down, in order to leave some room above for heaven and religion, but the old harshness is nevertheless to be reconciled with the new love, while the latter, in turn, is to procure for it a good conscience and give it faith in itself. We declare once more in this respect: It is not that Fichte sets forth these or those Ideas, which, to one who has once grasped the fundamental Idea, must surely issue from it of themselves and are not the property of any one man — (whoever could regard them as such must for that very reason never have truly received them) — it is not this that we regard as robbery, but that he only *makes use* of these Ideas, that love, the blessed life, and everything glorious that he appropriates are only to be the mask to conceal the fundamental defect, the original deformity of his system. Since he has attempted, with an intention not wholly pure, to work his way toward and over to the better, this affords us on the one hand the convenience of being able to assume him to be in agreement on certain principles and hence to mark all the more sharply the point where the error, where the complete [p. 29] failure to understand begins in him; on the other hand it calls upon us to do the opposite of him, and on this occasion to part from him thoroughly and down to the root.

We begin from the innermost center of the whole inquiry. — Philosophy is not a believing, a surmising, or a holding-fortrue, but a cognition and science of the divine, and indeed a thoroughly clear and adequate cognition, since of the divine there can be either none or only such a one. Since we have already said all that is necessary on this elsewhere, and since no further objection to the proposition in this generality is to be expected from Mr. Fichte either, we go on from here at once.

To God, or the Absolute, being is essential, or rather, God himself is essentially being, and there is no being but God; we cannot say: but the being of God. For the being of God would itself be God, because God is precisely nothing other than being.

Conversely, then, all being, merely because it is being, is in itself divine, absolute, neither explicable from another, nor become, but the eternal truth and thoroughly positive. Something that was not divine (if there could be such a thing at all) would for that very reason not be being, and it would therefore be wholly impossible to say that it is.

God is therefore the one and only actual, as certainly as he is essentially being; or he alone and wholly fills the sphere of actuality. To think something actual outside God is as impossible as to think an actuality outside actuality.

If philosophy is accordingly a science of the divine, then it is not a science of it as of a being that is merely in thought, or can be grasped only through thought, but it is a science of God as the one and only actual, hence also the one and only intuitable and, in everything intuitable, the one and only really intuited: (for an intuition that was not an intuition of the actual would not be an intuition either).

[p. 30] We wish to elucidate the same from another side for the one who grants that God or the eternal can be grasped through thought (cf. L., p. 19). If he thinks God truly, he thinks him as the one and only real, which is essentially itself *being*. God therefore cannot be in the world of thought without by that very fact being the one and only positive of an actual or natural world, and in regard to him there is generally no opposition of an ideal and a real world, of a beyond and a here. Whoever denies this may well dream of a nature that is not, or of an actuality that is not actuality. But how does he come to dream, when he ought to be awake? He grants that God is reality, pure actuality itself: let him now seek the world, or the sphere, in which God is actuality! No other world will rise for him, either now or hereafter, in which God would be actuality in some quite special way, apart from the present and so-called actual world, and if God is not actuality *in* this world, then he will presumably not be actuality at all, that is, he will not be God.

If, then, philosophy is science of the divine as of the one and only positive, it is science of the divine as of the one and only actual *in* the actual or natural world, that is, it is essentially philosophy of nature.

Were it not philosophy of nature, it would assert that God is solely in the world of thought, and thus is not the positive of the actual or natural world, that is, it would cancel the Idea of God itself.

Being is truth, and truth is being. What the philosopher thinks, and of what he speaks, must *be*, because it is supposed to be *true*. What is not, is not true. The philosopher, then, who speaks of nature as of something that *is not*, speaks not of the true, and speaks untruly himself, because he lends the truth that it does not have to the untrue, in that he speaks of it as though there were such a thing. True philosophy must speak of that which *is*, that is, of actual nature, of *existent* nature. God is essentially being, that is to say: God is essentially [p. 31] nature, and conversely. Hence all true philosophy, that is, all that is cognition of the one and only true and positive, is ipso facto philosophy of nature, and will probably bear this name as long as this cognition has not become general, in order to distinguish itself from the false, which is in the not-actual, that is, in the not-true.

From this Idea of the philosophy of nature, in its whole rigor, we may now make the application with greater freedom. In our view, the separation into a world of thought of its own and a world of actuality of its own is the proof that even in the world of thought *God* has not been posited. If (per impossibile) no nature existed for me, or I could posit it as annihilated, and I thought God truly and with living clarity, then in the same moment the actual world would have to fill itself for me (this is the sense of the often misunderstood identity of the ideal and the real). In between you speak of a given nature, and unfortunately it turns out that those who have been most zealous against such as cannot tear themselves loose from the given show the greatest incapacity for it themselves; but how do you come to this at all, and what entitles you to intrude it here? You were to philosophize, that is, you were to contemplate the Idea of God, or even merely (if you so mean) *think* it, and you were to think this purely and fill yourselves wholly with it; if you now do this, God becomes immediately real for you as the one and only actual, and you will no longer look around for another nature, since with God and through God you already have consummate actuality. To be allowed to speak to us of that given nature, you would first have to prove its actuality to us; this, however, you cannot do, and therefore resolve first to contemplate the *existent* that we call God, and not to turn your gaze at once back to the non-existent, like an eye that cannot bear the splendor of the sun and turns to the shade.

We go beyond mere thinking, then, with the Idea of the philosophy of nature, not only to cognition, but also beyond [p. 32] cognition in general one step further, to intuition in actuality and to the complete coincidence of the world cognized by us with the world of nature. Only in that point, namely, where the ideal has become wholly also the actual for us, the world of thought the world of nature, only in this point lies the last, the highest satisfaction and reconciliation of cognition, just as the fulfillment of ethical demands is attained only when they no longer appear to us as thoughts, e.g. as commandments, but have become real in the nature of our soul and in it.

In this alone lies also what distinguishes the philosophy of nature from all philosophizing hitherto. By being science of the divine in general, it would distinguish itself from everything that the nearest time, and also the earlier, after Leibniz, has brought forth in philosophy, but by no means from what the older and oldest has. Spinoza recognized his God-filled doctrine as a doctrine of nature; but the circumstance that he did not carry its exposition to that point of identity with actuality, and that, so far as he attempted it, the carryingthrough failed, was the cause that his doctrine too was regarded in later times only as an idealistic sketch, a view of thought for thought. Be the Idea of the philosophy of nature that which *Bacon* once grasped from the side of physics, but did not recognize from the side of philosophy, and therefore did not wholly penetrate, and so became only the originator of the age of empiricism, or have no earlier thinker ever grasped it: it is in any case a necessary Idea, not only occurring and lying on the way to consummation, but itself introducing this consummation, an Idea which sooner or later must be realized. It first sets the decisive goal, the determinate barrier, to the arbitrary choice of thinking, to the aberrations of abstraction; for it is the direct opposite of all abstraction and of all systems that proceed from it. Everything that in science, or in religion, or in any other sphere of human activity has ever attained to permanence and become partaker of true objectivity has won this precisely through that last [p. 33] step, which for ever after the science of reason has taken by becoming philosophy of nature; and even if it should be possible or permitted to us, who now live, to solve only the smallest part of the clearly recognized task itself: this can prove nothing against the truth of the Idea in itself, which, even when wholly going under, must nevertheless be taken up again and finally be wholly realized.

A reviewer of the Fichtean Erlangen Lectures in the Jena Literatur-Zeitung (1806, nos. 91 and 92), whose notice deserves to be called a model of forbearance, opens on this<sup>4</sup> occasion: he too does not consider the cause of the philosophy of nature the *best* (neither do we, we consider it only the good, namely the one right one), but it appears to him as an anticipation of a higher sphere of life, which, however, necessarily had to fail. — For this world, then, the reviewer gives it its dismissal, and to us he says what Mr. le Beau, the courtier, in *Was ihr wollt* says to the worthy Orlando: Farewell, my lord, in a better world than this I wish to have more of your worthy company. — But who may now say that there is such an anticipation, who say that anything is not philosophy but rather something better than philosophy? Is anything too good for philosophy, and is it not precisely in the representation of seeking philosophy in something lesser than that higher that the poverty, the doubtfulness, and the nakedness of the philosophizing hitherto have their ground? What if the consummation long prophesied by the fathers, what if that for which at bottom all the better spirits have longed, and which they have only failed to attain, were to consist in this: to present in actuality that which subjectivity has deemed inaccessible, eternally remote, and which, by every view other than that of a philosophy of nature, is in fact inaccessible and transcendent? This presentation of the life of God, not outside or [p. 34] above nature, but in nature, as a truly real and present life, is without doubt the last synthesis of the ideal with the real, of cognizing with being; and hence also the last synthesis of science itself.

<sup>4</sup> For which, by way of thanks, it is called by Mr. Fichte a *passionate* *review*. See the second supplement to s. L., which comes to our notice just before the printing.

To make the application of this to Fichte, what does it help him to have appropriated the teachings of the divine Idea, of God as the life and being outside which there is no life and being? He presumably thinks he can take up these comprehensive truths and yet persist in his one-sidedness. He errs. Whoever does not wholly penetrate those truths, let him stay away from them; in these clear regions half-measure cannot hide itself. The first, that philosophy is science of the divine, he lays claim to; but the consequence he neither grasps nor sees, and therefore does not understand the standpoint of the philosophy of nature either. The cognition which he has of God, that is, of that which alone is being, is a cognition through mere *thinking*, that is, through that which is opposed to all being, all actuality. “The eternal can be grasped only through thought” (s. L., p. 10). The divine life is irrecoverably *extinguished* in *actual*, *immediate* consciousness, and can be restored only in the thinking that raises itself above it (ibid., pp. 116, 117). Behold, the old root of error brought plainly to light again! A world attainable only by thinking, in which God is, and another, wholly empty of God, absolutely estranged from him, hence thoroughly ungodly, which he calls the actual, stand irreconcilably opposed. When he nevertheless speaks in his present writings of the divine as though he had a science of it, he merely falls away from himself and his own earlier and more correct system, without thereby gaining the true one. The one immediately cognizable is for true philosophy precisely the absolutely positive, the absolute-actual, that is, God; for him, however, the ungodly is the immediate, God the mediate, as in all dogmatic systems. Sooner, then, does he resort to dogmatism than let go of the opposition at which he has remained standing, and with which (though [p. 35] much worse) he now begins again, that of the ideal and real world, the world of thought and that of actuality.

Let Mr. Fichte by all means hold this for himself; but he moreover finds it necessary to make us in this respect equal to himself. “*In this, then, he says, in this firm resting upon the world* *of thought as the first (!) and most eminent*” — or, as he expresses it shortly before, “*in this, that they want to build up the universe* *purely from thought*, both, the science of reason and enthusiasm (which in that context means for him quite the same as philosophy of nature), are *completely at one*” (Gr., pp. 247—248). That he says this of enthusiasm, we are in that respect altogether in agreement with him. We believe that this is precisely already the whole and full enthusiasm, to posit a world of thought of its own and a world of actuality of its own; but that he equates the science of reason with enthusiasm in this, about that we are convinced that it has neither this nor anything else in common with it.

Upon this manifest ignorance of the first ground of our view Mr. Fichte now builds his ensuing chria against it, and thinks he is beginning very cleverly when he charges it with this: that it makes the incomprehensible, for the sake of the incomprehensible, the principle of science (Gr., p. 242). Has Mr. Fichte, then, slept through the four or five years in which he has not written, that he wants so utterly not to know what has gone on around him? Let him ask around among what he calls the age, and hear what complaint is most commonly raised against us. There he will hear a sighing, an accusing, a condemning of the presumption, the pride, the madness, of asserting a clear and adequate cognition of God or the Absolute. “What, say these clever ones, almost in the words of Mr. Fichte (Phil. J. 1798, no. 1, p. 17), “what, you are finite, and how should the finite ever comprehend the infinite?” and in doing so they puff themselves up no little on account of their speculative humility, and pretend as if they had quite beaten us.

[p. 36] How, then, does Mr. Fichte come by that allegation? We wish to try, since no ground for it is to be found in the subject matter, to derive it genetically from the other circumstances.

When the philosophy of nature and that excellent critique of the Fichtean system by Hegel appeared, Mr. Fichte was just then occupied with making it thoroughly comprehensible to the vulgarity of the age how bitter a wrong was being done him, and how he was in fact wholly in agreement with its own system of thought, only that he had sought to ground it more deeply and thus to secure it first properly. So, for example, nothing was more settled for that whole period than that the only religion consists in doing right, and that nothing else is needed; furthermore it was, according to the mode of thought of the same age, something quite dreadful that man must submit himself to the eternal laws of a strict necessity, that for the sake of nature alone he may not act as he pleases, and feels himself everywhere hemmed in by it. If only this restrictive and stiff-necked nature did not exist, one could live much more freely, and especially think much more freely. Is not nature still the one dam against the arbitrary choice of thinking and the freedom of abstraction! To this Mr. Fichte had from the first assented scientifically, since to him too nature always appeared only as a barrier to free activity, which is in our way everywhere; but in the Bestimmung des Menschen this arrogance and insane conceit of superiority over nature is declared altogether holy. (See the Krit. J. der Philos. loc. cit., p. 170.)

There can be no doubt that Mr. Fichte would have wholly succeeded with the age in this his intention, and that a complete reconciliation and peaceful fusion between him and the whole Enlightenment would have come about, had this good intention not been betrayed too early, and had it not been disturbed all too inhumanly precisely through this exposure.

How, then, was Mr. Fichte, who through that disclosure had perhaps come to his senses himself, to set about it, in order to squeeze through between the age and us; in order to [p. 37] maintain the Ideas he had acquired without spoiling things with the age, and to hold his plans fast to it without nevertheless falling wholly and utterly among the wicked?

Nothing is simpler than this. If he chastises the age with weapons borrowed from us, and us with weapons borrowed from the age, then to begin with he himself steps into the middle as the true and proper apostle, as the just judge who alone knows the truth and apportions it to each according to his cognition. The age will bargain some things away and put up with others, since the main matter can no longer be steered anyway, only that those who have dared to attack it so wantonly find their speaking made distasteful to them.

The fault of the age, according to Mr. Fichte, is that it wants to understand everything and to grasp it clearly (probably sun-clear), and that it will on no account allow anything to count as being or as binding except what it has thus cognized (Gr., p. 39 f.). At bottom this is a beautiful fault of the age; for the science of reason too wants to grasp everything clearly (Gr., p. 243), and the error lies only in the manner and way. We others, he thinks, have censured precisely this, and nothing else, in the age. But it was by no means for us to scold it so and to anticipate him (Mr. Fichte) in this, who alone is the right scolder and censurer of such wrong. Our censure was therefore merely a revolt of the age against itself, or, in the language of revolution, a reaction; and since on the one hand we have condemned the thoroughgoing wish to comprehend, yet on the other hand nothing rational can be expected of us either, we must necessarily have asserted the opposite unreason, namely, that the incomprehensible as such, and for the sake of incomprehensibility, must be set up as the sole principle. People who do this, and who can procure this incomprehensible, as we do, only through a free fabrication, have from time immemorial been called enthusiasts. But every enthusiast clings fast to nature and necessarily becomes a philosopher of nature, i.e., a kind of sorcerer, soothsayer, and [p. 38] exorcist, in short a kind of human being who must be expelled not only from educated but even from civil society. This the age has brought upon itself as a just punishment of heaven (Gr., pp. 275—276). Those who were sun-clear it would not grasp, for they were not yet palpable enough to it; now the generation that wished to comprehend throughout is “cruelly chastised for it”; nonsense breaks in; “the system of sober experience dies away; the system of wild enthusiasm, *with all* *its order-destroying consequences*, begins its dreadful reign” (Ibid.). Up then, while it is still possible, out with them, stone them; the age would be mocking its own principle of thoroughgoing comprehensibility and its well-earned enlightenment to its face, if it were to tolerate them any longer.

It is indeed true now that any other person who had only impudence enough could set himself up in just the same way and demonstrate the philosophy of nature just as a priori as anything agreeable to him that happened to fit his context; true, that any sophist of merely middling talent could have derived the philosophy of nature just as cogently from any arbitrarily assumed and far worse presupposition. It is further well known that authors thoroughly refuted have from time immemorial, when no other help appeared, sought first to bring the deaf god, the public, to its feet, then to call in the secular authorities, and to represent the cause of their opponents as destroying morals, right, and order; against Mr. Fichte too this has been used not just once, and he has not failed each time to raise an unbridled outcry about it.

“But with me that was in fact something quite different; the Nicolaites who called me an enthusiast, and others who decried my philosophy as ruinous to state and church, must now be ashamed of it themselves; but you —”

Quite right: “our fathers have sinned in that they stoned the prophets,” the Jews already said in the time of Christ, “but we are zealots for the law, in that we stone him who has come to abolish the law.” It was infamous and abominable that they [p. 39] actually burned Jordano Bruno, Vanini, and that I was almost burned too on account of my alone-true religion of right-doing (although nobody had anything of the sort in mind), says Mr. Fichte; I myself, too, would not advise burning, but I must say so, and I feel driven to call attention to the order-disturbing consequences of this doctrine, which threatens to displace mine.

Having thereby illuminated the origin of the rhetorical work of art and demonstrated its worth, we find in it, on the other hand, the occasion to enter into an inquiry closely akin to the present exposition, namely: where, properly, non-comprehension is at home in the age, and where, further, enthusiasm.

To have set up the principle of non-comprehension, or of the incomprehensible for the sake of the incomprehensible, is something with which, to our knowledge, the philosophy of nature has never yet been reproached; the merit of this invention belongs solely to Mr. Fichte. As for enthusiasm, he himself will make no claim to originality.
