Since for the moment it simply looks at itself in its presence-at-hand, there arises for it immediately, in this forceful direction upon itself (which is compared with what happens when a man *pulls himself together*, and what everyone can find in his self-observation) — there arises for it in that direction the view that it (existence) is *such and such* (which is what, if not that it is *not* being? whereby, however, no such-and-such and no positive character at all is given): with this, however, with the view that it has *this and this* character or is *such and such* — in this reflection upon itself inseparable from knowing, knowing cleaves itself by itself: that it becomes evident to itself, not in general, but determinately as *such and such*, gives the second from the first — one *leaping, as it were, out of the first* (O how many words to explain something that is not there at all!); it (knowing) and with knowing the divine being that has come to stand in it, that is, the world, springs apart into *two pieces* (into which two?); we would thus be out of the One into the Two; but not yet into the infinite multiplicity of existing things — but reflection, by virtue of its absolute freedom, can continue itself into the infinite (merely in the one of the two pieces, or in both?), and so for each new reflection the world must emerge in a new shape and *in an infinite time*, which likewise [p. 78] is generated only by the absolute freedom of reflection, must go on changing and shaping itself into the infinite, and flow away — *as an infinite manifold* (L. p. 112—115).

For those who might not care to compare our presentation with the book itself, let the assurance stand here that we have left out nothing of this derivation, but have given it, with the exception of the mere amplifications of the lecture-hall delivery, in its complete entirety.

Yet we would not wish to add anything to it; for with what could it, if we wished to consider it seriously, fill us other than with a feeling of infinite lamentation over the lofty emptiness that raises itself with such vanity of speech over nature, and with such vague, nebulous verbal trumpery wants to grasp her infinite determinacy and fullness! — “If someone, says Plotinus, wanted to ask nature for what reason she creates, she might answer him, supposing she deigned to give him an answer, in the following way: you should not ask me, but learn in silence, just as I too am silent and am not accustomed to speak.” — So, after the above deduction, one could wish nothing else for Mr. Fichte than that he learn to be silent, not merely outwardly but inwardly, and become still within himself, and put away entirely his willful speaking and imagining, in the hope that the divine in him might gain room to see and to speak.

We consider the cited deduction only in the respect that it shows us clearly how Mr. Fichte lives in the firm opinion that that standing dead world has an indelible actuality in consciousness; and likewise that that cleavage of being into an infinitely manifold is one that can never be canceled in actual consciousness (p. 120); for it is not *he*, the determinate individual called Fichte, but absolute consciousness that makes it, and must absolutely make it, without becoming conscious of it again itself. So it has always been, and so it will probably remain with him, that he, namely, what could be merely a psychological ground of explanation, referring to the peculiarity [p. 79] of certain individual natures, to which his own belongs, raises to a transcendental and universal ground; saddles upon the absolute I what is natural only to a hardened reflection, and then, by a very comprehensible operation, brings forth again out of it that very dead and distorted world whose image was drafted in that reflection.

What, then, is to be said against this, or rather, what can be said? — In truth nothing, except that that necessary transformation into a standing being, that whole supposed cleavage, is a complete fabrication, and that there is no such thing at all. “But he himself finds it there as having occurred and is not conscious of its execution: it must therefore have occurred beyond his actual consciousness, it must have occurred without his knowledge.” The latter we concede to him without further ado; his consciousness would precisely not be *his* consciousness, it would have to be quite other than it is, if he were to be conscious of that transformation; he would have to have not so determinately undertaken it and still undertake it, — not to be so grown together with it in his whole essence, in order to see that it is merely *he* who makes it, and not absolute consciousness.

Whence, then, does he have knowledge at all of this act of absolute consciousness? — Mr. Fichte was not present at it; he himself admits that, as soon as *he* comes to consciousness, this act has already occurred (p. 116). He can therefore only infer it, and he infers it from the circumstance that he finds that dead being so present in himself and cannot comprehend this presence-at-hand in any other way, of which we have just given the ground.

Against the fact of *his* consciousness, which he is pleased to pass off as a universal one, stands the fact that there have at all times been, and still are, human beings who have never known the world as such a standing being, and into whose soul Mr. Fichte would first have to push this view artificially or by force (as he would in truth gladly press it upon us), in order then to take it away from them again and be able to say [p. 80] that being is not in itself such, but a divine life (which latter he too has learned only now). On many his instruction would probably be lost for a lifetime; it would cost him just as much trouble to instill this standing being in them as it would cost us to free his imagination of it.

It is true, to be sure, that since the discovery of that opposition of object and subject was made, this opposition, together with the representation of the world as pure objectivity attached to it, has penetrated so far into all branches of culture and education that the unnatural has in most people now actually become nature, and could bear such blossoms and fruits as the Fichtean philosophy is. That view of being offers undeniable advantages for superficiality in life and in knowing, and at bottom it is precisely this arranging of things for so convenient a handling in which the triumph of so-called enlightenment and of present-day public instruction consists. At every time, however, there live some on whom the teaching of their age has had no effect, and so it is to be hoped that *even now* there are some who could convince us of the originality and imperishability of an immediate sense for the living, which must at least be the case with all those into whom the spirit of antiquity has penetrated, for whom that sense was not art but nature, and into which one cannot even find the entrance without it.

In the shortest terms, then: that whole representation of being as something dead, purely objective — as well as of the world as something actually cleft into infinite manifoldness — is a wholly arbitrary representation generated by empirical subjectivity, and since Mr. Fichte himself indicates five such standpoints of freedom, from which it can regard the world, he may by all means subordinate that view of being as something dead and infinitely many to one of these free standpoints (to which of them it belongs, we shall show more closely at once).

If, namely, it is nevertheless asserted by Mr. Fichte and [p. 81] others that the world as a lifeless, finite, and absolutely manifold one occurs in their consciousness, how must this fact be explained, and how alone can it be explained? — This point has already been touched upon before, without our having been much understood: we shall therefore try to state the answer more clearly here. What matters first of all is whether one can say in any way of that dead, absolutely manifold, or of the finite generally, as it is meant in those assertions, that it *is*, or whether one can in no way say this. The latter (that one cannot) was proved long ago and also in this writing; it was further inferred that that therefore cannot be intuited either; for what is intuited is ipso facto intuited as being, and what cannot be so intuited, because its nature resists all being, is not intuitable at all; it is thus shown that such a finite can be neither in itself nor in our intuition — that it therefore cannot be or be truly actual at all or anywhere. If, however, those people nevertheless go on demanding that this very finite be explained to them, and complain that we have not really derived this finite world for them: then it is evident that to the question: *why* they nevertheless assume that finite as existing, *despite its manifest and proven non-existence* — an answer can be given no longer theoretically, but only practically. It is, namely, by no means their science, but merely their guilt, that *such a finite* nevertheless exists for them, and this can be derived only from *their* own will, turned away from unity, which wills a being for itself, and for that very reason sees neither itself nor things as they truly are in God; and since, further, the religious standpoint is precisely that of seeing all things in God, without proof or further grounding, but simply and absolutely and with complete ignorance of the contrary, from *this* standpoint too the existence of such a finite [p. 82] world as we have described can be derived only in the way indicated, namely through a turning away of the individual will from God as the unity and blessedness of all things — through a true Platonic fall, in which man finds himself, who nevertheless holds for true and actual the world thought as dead, as absolutely manifold and separated. This answer is actually given in the writing Philosophie und Religion and carried out in accordance with the standpoint there: we have shown that the fact of the existence of such a world in the consciousness of men is just as universal as the fact of sin, indeed that it is this very fact of sin itself, and that, just as we can be redeemed from the latter, so too the former is no absolutely necessary, indissoluble, eternal consciousness. —

Mr. Fichte has, if not precisely this view, yet the speculative theory of freedom on which it rests, taken over — in<sup>6</sup> [p. 83] order to explain his five possible standpoints, but by no means also for the dead, standing existence, the cleavage, the infinite multiplicity and absolute manifoldness of his world. (See the determinate explanation p. 128).

<sup>6</sup> In order to put forward nothing without proof, the following parallels stand here. Philosophie und Religion. P. 28. The Absolute does not become objective to itself through the form in a merely ideal image of itself, but in a counter-image that is at the same time itself, a truly *other Absolute*. It transfers in the form its whole essentiality to that in which it becomes objective, etc. [VI, p. 34]. P. 36. What is exclusively peculiar to absoluteness is that it bestows on its counter-image, together with the essence, from itself also independence. This in-itself-being, this proper and true reality of the first intuited is *freedom*, and from that first independence of the counter-image flows what reappears in the world of appearance as freedom, which is still the last trace and as it were the seal of the divinity intuited into the fallen world. [= p. 39]. Anweisung zum seligen Leben. P. 228. Absolute being posits itself in its existence as absolute freedom and independence, to take itself and as independence from its own inner being; it creates not perhaps a freedom outside itself, but it is itself, in this part of the form, this its own freedom outside itself; and in this respect it does indeed separate Itself — in its existence — from Itself — in its being, and expels itself from itself, in order to return alive again into itself. P. 112. The ground of the independence and freedom of consciousness lies indeed in God; but precisely for this reason and because it lies in God, independence and freedom are truly there and by no means an empty semblance. P. 41. The for-itself-being of the counter-image expresses itself, carried on through finitude, in its highest potency as *I-hood*. But as in the course of a planet the greatest distance from the center passes immediately again into approach, so the point of the farthest distance from God is also again the moment of return to the Absolute, of the takingup again into the ideal. [= p. 42]. P. 40. The independence which the other Absolute receives in the self-intuition of the first, the form, reaches only to the *possibility* of real in-itself-being, but no further. [= p. 42]. P. 228. The universal form of reflection is I, accordingly — — an I and, what alone gives an I, an independent and free I belongs to the absolute form and is the proper *organic point of unity of the absolute form* of the absolute essence. P. 229. Freedom is certain, and truly there, and it is itself the root of existence; yet it is not immediately real; for reality goes in it only as far as possibility. That a theory of freedom according to which it has its ground in God stands in the most direct conflict with all earlier Fichtean doctrine, on this there can surely be but one voice among all connoisseurs. — On the whole the above writing seems to have found a better reception with Mr. Fichte than the others by the same author, and this is very understandable, since in it the great significance which his principle of the I has had for the age is fully acknowledged and presented with true interest. (It also contains (p. 41) the Fichtean interpretation of the absolute form as the λόγος). Mr. Fichte speaks several times, with a not indistinct reference to himself, of being plundered and decried by those very ones who plunder. We do not know exactly who today showed an equally great desire to enrich himself with ideas from Mr. Fichte: but who in the three writings is the decrier and who the decried, this is plain as day, just as everyone acquainted with philosophical literature will admit that that trick has been practiced against few with greater impudence than against the author of this writing.

To which of his five standpoints, then, does this belong, or rather, to which of them does his conviction belong that the [p. 84] aforementioned cleavage, infinity, etc. is *at least in consciousness* perfectly actual and real? To us it is, as we have already remarked to him before, wholly a matter of indifference whether what he calls the world of sense is outside us, or whether it is actual merely in us and for us. In both cases it has reality as such, which we concede to it neither as an objective nor as a subjective one, but precisely deny it entirely. *He*, then, who on our view attributes true reality to the world of sense — stands, while he supposes himself to be on the highest of his five standpoints, precisely on the very lowest — *He* it is, properly, who wants to preserve the world of sense for himself, in that he has it created by absolute consciousness; *He* has need of it not as a living but as a dead one, *He* — does not deify it, for it remains always and eternally something ungodly, but it has for him, as cleavage into the infinite, such an actuality through the form that *it cannot be canceled by God* *himself*, thus an actuality subsisting beside and with God.

Besides the general advantage of still placing the world as a world of sense high enough, of making it something inescapable and unavoidable, this theory of absolute consciousness offers yet the particular convenience of not merely asserting the objective, standing being against the philosophy of nature, but of foisting it upon her; while at the same time being able to appropriate from her that all being, considered in itself and in its original essence, is divine life.

On the whole, undeniable advantages accrue to this new system in comparison with the other philosophies. It is, as we may now, after having acquired sufficient knowledge of it, say without hesitation, the most accomplished *eclecticism* that was possible for our age. To Kantianism its portion of truth remains; Fichtean idealism is taken up again into the whole through the theory just cited; but the philosophy of nature too is right on certain points which she probably had herself [p. 85] not rightly understood. To Jacobi plainly belongs the third standpoint, that of higher morality, although He only grazed it — He who, so long as Fichte was still Fichte, wrote to him the passage: *Yes, I am the atheist, the godless one*, etc.; — a passage which we need not single out further; and should perhaps the various persons, from whose individual contributions this temple-building has been constructed, wish to assert their merit, one can furthermore answer them: Go, there is not a stone of you all in it, for if I could have used something from the one, I would surely have come away empty from the other, and if you think you have furnished me with pure gold, behold, here is nowhere gold, but everything stone!

Anyone who wished to hold in particular to individual passages in the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben* would be bound to find it incomprehensible how Mr. Fichte was not led, by mere formal consequence, to the true Idea of the philosophy of nature. One such passage is in part the following: “We know nothing of the immediate divine life; for with the first stroke of consciousness it transforms itself into a dead world, which moreover divides itself into five standpoints of its possible view. *Be it ever so much*, he continues, *God who lives behind all* *these shapes*; we do not see him, but only ever his covering; we see him as stone, herb, animal, we see him, when we raise ourselves higher, as law of nature, as moral law; but all this is still always not He. *I say to you*, who complain thus: simply raise yourself to the standpoint of religion, and all coverings vanish, the world with its dead principle passes away from you, and *the Godhead itself enters again into you*, in its first original form, as life, as your own life, which you shall live and will live” (s. L. p. 144, 145).

I was inwardly alarmed when I read this passage and recalled the earlier harsh and misinterpreting remarks about the philosophy of nature. Mr. Fichte wants, then, I said to myself, that the philosophy of nature should have intuited the herb as herb, the stone as stone, and made this herb as herb [p. 86] and this stone as stone into God ; for if this were not his opinion, why did he rage so against it? It would then merely have turned out that it had long since pronounced as the scientific standpoint what Mr. Fichte here proclaims to the astonished world as the religious one, and there would then be nothing to blame in it, except, if this should perhaps be his opinion, that the religious standpoint ought not to have been made into the scientific one. —

We have only borrowed the thought just expressed from Mr. Fichte, and in itself it signifies nothing. Our opinion is that the highest *standpoint* is everywhere the highest where true philosophy, morality, and religion are spoken of; for these are precisely the highest and want only the highest. Mr. Fichte, to be sure, takes a different view here as well. He wants his doctrine of morals and of right, which kept only to the second of the five possible standpoints, to have been nonetheless a true doctrine of morals and of right. He assures us that he never regarded that view of the world as the highest, but only as the one grounding those two sciences. I permit myself here to be of another opinion, and am convinced that, had he then recognized the higher view, he would certainly not willingly have presented the two doctrines according to the lower one; just as it is only a later reinterpretation by which that second standpoint must now metamorphose itself into that of Stoicism and even of Goethe’s Prometheus; for formerly he set himself against that very thing into whose dignity he now wants to pass over. — *Conversely* another recent author, who likewise could not yet free himself thoroughly from the Fichtean basic conception, thinks he could concede the science of the Absolute as the standpoint of philosophy, but not as that of religion. In his place I would not concede this; for if there were something higher than the Absolute, philosophy would have to reshape itself in accordance with it; otherwise, from the higher it would appear as false, that is, it would not appear as true philosophy. —

Suppose now that Mr. Fichte, in the above passage, were [p. 87] to grant for the religious point of view what he otherwise absolutely denies for every actual consciousness; this would be merely one more contradiction of which he makes himself guilty; for *irrecoverably* extinguished in consciousness, as regards its immediacy, is the divine life (p. 116). — Or, if there is really no contradiction here, then the religious point of view too must be possible for consciousness only mediately, namely through mere thinking and in contradiction to actuality; and it then remains with the mixture, or with the claim that the actual world belongs partly to God, partly to the devil — the whole passage then has also signified nothing higher and other than what we had already found in the rest. — Not to forget that even where, as he says, divine being steps forth “untroubled by any form lying in the self-subsistence of the I and therefore limiting,” the indestructible form of infinite manifoldness (and with it also of infinite time) is nevertheless expressly excepted; *in this* divine being then still remains broken, for it is a form never to be dissolved or brought to an end in actual consciousness.

Right at the beginning of the *seliges Leben* (p. 6) we find the following: “Not in being in and for itself does death lie, but in the death-dealing glance of the dead beholder.” So, I said to myself, I now comprehend how the philosophy of nature can deify the dead (which it does not know at all). Mr. Fichte shoots very embittered glances at it in the *Grundzüge*: these may well have had the above effect, the property of the basilisk’s glance, and turned living being in it into dead being.

Soon, however, I tried to reconcile the contradiction again in another way. The three works of Mr. Fichte, I said, must be regarded like the three parts of Dante, so that the *Grundzüge* are hell, the Erlangen lectures purgatory, the *Anweisung zum* *seligen Leben* the paradise of his philosophy.

But I convinced myself all too soon that even the *selige* *Leben* is by no means yet the true blessed life. If, for example, [p. 88] the last-cited remark were in real earnest, Mr. Fichte would have to give up at once his theory of absolute consciousness, which he carries out immediately after it. — Being is equal to existence; existence is equal to knowing or absolute consciousness; this is that which transforms the divine life into the dead, the reasonless — and it is hardly to be believed that this is the Johannine Logos, who had come to illuminate the darkness, but not to create it, in whom was life itself, but not death. If living being in itself is turned into death only through the dead glance of the dead beholder, then the absolute I is indeed the ground of all death and itself dead; it is then the true evil principle in the universe, the God of this world, but not the true God; the evil world-creator of the Gnostics, not the world-redeemer and Son of God. If it is religion to behold everything in God and thus as equal to the life of God, then absolute consciousness is the true principle of irreligion, of everything evil and ungodly in man.

As it is told of the devil that he maliciously changes into soundless coals the first ringing treasures of those who trust him, so for Mr. Fichte his absolute consciousness, or reflection, is the true devil, who gives back to him in actuality, as a dead coal, the bright gold of the divine life that he has grasped in thought.

But if there is such a consciousness, which, without our knowing it, indeed prior to our individual consciousness, transforms the divine life as with a single stroke into a dead slag and, irreducible for actual consciousness, calcines it: by what power of the heart are we then still to get beyond this consciousness?

Mr. Fichte answers: through thinking, which raises itself above actual consciousness — but also above the absolute? — How is it to break through this impenetrable deed, which separates us forever from the eternal? Is there, according to Mr. Fichte, perhaps a thinking, not only beyond all *actual* consciousness (as if thinking itself did not also have to be actual) [p. 89] — but also beyond absolute consciousness — a thinking outside or prior to the absolute I? — Woe to the poor Kantian who had formerly let himself be caught in such a nonthought!

Thus, a beholding of the divine life behind the sensuous coverings of things is, in Mr. Fichte’s system, for every point of view, the religious one included, a plain impossibility; that remark is therefore wholly foreign to his system and does not fit it in any way . Had it had more than rhetorical content,<sup>7</sup> the perfect identity of the standpoint of the philosophy of nature with the one he calls the religious would have had to dawn on him at once, at least in general; and he would not have been so astonished at the standpoint itself. But since he already raises an outcry over the mere Idea of the philosophy of nature, no differently than a man would do to whom it had never remotely occurred that the in-itself of nature could be something divine, this proves that the thought cited above was likewise only a passing appearance in him, but by no means cognition.

<sup>7</sup> In the repeatedly mentioned appendix, Mr. Fichte also protests most zealously against the interpretation of an ambiguously expressed passage in the *E. V.*, according to which it would follow that the majesty of God reveals itself most impressively in nature. Had he been able to say that, he says, he would have had to have forgotten himself. Since in a second review of this work we adopted the same interpretation, we wish by this remark to restore his honor on this point completely. [Cf. above p. 9].

After the three most recent works of Mr. Fichte it is hardly to be assumed that he has not read even One of the principal writings on the philosophy of nature thoroughly, that he judges them merely by hearsay or according to a rough idea; but would not, even in that case, some good spirit, some pupil at least, have been found to instruct him better on this?

Since in my presentation there lies absolutely no possibility of being misunderstood in such a way, but Mr. Fichte has nonetheless understood it in no other way, nothing remains to [p. 90] be assumed but that he could not understand it otherwise, that every other sense is in fact incomprehensible to him.

Or should one perhaps assume that Mr. Fichte understood the philosophy of nature quite well and merely does not want to admit it, for various reasons? Is the cause perhaps to atone merely for its originator? Was it perhaps not permitted him to express his views at a time when Mr. Fichte was still on the second of the five possible standpoints? Should he have kept respectfully silent until the philosopher in whom the Logos was one day, unexpectedly, to be reborn surprised the world with the exclamation: I say to you, only become religious, and all the coverings with which I myself provided you, the barriers and the whole rigid existence that I myself brought to you, will vanish, and you will behold God! — Is the philosophy of nature now to be pressed down quite low merely so that room may be made for *his* religious standpoint? Are *his* former errors to be left to us, so that he in return may the more securely take over a part of our truths, as religious ones?

Were the matter so, Mr. Fichte would have made himself guilty of the lowest of all literary arts, deliberate distortion. I abhor this thought and declare expressly that I do not harbor it.<sup>8</sup>

<sup>8</sup> In the appendix just mentioned, against the Jena reviewer, Mr. Fichte does indeed betray some knowledge of my writings. He cites: a) that I *posit a* *real independent of consciousness.* — What does Mr. Fichte mean to say by this expression, ambiguous either intentionally or unintentionally? If that real is being in itself, that which is still untransformed by absolute consciousness, as He would call it, then it is evident that, although not I, yet Mr. Fichte posits this being as independent of consciousness, since he gives it the relation of the mere image, of the *mere representation*, to it; I do not make this relation at all. Or if he understands the sensuous real, the stones as stones, the sand heaps as sand heaps, and the like, then Mr. Fichte could know that for me these things exist neither dependent nor independent of consciousness; that I deny them as such precisely all being, except in arbitrary thinking that abstracts from the real. b) that I *let this real independent of consciousness first break through into consciousness in intelligence.* — The answer to this already lies in what precedes. If being independent of all subjective consciousness, not to be set in opposition to it at all, in a word thoroughly absolute and being from itself — or God — is essentially a self-affirming, then it can well be maintained, with a deeper ground than Mr. Fichte is able to see, that this divine self-affirmation breaks through in intelligence to *the form* of self-affirmation which expresses itself as personal consciousness through the I am, and which Mr. Fichte otherwise regarded as the highest in the whole universe. — Moreover, it is further asserted in the remark in question: through those two assertions the Absolute or God is *incontrovertibly* turned into a *dead and standing being*, that is, naturalized; or conversely nature is deified. And all this as a remark to a passage in which the reviewer just mentioned, who after all is also not favorably disposed to the philosophy of nature, says in reference to it: *even the best cause is easily refuted if one imputes* *to the words of the opponent a meaning that they are not supposed to have!*

[p. 91] Thus the most honorable thing for Mr. Fichte, and what has the most semblance of truth in its favor, remains always this: that in his invectives against the philosophy of nature only his naturally common way of thinking about nature itself breaks out, just as his representation of it is really the only one that involuntarily occurs to him when the word philosophy of nature strikes his ears, as someone from the common people, when he hears the word nature or forces of nature, cannot refrain from thinking thereby of the devil or of sorcerers and magic powers, and that therefore in his own case those utterances in which the absolute vitality of all being seemed to dawn upon him were thought without any consequence and were really mere figures of speech.

Mr. Fichte has been rooted too long and too deeply in that representation of being as a dead thing standing opposed to him, has hidden himself too stubbornly against all vitality other than that of the I, for one to expect that, after he has devoted “half a life” to the presentation and grounding of this death, he will now all at once and without an extraordinary miracle become alive.

[p. 92] His last representation and opinion of nature, which he laid down in the *Bestimmung des Menschen*, was that it consists in affections of the I, which correspond to the qualities of the yellow and green color, of sweet and bitter taste, of the sound of the violin or trumpet — these affections — (not, as now, the divine life and being) — the I transformed into objects, spread over surfaces, and produced the standing or abiding thing for them: but in general nature was something absolutely ugly and unholy, without indwelling unity; something that was not supposed to be and only was so that it should not be, namely so that it could be canceled.

This very representation still assails him at every moment, as often as he hears the name nature, and before just this nature, consisting of herbs, grass, stones, and so on, he pictures the philosopher of nature sitting, in order to *speculate* about it, to *think up all sorts of things*, “and to investigate certain inner properties, beyond further comprehension, in the grounds of things, through the use of which effects going beyond the ordinary course of nature might be achieved”; this very nature, consisting of sand heaps and the like, the same philosopher of nature strives to deify.

I do not believe that any reader, however good-natured, will put forward the possibility that in Mr. Fichte’s case there is talk of some philosophy of nature unknown to us, say one on the moon, or that only a problem was to be posed: What if someone one day came upon this mad thought? so that his listeners might then know how to set him properly right. No, the talk is of the philosophy of nature well known to us all, and we do not even credit him with the excuse that he did after all name no names, and so one cannot really know whom and what at the time he meant by it. Rather, he knows quite well and has reckoned on the fact that, without naming any name, the whole public would nonetheless know to whom these civilities are meant to apply.

Granted, however, that Mr. Fichte, at the word philosophy [p. 93] of nature, simply cannot think anything else, whence nonetheless the exuberant assurance with which he ascribes this representation to *us*? Did no shadow of a doubt arise in his inner mind that the matter might after all have quite a different character? With such monstrous and thoroughly incomprehensible errors one otherwise seeks every other explanation before one, at last compelled by necessity, recognizes them as real; “the man may well simply not have expressed himself exactly or well, one says, he may well connect another concept with the word nature” — such humane<sup>9</sup> and tolerant interpretations, by which one would gladly remove an assertion that seems dangerous, are not unusual for the vigorous superiority of Mr. Fichte either.

<sup>9</sup> Against the Jena reviewer, who points out to him that he himself called the splitting of the One life of reason into several individuals an arrangement of nature, Mr. Fichte avails himself of the excuse: the word nature is taken here, as in *several* passages, in another and higher sense, for everything that follows from the eternal form. — To the philosophers of nature alone such a cheap excuse cannot be allowed, one that moreover makes use of a distinction which they themselves have made (see the Aphorisms in the *Zeitschr. für spek. Physik* II, 2, § 15, Addition 1 [IV, p. 120]); they must necessarily have understood by nature what Mr. Fichte is pleased to call so, the pure limit, the mere sensuous world, rigid existence.

This assurance too, however, I must again acknowledge as laudable; it proves the firmness of the man, the triple brass about his — breast.

Man’s asserting is his seeing; what a man earnestly asserts, that he also really sees, and no one can dispute it with him; what he asserts and does not see, on the contrary, that he is lying. So I think also of Mr. Fichte. Who knows what the man does not still see, of which the rest of us in dreams have no inkling. For as it can go on to infinity with the intuition of the living, so that the point at which it may still arrive cannot be determined at all and cannot be foreseen at all, to what [p. 94] degree the mediate cognition, which after all is only the surrogate of the lacking immediate one, will vanish — so it can also go on to infinity with the view and the finally actual *seeing* of death, and it cannot be determined what is possible for man in this direction. — Thus Mr. Fichte describes among other things (p. 258) a picture of his own invention, representing a holy woman who is raised to heaven, and then adds: “What is it now that makes this figure beautiful? — Is it *her* *limbs and parts*? Is it not rather wholly the One feeling which is poured out through these limbs?” — I ask in reply: whose imagination is so unhappily constituted as, at such a picture, to think immediately of the *parts* or limbs, or even of the feeling that fills them, separated from the whole? Who will not rather grasp and contemplate the indivisible whole — in its indivisibility? — — What other ugliness may Mr. Fichte still have in readiness, in order to free the age from it, in his opinion? Thus the idea of a *willful, capricious* God, whom one must make favorable to oneself by services, has pursued him for many years now, and occurs to him even in connection with the philosophy of nature. One must not, he says, let oneself be led astray by fanaticism, by the fact that it has often wanted to betray to us the means of binding and banning angels and archangels or even God himself; this has still always happened only in order to bring about *effects of nature*: those spirits were therefore not conceived as spirits — (that would still be tolerable) — but as *forces of nature* (Gr. p. 262). The forces of nature and nature are thus the properly and always abominable; a spirit, to be sure, a pure spirit can still, as in the *Bestimmung* *des Menschen*, keep catechism-lessons with one and free him forever from all nature — but nature is so wholly of the evil that even an angel of light, indeed an archangel, if he appeared as a force of nature, would be unholy, an angel of darkness. In all of this there betrays itself no other feeling of [p. 95] nature than that of the crudest and most deranged ascetics, of those who rolled in pointed thorns, not out of holiness, but in order thereby to flee from their unholiness and innermost impurity.<sup>10</sup>

<sup>10</sup> Into what hiding places of base thinking, one might also still ask, may the man have looked, whose bitterness against his opponents can sketch such a picture as that in the *Grundzüge*.

Mr. Fichte *sees* just such a nature once and for all (we have already conceded it to him, for his own person), and because he sees it, he also asserts it and derives it, and thereby accommodates it in his system. We others must surely see it too, he thinks; but with us it is nowhere derived (as we likewise feel no vocation to give a deduction of other ugliness or absurdities of human view); since it must nonetheless occur somewhere with us, it is without doubt harbored in the philosophy of nature; and since at the same time it is rumored that this regards nature as a divine life, but by no means as a rigid, dead being, we must have deified just this dead being — that J. G. Fichtean nature.

Who does not know the universal suffering of the present generation: that it cannot see the living as actual and, conversely, the actual as at the same time living; that for it time cannot be as eternity, eternity not as time, which they have long since revealed in all forms of the world? But this discord at least makes itself known in others as a suffering, as a pain, which has merely not wrestled itself out and therefore also has not found its end. Fichte alone is of quite good cheer about it, he gives himself and others the best of consciences about it; for him what manifests itself in others as sickness is health; that against which even those who cannot live rightly and cannot die rightly philosophically balk as against death is the actual, proper life.

We have asserted, and assert as a proven matter, that the world as unbroken and colorless is not only to be thought, [p. 96] but in fact to be beheld and is actually beheld; just as we also see in color not properly darkness, but precisely light, and only by means of it notice its opposite; we *assert* that the divine in nature is by no means veiled and invisible, to be grasped solely by thought, but that it is manifest, intuitable, present, the properly immediate, just as, on the other hand, everything ungodly is the merely mediate, solely to be thought up; we assert that it is impossible for us to comprehend even any part of matter other than as a life, just as it depends only on each person himself to see eternity as actual in time itself, and accordingly to be rid of time in actual consciousness.

That Mr. Fichte now does not see the possibility of this and denies it, we know, and herewith accept it as a fact. There, however, the matter rests. By this confession of his we are separated forever. He cannot come into the world in which we find ourselves, since he himself confesses that it is closed to him, and that a life which is at once divine *and* actual (actual in the strictest sense of the word) belongs for him among the utter incomprehensibilities.

Our difference lies, as has now clearly emerged, far deeper than Mr. Fichte imagines and is able to imagine. He is with his thoughts still always at a wholly different inquiry. — Whether things, in their pure objectivity and rigidity, are actually outside us, or whether they are merely within us (the latter of which Mr. Fichte considers his discovery), of this there has long been no talk; it is a matter of something wholly different: namely, whether they are then even *within us* actual.

He seeks us where we never are, in what he calls the sensuous world, and wants, to the amusement of all who understand the matter, still to go on instructing us that it has no reality in itself. While He, on the contrary, imagines that he has freed himself entirely from this sensuous world, indeed has himself annihilated it, he finds himself in the midst of it, or rather, it finds itself in him, in the center of his consciousness, [p. 97] and in such a way that he cannot shake it off at all, cannot in any way eradicate it.

What he calls nature is *nothing to us*; not because we do not know it, but rather because we clearly cognize it as a specter of his reflection, a creature of his merely mediate cognizing. What we, on the other hand, call nature is, to be sure, nothing to him either, but not out of cognition, rather out of a lack of cognition and manifest ignorance.

Mr. Fichte denies in the most proper sense the *things in* *themselves*, namely he denies that the in-itself is the actual; of his actual, which is not the divine, he then supposes that we deify it. Quite the reverse, we say: that there is nothing actual either in us or outside us but the divine.

We do not directly deny his theory; we deny the fact of his world of appearance; there is no such world of appearance as he assumes, except for a corrupted reflection. Once he has made such a world for himself, his theory may well be necessary and fit quite nicely; what the poet says applies here: once the cross of wood has been soundly timbered, a living body is of course fitting to be put upon it as punishment. — Were Fichte to understand the world, there would be need neither of a splitting for him nor, therefore, of any explanation of this splitting.

Outside the divine world, which as such is immediately also the actual one, there is nothing at all but only individual, arbitrary thinking, through which that world can be turned into something dead and absolutely manifold, but is not necessarily so turned. Mr. Fichte has now also thought up for himself such a dead and infinitely fractured world, *thought up*; if he wanted to assert that it is actual for him, he would have to assert that he can see and does see what is not and cannot be, that is, he would have to assert that even the *sense* in him has become delusion, hence *delusion-sense*, nonsense. He who lives and moves in what is merely thought up, and takes it for something necessary, nevertheless presumes, from out of this thought-up world, to tell the philosophers of nature that they [p. 98] *all manner of things* think up; he, the dreamer, to interpret the intuitions of the waking as dreams!

With that absolutely reasonless world, whose creator, in Mr. Fichte’s opinion, is the absolute consciousness, the principle of his polemic against all rational cognition of nature, against all speculative physics, is then given at once. That theory of the transformation of divine being is the means of turning the world once more into something arbitrary, and precisely here, where the purest necessity prevails, of keeping open still a sphere for free imagination and for mere opining. According to what law does the absolute consciousness proceed in that transformation? Answer: there is no law here at all, reflection is wholly free; “if there is no reflecting, as by virtue of absolute freedom may well be omitted, then *nothing* *appears*; but if reflection goes on infinitely, as by virtue of the same freedom may well occur, then with each new reflection the world steps forth in a new shape” (s. L. p. 114); why the shape is this determinate one — its wholly individual liveliness and uniqueness — is not thereby comprehended; these actual shapes, into which the real is split, can only be lived through, so that one must give oneself over to them observingly, just as we simply have to take it when the sky rains down on our heads, but by no means can they be thought out or derived a priori.

Who would object to this? — About the absolutely reasonless no reason can cognize or know anything, such a thing can indeed only be lived through, and the opposition of a priori and a posteriori is quite in its place here. The a posteriori is the purely reasonless; but the a priori is also not the rational, rather the empty understanding. This can well derive a priori “the *general properties* of those shapes of the One Real from the fundamental law of reflection (that it splits, namely), it can accordingly order them into classes and kinds”; as to what goes beyond this, however, mere experience takes place: in the golden age of rational science a regulative will be set up, [p. 99] according to which it can be investigated by experiments; so long as this is not given, and rational science “has not yet fulfilled its duty toward physics,” one must of course permit the physicist to have notions about the thought-of reasonless (the gift of such notions, afterwards dispensable, is called genius); but he must test and confirm these by experiment: to want to have notions about the empirical without any empirical knowledge at all, that is manifest nonsense, is, as the public readily sees, just as foolish as wanting to bake butter-cakes without butter — is possible only for a speculation so little understanding itself, of the kind the unhappy philosophy of nature is. (See on all these remarks Gr. p. 206 ff.).

The zeal for the good cause of the understanding makes the worthy orator once again overlook only one small point, namely the insignificant question whether the philosophy of nature even concedes that reasonless thing, indeed whether even empirical physics concerns itself with investigating it?

In a Fichtean system of the sciences it might well constitute pretty much the main subject matter; for divine being is to him a pure One and absolute sameness, which is by all means tedious, and with which one is at once done, so that one must be truly grateful to the absolute consciousness for transforming and splitting divine being for us. The philosophy of nature, on the other hand, seeks to grasp multiplicity rationally, namely in unity with unity, and not reasonlessly, and that unnecessary world imposed upon us by the absolute consciousness does not exist for it at all. — But the genuine investigator of nature too, what does he actually want to find out through the experiment, and what alone can he want to find out? — I answer: *that which is*, or what he actually sees in the appearances of nature. He by no means wants to investigate the reasonless, to make what is not into an object of cognition; it is rather precisely this that he seeks to separate off, to posit as a not-being and for that very reason not properly cognized and experienced.

[p. 100] I presuppose that one knows, with Lichtenberg, how to distinguish between physicists and physicasters, as between musicians and musickers. The latter forget the end in the means, or rather they know only the former and not the latter at all; they are concerned not with the living but only with the arrangements for its presentation, which they then take for the essential itself. For the true physicist, of whom alone there can be question, the reasonless is an object of handling and by no means of cognition; to the latter he stands only in the relation of a technician; but as one who knows, and who strives after science, he is directed solely toward *what is*; he is a liberator of this which is, the true priest of nature, who sacrifices what is not so that what is may be transfigured into its true essence. Thus, to make ourselves clear at least through one example, physics attained science concerning the course of the chemical process only since it recognized that what truly *is* in the chemical appearance is not matter as such, the combined as the combined, but the living bond, or the copula of the two electricities. —

In this aim directed at the cognition of what is, philosophy is now wholly and immediately at one with physics, as was already shown before; and it is a futile undertaking to want to stir up strife or disunity between the two, and a ridiculous one besides, when it is undertaken with such evident ignorance of the essence of both sciences as by Mr. Fichte.

His whole judgment of the matter rests on his first positing an absolutely reasonless world, which is for him the actual one: since we do not concede such a one, but only a world which is living reason itself, there arises *for him* thereby the semblance that we raise ourselves above the actual world and yet in this elevation want to cognize the actual. The word experience, which he uses here, is to be sure a very ambiguous word, designating a, commonly, highly mixed concept. If it means cognition of the actual as the actual, then the philosophy of nature is concerned precisely with the purest experience; but if it means cognition of the not-actual, of the reasonless, either for itself or in its admixture with the actual, then philosophy of nature is of course wholly different from it; but it does not raise itself above the world of such an experience, [p. 101] rather it sublates it itself and denies that it is. Just as the art of the artist does not properly consist in surpassing nature, but in presenting what is in it, and in removing what is not, which in common occurrence is noticed along with it, even for perception — (which, as mere for-true-taking, is expressly opposed to actual seeing) —: so too the aim of the philosopher of nature is by no means to soar over nature, but to present and to cognize purely the positive, or what in it actually is.

That such a cognition is possible, the proofs have long since been given, and it is too late to doubt the possibility where the actuality already lies before our eyes. In general this eternal and necessary bond of philosophy with nature and physics, in its true significance, has still remained a mystery to the age. Here individuals still rise up, as if drunk with sleep, and speak against this view in the old way, in the accustomed phrases, meaning that their abstract concepts have power also against this science. No, it is no longer a matter of mere thinking, to which another thinking can then be opposed; it is a matter of *seeing*; it is no longer at your discretion whether you accept what is here at issue and let yourselves be convinced of it; you may leave it undone, you may look away from it, ignore it; it is nonetheless there, and you cannot get rid of it, for it is not *our* opinion, but is something actual and to be seen with eyes as in mathematics; and you will not demand that we exchange this visible truth for your webs of thought.

But how does Mr. Fichte come, after all — — to speak of physics, *he of all people*, to hold himself called to be the patron [p. 102] of experience? Suppose the philosophy of nature did not accomplish, as speculative physics, what it undertook, indeed that by the nature of the case it were not even capable of accomplishing it, what has Mr. Fichte gained thereby? An undeniable merit would still remain to it with respect to him. Of this, that it has reinstated philosophy in its ancestral dignity of being cognition of the divine — after it had in him divested itself of this majesty entirely and to the last trace — of this Mr. Fichte most cleverly keeps silent, and, instead of going back to the principles, attacks the results, as only a sophist does.

And what concepts of physics as a science does Mr. Fichte himself betray, which could give him a right to sit as judge in this field? — “The true physicists, according to him, always proceeded from phenomena, seeking only the *law of unity* (not the living itself), in which these could be comprehended, and, as soon as they had conceived their thought, returned to the phenomena in order to test the thought on them — doubtless in the firm conviction that it expects its confirmation only from the explicability of those from it” (Gr. p. 252) — in other words: they first sought to guess the ground of the phenomena from the phenomena themselves, naturally they put into the latter nothing but what seemed to them serviceable for explaining the phenomena; thereupon they found, going back, that these were indeed explicable through that — and now the thought was confirmed — confirmed through a palpable circle in which one had gone round. It cannot well be unknown to anyone acquainted with the history of science that it was precisely this circle — this inferring from the appearances to the ground, and deriving the appearances again from the ground — that produced the most absurd theories in physics; just as there is probably no genuine physicist who would not abhor this way of wanting to attain cognition of nature.

What proofs of self-acquired knowledge may give Mr. Fichte the heart to say of the philosophy of nature: that it [p. 103] relieves one of laborious learning and is welcome to the young for that reason; for even the pupils who adhere to this doctrine he does not spare in his wrath and follows them with envious and jealous glances. — I will remark here that my chief error with respect to the age really consists in this, that I regard nature not mechanically but dynamically. Could one only convince me that it consists in mere mechanism, my conversion would be accomplished at once; then nature is undeniably dead, and any other philosopher can be right, only not I. According to this mechanical view all prevailing philosophy since Des Cartes has been modeled; a dynamic living nature has not been reckoned with in it at all, and it therefore comes most inopportunely to all philosophy already there beforehand and completed. Since the strife of the latter against the philosophy of nature is at bottom a strife of mechanics against dynamics, the former enters upon an unequal and, on its side, highly imprudent combat. For it may well happen (as it has already happened) that it is refuted by physics and must yield to experience, since it would not yield to reason. — So it now fares with Mr. Fichte. He is in physics, as in philosophy, a mere mechanic; never has a glimmer of dynamic life illumined his spirit. Equipped with this mechanical view, he now wants to conduct the cause of the physicists at a moment when they themselves have for the most part ceased to be mechanics. But nothing, in fairness, causes more vexation than an unbidden advocate who does not understand the cause he wants to conduct. — Still no more comprehensive knowledge of nature wants to betray itself in Mr. Fichte than that now already often shown: “that several tracts of the earth still lie covered with putrid marshes and impenetrable forests, whose cold and dull atmosphere breeds poisonous insects and exhales devastating plagues” (Gr. p. 87). With such poverty, indeed one may well say such a complete lack of any intuition of his own in the field, it is natural enough to seek foreign assistance; but a wholly vain hope, even now to win the investigators of nature [p. 104] for his mechanical view and to incite them against the philosophy of nature.

“It must, he supposes, greatly vex the older physicists, who had carried out fruitful and fortunate experiments, that they undertook this fruitless and inglorious labor, since they must now see the discoveries of their experiments demonstrated a priori in a couple of periods.” — Ah, no! the physicists are not of so vexable a kind as to let it annoy them when an enlargement is granted to human insight; or when what they found factually from a limited standpoint is now also recognized as necessary from a higher one. Galileo’s experiments have not sunk into ungrateful oblivion through Newton’s mathematical proofs, and the physicist who, out of the confusion of the surroundings, has lifted out the living by the happy stroke of an experiment retains his high merit undiminished, even when what he found has long since become an object of immediate and necessary cognition.

On the other hand, Bacon’s prophecies, for example, have lost nothing by being fulfilled only long afterward through experiments not foreseen by him. If experiment has in some points of science run ahead, it will on the other hand perhaps take centuries until it has lifted the life of nature up out of the depth in which reason and science already now clearly behold it. Man should indeed demand no signs and wonders; true inwardness of sense sees the full life in the faintest weaving and working of nature; yet I believe that that sleep-drunk and dreaming world of monads, as our Leibniz calls it, must answer the questioning investigator with quite other signs of life than has happened hitherto, that it will then no longer be possible to pass off Ideas such as those as mere *thoughts*, since we shall then see living nature ascended, speaking with us face to face. —

So far Mr. Fichte’s conceptions of the philosophy of nature do not reach; for his thoughts of nature itself do not go so far. [p. 105] Since he is accustomed to regard it only as to the mechanical and its usefulness for man, he supposes that by means of the philosophy of nature too all sorts of things profitable for human life, for example the genuine preparation of Berlin blue or the making of the most durable mortar and the like, are to be deduced a priori, and then of course cannot see what for all this is to be derived a priori, since one could take it quite simply and much more surely from the nearest hand, experience. That such derivations are beneath the dignity of philosophy, this ground he does not even make use of. On the contrary, they belong quite properly to philosophy, and are quite in their place, where the question is of arrangements that can be made by human freedom itself. There, for example, men long practiced and rich in experience have taken pains to devise how the police in a city may best be organized, the forgery of bills of exchange or state papers prevented, and the greatest possible commercial advantage for a state achieved. Now Mr. Fichte comes and deduces to them a priori the whole arrangement of the police, in minute detail, down to the duties of the gatekeepers; and if the Prussian state had consulted him in the production of its treasury notes, the thoroughly learned man could have served it with his knowledge, as he had already derived a priori in the closed commercial state the true archetype of the Prussian commercial constitution, only, it goes without saying, with a consistency exceeding actuality. How it must vex the many writers on the police and the Prussian statesmen, if they were of Mr. Fichte’s humor, to see a great part of the arrangements made by them, without any aid from philosophy, deduced a priori by Mr. Fichte — not in a few paragraphs, to be sure, but in many pages and whole books!

Such real merits the philosophy of nature cannot boast; and since Mr. Fichte, on a cursory glance through its propositions, [p. 106] could find no such truths profitable for human life derived in them, and yet on the other side could not comprehend how nature or anything in it could be the expression of pure rational truth, the whole had to strike him as *allegorical*; for how else should nature, which in its innermost essence is reasonless and ungodly, be brought to a semblance of original rationality than through laborious allegorical interpretation, a rationality which in any case comes into it only by its being made useful and serviceable? Accordingly Mr. Fichte assures us: “the essential of the knowledges cited by way of example was never *deduced a priori* in the philosophy of nature, but only forced into allegorical form”; Mr. Fichte is without doubt the man to judge what the *essential* is in any natural phenomenon: but that the philosophy of nature neither *deduces* nor deduces a priori, this is a side issue, which does not matter in the judgment.

That resistance to the innermost identity of nature with reason, and that incapacity to see in their agreement anything other than allegorical play, has expressed itself in others in an inverted way, in that they have censured our peculiar scientific language as one taken from nature and for that very reason unlawfully transferred into the realm of reason. I ask them in return whence all scientific language was originally taken, if not from nature, only that through long use this origin of all our philosophical expressions has long been obscured. Given the original unity of the real and ideal world, this intuitive language is not an arbitrary but a thoroughly necessary invention, which, notwithstanding the abuse that some have made of it, must be preserved, and is an essential gain for the evidence of philosophy. That it has over the ordinary abstract language the advantage of clarity, and serves to designate distinctly with a single word relations which it would otherwise take a multitude of words to make comprehensible, no one who understands it will be able to deny. Suppose, for example, someone asserted that Mr. Fichte and [p. 107] Mr. Nicolai are innermostly akin and at bottom wholly at one; this would seem to have uttered a great paradox. Let one use for this relation the word polarity, and all is clear. One sees, namely, how, notwithstanding the most direct opposition, both are nevertheless one according to their innermost foundation, and how they, represented perhaps as the two gases burning together, Nicolai as the hydrogen, Mr. Fichte as the oxygen, in reciprocal interpenetration and depotentiation would have to yield as product the pure indifference, the true water of the age.

“The wonder-worker (the philosopher of nature, that is), says Mr. Fichte, should at least document his higher mission by *one* prophecy that has come true, he should, in a region unattainable by inference from previous experience, specify an experiment made neither by himself nor by others before, and predict its outcome determinately, so that, on the actual carrying out of the experiment, it would turn out just as he had said” (Gr. 271).

It may now be some eight or nine years since Mr. E. C. E. Schmid at Jena rolled this heavy stumbling-block into the way of the philosophy of nature just beginning, which now, after no one had been willing to lift it until then, is pushed a stretch further by Mr. Fichte, in that he has sharpened the task so that it is wholly unfulfillable. “In a region unattainable by inference from previous experience the sorcerer is to specify an experiment.” Let him give him this task too: that he build a palace in a world that does not exist at all! Nature is an absolute continuum; each thing is determined through all and all through each; it would therefore have to be explained how there could be a region unattainable by inference from previous experience. — In the end the demand is this: the sorcerer should have no experience at all, break off the ground on which he stands from under himself and so, stepping upon the nothing, prophesy like a pure Fichtean spirit. Yes, even that would not be enough; for he himself would still exist, and [p. 108] he might have some experience of himself and from this infer, for example, that he must have a body consisting of tough and modifiable matter, from which he could then at last arrive at the whole of nature. He would therefore have to not exist at all, and so, not existing, prophesy to Mr. Fichte something that no eye has seen, no ear ever heard, which — considered precisely — likewise did not exist!

Such a complete nothing of reality is therefore the Prius of Mr. Fichte: for the *purity* of his cognition it is already disturbing that anything exists at all, that the eternal is actually real, and only *after* it is actual is also cognized, because this cognizing itself belongs to its actuality. It would rather have to be not there at all, so that the cognition of it might be wholly pure and absolutely a priori. — These are necessary consequences of the Fichtean distinction of the a priori and a posteriori, which He, although we wholly reject it and admit no other distinction in knowing than that of the immediate and the mediate, nevertheless thinks he may apply against us.

Whether, moreover, the philosophy of nature has always prophesied only after the deed, as Mr. *Fichte* wants to have it, *connoisseurs* — upright, conscientious ones — may decide. That, for example, at a time when physicists knew magnetism only as the property of a single metal, explaining the traces of it in some others only from admixed parts of that very metal, the philosophy of nature asserted its universal generality and demonstrated magnetism to be a necessary category of matter — that it was then, over this assertion, set right by reviewers and others, as is fitting, through experience, which was said to show that magnetism is by no means a general property of bodies — until then, several years afterward, a French physicist, who knew nothing of that assertion, finds through experiments that no solid body in nature is unmagnetic — this of course makes no prophecy in the Fichtean sense. Or that the [p. 109] author in his aphorisms on philosophy (Zeitschr. f. sp. Physik II, 2, § 75 [IV, p. 156]) sets up the general proposition: “Any two bodies differing from one another (in quality) can be regarded as the two sides of a magnet, and the more so, the greater their relative difference,” and that afterward a German investigator of nature composes from silver and zinc a true magnetic needle pointing to the poles, this is again no proof that the wonder which Mr. Fichte holds impossible is nonetheless possible; for besides the fact that the author, in setting up that proposition, did after all actually exist, he would moreover have had to specify not merely the truth or the proposition itself, but also the experiment, if Mr. *Fichte* was to believe him!

For him, however, we shall specify a quite simple experiment. What the physicasters will say to his utterances we leave undecided; his concepts of physics come roughly closest to theirs, yet they will find that he has learned nothing thorough in the matter. We propose to him, on the other hand, that he once take a poll among the true physicists, to find out which of us two they declare to be in the right. I hereby assure him and prophesy a priori, with the firmest conviction, that it will in fact turn out just as I have predicted: the physicists will politely thank him for his instructions on experimenting and will not carry out even one of the experiments he may put forward, so that he will never run the risk of being found a false prophet.

What is the true spirit of the investigator of nature? — It is devotion, piety toward nature, religion, unconditional submission to actuality and truth, as these are expressed in nature and are one with nature itself. Precisely this submission is, according to the Fichtean doctrine, the most terrible thing, at which the spirit of a free being recoils in horror: the agreement of nature with thought is possible, according to it, only in such a way that nature conforms to thought (Gr. p. 253), but not in such a way that truth itself is being, that being or [p. 110] nature itself is truth. — What does the physicist desire? Life, and only this is the prize he wants to carry off from the struggle with death. — The Fichtean theory here draws an absolute boundary before him, that blow of absolute consciousness which irretrievably transforms life into death for every actual intuition and leaves only the empty husk for contemplation. What impulse can a rational spirit feel to investigate a world that can be explained to it by so wretched a conjuring trick, whereby, if there is no reflecting, nothing appears, but if there is reflecting on into infinity, then on into infinity something appears as well? — And what is there, in fact, to investigate? We may perhaps undertake to derive the universal properties of things a priori, to classify them systematically and divide them into species and genera — behold the astonishing results of Fichtean rational science! — What is more repugnant to the genuine investigator of nature, in the innermost depths of his soul, than the teleological view and consideration of things? In older systems it was at least the revelation of the goodness, wisdom, and power of the eternal essence that was laid down as the primordial purpose of nature: in the Fichtean system it has lost even this last remnant of sublimity, and its whole existence amounts to the purpose of its cultivation and exploitation by man. Could there really be any physicist living who thought so meanly of the object of his science as to listen with equanimity to the Fichtean deduction of physics in the Erl. Vorles.? The forces of nature, according to it, are there only in order to be subjected to human purposes. This subjection is expressed at one time as a gradual cancellation and annihilation of nature (so, then, an actual nature?) by man — at another as an animation of nature through the life of reason; as if every subjection to human purposes were not a killing of the living, or as if that could be animated which is supposed to be a mere limit. For the sake of this purpose, knowledge of the laws according to which those forces work, that is, physics, is necessary. But nature is to be not *merely* useful and serviceable to man, [p. 111] which was its first purpose and the economic view, but “it *shall* at the same time surround him fittingly,” that is (how else can one interpret it?) it shall be refashioned into agreeable gardens and country estates, beautiful dwellings and suitable furnishings, which is the second purpose and the aesthetic view of nature.

What can be reconciled with such a cast of mind and with the representation of such a nature, which is worth only being refashioned into tools and household goods, other than the blindest contempt for all nature, which boldly believes it cannot revile *man* more forcefully than by saying of him that he is a force of nature that produces and thinks in him (Gr. p. 253 f.)? To be sure, it is not to be seen how in such a nature a force can be thought to think; by that utterance, then, only a force thinking with inner necessity is presumably meant, as opposed to the free, self-owned force of the individual. Now Mr. Fichte, like much else that does not suit his system, also takes it upon himself to say: “that everything wrong in man rests solely in his selfhood, “that only when *a foreign power* *seizes man, drives him on, and instead of him* (as a finite being) *becomes alive in him*, does real and true existence (thus, since existence = knowing, also true and real knowing) “come into his life” (E. V. 7). Now even if this foreign power, as Mr. Fichte assures us, is always the power of God, it still remains foreign in relation to the individual — likewise a necessarily working force, neither his own nor free. It would follow, then, that the later work teaches what was reviled in the earlier, which in Mr. Fichte’s case is not so only once. Yet, to be fair, we must regard even the last utterance merely as a decoration borrowed from the philosophers of nature: the orator’s actual basic opinion and innermost conviction is that *he himself* thinks within himself, and that *he alone* thinks in him, and no one else. He has “risen above all power of nature, and would long since have stopped up this source in himself” (Gr. p. 254), [p. 112] if it had ever flowed in him; anyone will testify that it is not nature that thinks in *him*, and how should it even get a word in before him? If it were to give any trace of an expression of life, he would shout it down at once and talk it utterly into the ground with his wisdom. Between nature and him there is eternal enmity, like that between the seed of the serpent and the seed of the woman; *he* has long since trodden on the head of all nature in himself; yet it remains doubtful, to hear him tell it, which of the two does the other the most harm. Nature thrusts him, presses him, stings him not merely in the heels but threatens his whole life everywhere and constantly (so he says himself; what else it does to him, and what pitiful irony it plays on him, he of course does not notice). He repays it for this in his own fashion; he would gladly persuade himself that at bottom it does not exist at all; yet he fights it, and in his inability to find words that express his whole loathing, he assures us that it will at least still be annihilated, if it is not so already.

The question might still arise whether in Mr. Fichte the hatred of nature engendered that of the philosophy of nature, or whether the fury against the latter first produced the supreme loathing of the former. But one can hardly hesitate to declare for the primordiality of that hatred which he has sworn against nature and its works; only retroactively has the philosophy of nature aroused its flames to a still greater violence. — Had it succeeded in drawing even a few drops from the wellspring of all joyfulness, nature, it would have to be a poison to the will standing in the fiery torment of subjectivity, which it thrusts from itself with force and vehemence. Pour into a boiling, seething metal a few drops of refreshing water, and see how it flares up with hissing and roaring; such an explosion is that by which the hell of self-ness, whose root in nature has been cut off, has given vent to itself in Mr. Fichte.

To *him* the philosophy of nature is comprehensible only as arising from a thinking that stands *solely in the service of craving*, that goes back to the person alone, that for precisely this [p. 113] reason strives back into that from which the life of the person descends — into *sensuous* nature, which is *for that very* *reason necessarily* speculation on nature (Gr. pp. 256–258).

At all times embittered people, who are at the same time weak or defend a weak cause, have seized as their last defense upon the expedient of shifting their opponents’ assertions onto the immoral character of those opponents and deriving them from it as from their hidden source. By this means all troublesome investigation and further defense was spared once and for all. — There is therefore nothing remarkable in that deduction of the philosophy of nature, except perhaps (if one wished to find it so) that — even Mr. Fichte feels himself driven to this kind of polemic. Noteworthy alone is the confession it contains; namely that *He* has, up to now, been able to think nature only in relation to his sensuous person; and this is then — one cannot say the opinion, but — the disposition that was bound to become manifest in many in opposition to the philosophy of nature. Because *they* see in nature nothing but the mirror of their contemptible lust — therefore it is to be shattered and damned. To them nature must appear dead, repugnant, and abominable, if they are to feel no temptation of desire; were it the opposite of that, their supposed virtue, or at least that of the rest of the world, whose guardians they consider themselves to be, would run the highest danger. For that reason the divine too must be moved out quite far — beyond all boundaries of consciousness and actuality — so that it may not be stained by the impurity that they transfer from themselves into nature.

At the same time, however, in presenting nature as worthy of hatred and annihilation, they nonetheless demand that it remain, so that they may have something their heart can hate, so that their will may not be a single one that wills only One thing, but a contending one, in which a twofold desire lies. While they pretend to contend for the honor of God, they contend at bottom for this very ungodly world, which they call the actual one. As a divine world they do not want it, but [p. 114] certainly as an ungodly one. — There is only One way to cancel the discord between the divine and the ungodly, namely, that only the one *is*, but the other is not. Since we, then, certainly cancel that opposition, but in such a way that we wholly deny the existence of the ungodly and assert that only the divine *is*, while those others nevertheless cry out because of this cancellation and accuse us of a deification of nature, it is clear that what concerns them is precisely that lower, or in our opinion wholly non-existent and ungodly thing. — We are far from charging any of these criers with wanting to preserve this world for himself as an instrument of his lust or desire. Their personality is wholly indifferent to us, we know nothing of it, nor have we ever had to do with it; moreover, we are convinced that the ground of that crying out lies, in most of them, quite elsewhere than in their lust; rather, precisely in their moral concepts; for to the will that is only a single one and wills only One thing, it is no merit to will this One; but those others want a merit and therefore need the opposite; the concept of sin is engraved in the depths of their hearts, and with it the concept of a dead world, a lost world, one cast out by God. They themselves, to be sure, do not demand to be sinners; but were sin eliminated from the world, then merit would be too, and there would remain only faith, that is, the disposition which is itself divine and sees only the divine. — Finally it must be uncovered what the struggle waged by them is really about, and what cause it is to which they dedicate their highest interest.

According to our proofs it is absolutely impossible that in itself or objectively any ungodly thing *be*; its existence can therefore arise only from the ground of the subject, and indeed of the individual, empirical one. Here, accordingly, is the point where our doctrine, like all other philosophy, must refer to the formation of human life itself and takes this up into itself as a necessary requirement. Until the root of the ungodly has been torn out in disposition and thought, it will [p. 115] go on putting out its branches over into the actual world as well, and perverting it and obscuring the divine in it.
