I am not speaking of isolated, misjudged utterances of genuine ethics, but of all morality valid hitherto, when I say that it has not merely confirmed but demanded, and had to demand, belief in the actuality of an ungodly thing in us and outside us, in order to subsist itself. The feeling that spread from this ethics could be no other than that general to the science of this age, that God is essentially, namely as actual, *dead*, and as such to be awakened only by the power of our thought, and as our creature: the assurance with which this thought was ascribed to those who proclaimed the joyful message of the life of God proves only how deeply that opinion of God’s nonactuality had been impressed on all thinkers. — Our fathers were strong in faith without the false pomp of ethical life and of one’s own merit. The question of their heart and spirit was: Death, where is thy sting? Hell, where is thy victory? Instead of that, the learned have by their opinions reintroduced death and set their systems, which mechanically pervert nature, above the living ground of nature itself, to a merely historical faith in the word and not in the spirit, in the concept and not in intuition; instead of the confidence of our being-one with God, however, they have given man a self-created and selfcontemplating ethical life, and with it placed him again under the law, and through the law under sin.

The appearance of a doctrine that denies all existence of the ungodly, in an age whose morality rests on precisely this existence, must necessarily produce, in this age, quite peculiar moral effects, at which only the ignorant can wonder. Would we perhaps be right in what we say of the morality of the age, if our doctrine were not being combated in the most unethical manner — on grounds of ethics — by people who display toward us ourselves the highest lack of ethical conduct — in honor of their ethics? What have we ourselves posited as the [p. 116] two poles of life? Sacred custom on the one side, religious inspiration on the other. But precisely these have died out and been extirpated in the dominant doctrine and culture, and in their place something has stepped that contains nothing of either and excludes both from itself. Can it now surprise us that our doctrine itself first of all feels the wildness of the age, and must it not calmly bear its consequences and accept them as so many proofs of the truth of what it asserts about the character of present-day morality? Can I myself be surprised that for a long time now I have been contested here and there with reasons, but generally have become a target of lies, malice, and personal persecution? Have I not deserved all this richly? Have I not, as occasion and circumstances allowed, done much evil to the bad and the spiritless, not spared the Pharisees and hypocrites, stripped the sheep’s clothing from some of them and unmasked their inner malice? So too I have always been heartily out of sorts with sentimentality of every kind, and have thereby betrayed my wicked heart plainly enough. Had I counted on principles of honor, it would serve me doubly right; for I should have known that inner dishonorableness confesses itself without fearing dishonor, and that nothing is harmed in it when it is exhibited as such. The man to whom my ear and my door are closed can nonetheless go and slander me publicly, and he can know that I know it, without his needing to blush before me. Another may have eked out his living by senseless authorship with words and ideas borrowed from me, and may still do so, and if the times so bring it, may still write a book full of invective against me with the same ideas; this brings him no disgrace and does not even make him ridiculous, but does honor to his courage and his free way of thinking. I myself, to my knowledge, have never burdened the public with my person, having never spoken of it; but precisely this is a new proof of my obduracy, and it must surely be permitted to think and say the worst of him who has not made the public a witness to his [p. 117] heart and his personal feelings at all, but has always spoken only of the matter or against the matter, in a cold and merciless manner.

All this is therefore in order, and the opposite would be astonishing, but not that it is now thus. But if the power of that against which these preparations are made could otherwise be doubted, it would emerge from this alone, that so many who fight against it must at the same time reveal their innermost to its deepest ground, that not only wretches and those worthless from the beginning, but men who otherwise, especially in scientific intercourse, even with respect to themselves, demanded principles of honor, integrity, and shame, now deny these very principles against it and cast them away without scruple.

I can only lament that Mr. Fichte has placed himself in this class of combatants.

After everything earlier against the philosophers of nature failed to prove sufficient, the following traits of their personality are then (Gr. p. 265 f.) to decide the issue.

The enthusiasts — not in general, but specifically, and as is expressly distinguished (p. 264) — those of the present age, of whom it had already been declared and is further declared that they are the philosophers of nature — *these*, then, the philosophers of nature, intoxicate or inspire themselves, when the ideas do not quite want to flow, by physical stimulants. — Mr. Fichte does not say: the author makes use of such means, but first of all, he thinks, and *cannot* suppose otherwise, the public will nevertheless relate it to him; for it is of course known that some ill-wishers, who made it their business to speak ill of him, spread this very thing about him long ago, with the addition that the physicians give him only a few more years to live. Now he is indeed still alive and enjoys the best of health, and no decline of life is to be detected in him. All the more necessary, then, to bring the rumor back into [p. 118] circulation, and an old proverb says: slander boldly, something always sticks!

Does Mr. Fichte know that circumstance from my servant or household staff; for from somewhere he must surely *know* it, since he asserts it as a fact, otherwise he would be in the position of having knowingly put forward an untruth or (which is the same) a fabrication. Or has he merely inferred this too, and does he reason as the Jews did at Pentecost, when they heard languages they did not understand, and must all whom *He* does not understand be full of sweet wine? — Do my writings bear the mark of intoxication and of a forced inspiration? — (We have heard quite different judgments of them) — perhaps, however, for Mr. Fichte, whose mental capacity, as is easily shown, is confined to a couple of ideas (if one may even call them that), which he has communicated in endless breadth and wearying prolixity, which blurring of thoughts *He* calls his art as a writer. Mr. Fichte gives us to understand several times that we lack clarity about our own thoughts, that we cannot give a clear account of them. How matters stand with Fichtean clarity and transparency we have found in what precedes. A world in which, on into infinity, everything possible appears, merely when there is reflecting, is no doubt transparent enough: but the most transparent thing is the vacuum, and it is easy always to seem clear to one who never raises himself to the place where, for common understanding, the darkness first begins. — By the Fichtean explanation of clarity, Mr. Nicolai would be the clearest man of the century, since he surely at every moment surveys his whole stock of thoughts and knowledge and knows exactly of each part to which pigeonhole it belongs. We do not boast of such clarity, and have long since confessed that it is impossible to render a sun-clear report of the universe. Moreover, let Mr. Fichte just try our clarity: we shall answer to him from beginning to end; Heaven grant only that he answer to us, instead [p. 119] of railing at us in generalities and from out of his corner and heaping abuse on us. Can drunken courage so bring sober wisdom out of its composure; can wild intoxication so make sober, cool, frostily begotten science come to grief, as it appears that in this work we have indeed brought the Fichtean knowledge to grief? — To be sure, you still hold it possible even today that one can cast out devils through Beelzebub, the prince of the devils.

But it is not only with physical stimulants that the philosophers of nature inflame their fantasy, but also with the reading of enthusiasts; the most decried and the rarest are the most agreeable to them for this purpose (Gr. p. 260). — Whoever is at all acquainted with the history of the sciences in the last centuries will have to agree that among the learned of those centuries there seemed to prevail a kind of secret and tacit compact never to go beyond a certain boundary in science, and that the much-vaunted freedom of spirit and of thought has at all times been valid only within this boundary, while no step outside it could be ventured unpunished and unavenged. I need not designate this boundary more closely to the true connoisseur, and remark only that even the most gifted men who really did cross it, like Leibniz, nevertheless avoided the appearance of having done so. Hence that true depth of science, and the real permeation of all parts of cognition with its innermost center, was left to the unlearned and simple, whom unstilled longing and original inspiration drew toward the investigation of the indwelling and living ground of all things. These, then, because they were not learned and aroused the envy of the so-called learned, were designated by them without distinction as enthusiasts; not only those whose wild and extravagant fantasy had really given birth only to fantastic phantoms, and who were for the most part already degenerate descendants of the originally inspired, but these latter themselves as well, and indeed solely because they were non-scholars or men of simple and plain conduct. Thus the pride of the learned and of the schools has banished them and [p. 120] pronounced the ban upon them in all the marketplaces of science, driven them even out of the temples, where meanwhile the sellers and buyers bustled about and the moneychangers set up their tables.

So Mr. Fichte, too, may speak of these enthusiasts with the most comfortable scholarly pride; although it is not to be seen what he can be so conceited about toward them in general, unless it is that he can write orthographically, form periods, and has the façons of authorship in his power, whereas they, in their simplicity, revealed it as purely as they felt it. Only one who is already cleverer than they, Mr. Fichte opines, can learn anything from the reading of their writings (Gr. ibid.), and so he thinks himself a great deal cleverer than they; yet Mr. Fichte might well give all his rhetoric if he had revealed in all his books taken together the fullness of spirit and of heart that a single page of many a so-called enthusiast often makes known. When I think of the many soulful and heartfelt utterances of our Leibniz, Kepler, and many others, which according to Mr. Fichte would all have to be held for nonsense, I cannot help holding that he has shown himself the most spiritless and heartless of all philosophers who have become famous by name. Those men, and all like them, have been charged with enthusiasm, at least on account of individual utterances; and what philosopher would not be, who has so much as singly pointed to the ground and the eternal birth of things! I am not ashamed of the name of many so-called enthusiasts, but will rather confess it aloud and boast of having learned from them, as Leibniz too boasted, as soon as I can boast of it. My concepts and views have been scolded with their names, even when I myself knew only their names. This scolding I now mean to try to make true: if I have not seriously studied their writings hitherto, it has by no means happened out of contempt, but out of blameworthy negligence, which I do not intend to let myself be guilty of in future.

The old compact among the learned has expired and no longer binds us; for they themselves have broken it toward us [p. 121] by their deeds, and in every way there is a new covenant. Now neither resistance nor covering up is of any use, for the fruit that is ripe breaks forth into the day with power. In the hearts and spirits of many men there lies a mystery that wants to be spoken out; and it will be spoken out. All peculiarity, all constraint of the schools and separateness of opinions must cease, and everything flow together into one great and living work. Now what is written of them will once more be fulfilled upon the scribes: Woe to you who hold the key of knowledge; you yourselves do not enter in, and you hinder those who would enter. That which they left to simplicity to know and to fathom, this very thing must step forth, clothed with all art and in noble form, with which *they* have hitherto sought in vain to adorn their own nothingness.

This very thing is our crime, and must be, in view of the prudence of the age, that we, ourselves learned in their schools and instructed in their art, did not heed the disciplina arcana, but in all earnestness grounded ourselves on the living ground of free nature, with which all separate systems and sects must vanish. If there is anything blameworthy in this, it is solely the fault of those who were before us. We too sat at the feet of Gamaliel for a long time, and increased in knowledge after their manner. Why did they not quench the thirst of those languishing in the desert, and compel them to dig out for themselves the living spring? When we adhered to them, clarity and soberness were not denied us; our thoughts were not whims, but real thoughts, and the praise of us and of our works, though neither we nor they deserved it, was not small among the masters. Now that we have come to know better and have arrived at insight ourselves, all at once every gift we formerly had is lacking, now we are dreamers and blind enthusiasts.

Yet in this last reproach, common as it has become, Mr. Fichte has made a better choice than one might believe at first sight. By virtue of it he may bring our whole knowledge [p. 122] to himself by degrees, and yet go on belittling us and praising himself as an original; for I, he can say, have thought the whole thing myself, and with me it is science, but those others are only contemptible enthusiasts, in whom it was merely nature that thought; and it is something quite different when I pronounce it and when they pronounce it. We grant him this joy from the heart.

I have spoken of his personalities neither in my own defense nor in order to gain anything against him thereby. Upon me they could only have the effect that I might regret every word I have written against Mr. Fichte. I have known in him too truthful a sense of honor for me to explain his resolve to use such weapons otherwise than from a state of extreme constraint, which knew how to give itself air only in this way, and which may well arouse my painful regret, but neither my resentment nor my wrath. For this reason I have forbidden myself to mention it earlier, because after this mention I could not well, with honor, bring forward anything further against him.

I have never, to my knowledge, offended Mr. Fichte, and have always kept my personal relation to him pure. My sole offense against him consists in my having dared to go further in science and cognition. Nor has Mr. Fichte ever known me as he would, if it were possible, depict me to himself and to the world. I have hitherto let pass what he, likewise in a personal way, would have his hearers and readers believe about the desire to bring something new into vogue as a motive of our doing. He himself knows full well, or can at least know, how thoroughly I never deemed it robbery to set up the better in place of Him. Had I felt so great a need to appear original with respect to him, I would have taken the worst road in the world to it, and gone about it most foolishly, when in the preface to my Presentation of the System of Philosophy I wrote the words: “It is according to my conviction impossible that we (he and I) should not agree in the sequel,” and when I [p. 123] there declared in the most honest manner “that his cause is still far from its end,” and aroused the expectation of a still impending development of it, wholly unexpected by his opponents (Zeitschr. f. spec. Phys. II, 2, Preface pp. VIII, IX) . That<sup>11</sup> boldly cast-out assertion would therefore have to rest tacitly on the ground that whoever goes beyond him at all can do so merely out of a desire to be new, since he himself is the A and the O, the beginning and the end. — Even after I had convinced myself of the complete impossibility of our union and had finally had to give up all thought of it, I have nevertheless spoken against his view only so far as was necessary to elucidate my own, and more through this itself than through express words. In the year 1802 there appeared the characterization of his system in the Critical Journal of Philosophy, whose penetrating force would be evident from this alone, that Mr. Fichte has never yet, and not even now, attempted so much as to touch it from afar. I have not the slightest share in it; which I remark, not as if I could not fully subscribe to it in content, but to show how little need I had to bring my opposition to Mr. Fichte into the light. — Why does he now compel me to use harsh words against him, when I would prefer to speak only gently? Why does he himself break, in so striking a manner and one far surpassing his thinking at that time, the rule which he generously prescribed to himself and to me, or to one of us who have been formed by him, for the case of an expansion of the human view beyond the limits of the Wissenschaftslehre? “It is the rule,” he says in his publicly known letter to me, concerning *Kant’s* declaration against him — “It is the rule that, while the defenders of the pre-Kantian metaphysics have not yet ceased to tell Kant that he is occupied with fruitless subtleties, Kant says the same to us; the rule that, while those assure us against Kant that their metaphysics [p. 124] still stands undamaged, unimprovable and unalterable for eternal times, Kant assures us the same of his own against us. Who knows where the young fiery head already lives who will seek to go beyond the principles of the Wissenschaftslehre and to demonstrate its inaccuracies and incompleteness. May heaven then grant us its grace, that we do not stop at the assurance that these are fruitless subtleties, and that we would certainly not engage with them, but that one of Us, or if this should no longer be expected of ourselves, in our stead one formed in our school, stand there, who shall either prove the nullity of these discoveries, or, if he cannot do this, gratefully *accept* them in our name” (See Jen. A. L.-Z. 1799. Int. Bl. No. 122, pp. 991. 992) . Why, then, has heaven’s<sup>12</sup> grace so deserted him that he preferred to give the world the spectacle of a personal quarrel, breaking out on his side in bitterness and slander, rather than that of an honest scientific dispute? Does he think that it is *my* intention to surpass him personally? How little he knows me! So I have indeed not treated him gently in this writing: I have shown that in his polemic against my view he proceeds from a pure invention, a wholly arbitrary and fabricated concept of it, and reviles it although he does not know it; I have had to uncover the contradictions, the superficiality, and the shallowness, almost incredible even to me, of his whole present doctrine. But I also know that all this is not He himself, and I esteem his truthful essence, hidden behind the veils of his reflection, infinitely higher than all his utterances, and than himself regarded in these utterances. What I have said harshly and unkindly against him I have not said from inclination, but from principle. Not to the original Fichte, but to the Fichte who has expressed and conducted himself in the Grundzüge [p. 125] and his other recently appeared writings as he has expressed and conducted himself, to him I had to respond precisely as I have responded to him, had to do so from insight, and could not do otherwise.

<sup>11</sup> Vol. IV, p. 110. Cf. Briefwechsel Fichtes und Schellings, pp. 63, 74ff. D. H.

<sup>12</sup> Philosophischer Briefwechsel Fichtes und Schellings, p. 16. D. H.

I call upon every upright man and thinker to say whether Mr. Fichte’s sally against the philosophy of nature is not conducted from behind the opponent’s back and treacherously, so that he must still turn around, turn his face to the crowd following, and say: It is I whom he has wounded. *We* have stood against him in honest, open combat, with scientific weapons and in scientific form, in the sight of the thinking men of our nation. He — delivers his blows against us before Berlin women, cabinet councillors, merchants, and the like; scatters in the dark of a private lecture slanders against those who cannot defend themselves, until — I know not what — gives him the courage to come forward publicly against them as well.

These attacks he concludes, in the manner of all pious persecutors, with the sanctimonious exclamation: “Blessed in this the wise man, who rises above his age and above all time; who knows that time is altogether nothing, and that a higher guidance, through all apparent detours, leads our species quite surely to its true end!”

Yes indeed! I too hope for this final decision. In time, too, the day will come when sincerity of inquiry will again be prized, and the principles of honor come to honor: whatever this philosophy may be, this at least it has from the good principle, that it has never sought to assert itself by other means than the weapons of the spirit and the grounds of science — and this honesty of conduct will be laid in the scale against the imperfections of its appearance and the defects of the man in whom it expressed itself. — But what will then become of its opponents? Most of them have now for years not brought forward a single rational thought against it, but have only striven to make its name unrecognizable before all the people. A view that, in order to be grasped, demands the [p. 126] deepest stillness of the heart and composure of the spirit, they have received with passionateness and fury, or have summarily judged it as a talk of long-known things, according to their representations of the world, of God, and of nature. Yet the judgment upon it will be the smallest thing in that final decision. Long-misjudged nature itself will, filling all things, break through; all little leaflets and books will not hold it back, all systems of the world will not suffice to dam it. Then all will become united and one, in science and cognition too: as from eternity all was united and one in being, and in the life of nature.

[p. 127]

### Vorrede zu den Jahrbüchern der Medicin als Wissenschaft. — Preface to the Yearbooks of Medicine as Science.

As many as have at all times been granted not merely to greet the sanctuary of organic life from the threshold, but themselves to behold it, more or less: so many have also recognized that a higher spirit, the spirit of the All, holds sway here; just as, in a sublime temple building, the eternal seems to address the beholder more immediately, as it were. If the investigators of nature are all, each in his own way, priests and interpreters of certain natural forces, the physician, by contrast, keeps the sacred fire at the center and beholds the immediately present God in the working and living of an organic body.

The science of medicine is the crown and flower of all the natural sciences, as the organism in general, and the human organism in particular, is the crown and flower of the world. From this it is evident that it is no slight undertaking, and one that requires many forces working together in concord and harmony, if in this domain of science the perfected is to be brought about.

A particular good fortune of our times has willed that it should become possible, through this journal, to show what many centuries were unable to show, namely the philosopher and the investigator of nature of every kind, the chemist and the anatomist, the zoologist and the practitioner of healing, united in a common work, to raise the science of the organism, and through it the art of healing, to the summit it ought to occupy, and gradually to develop it further.

Honesty of cooperation, unity of purpose amid manifold [p. 132] diversity of means and the greatest mutual independence, might perhaps have let us hope for something not yet achieved, were it not that the observation of the course of things teaches us to be moderate in our expectations, and rather to promise the lesser in order to achieve the greater, than the greater in order to fall behind it.

This journal has no other purpose than the one indicated. It wishes to have nothing in common with any other undertaking and for that very reason also to be opposed to none.

Just as little is it its intention to wage a war against presumptions, false opinions, or the impure remnants of a state of anarchy in the sciences. The time is indeed past when the view from which the idea of this journal also emerged could seem to need war for its consolidation. At the moment when the great mob, giving up the attack on the cause, turns it against the person, or, for want of the spiritual arm, calls the worldly one to its aid, that cause may well be left calmly to its natural development, and philosophy, as a now pacified world, may reveal its innate formative drive more and more in enduring creations. The literary wars through which this new world, into which the best forces are now beginning to intervene in their own way, had to force its way into existence, have left behind no other trace than civil wars leave in the dregs of the people, who found in them a momentary existence and who now, dissolved, may indeed trouble the highways but cannot penetrate into the heart of the country itself.

Every cause that is good and sound only in its ground soon ceases to be the cause of an individual, even if it bore that stamp at the outset; it becomes the common possession of several spirits who sense the higher and strive toward the whole, and must at last grow into a universal intuition which, like the worthiest and best that has ever been in the world, unites spirits without fettering them, and makes them free without permitting the nullity of individual doings or the lawlessness of arbitrary choice. Yes, even the more serious philosophy, [p. 133] which, in ages of reason petrified in reflection and in opposition to them, likewise assumes strict forms, and appears armed and equipped like Minerva, lays down harness and weapons, like her, when, after the battles of mortals are ended, she hastens back to Olympus and the circle of the gods.

As it is One nature that generates and brings forth all things and rules over them omnipotently in her freedom, so there must be One fundamental intuition and view of the spirit, divinely overpowering to human beings, from which everything of a divine kind in science and art proceeds; what does not spring from this is vain, is artifact, is something human, not a work of nature. From this it can be seen how foolish it is to demand a diversity of fundamental views and, as it were, deliberately to wish to found a party in the realm of beauty and truth. The sacred bond that unites the things of nature without suppressing them is possible also among spirits, and possible to the degree to which the intuition of nature and of the universe is reborn in them. It is the bond that unites the great masters of art in a universal, boundless intuition of beauty and truth, or that often makes one and the same being equal to itself and free from itself: as the same *Plato* now describes, with indescribable sensuousness, the welling up and growing of the plumage of the soul, as it were audibly, now, a royal eagle, vanishes from the sensuous eye in the rays of the world of Ideas, now seems to play without purpose, now with the deepest art marshals the phalanx of dialectical consequences.

Let us confess that the most glorious thing in human nature is what we call originality or originalness; indeed, it is the reflection of God in it! But this originality is for that very reason wholly different from personality; it is no peculiarity of spirit that human beings could win for themselves from vain motives, but everyone who strives in this way to be free is for that very reason a slave. For only God is able to create what is peculiar in things, and it is the seal of divinity upon [p. 134] them. Thus also only the one touched by God can be truly original, but not the selfish human being who, forsaken by nature and God, can create nothing, can only put together and join together.

If a certain anxiety before science, under circumstances a not unfounded fear on the part of the better, at seeing a standard still given only in generality boldly applied to every object, then we observe, by contrast, others who, seized by the same anxiety, stubbornly pursue their one-sidednesses to a pinnacle, and, as it happens, force them even upon education and the first objects of the common weal. Such pushers and drivers, who stand with raised cudgel behind youth and the dependent part of the age, to shape them into instruments of their concepts, nevertheless accuse as oppressors those who hold sway in the realm of truth without alien or constricting purposes. But whoever conquers spirits and hearts by the power of truth may rely upon it that no one shares that feeling except bad imitators, or the mannerists, who have taken for themselves a single form of his spirit, in which they are imprisoned and weary themselves hunting after the never attainable truth, or those who would like to found in the sacred domain, in place of an unconstrained spiritual dominion, a worldly one, though in vain.

From the other side, however, it cannot be a hindrance to truth but only a furtherance that seriousness and severity, indeed even that hatred and ill will, are directed against the personality of its appearance; for what is not of nature is vain, and what belongs to the person shall not endure. That madman who, to make a name for himself, set fire to the temple of Diana at Ephesus was certainly not in a position to build one, indeed perhaps not even an ordinary dwelling house. But what are you seeking at this temple of nature, which some who are of like spirit are striving to build? Its foundation pillars and the primal form that rises from the depths of nature itself, you will neither burn nor destroy; but everything that is false ornament, superfluous addition, may purifying time take [p. 135] away, so that it may ever more worthily and more like its archetype arise!

Let us now turn to our nearest subject, and seek to bring under certain main points what might be worthy of the most special attention and discussion by the present journal!

*Possibility of a Cognition of the Absolute.* After attachment to the I and to one’s own subject had made itself known in German philosophy for a considerable time in several opposing, indeed in part glaring forms, it was bound at last to turn out that this same attachment also emerged in a more pleasing and, in a certain measure, beautiful form, as longing, devotion, feeling, faith, and was rebaptized; and since an interesting individuality has communicated itself in this manner, there has remained in a certain class of writers almost no one who has not wrestled for this crown of faith. The representation of philosophy that lay at the basis of it is clearly enough this. The Absolute is the original or archetype; philosophy as the work of the human being is the copy or the afterimage; the soul hovers between the two, in order to judge the likeness of the latter to the former, and in this gazing *in* the Absolute it necessarily behaves as one that is itself outside the Absolute. It would be incomprehensible how this simple inference could have remained hidden so long, if the first claim were correct, and the philosopher in the cognition of the Absolute really and immediately reflected upon himself in such a way that he gave himself a relation to that, and did not rather forget himself in it. Honor to this striving, if its sole intention is to make clear that the divine can never behave as something cognized, proven, intuited (in the passive sense)! Only this declaration seems to have been set forth neither early enough nor against the right target. For this very distinction of a particular sphere of cognition outside of and beside the Absolute, *into* which the Absolute could be *drawn*, [p. 136] philosophy denies altogether, and on this rests its character, as different as can be from all non-philosophy and unphilosophy. In general, then, that faith might have significance against the dogmatic representation, to which the Absolute hovers insuperably as an object; but against philosophy, whose limit it cannot determine, since it has not yet recognized its essence, it necessarily becomes meaningless. Meanwhile, of this kind of feeling holds what a witty critic recently remarked of poetic sentimentality: it is, as the expression of a beautiful soul, pleasing and good at first hand, but it is a pity that the well-known imitative tribe attaches itself most readily to that in which there lies no objective content.

*Experience and Theory.* As long as this opposition between unconscious and conscious intuiting subsists in its present confusion, so long will it be important, indeed necessary, to show wherein it has its ground, to what extent it can vanish and to what extent not. We are glad to be able to communicate, in this very first issue, a significant word on this subject from a master of science and art.<sup>13</sup>

<sup>13</sup> On the Speculative Tendency of the Experienced. By Prof. J. Ad. Schmidt in Vienna. Note of the Editor.

*Particular Relation of the Philosophy of Nature to the Art of* *Healing.* As is well known, various people have in various ways striven to transform and reshape medicine for the better by means of certain principles drawn from the philosophy of nature. Yet we must confess without exception that none of these attempts has given a thoroughly worthy proof of what the fundamental view of nature could accomplish in the doctrine of the art of healing. In times when new views open up in science, very few are seized by the principles, but *they* seize the principles, and their commerce with them is that of a *using* in the most proper sense. In this way some transcribers and copyists, in so far as they could be that, have sought to [p. 137] make an easy harvest in this field. A truly responsive spirit, by contrast, is easily fertilized under the same circumstances; only it must not be with overly general concepts and words, such as contraction and expansion, receptivity and activity, with which one can explain everything, but for that very reason also nothing. Otherwise the fertilization would resemble only the impregnation of clouds by dissolved vapors, which, to be sure, when the sluices of heaven open, act fructifyingly where they find soil with living germs, but themselves bring down none. — The spirit, when it has to some extent satisfied itself inwardly, looks indeed less outward; yet since it cannot help acting upon human beings, and at least wishing not to act harmfully or destructively, it must sooner or later seek also to make its relation to the outside clear to itself. When in the individual human being, or in the whole of a generation, the universal spirit of higher scientificity and of illumination through Ideas is joined with the liveliest and most manifold cognition of the individual and altogether particular, there arises that pleasing evenness of formation from which only what is sound, upright, and capable in every kind of knowing and acting can grow. But when, in a given scientific condition, neither the fullness of classical learning nor that of a true experience grounded in the intuition of nature holds the necessary counterweight to the drive toward the comprehensive and universal, which is perhaps stirred up by philosophy, then it is unavoidable that the whole, inclining to the one side, will sooner or later topple over, in which sad case, however, philosophy is not to blame, but the weakness or lack of that which is to stand over against it, and together with which alone it is able to present the perfected organism of formation.

With the heightening of science the demands upon empiricism also heighten, which, once awakened, cannot be driven back again. All true experience is religious: the praisers of empiricism in words but not in deeds, or, as one distinguishes sham Christians and mouth Christians from the true, [p. 138] the sham- and mouth-experienced, whom you can find in journals, at the universities, and everywhere, are as little able to silence science and its demands as to bring about an organic relation between it and experience. Whoever lacks a thorough intuition of nature, and to whom the art of healing has never appeared in connection with general investigation of nature, cannot now, when one is beginning to grasp the organism in general, and the human organism in particular, as the center of nature and the sum total of all its forces, possibly pass for a learned or truly experienced physician, but only for a flat routinier, even supposing that he had mastered the empty formalism of a theory, such as the Brownian, for example, and thereby, since he cannot take up the former into himself and under its universal, compiled together the experiences of earlier physicians.

This relation, by virtue of which either science and the spirit of thinking must gradually yield to the trade, or conversely the science of the universal and highest is developed out of proportion to the cognition of the particular and concrete, seems to be growing ever more oppressive in most schools of learning, and has expressed itself in the almost desperate proposal of one of the most scientific physicians to establish special institutions of education for medical routiniers or tradesmen, and others for learned practitioners of healing educated through science.

If in this journal, at least for the time being, a preponderance of scientific treatises over reviews and notices should be found, the reason lies in the fact that we believe we can first of all act more determinately through the communication of our own views than through the judging of others’, and moreover that criticism itself presupposes certain ideas already pronounced. In this connection we further remark that in such a thoroughly free association each one has to answer for his own view alone, and that apparently or really different ways of representing things cannot be unexpected here.

Since the presentations of the *Journal for Speculative Physics* [p. 139] were carried precisely up to the limit of the organic doctrine of nature, the present Yearbooks connect directly with it, but, in accordance with the idea underlying them of the science of the organism, which has reference to the whole doctrine of nature, just as the whole doctrine of nature has reference to it, take up, like that journal, every idea and consideration that has significance and worth in reference to general natural science.

Würzburg, in June 1805.

[p. 140]

### Aphorismen zur Einleitung in die Naturphilosophie. — Aphorisms as an Introduction to the Philosophy of Nature.

1. There is no higher revelation, whether in science or in religion or art, than that of the divinity of the All: indeed, it is from this revelation that those first begin, and they have significance only through it.

2. Wherever, even if only in passing, that revelation has occurred, there was enthusiasm, a casting off of finite forms, a cessation of all strife, concord and wondrous harmony, often separated by long ages, together with the greatest individuality of minds, and a general alliance of the arts and sciences was its fruit.

3. Where the light of that revelation vanished, and human beings wished to cognize things not from the All but out of one another, not in unity but in separation, and likewise to comprehend themselves in isolation and severance from the All: there you see science laid waste over wide expanses, with great exertion small progress in the growth of knowledge, grain of sand counted to grain of sand in order to build the universe; you see at the same time the beauty of life vanished, a wild war of opinions spread over the first and most important things, everything fallen into singularity.

4. All strife in science can by its nature have only One source, the turning away from that which, as the All-blessed, can have no strife within itself. Those who set themselves [p. 141] against the Idea of unity are fighting for nothing other than for strife itself, on which their existence depends. If all false systems, all degenerations in art, all aberrations in religion are only so many consequences of that abstraction, then the rebirth of all sciences and of all parts of culture too can begin only from the rerecognition of the All and of its eternal unity.

5. This cognition is no light that shines merely outwardly, but it stirs inwardly and moves the whole mass of human culture; there is nothing so great or so small in which it would not be at work, and as it drives and creates in the whole tree of knowledge, so also in each single branch of it.

6. But not only are the separations of the sciences from one another mere abstractions, but also that of science itself from religion and art.

7. As all elements and things of nature, as mere abstractions of the All, finally enter into the all-life of nature, whose image are the earth and the stars, each of which bears divinely within itself all forms and kinds of being: so must all elements and creations of the spirit likewise finally pass over into a common life, which is higher than the life of each of them in particular.

8. This collective life of science, religion, and art would be, in the whole of humanity, the state formed after the divine prototype. But the relation that reason has to the structure of the world, the same relation philosophy has to the perfected state, namely that it can see its own image presented and living only in such a one.

9. Science is the cognition of the laws of the whole, thus of the universal. Religion, however, is contemplation of the particular in its bondage to the All. *It* consecrates the investigator of nature as priest of nature through the devotion with which he tends the single thing. It assigns to the drive toward the universal the limits set for it by God, and so mediates, as a holy bond, science with art, which is the forming-into-one of the universal and the particular.

[p. 142] 10. As in the state legislation is nothing without the heroism of upholding it and the religion of observing it in particulars, and as only the union of the universal of the former with the particularity of all and each, through the spirit that animates and governs the whole not mechanically but artfully, gives birth to the perfect beauty of public life: so philosophy attains the divinity befitting its Idea only in the actual interpenetration of science with religion and art.

11. Not only is the eye never satisfied with seeing, and the ear never satisfied with hearing: reason too is never satisfied with contemplation. This can be objected to science in its severance, that no one can think out or talk out to the end the thought of the All. As legislation pressing for closure, it necessarily has another side, from which it is open and unbounded, and the recognition of which is the religion in it.

12. Religion, on the other hand, loses itself in devotion to the particular, without return to the absolutely universal, the All, necessarily in superstition, and I ask every unprejudiced person whether he could describe otherwise the representations that an often pious zeal, without knowledge of the laws of the All, has made for itself of the individual things and appearances of nature.

13. To see the finite only as dissolved in the infinite is the spirit of science in its severance; to behold the infinite in the whole comprehensibility of the finite, in the latter, is the spirit of art.

14. To present, with the seriousness of science, those laws in which, in the expression of an ancient, the immortal God lives, but with equal love to embrace the particular, even the most singular, in order to present the All in it, and thus to form the universal and the particular into one in an infinite manner: this is the spirit of true philosophy.

15. In whatever form this enthusiasm may otherwise reveal itself, whether in the lyrical outpouring of a harmonious individuality that lets the accord of the universe resound within [p. 143] itself, or, with epic expansiveness and fullness, composing the history of the universe, or finally in strictly plastic delimitation, be it in the still austere style that the system gives birth to in science as in art, or in that moderated by grace of an art already grown freer, or in the last perfection with dramatic life, in sublime assurance over the matter, where the deepest seriousness and the freest play, mutually transfiguring one another, mutually exalt one another: this is, with respect to the infinity of the material (provided only that it be drawn from totality) and to philosophy itself, a matter of indifference, and designates only different stages of the culture and maturity of art.

16. But just as, according to Winkelmann’s words, the still austere and severe style of the oldest plastic art had to precede the products, made beautiful by grace, of later art, and as only those states have the disposition to become great that begin from strict legislation: so the seriousness and severity of scientific culture must have overcome the ignorance of minds before the sweeter fruits of philosophy can ripen. The Platonic saying, that no one uninitiated in geometry should enter, holds in a far more general meaning.

17. Not formlessness is the true infinite, but that which is bounded in itself, closed off *from itself* and perfected. This inner perfection of the infinite, which is imprinted in the greatest as in the smallest, gives in the particular a type of contemplation and in the whole a Systema of cognitions.

18. But not only the whole as whole is divine. The part and the particular is so too, for itself. Even if the scientific form were merely the band around the full sheaf, and I held out to you only the single ear, as a growth of divine kind, you would have to thank me. How much more, since it is an inner organic connection, in which each part is of the nature of the whole, and lives in itself as it lives in the latter.

19. What do I boast of? — Of the One thing that was given me, that I have proclaimed the divinity even of the particular, [p. 144] the possible equality of all cognition without distinction of object, and with it the infinity of philosophy.

20. In brief propositions, with traits as simple as seemed possible to me at that time, I first presented, in the year 1801, the doctrine of nature and of the All in a new way . I have<sup>14</sup> found cause to improve or alter my view on much in the part where the consideration enters into the particular, and in general to broaden it. The general grounds, however, as they are set forth there , have proved themselves to me mar-<sup>15</sup> velously in every subsequent investigation, even in that which had sprung more from divination than from conscious cognition: the fury of the raging crowd, which regarded this doctrine of the All as an apple of discord thrown among them, has, to the best of my insight, not made even One of those propositions merely doubtful, still less been able to cancel One; and my sole intention is to go on maintaining the whole and the universal, as it was pronounced there, and to set it in every possible light.

<sup>14</sup> *Zeitschrift für speculative Physik* (Jena and Leipzig) vol. 2, no. 2. [vol. 4, p. 105 ff.].

<sup>15</sup> §§ 1–50 of the presentation contained in the cited work.

21. I hereby give thanks for all the improvements in matter and form, well or ill meant, that have become known to me up to now and that have been intended for that presentation.

22. First of all, whether religion is higher than philosophy, and whether what is in the latter can be raised higher by the former, may be judged from what precedes and follows. Religion, to be sure, is not philosophy; but the philosophy that did not unite religion with science in holy harmony would not be the latter either. The religion of the philosopher, however, has the color of nature; it is the vigorous religion of one who with bold courage descends into the depths of nature, not the hermit-like religion of idle self-contemplation, which can in no way be brought into connection with this philosophy grounded wholly on the totality of nature.

[p. 145] 23. Philosophy too is poetry, but let it not be a forward poetry sounding only out of the subject, but an inward one, implanted in the object, like the music of the spheres. Let the thing be poetic first, before the word is.

24. Most of all I decline the rhetorical additions with which some have sought to improve this simple doctrine. In many writings of such authors the well-known plant has tasted to me no otherwise than as a wine that has turned sour with them, which they, like bad innkeepers, seek to help along with honey or sugar.

25. I do indeed recognize something higher than science, and what you say of it, you say not of yourselves; but has one therefore reached the higher because one bungles in science? As surely as someone is an excellent poet because he writes bad prose.

26. Those who most condemn their consciousness of being pupils cry loudest against the compulsion of the school, and place-hunting applicants of every kind plant themselves in the philosophy of nature no otherwise than the arrogant revelers in the house of Odysseus: no wonder if in the end even impudent beggars, poorer in spirit than Irus in possessions, challenge to a fistfight the man from whose table they are still eating the scraps.

27. How narrowly, however, have even some of the better ones regarded this matter, who do not see that it is no matter of this age alone, and that I have done nothing but supply the element for an endlessly possible culture. Never will philosophy, unless the whole age should change, be able again to exclude from itself the eternal relation to nature and, with the one-sided abstractum of the intelligent world, to want to embrace the whole.

28. Whether I want a school? — Yes, but as there were schools of poets. Thus may those jointly inspired go on composing in the same sense in this eternal poem. Give me a few of the kind I have found, and see to it that the future too does not lack the inspired, and I promise you that one day I shall [p. 146] yet give you the Ὅμηρος (the uniting principle) for science as well. For this there is need of no pupils, nor of any head or master. No one teaches the other, or is obligated to the other, but each to the God who speaks out of all.

29. For a long time I have set iron and bow before opponents and others, to see whether they can shoot through: what follows will show whether they have been able to bend the bow.

30. In keeping with the particular purpose of the present journal, I have wished to send ahead those principles that are necessary for following the philosophy of nature in particular, not doctrinally, or so that I always carried out the proofs in the strict manner, but rather historically, as testimony to the matter; and it seemed most appropriate to treat of them in the following order.

#### a) Von der Ein- und Allheit. — a) On Unity and Totality.

31. Reason cannot be described to anyone: it must describe itself in each and through each.

32. The senses are divine in that they apprehend the particular, to be sure, but each thing for itself, as if nothing were outside it, like a world of its own. They behold, unconscious of themselves, a present infinity, they behold therefore in each the totality, but without redissolution into unity. — Hence the unfathomability in everything sensible, the chaos, the confused fullness. The senses are to be equated with religion.

33. The understanding, on the other hand, cognizes the empty unity without fulfillment or totality; clarity without depth is its essence. Forming general concepts, it compares things and cancels the divinity of all and of each in particular, in that it comprehends it only in the reflection of others, not in itself. It is at once the positing of all distinguishability and multiplicity of things, and insofar as it apprehends the universal at the expense of infinity in the particular, comparable to science in its severance.

34. Clarity with depth, uniting the fullness of the senses with the comprehensibility of the understanding, is the imagination: [p. 147] this is itself only the senses conscious of their infinity, or the understanding that at the same time intuits.

35. Reason, however, bears within itself senses, understanding, and imagination as so many finitudes, without itself being any one of them in particular. It cognizes neither merely the confused infinite (without unity), like the senses, nor the empty unity (without infinity), like the understanding, but unity and infinity, clarity and fullness are themselves one in it, and not merely in a particular manner, as for the imagination, but absolutely and in an infinite manner.

36. Reason can affirm nothing that would have reality only in relation or comparison (for thereby it would become like the understanding and posit only finitudes): it can therefore, first, affirm no differences, of whatever kind they may be, then it can also cognize or posit nothing that would be only through another, but only that which is absolutely and in every respect out of and from itself, or which is the infinite *position of itself*. This is the Idea of absoluteness.

37. Reason may therefore be filled only with that which [not only in the particular, but which is absolutely and thoroughly universal, thus] is in everything and each thing the self-same in an infinite manner, the self-affirming, and which therefore, *as* the self-same, or *as* unity, is immediately also infinity or totality. [This only God. For He is affirmation of Himself, that is, the indissoluble identity of the predicating and the predicated. Since only this is the subsistence and the essence of all things, so God is the position of all things, the self-same in all things].

38. The affirmation of infinite unity and totality is not accidental to reason, but its whole essence itself, which is also expressed in the law of which it is conceded that it alone contains unconditioned affirmation within itself, the law of identity (A=A).

39. You regarded this law as a merely formal and subjective one, and could recognize in it only the empty repetition of [p. 148] your own thinking. But it has no relation to your thinking, rather it is a universal, an infinite law, which states of the universe that in it there is nothing as merely predicating or as merely predicated, but that eternally and in everything there is only One, which affirms itself and is affirmed by itself, manifests itself and is manifested by itself, in a single word, that nothing is truly that is not (36) absolute, not divine.

40. Consider that law in itself, recognize the content it has, and you will behold God.

41. The infinite clarity in inconceivable fullness and the inconceivable fullness in infinite clarity is God — infinite affirmation and equally infinite being-affirmed of himself, in an absolutely simple, indivisible manner.

#### b) Von der Vernunft als Erkenntniß des Absoluten. — b) On Reason as Cognition of the Absolute.

42. Not we, not you or I, know of God. For reason, insofar as it affirms God, can affirm *nothing other*, and at the same time annihilates itself as a particularity, as something *outside God*.

43. There is truly and in itself nowhere any subject and any I, and for that very reason also no object and no not-I, but only One, God or the All, and besides that nothing. If, then, there is anywhere a knowing and a being-known, what is in the former and what is in the latter is nevertheless only the One as One, namely God.

44. The *I think, I am* is, since Cartesius, the fundamental error in all cognition; thinking is not my thinking, and being not my being, for everything is only God’s or the All’s.

45. The One kind of cognizing, in which not the subject but the absolutely universal (thus the One) knows (43), and in which for that very reason also only the absolutely universal is what is known (39), is reason.

46. Reason is no faculty, no instrument, and cannot be [p. 149] used: in general there is not a reason that we have, but only a reason that has us. To seek out in oneself the faculties for the cognition of God, and to count or weigh them, is the utmost limit of confusion and of the inner darkening of the spirit.

47. Reason too is not an affirmation of the One that would itself be outside the One, but a knowing of God that is itself in God. If nothing is outside God, then the cognition of God too is only the infinite cognition that God has of himself in eternal self-affirmation (36), that is, it is itself the being of God and in this being.

48. Reason does not *have* the Idea of God, but it *is* this Idea, nothing besides. Light does not have the Idea of bodies, but it is this Idea. As one cannot ask of light whence its clarity comes, since it is precisely clarity itself, so one cannot ask of reason whence the Idea of God comes to it, since it is precisely itself this Idea. Further, as little as one can describe light any further, or communicate the idea of it again, so little can one describe or communicate the cognition of God any further, for it is, even in expressing itself in the subject, nothing subjective, but proceeds from the annihilation of all subjectivity. As each can only intuit and contemplate light as a true objectivity and as shining in nature, so must he acknowledge the Idea of God as shining in itself in reason and in those who speak of it not from the power of selfhood but from the power of God; for without divine enthusiasm no one is able to cognize God or to speak of God.

49. This Idea is no object of contention or discord; all particularity, from which alone strife comes, perishes in it. The senseless man who denies it pronounces it without knowing it; he is unable to connect two concepts in accordance with reason except in this Idea.

50. God is not the highest, but he is the absolutely One; [p. 150] he is not to be regarded as summit or end, but as center, not in opposition to a periphery, but as all in all. Even the highest is this only in relation to something lower; but God is the absolutely relationless, affirmable solely from himself and through himself.

51. There is therefore no ascent of cognition to God, but only immediate cognizing, yet also none immediate that would be man’s, but only that of the divine through the divine.

52. In no kind of cognition can God relate himself as *known* [as object]: as known he ceases to *be* God. [We are never outside God, so that we could set him before us as object]. Rather, as the *feeling* of heaviness is itself the *being* in gravity, so the cognition of God is itself the being in God. It is neither a subjective nor an objective, because it is not a different thing that cognizes and that is cognized, but only one and the same (51), God.

53. Intrinsically objectionable likewise is every kind of contemplation in which the *subject* subsists as subject. You speak of a presentiment of the divine, of a faith that you place higher than cognition. But the divine does not have presentiments of the divine, for it is itself the divine; nor is there any faith in God as a quality of the subject. You wished, then, only to rescue the latter, but by no means to transfigure the divine.

54. As there is a boundness of the will that compels man not in a human, physical, or psychological, but in a divine manner, to act as is right [as there is an acting in which the individual forgets himself]: so there is a divine boundness of cognition, which does not originate from man himself, and in which the cognizing as such, just as there the acting, but with it also necessarily the cognized, as cognized, vanishes.<sup>16</sup>

<sup>16</sup> These propositions show the worth of the most notable, but without doubt also the last attempt thus far to transform the cognition of the Absolute into a subjectivity. Unexpected, to be sure, it could not be to the author, who predicted it in the *Vorlesungen über die Methode des akademischen* *Studiums* p. 149 [vol. 5, p. 278] so definitely that he could not now write more definitely about it. This age demands a knowing as knowing of the subject, an ethical life as a self-given one of the individual. In such a sense I do indeed exclude this as well as that from the system of reason, and indeed exclude it in an entirely positive manner, and I rejoice that people have begun to recognize this.

[p. 151]

#### c) Von der Untheilbarkeit der Vernunfterkenntniß oder der Unmöglichkeit etwas von der Idee des Absoluten zu abstrahiren oder aus ihr herzuleiten. — c) On the Indivisibility of Rational Cognition, or the Impossibility of Abstracting Anything from the Idea of the Absolute or Deriving It from It.

55. Scarcely has the Idea of God been born from the fullness of reason when the understanding steps up in order to have a share in this good. It would like to consider separately what is posited in that Idea as eternally and absolutely one, and to give reality outside unity also to that which has reality only *in* *unity*. Every such abstraction declares its nullity immediately through the contradiction that it has as its necessary companion.

56. You believed that, with these contradictions into which the Idea dissolves as soon as its indivisible unity is canceled, you were contending against reason and against the Idea itself, while in truth you were only revealing its inner essence. Precisely thereby it was and is made manifest that the understanding can affirm none of the possible opposites for itself without contradiction, that to each such another like it is opposed with equal right, and that only the indivisible unity of the Idea in its indivisibility has truth.

57. Of the rational Idea of God, that he is the infinite affirmation of himself, the understanding would first of all separate the affirmative and the affirmed and grasp God as the one or the other for itself. But of each of the two members into which the Idea seems resolvable, the contradictory can be shown, precisely *through* the Idea itself.

58. The Idea that God is the infinite affirmation of himself, [p. 152] seems resolvable into the two consequences: God affirms himself infinitely, and: God is affirmed by himself. If you consider the first for itself, it is impossible that God affirms himself, for the affirmative (the concept) is always greater than the affirmed (the thing). But God as affirming himself is absolutely equal [with] God as the one affirmed by himself [only one and the same]. God does not grasp himself, because he cannot be greater than he himself is. Accordingly the proposition: God affirms himself, taken for itself, is by virtue of the Idea itself an impossible one. The same holds of its opposite. God can just as little be the affirmed of himself; he is inconceivable to himself and is not grasped, because he cannot be smaller than he himself is, because he is not a different thing, but only one and the same.

59. In the same way every possible affirmation of reason, whatever its expression may be, can be dissolved into contradiction if you pick out the single member of the identity expressed in it, namely in such a way that what has been abstracted can be posited neither nor yet not posited. For example, by virtue of the Idea of the Absolute, that it is that whose essence is also being, no *being* can be ascribed to God; for being as such exists only in opposition to essence, whereas in God it is absolutely one with it. Nevertheless the being of God also cannot be negated, on the same ground, and precisely because in him it is the same as essence.

60. Of the proposition “God is unity and totality,” the unity cannot be posited for itself. God is not the absolutely One; for the One exists only in opposition to the many, but in relation to the absolutely One there is no many. Thus this Idea cancels itself, and God is also not One. Yet he is also not not-One and many.

61. All cognizing is nothing other than an affirming. Science has always sought the point where being includes cognizing and cognizing includes being. But how could they be more perfectly one than in the Idea of the universal substance, of God, whose being is the infinite affirmation of [p. 153] itself, whose being therefore includes cognition within itself, and indeed in an infinite manner, and conversely cognition includes being. But precisely for this reason it is impossible to ascribe to God a being or a cognizing in particular. For the self-affirmation of God is an infinite one, the cognizing and the cognized are therefore *one and the same* in him , and<sup>17</sup> to that extent there is no cognizing in God. Nevertheless God is also not the negation of all cognizing, a wholly blind Absolute, mere being. For being as such exists only in opposition to cognizing, but the being of God is the infinite affirmation of itself, and so not the negation of cognizing.

<sup>17</sup> Correction in the author’s own copy: For in the self-affirmation of God the cognizing and the cognized are one and the same. Remark of the editor.

62. The same can be shown, in a more general sense, of the opposition between being and acting. In God there is neither an acting nor yet a negation of acting. Not an acting, for the infinite self-affirmation of God flows together with the being of God, and is itself this being (61); yet the acting in God is also not negated, because in being he is the infinite affirmation of himself. Thus the circumference of the circle can be regarded as a being, but as being it includes an acting within itself, namely the absolute self-cognizing of unity as totality.

63. This brief consideration (55—63) suffices to prove that the Idea of the Absolute resists every abstraction, that it is absolutely indivisible, and that it is therefore impossible to develop anything out of it by analysis or abstraction.

64. The proposition that the Absolute has no predicates,<sup>18</sup> is correct only insofar as the predicate itself is possible only in [p. 154] opposition to the subject (an opposition that is unthinkable in God), and insofar as to every possible predicate another can also be opposed. But nothing that stands in relation, nothing therefore that can stand in opposition, is affirmable by reason (36) and of God.

<sup>18</sup> The author of the well-known *Aphorisms* on the Absolute, which are supposed to be a parody of so-called most recent philosophy but were faithfully transcribed by its opponents, has also taken up this proposition. Yet, particularly in this respect too, an excellent essay *On the Relation of* *Skepticism to Philosophy and Its Various Modifications* etc. would be worth recommending to him for careful reading. It is found in the Kritisches Journal der Philosophie. Vol. 1, no. 2.

65. The Absolute can therefore be expressed eternally only as the absolute, absolutely indivisible identity of the subjective and the objective, an expression that is equal to that of the infinite self-affirmation of God (36) and signifies the same.

66. In this Idea reason posits neither the negation of oppositions, nor does it posit oppositions as actual in it. Not the negation, for then unity itself would be a merely negating and to that extent conditioned one. But the oppositions are annihilated in that Idea not in a negative but in a positive manner; it is not their difference that is negated, but their absolute identity that is posited. But just as little does the opposite hold, that the oppositions would be posited as actual in that Idea. They *are* not, for their positive identity is posited, and they are also not not, for it is not their negation that is posited.

67. Absolute identity of the subjective and the objective cannot be a mere equilibrium , or synthesis, but only com-<sup>19</sup> plete being-one.

<sup>19</sup> An equilibrium of opposites is the highest one can reach with relations: hence this misunderstanding of the Idea by those who comprehend nothing but relations. Most of them have nonetheless contested this product of their own failure to understand. But what is one to think of those who want to contest not against it, but — with it — against me?

68. We shall try to make this distinction, which is in itself indeed very clear but to most people nevertheless not clear, plain through a few examples. The fulcrum of a lever represents the equilibrium of two opposed forces; it is what unites the two, but it is by no means their absolute identity. It is what it is, namely fulcrum, only relative to the two opposed [p. 155] forces, not in itself; these reduce each other to zero in it, but not it itself, as itself; it is the *positive* zero of both.

69. Examples of the absolute being-one of opposites are necessarily offered by the whole of nature, and offered in abundance by all the sciences. Whoever tried to comprehend matter even in the simplest manner from contraction and expansion would never arrive at a real matter, so long as he assumed those two to be opposed like the forces of a lever, unless he thought matter as thoroughly and *at every point* both expansive and attractive in an indivisible manner.

70. Or let one think of an organ of sense, an organ of sight, for example: such an organ is, at every point of its essence, a being and a seeing and yet only One. Seeing and being do not relate to each other like factors that would reduce themselves to zero, and yet the organ is also not mere being, abstracted from seeing (otherwise it would be only matter), nor mere seeing, abstracted from being (otherwise it would not be an organ); rather it is wholly being and wholly seeing. It is *in* being also a seeing and *in* seeing a being.

71. The Idea of the circle is an absolutely simple and indivisible Idea. — Although center and circumference lie spatially (in the concrete circle) outside one another, they are nevertheless one in the Idea of the circle. One cannot abstract from the circle; for the center by itself, without the circumference, is also not center; the circumference by itself, abstracted from the center and thus from the whole circle, is also not circumference. Truly, then, in the Idea of the circle neither the center by itself nor the periphery by itself is posited, but in each of them necessarily already the circle, that is, the absolute unity. The center is the circle intuited in its affirmativity, or the ideal circle; for what is the point at all but a circular line of infinitely small diameter, or a circle whose periphery coincides with the center? The periphery, on the other hand, is only the circle intuited in its being-affirmed, or [p. 156] in totality. Unity here, as such, is equal to totality, the center as such equal to the periphery (for since the size of the periphery is a matter of indifference, it is = the point). The being-one of the two is not that of two parts that first together make up a whole; the two are not factors of the circle, nor is the latter the product or the synthesis of the two: it is their *absolute identity*.

72. The whole of nature contends against every abstraction, for example that of matter as a pure being from which all subjective, inner life, all perception is negated. Even if in the lower spheres of nature the perceptions are darker and less distinct, they are still unmistakable in the animals, which for that reason we nevertheless regard as mere material beings. How, then, does perception come to matter here, if the latter is not already in itself and *as being* also perceptive? The acting of animals is a wholly blind one. We do not think of them themselves as acting, but of something else, an objective ground, as acting in them; nevertheless we recognize with irrefutable certainty, which the purposiveness of those actions, especially of the instincts of art, forces upon us, that this principle, merely objective relative to the animals, *in itself* considered, is also a subjective one, one similar to the conscious in unconsciousness, without our positing any dualism thereby. The most obstinate habituation to seeing mere objectivity in nature could long since have been overcome by the phenomena of extraordinary states of man, in which, even by the common conception, the soul has no part, for example the skillful and sure actions of the sleepwalker, which take place wholly so unconsciously and yet not seldom betray as much purposiveness as the actions of animals, of the constant somnambulists.

73. The meaning is therefore by no means that the absolute identity of the subjective and the objective is only the particular essence of God (for the essence of God is not anything particular), but that it is the essence of all things, the absolutely universal, and that nothing may be affirmed or may be [p. 157] which is not equally affirmative and equally affirmed without any dualism. For just as little as it is a real opposition when one and the same essence bears two different names, A and B, and just as little as the essence A and the essence B are in this case two different essences, being rather only One essence, so everything affirmable through reason is only One essence, and as the One thoroughly affirmative and thoroughly affirmed, *wholly ideal and wholly real*.

74. But that this absolute identity of the subjective and the objective is the same in all things, the ground of this lies only in God, who is *the infinite affirmation of himself*, and through whom, as universal substance, all substance is likewise in itself unity of the affirmative and the affirmed.

75. Just as little, then, as abstraction (55—74) is able to do anything against the Idea of God, to bend it or to take something particular out of it and posit it for itself, so impossible is it to derive anything from this Idea by way of coming-to-be or of issuing forth from it.

76. Everything is without origin, *eternal* in God. For what can be by virtue of his Idea *is necessary* and *is eternal*, and what cannot be in this manner is altogether incapable of being. Nothing can therefore truly come to be in God or out of God.

77. God inclines to nothing, neither in him nor outside him, for he is all-blessed; he effects nothing, for he *is* everything. The infinite affirmation of himself is no action to which God would relate as subject; rather it is itself the being of God. God does not *become* through affirming or cognizing himself, but he *is* an infinite self-cognizing *in* the infinite being, not outside it and in a separate action.

78. As simple as this Idea of the infinite self-affirmation of the infinite being-from-and-out-of-itself is in itself, so difficult is it for the understanding, which has its essence only in oppositions. To the understanding it is either a self-division of God, so that he, for example, posited one part of himself objectively (as world) and kept the other for himself, that [p. 158] is, that he posited himself as negated in the subject and in the object, which conflicts with the first Idea of God, to be the infinite position of himself; or a self-differentiation, since, if there were an acting in God at all, it would on the contrary have to be God’s self-identification. It is not, because God does not identify himself but is the absolute identity.

79. Of the same worth, that is, wholly contradictory, is the representation of a going-out of the Absolute from itself. Could God go out from himself, he would for that very reason not be God, not absolute. Absoluteness, or the infinite self-affirmation, is rather the eternal going-back, not as action, but as the eternal *being* and subsisting of God in himself.

80. This consideration (75—79), like the earlier one (55— 74), shows that the understanding can have no part in the Idea of the Absolute, and if only these two ways to cognition are open to science, that of analysis or abstraction and that of synthetic derivation (as is indeed the case according to the prevailing conception), then we *deny* all science of the Absolute. Nothing can be separated off from God, for precisely because nothing can be abstracted from him is he absolute; nothing can be derived from God as becoming or coming-to-be, for precisely because he is everything is he God. — *Speculation* is everything, that is, beholding, contemplating what is in God. Science itself has worth only insofar as it is speculative, that is, contemplation of God as he is.<sup>20</sup>

<sup>20</sup> Compare with this the treatise on the manner of presenting all things in the Absolute in the *Neue Zeitschrift* für speculative Physik, no. II, § IV. [vol. IV, p. 391].

The explanations so far contain the mere *beginnings* of philosophy, about which to dispute with anyone is utterly pointless. To those who, according to their many utterances, simply cannot form any other representation of the Absolute than that of a *thing*, and indeed of a thing to which the identity of the subjective and the objective inheres as a property, to want [p. 159] to give further explanations would likewise be utterly useless. — Of all explications of the simplest Idea, moreover, what Leibniz says somewhere holds true: “On a dit, que si l’esprit avoit une vue claire et directe de l’Infini, le P. Malebranche n’auroit pas eu besoin de tant de raisonnements pour nous y faire penser. Mais par le même argument on rejetteroit la connoissance très-simple et très-naturelle, que nous avons de la Divinité. Ces sortes d’objections ne valent rien, car on a besoin de travail et d’application pour donner aux hommes l’attention nécessaire aux notions les plus simples, et on n’en vient guères à bout qu’en les rappelant de leur dissipation à eux-mêmes. C’est aussi pour cela, que les théologiens, qui ont parlé de l’éternité, ont eu besoin de beaucoup de discours, de comparaisons et d’exemples pour la bien faire connoître, quoiqu’il n’y ait rien de plus simple que la notion de l’éternité etc. etc.”

#### d) Von der Art, wie die Einheit Allheit und die Allheit Einheit ist, und von dem ewigen Nichtseyn des Endlichen. — d) On the Manner in Which Unity Is Totality and Totality Unity, and on the Eternal Non-Being of the Finite.

81. All true contemplation, even of the individual, is intuition of actual infinity.

82. In what precedes we have considered the Idea of God in its simplicity, insofar as it is absolute identity of the subjective and the objective in general.
