CCIX. Gravity is the positing of time only because it (CVI) posits the positive of all time in the individual. So, on the contrary, the essence of light must posit space in things, but not *as* space, but the positive of all space (CCV), which is above all space, and contains it in itself as the universe does, without being in it.

CCX. Nature is a gradual (CCI) positing of the positive of time in the individual; for that very reason it itself appears, as a whole, to be enclosed rather under the form of space. Only with the completed in-formation of the in-itself of time into the individual does the dominion of time begin (in history).

CCXI. The soul (CXCV) is in the individual the positive of time, just as the infinite and omnipresent thinking is in the whole (CCVIII). Hence in the soul there is the time-penetrating power, the presentiment of the future even in animals; the [p. 238] constant revival of its unity out of time, and the consciousness positing all of it again in itself as eternity.

CCXII. At the basis of time, or rather of the observation of time, lies only the inverted opposition of that which lies at the basis of space (CII, cf. CVIII). Both must therefore contain the same elements in themselves.

CCXIII. Time, in complete opposition to space, would be the affirming in complete separation from the affirmed; but since this is unthinkable, complete opposition to space is impossible in time itself too, and it itself must comprehend space, as space (CXIV) comprehends time.

CCXIV. What is properly temporal in time is the *future*. For the future is that whereby the affirming is connected with its affirmed, possibility with its actuality; the concept of it therefore rests most upon the opposition of these two.

CCXV. But since the future as *future* is merely *thinkable* and the manifest product of mere imagination, the only real in the temporal of time (CCXIV) is just the *bond* of the affirming with the affirmed, that is, the non-temporal .<sup>40</sup>

<sup>40</sup> Just as the real in the first dimension of space is not the spatial itself, but that in which space is negated, and insofar as it is negated in it — mass (CXVII).

CCXVI. As the inner unity of things can reflect itself in space only as the negation of it and thereby of all being and *subsistence*, as the constant passing away of things: so the *eternity* of things can reflect itself in time only as the negation of time and thereby of all *becoming* — as *past*, in which all time is extinguished.

CCXVII. The past is time posited as *space*, or the spatial in time, and as the future is only the (one-sided) synthesis of the affirming with the affirmed: so the past is only the (one-sided) synthesis of the affirmed with its affirming — abstract or lifeless eternity.

CCXVIII. True eternity, however, is not the eternity in opposition to time, but the eternity that comprehends time itself and posits it in itself as eternity (CLXIX) — not being in opposition to becoming, but being in eternal unity with eternal [p. 239] becoming.

CCXIX. What is truly living in time can for that very reason emerge only in the present, as the unity of past and future, being and becoming, just as the properly real in space is only the third dimension as the synthesis of the first two (CXVII).

CCXX. No differently than the future, the past too, as the past, is merely *thinkable* and solely a product of imagination. In the real, as such, there is as little past as future; but in the present too there is not the temporal, but the living bond of being and becoming, that is, the non-temporal (CCXVIII), the only real.

CCXXI. Time in general, therefore, has, as *time*, reality only in abstracting thought, that is, in thought that abstracts from the real.

CCXXII. Every thing is, in opposition to time, actu eternal, as it is, in opposition to space, actu infinite (CXXVII).

CCXXIII. The temporal is related to the eternal no differently than the affirmed is related to the affirmation . Just as<sup>41</sup> [p. 240] now the affirmation cannot be without the affirmed, and both are not in a transitory or accidental, but in an eternal and necessary manner at once: so the temporal is at once with the eternal in an eternal manner, and yet itself eternal.

<sup>41</sup> To prevent a possible confusion, let the following reminder be given here. — The absolute in every respect, we have maintained, is the eternal unity of the predicating and the predicated, grasped *as unity*. We cannot ask: how does the affirmed arise? or: whence does it come? for it is equally eternal with the affirming, just as, conversely, the latter could not be, as such, without the affirmed. Being itself, or the properly eternal, is therefore only the absolute necessity that the affirming be at once and inseparably linked with an affirmed, the infinite with a finite, as prototype with counter-image. Through this necessity, and in and with it, both *are* for the first time; but it itself is exalted equally above both, as their bond or essence. — We can now, however (and this is the point that matters here), consider that unity of the affirming and the affirmed either formally or really. Formally: in that the affirming = A is posited as one with the affirmed = B; whereby, however, it is evident of itself that neither A as A nor B as B can ever emerge on its own, since only the unity of both is the real. In other words: A as A and B as B are themselves only formal or ideal factors. — The real B is itself A posited in B; the real A itself B posited in A. — A is posited in B means: the unity of A and B is itself posited as affirmed. B is in A means: the unity of both is itself posited as affirming. As eternal as the living bond of A and B, just as eternal, and at once with it, is also that which is bound together out of A and B. The real affirmed is thus the bound-together of A and B; the real affirming is the bond of both or the affirmation itself; and this is the sense of these words in the above proposition. — Everything that holds of the relation of the affirming and the affirmed in the formal sense holds also of the relation of both in the real sense; one can be substituted immediately for the other, as one dissolves immediately into the other. — Whoever wishes to combine with the above propositions the explanations contained in the *Statement of* *the True Relation between the Philosophy of Nature and the Fichtean Doctrine*, and further in the treatise added to the new edition of the writing *On the* *World Soul*, will find that nothing obscure can well remain here.

CCXXIV. As the real in the affirmed is itself only the affirming: so the positive in the temporal is itself only the non-temporal, namely the eternal.

CCXXV. The eternal and temporal life of each thing is only one and the same life; and there is no numerically *other* life apart from the temporal. Rather, the same life that is eternal according to position is, in the affirmed, the temporal, and conversely.

CCXXVI. Only to the All is it essential to be, and only through the All to things (159). Things *are* therefore only in totality; and this is the natura prius of them; or: totality must always already exist whole and *complete*, in order that the individual may be possible and actual.

CCXXVII. But if the individual is posited abstracted from [p. 241] this totality, a necessary contradiction arises. For since it is not to precede it, according to the Idea, by virtue of abstraction, and yet the individual can be only in it, this must be taken up into the totality and also not taken up at the same time. Imagination can resolve this contradiction only through the mediation of an infinite series, that is, not at all. The abstracted is synthesized with another abstracted, this again with another, which needs the same linkage, and so on (after the indivisible unity of position has once been canceled) to infinity.

CCXXVIII. Reason, however, posits the unmediated and incomprehensible totality with a single stroke, and only *after* it and *in* it the individual things.

CCXXIX. In this totality the existence of each thing too is an absolutely unconditioned and thoroughly indivisible existence (position); eternal, irrespective of all time.

CCXXX. In abstraction from totality, however, the *essence* does not immediately include also *being* in itself (CCXXVI); the thing (since it is now necessary in the totality) appears as one that could be and also not be, that is, as a contingent one; further, as one whose existence can be determined as greater or as smaller.

CCXXXI. This abstract existence, which, irrespective of the concept, can be determined as greater or smaller, is called *duration*.

CCXXXII. But if the positive of duration were not itself eternity, that is, indivisible position of infinity, not even a time could elapse ; just as that loose linkage of things in time,<sup>42</sup> which abstraction alone sees, would itself be impossible without the constant actual presence of the whole.

<sup>42</sup> Ubi quis durationem abstracte conceperit, nunquam poterit intelligere, qua ratione hora ex. gr. transire possit. Nam ut horat transeat, necesse erit, ejus dimidium prius transire et postea dimidium reliqui et deinde dimidium, quod hujus reliqui superest, et, si sic porro infinite dimidium a reliquo subtrahas, nunquam ad finem horae pervenire poteris. Spinoza in Opp. posth. p. 468.

[p. 242] CCXXXIII. The concept of duration is different from that of eternity toto genere, and things are eternal irrespective of duration. Their life is short, but eternity is much shorter still; for it is in the moment the whole (LXXXIII); as substance too is in the point the whole and infinite (CLIV).

CCXXXIV. Even infinite duration, were it thinkable, could not create eternity; for that very reason even the smallest duration cannot annihilate eternity.

CCXXXV. Through the application of time to the universe an irresolvable conflict arises. For time rests on the opposition of the affirming to the affirmed (CVIII); in the universe, however, the affirmed is absolutely equal and adequate to the affirming; it is neither exceeded nor overflowed by it; the same that is as identity is also as totality.

CCXXXVI. You want the universe as totality; but this is possible in time only if the universe is infinite in respect of time; but now unity is lost. You want it as unity; but this is possible in time only if it is finite in respect of time. You now have unity, but totality is lost .<sup>43</sup>

<sup>43</sup> It is noteworthy that common understanding has in this conflict always decided, with regard to space, rather for infinity (the boundlessness of the world), and with regard to time rather for finitude (a beginning of the world). So too has public religion. This decision as well rests on the original opposition of space and time: since in the latter unity, in the former infinity, predominates.

CCXXXVII. Had the world ever begun to be, that is, were its being referable to a determinate time, and the transformations and motions in it to a determinate number, it would have to be asserted that being does not follow from the essence of God, that is, the Idea of God itself would have to be canceled. For being, that is, the All itself, follows just as essentially from the Idea of God as it follows from the Idea of the triangle that its angles together equal two right angles.

[p. 243] CCXXXVIII. Conversely, however, that the world has not begun and must endure from an endless time could be asserted only by thinking, not the whole as preceding the parts, but, inversely, the parts as preceding the whole; just as the generation of a line would also require endless time, after one had first thought it composed of infinitely many points; all of which is the utmost absurdity.

CCXXXIX. Only the whole as the *whole* is, and with it the parts; but this has begun just as little as not begun; for it surpasses all time; it is not from eternity, but in an eternal manner, as the truth in the law of identity is not from infinite time, but eternal by nature.

CCXL. The universe is not generated, for all existence is only its existence; just as little can it perish, for there is nothing into which it could pass over, since it is itself all being. It can neither grow nor diminish, for the infinite can become neither greater nor smaller. It suffers no change, neither one that would be effected from without, for there is nothing outside it, nor one that would spring from itself, for it is everything that it can be, in actuality and without time at once. Since, then, the possibility in it is constantly fulfilled by actuality, it is in an immortal rest, which however is only the consummate fullness and infinite power of its self-affirmation.

CCXLI. The essence in gravity and the essence in light are, in their separation from each other, still merely ideal factors of nature; for creative nature unites even them themselves again (CLXXII), and nothing real is in nature that belonged merely to the one or the other of the two (ibid.).

CCXLII. The *actual* potencies in nature therefore cannot conduct themselves merely as gravity, light, and the identity of the two; for in everything actual the threefold bond of both is expressed.

CCXLIII. Creative nature, as the living unity of light and gravity, first of all affirms itself absolutely in the individual, [p. 244] and this is the first potency of its affirmation = A¹, in which gravity, light, and the unity of both are jointly subordinated to gravity. It affirms this its affirming again = A², so that gravity, light, and the identity of both appear under the common exponent of light. Uniting both again, being = A¹ and the position of this being = A², = A³, it reveals itself for the first time as the truly absolute copula; and light with gravity appears subordinated to the common bond in which both are originally enclosed.

CCXLIV. This sequence of the real potencies presents itself to consideration thus — the first as the universal metamorphosis of nature, or as the first blossoming of things out of gravity; the second as dynamic life, as the first inner linkage of things; the third as organic life, as the equally perfect unfolding of the inner and outer life.

CCXLV. The consideration of these real potencies of nature is the subject of the special philosophy of nature.

[p. 245]

### Kritische Fragmente. — Critical Fragments.

Someone who has purged theories and common concepts utterly from himself, and applied the straight, fresh understanding anew from the ground up to the particular, has not yet been found, says *Bacon*.

But involuntarily, sooner or later, this operation will be undertaken, and the surfeit of abstractions and empty concepts will itself indicate immersion in the particular as the soul’s sole remedy.

The man whom at that time the intuition of the concrete left empty, and did not fill with the Ideas of the divine, the eternal, and the All-living, would have to be accounted lost to science as to religion.

The formation of every stone (e.g., the passage of the layers) presents problems that cannot be resolved without the loftiest Ideas.<sup>44</sup>

<sup>44</sup> Cf. *Darstellung der rein rationalen Philosophie* II, 1, p. 360. Ed.

We know nothing except what is in experience, says Kant. Quite right; but that which alone is in experience is precisely the living, the eternal, or God.

God’s existence is an empirical truth, indeed the ground of all experience.

Whoever has grasped this and known it inwardly has had the sense for the philosophy of nature opened to him.

[p. 246] It is no theory, but a real life of the spirit in and with nature, which can express and present itself in as infinite a manner as nature itself. Therefore, if anyone shall say to you: here it is, or there, do not believe him; if they say to you: behold, it is in the wilderness, do not go out; behold, it is in the letter or the word, do not believe him.

Is poetry then present somewhere and in stock, so that you could take it up and carry it about with you? But in every true appearance you recognize it whole, though never completed in its appearances themselves.

One man I pity, that so great a wrong is done him. A mystic the people call him, and he is, alas, only mystified.

One man I esteem and call him the Ossian of the philosophy of nature, — Another has composed in philosophy the first idyll in the manner of *Geßner*. Let a philosopher of nature now compose for us a *Theocritean* one.

⁂

Nature knows not through science, but through its essence, or in a magical manner.

The time will come when the sciences will cease more and more, and immediate cognition will set in. All sciences, as such, were invented only from lack of the latter; e.g., the whole edifice of astronomical calculations, because it was not given to man to see the necessary in the celestial motions immediately as such, or to live spiritually along with the real life of the All.

There have been and will be individuals who have no need of science, in whom nature sees, and who in their seeing have themselves become nature. These are the true seers, the genuine empiricists, to whom those who now call themselves by that name are related as political tinkers are to prophets sent by God.

What is accomplished by such a seer in the art of medicine [p. 247] or any other work is a miracle, for it is cognized and done without mediation.

Miracles of history, riddles of antiquity, which ignorance rejected, nature will unlock for us.

One I know who is by nature a subterranean man, in whom knowing has become substantial and turned into being, as in metals sound and light have turned into solid mass. He does not cognize, but is a living, ever-mobile, and complete personality of cognizing.

Do not speak, for heaven’s sake, of science, since you have scarcely scratched the surface. To behold the truth just as it is, no one has yet had the heart.

You complain of its too sensuous expression. I tell you, it is not nearly sensuous enough. You have so far been able to repeat words without intuition. Were its sense to open to you today, you would be terrified, and at least half of you would flee from the holy place.

⁂

One stands alone, on the mountain, as he says, from where he looks only from afar into the promised land, and where he wants to be buried by the Lord God.

Even if one glimpsed the eternal from there only in the mist of presentiment, one would still have to stand on the summit in order to know it.

Where the creature vanishes to itself and becomes transparent to the Creator, there is reason.

For him to whom reason is the archetype, the Absolute a counter-image of this archetype, philosophy the copy of this counter-image, and thus again something other than reason, he descends instead of ascending, and ends up in the midst of the wilderness.

The cognizing and the cognized are the same in reason, and that which cognizes this unity is again only the same. This [p. 248] trinity of cognizing no abstraction can dissolve. Whoever does not comprehend it has as yet cognized nothing in an eternal manner.

Reason is not an objectifying *of itself*, for it is nothing for itself, that it could objectify itself. Rather, the eternal is *essentially* the cognizing of itself, and this self-corroboration of the Absolute, which is its being, is the whole and sole content of reason.

He strives toward the transcendent who is still rooted in something other than this, for whom the One and All, the sole reality, has not become his own.

In the stillest existence and without reflection the plant reveals eternal beauty. So it would be best for you to know God silently and as though not knowing.

This unknowing knowing cognizes, before you proclaim presentiment and faith as the highest!

Only in the highest science does the mortal eye close, where it is no longer the man who sees, but the eternal seeing itself has become seeing in him.

The old seer had known God face to face before he was buried, in the place that God alone knew.

⁂

There are already more theories of the senses than senses. Those in which there is sense must all dissolve themselves and find themselves again in one comprehensive theory.

There is an objective order of the senses, in accordance with the type that is expressed in the forms of universal natural activity.

To the activity which is magnetism in the product, and sound in the in-itself or essence, there correspond among the senses the senses of touch and of hearing.

Electricity, light (the in-itself of all electricity): to these correspond the senses of smell and of sight.

Chemism, heat (the in-itself of all chemism): parallel to them are the senses of taste and of heat.

[p. 249] In the universal conformation of the animal kingdom the union of the soft and the rigid is nature’s highest problem.

The gradual pushing back of the bone system toward the interior is a gradual union of the hearing-animal and the touch-animal.

The organ of touch is the totality of the soft parts, that of hearing the totality of the hard parts of the body.

On the lowest level nature produces a mere touch-animal; the hearing-animal falls into the coral, outside the touch-animal. The shell of the mollusks prefigures the spiral windings of the future organ of hearing; but as yet it is outside the touch-animal, as something other, though in closer connection with it than in the polyp.

In the most perfect hearing-animal, on the contrary, nature almost loses the touch-animal; the bird has, in proportion, the least flesh, and even this passes over into the vegetation of an outer covering.

The union of initially mutually exclusive systems is not the least of the distinguishing marks of the mammals from the lower classes of animals.

Every animal is at once a light-animal and a gravity-animal; the former in the system of the soft parts, the latter in that of the hard.

Man is the most successful union of the most perfect hearing-animal with the most perfect touch-animal; an inner and an outer man.

The relation of the two systems is like that of the earths and metals in the universal body of the earth.

The senses of touch and hearing are senses of succession; those of smell and sight senses of the outside-one-another and side-by-side, those of taste and heat senses of the within-oneanother.

According to *this* view the order of the senses is that of the three dimensions. In each of them, however, the sense is doubled according to the soft and the hard, as the animal itself is a doubled one.

The opposition of the senses according to the soft and the hard also corresponds to the opposition of space and time.

Taste is the sense most closely akin to the soft among [p. 250] those that belong to the hard; therefore it senses the present, i.e., the most spatial in time. Smell is sensation of what is to come, i.e., of the most temporal in space, of the outside-one-another without side-by-side. In hearing time itself has become absolute, and space has been taken up into time, and so overcome as space.

Of the senses that belong to the soft, touch, especially in the principal organs of cohesion, the fingers, comes closest to the hard; hence it is a sense for succession or the temporal in space. Since the opposition of time and space is itself that of the first and second dimensions, time must be negated most completely in the sense of sight (the softest), as space is in the sense of hearing (the hardest). The third, enigmatic sense, for which we have no wholly adequate name, takes time up again, relative to the sense of sight; it unites nearness and distance, which are separated in touch and sight; it is touch at a distance, sensation of the temporal or of what is to come as present, a divinatory sense.

Sight cognizes infinity in unity; hearing, unity in infinity.

Gravity, overpowering the particular, for that very reason posits light or the inner identity of all things *in* the particular. Hence the senses that belong to the hard are senses to which the inside of things is distinct, the outside dark.

Conversely, light, unfolding the particular as the particular, posits in it gravity itself as the bond or the cognizing. Hence to the senses that belong to the soft only the outside is light, the inside night.

In hearing, smell, and taste gravity is properly the constructing, because it posits light inwardly; in the senses of sight, touch, and heat the light-essence or the ideal is the constructing, because it posits gravity as inward or cognizing.

Only through its own original opposition can nature become intuitive in the particular, i.e., only through that opposition are senses possible.

[p. 251] Nature is wholly inward (ideal) and wholly outward (real). Wholly inward, for everything is only in it; wholly outward, for it is wholly being as well, since nothing is outside it. It is thus neither the one nor the other in particular, but the absolute identity of both.

Through the isolation of the senses, by virtue of which the inward and the outward are held apart and set forth for themselves, the animal is posited out of the absolute unity in which nature lives.

This unity, however, breaks through in the instinct and the reason-like actions of animals.

Animals, we said, are the natural somnambulists (Aphor. 72); but others before us said more truly that the whole of nature is in somnambulism.

The first or objective order of the senses already comprises within itself the division of the senses into material and immaterial.

Touch, smell, and taste are the senses for identity, difference, and totality in the particular or in the product.

The three immaterial senses are senses for the essence or the ideal of the things themselves; hearing the sense for the in-itself of all identity, sight the sense for the in-itself of all difference, the sense of heat the sense for the in-itself of all totality.

The sequence of the lower classes of animals cannot be determined according to the emergence of the senses in them; for rather the higher or lower senses emerge in them according as they are held back at the lower (the reproductive) level or are already transfigured into a higher one.

Since struggle with mass and the production of it is the most distinguished moment in the life of animals of the lowest order, there is on the lowest level a succession of creatures through which the inorganic, the corals, is produced; difference is wholly dominated by identity; in the class of the worms and mollusks the first decisive *falling apart* of the species into individuals is manifest, where each carries its own [p. 252] shell for itself; in the bloom of the insect kingdom, represented by those which are animated by the art-instinct, nature gathers itself; what happened successively in the polyp happens *simultaneously*; what prevails is — unity of the art-instinct with separateness of the individuals; identity, but as totality.

Homer was only one, and yet many; and many

Being yet only one, think of him as a race of bees.

The sequence of the lowest class of animals is therefore: polyp (worm), mollusk, insect.

The place of each class of animals is to be determined by what first emerges decisively in it; for this marks an epoch in the history of creation.

What first emerges in the fish is the heart and the simple circulation. Hence among the animals of the second dimension it asserts the first dimension again.

The nature of every animal is mixed from the determinations of the universal dimension to which it belongs, and of the particular place within it.

To the latter the fish owes its all-surpassing fertility; to the former the considerable but as yet less substantial irritability, the galvanic articulation of the bony plates, and the electric force.

In regard to respiration nothing is changed in the fish; what was already created in the mollusk is merely reproduced.

First emergence of a widely extended and well-formed lung; independence of respiration, double circulation in the best-known genera, persistence of irritability and its inseparability from matter even in individual parts — these are the characteristic moments of the formation of the amphibian.

Maximum of swiftness, vitality, and variety of voluntary motion clearly enough assigns the summit of this stage of formation to the race of birds.

[p. 253] The sequence of the animals of this dimension is therefore: fish, amphibian, bird.

The order in which the senses emerge in particular is determined by the measure in which the inner perfection of the organism for itself attains a higher degree through them.

It is not true that the senses emerge in the order in which the outer world of the organism is enlarged through them.

The inner perfection of the organism for itself has the following stages. *First*: it is limited to itself, and contains only the infinite possibility of itself. *Second*: it takes up into itself the possibility of other things, but as other, or with difference. *Third*: it contains the possibility of other things, but remaining within itself, and persisting in identity with itself.

This sequence of stages too reproduces itself in the senses.

The senses in which the organism contains merely the infinite possibility of itself are touch and taste (by virtue of its relation to nutrition).

Those in which it takes up the possibility of other things, but as other, are sight and smell, of which two the latter is the more inward.

The senses in which the organism, taking up the possibility of other things, at the same time remains wholly within itself, are the sense of heat and hearing.

This order, the subjective, is that of the emergence of the senses in the animal kingdom.

Since two senses correspond to each dimension, the most is in favor of assuming that of the two the one emerges earlier in which outwardness rather than inwardness is dominant; or, what is here the same, that which belongs to the soft before that which in the same dimension belongs to the hard. So, e.g., touch before taste.

Only by such a general principle could it be decided to which sense each particular class of animals corresponds.

[p. 254] Experience leaves the matter the more doubtful because nature knows no sharp distinctions and reproduces all of them, more or less distinctly, in every genus. So in creating a new level it too sinks back relatively to the most perfect of the preceding, in order only then, as if by a new running start, to create the new sense in its highest perfection. Conversely, in the lower sense the higher one of the same level is at once germinating.

Where the senses still emerge in isolation there is no totality, and for that very reason no unity either. The animal does not have sense, but is itself the sense laid out externally in its isolation, as Harvey says of the egg that it is an *uterus foris* *expositus*.

The six lower classes of animals are the six senses presented for themselves and laid bare.

The polyp is the first papilla of touch, nothing more; the development of this sense into the sense of feeling, which is not a separate one, is set forth in the naked worms, the purest organs of the first dimension.

The sense of taste is exposed in the mollusks. The tongue of the higher genera of animals is a true mollusk, which has deposited its shell outside itself in the organ of hearing. Hence the connection of the two; the eventual elevation of the tongue to the organ of speech.

The tongue of animals is either semi-fluid, like that of most of the dwellers in shells; in other genera almost cartilaginous, horny, furnished with bristles, or, as also in diseases, incrusted — Crustacea, Testacea.

Salt is the indifference of all dynamic potencies in magnetism, as the (one-sided) water is in electricism. In the water of the ocean the most primordial and absolute indifference of all directions is for that very reason preserved.

The insect, as the first personification of the sense of light, has found eloquent defenders; and according to the principle just set forth, the sense of sight would indeed have to emerge before the sense of smell.

I acknowledge that nature in the insect tends toward the development of the sense of light and puts forth the first eyebuds [p. 255] in its hemispheres , which perhaps unfold fully only at the highest summit. But by the principle that the place of every animal must be determined by what emerges in it *first*, though, for that very reason, in a more imperfect formation, the insect is to be regarded as the animal corresponding to the sense of light.

As the mollusk is *wholly* organ of taste, so the developed insect is *wholly* organ of sight; yet for that reason this organ is less demonstrable in it in its determinate formation and independence from the whole.

The only insect that has a mobile eye, i.e., one independent of the whole, is one that lives in water, and the fish, in which the identity of the sense of smell is moreover decided, and which is rightly set parallel to it, shows the eye first as single, distinguishable with determinateness; just as, conversely, this organ in its higher formation has a salty moisture for its element, and corresponds less to the cornea of the eye and the color-sheen of the iris, apart from the shining coverings of insects, than the scaly skin of fishes and the often wonderful luster in their coverings. Likewise to the shining of the eye nothing corresponds so determinately as the shining of some insects and the phosphorescence and electricity of fishes.

Swiftly and often, with the change of life-force and passion, the fish, like the eye, changes its color. It plays in the light, and, befooled by nocturnal gleam, goes into the encircling net. Boldness and rapacity, whose force lies in the sense of sight, become mighty first in the realm of fishes after the insects. Their crystalline lens is far more convex than that of birds, of quadrupeds, of man; their retina is more finely formed than their olfactory nerves — taken together with the other, if the general principle did not contradict it, seductive grounds for regarding the fish as the exposed form of the sense of light, the insect — (consider that they are almost throughout organs of respiration, that they are guided in the dark by smell and dwell in the proper realm of scents) — as the first, still free, organ of smell.

[p. 256] The eyes of fishes lack, strangely enough, the *corpus* *ciliare*, a gill-like formation of the inner eye, likewise lashes and lids, gill-like formations of the outer coverings.

As gravity is the totality of things according to the universal, so heat is it according to the particular or difference.

No more intimate communion of things, penetrating more deeply into essence, than that through gravity and heat! As there is an equilibrium of gravity, so there is an equilibrium of heat.

Heat, as corresponding to the third dimension, can also be thought as the indifference of magnetism and electricity. The former corresponds among the dynamic potencies to gravity, the latter to light; heat therefore, in the potency of dynamic life, = identity of light and gravity (as *Steffens* also maintains).

Of the utterly absolute identity of light and gravity, however, heat is only the most immediate objective or dynamic expression, by no means that identity itself.

Hence the immediate appearance of heat, and of independent heat, where that absolute bond of light and gravity unfolds.

Every other principle has answered your questions with signs; do you think that this one will be silent when you ask it? The experiment still stands still before it, as before the innermost sanctuary, and has no inkling of the wholly new world of phenomena that would open up in it.

Perhaps, without knowing it, animal magnetism has experimented with that essence of all life and organism.

The sense of totality can be called the sense of heat only as the sense of sight can be called the sense of light, since it is not so much a seeing or sensing of light as such as rather of things by means of light.

As sight is a sense for things in their merely ideal difference: so the sense of heat is a sensation of things in their ideal totality, or in the temperature of particular life within universal life.

[p. 257] As all dynamic potencies become indifferent in heat, so do the senses corresponding to them in the sense of heat.

Hence it is the darkest of all immaterial senses and that through which the sensibility of the animal, even of lichens, is capable of immediate sensation of the universal states of nature in its universal life-process.

The immediate organ of sense for heat is the entire system of the skin; through this the animal is most determinately connected with the universal life-temperature of nature and its changing states.

The skin is the eye for heat — the different color of the iris corresponding to the different color of the skin. — Black pigment of the eye and (though developed only in one race) of the skin.

Nature forms the first true skin in the amphibian, although here too, as everywhere, only repeating earlier stages (e.g., the mollusk in the genus *Testudo*). In the fish the skin was still covered with scales; in the sloughing of the snake the great significance that the formation of this organ has for nature is revealed.

The sense of heat is hypostatized in the amphibian, which of all creatures stands in communion with all the potencies of nature most of all. Heat itself is an amphibian, living always between the solid and the fluid, indeed real and possible only on the constantly changing boundary between the two. — Dependence of the amphibian on the universal temperature — (snakes stiffen through nocturnal cold and are revived again by the warmth of day).

Presentiment of meteorological changes in the amphibian.

Since heat is the soul of the third dimension, the sense of heat too must emerge, besides its immediate organs, the amphibians, in the animal kingdom wherever in any significance the third dimension is reached. So the insect does not lack the sense of heat and with it of totality, and it produces a foreboding of future changes.

[p. 258] Art can emerge only in pure opposition. Therefore art-instinct is connected only with the senses of hearing and sight, because in them space and time are held most separate. The one-sided, spatial — architectonic — art-instinct dwells in the insect; in the bird, the personification of the sense of hearing, the musical joins with it.

Unity of a whole with itself, i.e., with its parts, is inner repose; motion posits difference of the parts and of the whole; the activity of re-forming-into-one after disturbed equilibrium is *sound*.

Sound is not magnetism nor cohesion, but the essence or the ideal, intuited as the in-itself of all cohesion.

Matter is the spoken word, sound the speaking, the living word.

Sound is the first in-forming of the infinite into the finite; therefore in the completed in-forming, where the eternal breaks through the temporal, affirmation through the affirmed, it must become living again and, as the first, be the last.

In hearing nature finds itself and enters again into the first consciousness of its original unity and selfcomprehension.

The sense of hearing is the most inward of the senses and therefore the highest with respect to the perfection of the organic essence in itself.

After nature has created one-sidedly in the subordinate genera, it begins its many-sided creations in the mammals, and, placing the senses ever more concentrically, gradually gains the focal point where reason ignites.

As human flesh is a chaos of all colors, so human speech is the chaos of all tones and sounds, and therefore quite properly the word made flesh.

In the plant nature forms out more the relation of the earth to the center, in the animal more the relation of the center to the earth.

The potencyless image of potencyless identity must be, of both directions of nature, not so much the syntheses as the absolute identity.

[p. 259] Man is already, by the form of his outer shape, nature’s most successful cube. In man too, as in the cosmic body, the relation of the universal or subject to the particular or object is a relation of the square to the cube.

As in revolution the universal of the cosmic body holds fast the particular, and intuits itself in it, i.e., intuits it as itself, so the universal of man grasps itself in the particular through speech.

In speech is the highest identity of soul and body.

Speech immediately makes the infinite present; it is the [p. 260] absolute seizing of space by time, of totality by identity. -<sup>45</sup>

<sup>45</sup> Here there followed in the original a further remark, in which the author complains that, by means of badly transcribed notebooks, his ideas have to serve all sorts of book-manufacturers, whereby, unfortunately, a great lack of discrimination shows itself in the public, since “such ware is regarded by one part quite properly as authority and document.” — The announced continuation did not appear. Ed.

### Vorläufige Bezeichnung des Standpunktes der Medicin nach Grundsätzen der Naturphilosophie. — Provisional Characterization of the Standpoint of Medicine According to Principles of the Philosophy of Nature.

§ I. Every thing, as it attains to existence in appearance, but above all the living organism, presents to consideration a twofold side. For either regard is had to its transient existence, insofar as it consists in relation and reference to other things, or to its eternal ground, its essentiality and archetypal character. The former is the finite, the latter the infinite side of the object.

§ II. To cognize exactly each of these two sides for itself, as well as the manner of their union in the organism, would then without doubt be the task of a true science of it.

§ III. But if we set aside those ancient heroes of the art, whose correct intimations were outwardly veiled by the obscurity or formlessness of language and presentation, and who revealed the essence of the organism only in isolated flashes of spirit, then it would seem that in earlier times there is nowhere to be found any proper cognition either of the divine or of the natural relation of the organism, or of the manner of their union within it.

§ IV. According to a general law, science, like every other kind of formation, seems to have to arrive at self-conscious [p. 261] clarity and perfection only after the age of unconsciousness, and only by passing through opposition and separation. The most unblessed ages of science are those in which the barren understanding has brought matters to the point of not merely confusing the cognition of the object, but of making the object itself unrecognizable. In such an age there appears, as a beneficent and stirring figure, a vigorous man who, seizing one side of the object with power, singles it out alone and subordinates all others to it. Hereby there arises an immediate clarity, the appearances receive a reference; what is different separates, what is alike comes together, and since a kind of simplicity cannot fail to accompany one-sidedness, everything is for a while delighted, edified, in part even calmed.

§ V. Such a man appeared to medicine toward the end of the last century: Joh. *Brown*, who, like all who mark the initial moment of the rebirth of a science, is exalted by force of spirit and depth above his nearer, and by clarity above his more remote, predecessors. Since science before him had recognized the natural and divine relation of the organism neither in clear distinction nor in true unity, he brought the first decisively to the fore, established a doctrine about it, and grounded organic life itself and the alternation of its states, in particular that of health and sickness, solely on that side of the organism by which it is determinable through external things and is always actually determined.

§ VI. Given the aim of the present exposition, merely to indicate provisionally the standpoint that results from the principles of the philosophy of nature for the science of medicine, we shall be permitted to adopt the doctrine of that man as the fixed point from which we follow the metamorphoses that, in our opinion, it must pass through in order to raise itself stage by stage from its limitedness and opposition to the perfection possible to it.

§ VII. When we assert that Brown grasped only the relative side of the organism, that of its being determined through other things, our meaning is this: that he seized only [p. 262] that side with consciousness, but did not positively exclude the other, merely left it undiscussed, as it were in a background, from whose darkness he drew back with an awe, rightly felt from his standpoint. In positing the organism as excited from without, he had involuntarily to posit also the excitable, which, as such, had to have a being and essence independent of the merely external determination, since the latter could be neither the ground of that upon which it acted, nor the cause of the property by virtue of which it was determined from without to activity. However obscurely, then, Brown himself had to acknowledge a domain of the organism independent of external influences and unreachable by them, a ground that, prior to all actual excitation, posited excitability itself. This remark has already been made, and carried further there, in the *First Outline of a System of the* *Philosophy of Nature* , to which we therefore refer the reader.<sup>46</sup>

<sup>46</sup> Pp. 258, 259 ff. [vol. III, p. 222 ff.]

§ VIII. Faithful to that empirical mode of consideration which, through Bacon, Newton, and Locke, had gradually spread over all scientific nations, and according to which the in-itself, the relationless ground of appearances, was regarded as eternally unfathomable, while the negative conditions or the external causes of them were regarded as alone knowable, *Brown* warned against any causal explanation of excitability, confining himself solely to the phenomenon, to excitability itself; in this too of sounder mind than most of those who, before him or after him, without the vocation of a higher kind of cognition, wished to reach the essence of excitability by explanations. For all explanation by causes begets eternally only opinion, never science.

§ IX. Yet in that way excitability itself, as a property unknowable in itself, was only *inferred* from the phenomenon of excitation, and only as the necessary presupposition of the [p. 263] latter, not cognized in itself. But excitability, insofar as it is mere determinability to activity by external influence (and more was not cognized in it in the manner indicated), is by no means what distinguishes the organism, since in this sense it belongs also to inorganic and so-called dead things, of which the chemical and the whole dynamic process furnish examples in abundance.

§ X. If we are to express what alone distinguishes organic beings from inorganic ones in this respect, it is that the former, excited by external influences, nevertheless persist in the form of their being, while the latter are either transformed, or lose their independent being, or are even wholly destroyed as to form. That determination was therefore added by the philosophy of nature to the concept of excitability, and the latter was made to consist in this, that the organism is determined by external influences to self-reproduction . Insofar as the<sup>47</sup> energy or the capacity for action of the organism was also regarded as that by which it asserted its objective subsistence against the external world, the same synthesis was clearly expressed in the familiar idea of an equilibrium of receptivity and activity as the most perfect organic state.

<sup>47</sup> Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie. P. 158. [= p. 145].

§ XI. But this synthesis (of the activity determined from without and of the peculiar being of the organism, determined according to form) lies, strictly speaking, no longer in the concept of excitability, but is grounded on a higher view, merely mixed with the original Brownian one and lent to it.

§ XII. This we shall express in its highest form thus: that in the organism generally the finite, what is determinable through something else, is posited as equal to the infinite and as itself essential. For just as with the archetypal things there are posited, equally eternally, their relations too, but as eternally null in respect of the All, so that the former subsist [p. 264] unchanged by the latter: so the living organism, as a partial All, a temporal eternity, posits the relations of its life, and the determinations which it receives in them, eternally as null in respect of itself, and asserts the particular form of its being as one itself essential and archetypal. What is taken up into it lives, so long as the whole subsists, a life withdrawn from transformation and from time; only the unessential has its alternation, posited together with the essential, and constantly arises and passes away; but the primal form, the particular form raised to identity with the essential, remains, as if by divine sanction, from the first germ to the last development unchanged, the same.

§ XIII. What has just been said already indicates that the ground of the organism as such cannot lie in any particular principle of nature. For only absolute nature, the infinite substance itself, bears the particularities of the world as eternal growths just as the organic whole, so long as it endures, posits the individual members as unchangeable even in form: only in the former, then, is the finite originally and absolutely equal to the infinite and raised to essentiality. Just as in created nature there are some things in which the form of particular being does not appear equal to the universal, but the latter (the substance) indeed subsists, while the former (as the accident) is constantly transformed and passes away: so, on the other hand, in other things the essential being of the particular in the All may also come forth in appearance, so that these themselves are images of the All and presentations of the way in which the particularities of things are comprehended in it in an eternal manner. Further, if the things of the first kind have through what subsists in them only an immediate relation to the one attribute of substance (gravity), then those of the other kind will have an equal immediate relation to substance considered absolutely, which, entering here as a higher gravity, is the ground of that activity by which in the organism the contingent is posited as equal to the necessary, the form as equal to the substance and itself essential.

[p. 265] § XIV. Every organic activity therefore breaks forth from the essence and innermost part of nature, and can no more than gravity be explained further empirically. The organism as product relates to substance as its counter-image, in which it beholds itself. Through affections from without, only this, the object, can be immediately altered; but mediately, and through the alteration of the product, substance appears determined to act, in that it always posits the object as similar to itself, as absolute identity of form and essence, as All, which annihilates all determination and relation through its own timelessness.

§ XV. Excitability, as indirect determinability to act, cannot therefore be posited as a property of the organism; for it is by no means the organism itself, as product, that is determined to act, but substance as the immediate ground of its existence. Just as little can excitability be regarded as a property of substance as such; for this too is by no means determined, or determinable, to act indirectly in itself or considered absolutely, but only in relation to the organism as an individual thing. The same holds of the concept of the capacity for indifferentiation or capacity for action. For the absolute ground of the organism can appear only in relation to the individual thing as the mere ground of the possibility of an acting, since the actuality of the acting is conditioned from without by the affections of its object; in itself, however, it is that in which possibility and actuality are unconditionally one.

§ XVI. In general, then, the concepts of excitability and of the capacity for action belong to the indistinct mode of cognition which mixes the consideration of the in-itself with that of the concrete. For they determine neither the in-itself of the organism purely, nor the organism purely as object, but the mere mixture, and for that very reason not the absolute identity of the two either.

§ XVII. But as to how matters stand with the being-determined to activity, as well as with the subject of this beingdetermined [p. 266] (for we too have treated of it not absolutely, but only in relation to the view of excitation), the most important inquiry always remains that into the possibility of different states of life. For if life rests on constant excitation, or on the activity of that empirically unfathomable principle which is nevertheless excitable by external influence, the question arises whether that activity can be different merely in degree and magnitude, or whether it can be different in kind and quality.

§ XVIII. The former is asserted by the purely Brownian theory, and this must be regarded as what is properly distinctive of it, since the concept of excitability can still be dissolved into other views, or combined with higher Ideas. However simple the assertion seems, that all difference of the states of life rests on a mere more or less of excitation, it must prove so much the harder to derive from the evolutions of a homogeneously running series of degrees two states as opposed as health and sickness are, which according to the general conception relate to one another as position and negation. Here we are willing, by a violent leap, to grant that view hypersthenia and asthenia (for there would still be much to discuss as to how, either from the relation of the exciting causes to excitability, or, as was likewise attempted, though with not much better success, from the relation of receptivity and capacity for action, even these two states alone could be derived). But granting these two states, it is in no way to be seen how they, as such, which lie in the same series of degrees as that of health and form no true opposition to it, could be sickness in themselves .<sup>48</sup>

<sup>48</sup> Cf. loc. cit., p. 273. [= pp. 235, 236].

§ XIX. Every excess, every too much, of stimuli for example, can be thought only relative to something wholly determinate and bounded, here perhaps relative to excitability, not in general, but as one bound to a determinate product. But if, [p. 267] once the product must be taken into consideration in order to give excitability a limit, why should it be reckoned for nothing in the case of sickness itself, and the more or less of activity alone constitute it? Likewise, from a relative preponderance of receptivity and of the capacity for action nothing further could follow than, in the first case, a lesser, in the other a greater measure of energy, with which the organism asserts itself against the onslaught of external nature, that is, mere weakness and strength. But that the organism subsists with greater or lesser energy of self-action is, provided only that it subsists at all, a difference without real significance, as we indeed do not call that organism sick which has a weaker life-energy, and place health or sickness by no means in the degree of strength with which the organism subsists, but in subsisting or not subsisting at all. Hence also the most acute defenders of that view transformed Brownian strength into over-strength, and with equal right could have transformed weakness into over-weakness. But that in relation to which strength or weakness could be too great must necessarily be something insofar independent of excitation and otherwise determined: already with that addition to the concepts of strength and weakness, therefore, a relation different from and independent of the external and quantitative relation of the organism is tacitly conceded.

§ XX. The complete emptiness of the concepts of sthenia and asthenia in respect of the phenomena of life shows itself most clearly in their application to the diversity of manifold organs which are united in a total organism. The equilibrium of receptivity and energy is either regarded as an absolute one for every organic whole; then no manifoldness is possible anywhere, unless all organs but one were to be thought of as sick and either in the asthenic or in the sthenic state. To one organ, in comparison with another, there belongs an evident [p. 268] plus of energy ; to another a plus of receptivity is peculiar: at bottom, then, both would be sick, the one through strength, the other through weakness. This cannot be the meaning. The equilibrium must therefore be determined as a relative one: namely, a certain degree of energy and a certain degree of receptivity belongs necessarily to the subsistence of every organ according to its determinateness, and only insofar as the actual degree of activity or receptivity is below or above the degree of the first or of the other required by the determinateness of the organ can it be called sick. This has then been indicated in various ways, among others by speaking of a *normal and abnormal* degree of excitation. But where, then, is *the norm* to be sought, according to which the excitation is determined? Certainly not in the excitation itself! But once that determination is added to the degree of excitation, the ascertainment of the norm must be the most important and the first thing, in order to find the real definition or construction of sickness. Yet precisely this question was left in complete darkness until a certain time.

§ XXI. In order to put in a still brighter light this point, at which the theory of excitation, if carried on scientifically, as happened in Germany, had sooner or later to strike and to recognize another side of the organism as its limit, we shall conduct the following general proof. In regard to the organism the demand is made that the accident too be equal to substance, the particular to the universal (§ XII). Supposing now that the essence of the organism consisted in a quantitative equilibrium of receptivity and energy, that demand is without doubt not that there be an equilibrium at all, for this is indeed (ex hypoth.) the universal of the organism itself, but that there be something determinate, bounded, and this boundedness constitutes the accident here. The ground of this boundedness cannot now lie again in the quantitative relation. For this is posited rather as what is bounded by it, and accordingly in itself as unbounded and infinitely variable. [p. 269] Since now it is not excitation as such, but the too much or too little of it relative to the indicated limit, thus in general the overstepping of this limit by excitation, that is sickness (because only thereby is difference of the accident from the substance posited), and this limit cannot be given by the quantitative relation: so it is also impossible to comprehend sickness in general from the merely quantitative relation of excitation.

§ XXII. In this discussion we have still let the concepts of hypersthenia and asthenia themselves rest on their worth: but what is one to say of those physicians who to this hour posit the essence of sickness either in asthenia (direct or indirect), or in hypersthenia, and yet maintain that a sickness which is the same in kind and essence can nevertheless be now of a sthenic, now of an asthenic nature! The unheard-of demand to believe such a contradiction lets us expect beforehand that this opposition too will yet vanish, and that science here, as elsewhere, must proceed from opposition to the unity of the ground of explanation and of cognition.

§ XXIII. Meanwhile we have shown how the mere view of excitation is driven to the acknowledgment of an original and essential relation independent of external determination: which we have long since designated as the relation of metamorphosis . It is that by which the organism has no reference<sup>49</sup> to external nature, but to the archetype. It determines the degree of its perfection or the place it occupies in the scale of metamorphosis, and is an inner and qualitative relation of the real and the ideal, or, in the determinate expression, of matter and light, whereas that of excitation designates a merely quantitative and external relation of factors.

<sup>49</sup> Zeitschrift für speculative Physik (Jena and Leipzig 1801), vol. II, no. 2, p. 159. [vol. IV, p. 211].

§ XXIV. With this relation there comes into organic life, [p. 270] for the first time, manifoldness , in place of formal unity there enters the true unity, which is at the same time allness of forms, and makes the organism a true, self-enclosed, completed whole. *Brown* in his view of the organism and *Kant* in his doctrine of matter were alike in this, that they recognized a merely quantitative or properly arithmetical relation of the two factors of their construction, and that for that very reason they overlooked all qualitative difference, or refused its construction. This, however, rests, in regard to matter and the organism, as to nature in general, on the triplicity of the potencies or dimensions.

§ XXV. For if the qualitative or essential of the organism is in general identity of matter and light, then according to the general type (which we cannot derive here) this identity itself can again appear either more under the exponent of the real principle, as the in-forming of light into matter, or more under that of the ideal, as the dissolution of matter into light, or finally as the absolute forming-into-one of both. These three possibilities correspond to the three dimensions of matter, and can therefore, in order to follow the manner of presentation already given elsewhere , also be expressed thus:<sup>50</sup> Either light, the infinite possibility, is bound to matter only for the first dimension, that of being-in-itself; the organic being then contains merely the infinite possibility of itself as individual or species; this moment is designated by *Reproduction*. Or light is bound to matter also as possibility of other things, as of others; the expression of this moment, corresponding to the second dimension, is *Irritability*. Or finally matter and light are wholly and absolutely one, the ideal is wholly also the real, the productive; and conversely, the productive [p. 271] of the first moment is united with the ideal of the other; this moment is that of *Sensibility*, which accordingly corresponds to the third dimension.

<sup>50</sup> Vorlesungen über die Methode des akadem. Studium. Dreizehnte Vorlesung: Ueber das Studium der Medicin. P. 291 ff. [IV, p. 335 ff.].

§ XXVI. This is not the place to justify this sequence of stages in detail, or even merely to set out our view of it completely. We refer him to whom it may seem strange to the following extract from a treatise already published in the year 1803(51), in which it is set forth clearly, simply, and correctly: just as readers in general who might find themselves in the same case with regard to the whole of the present treatise would do well, before they read it to the end, to make themselves first more familiar through that extract with the spirit of the consideration proper to the philosophy of nature. Here we wish only to remark that this sequence of stages has been variously misconceived, in that, for example, reproduction was given as the synthesis of sensibility and irritability (which is neither true in itself, nor can be assumed without significant confusion of the sequences), or as the third dimension, which error already had its beginning in the *First Outline of the* *Philosophy of Nature* itself, where reproduction was equated<sup>51</sup> with light (in so far indeed not incorrectly, as light in its expansion is archetypally the same as cohesion, magnetism, formative drive are counter-imagewise) and at the same time with the chemical process. *Röschlaub* with acuteness already equated reproduction with magnetism in an earlier essay, and what follows will show what light this view affords, according to which it is considered not as synthesis, but as the simple, namely first, dimension.<sup>52</sup>

<sup>51</sup> Cogitata nonnulla de Idea Vitae, hujusque formis praecipuis. Autore Carolo Eberh. Schelling. Tubingae 1803. The extract from this treatise mentioned above, whose author is Schelling’s brother, stands in the Jahrbücher der Medicin als Wissenschaft, vol. I, no. 2, p. 134 ff. Ed.

<sup>52</sup> P. 236. [III, p. 207].

§ XXVII. This presupposed, we can, passing over the unessential metamorphoses of which the view of excitation [p. 272] was capable without giving up the principle of the merely quantitative difference of all phenomena of life, designate the next stage which it could attain by combining itself with the qualitative view. The concepts of hypersthenia and asthenia remained standing in this; they required still another moment in order to form sickness, and were thus only not the whole sickness alone. All external influences could originally posit in the organism *only* hypersthenia or asthenia, for they could raise only either the ideal factor at the expense of the real, or conversely the latter at the expense of the former. But in order to find when *sickness* arises, and what *sickness* is, not merely the subjective, but also the objective of the organism had to be taken into view, the general factors of life had to be considered not only for themselves, but in relation to the organic mass and its various formations. The alternation of the factors, considered in the whole and in itself, appeared as free, but in the individual formation and viewed as real as bound; and sickness could therefore consist merely in the conflict of the universal (of organic activity) with its given exponent, the particularity of a formation .<sup>53</sup>

<sup>53</sup> Ideen zur Grundlage der Nosologie und Therapie von Dr. Troxler. 1803. Pp. 19, 21, 28. — Indisputably in its general part the best that had been written on medicine proper, according to views of the philosophy of nature, up to that time. — That we do not mention in this critical survey the great many stillborn and spiritless productions which made similar claims and are already forgotten will be found natural.

§ XXVIII. The possibility and the manner of the disproportion between excitation or organic activity and the qualitative of the organism could be demonstrated more precisely in the following turn. Of every determinate manner of the essential being-one of both factors (the real and the ideal) there is a determinate quantitative relation of both, the objective or formal side. Reproduction, for example, as that dimension of the organism in which the greatest inner preponderance [p. 273] of reality obtains, posits also externally and in excitation an equal preponderance of energy over receptivity. This relation of both factors in excitation can now be altered by external influences without detriment or suffering to the organism itself, as long as the qualitative is not thereby attacked; but as soon as the degree of excitation, and thus also the relation of the real factor to the ideal, becomes either so great or so small that the inner or qualitative determinateness of the organism, in the whole or in the individual part, cannot subsist with it, the identity of the organism with itself is canceled, a necessary conflict is posited. For if, through excitation, the ideal factor has received to the real such a relation as is compatible only with the higher dimension, for example irritability, the demand will now also be made on reproduction to raise itself to irritability; but since the demand, by virtue of the relation of metamorphosis, cannot be fulfilled, the organism is thereby posited in disharmony with itself. Sickness, according to this view, is in general a conflict of the relation of excitation with that of metamorphosis, just as, on the other hand, equilibrium and agreement of both is the most perfect state of organic life .<sup>54</sup>

<sup>54</sup> The further elaboration of this view is found in the following extract, to which reference was already made above (§ XXVI).

§ XXIX. One must admit that through this view, which has also received the assent of the most distinguished founder of the theory of excitation among the Germans , a relatively<sup>55</sup> significant step toward the cognition of the nature and origin of diseases, especially as to the manifoldness of their forms, has been taken. But according to our gradually acquired and ever more firmly established conviction, the matter must be grasped still more deeply and a view adopted at which it is unavoidable to arrive as soon as one wishes to draw into the light a question, hitherto always left in darkness in the investigations, [p. 274] though as it were forcing itself upon us. In the conception last set forth, excitation is still always presupposed as something subsisting for itself, independent of the relation of metamorphosis; still always asthenia or hypersthenia is posited directly through external influence; sickness indeed takes place only insofar as the relation of metamorphosis is altered; but the middle term of this alteration is and remains excitation. — But what, then, is this excitation itself? *How* does it occur? How can the relation of the factors of the organism be altered through it, the real raised at the expense of the ideal and conversely? In a word, how is that hypersthenia and asthenia itself possible, which, by collision with the qualitative determinateness of the product, engenders sickness?

<sup>55</sup> Erster Entwurf eines Lehrbuchs der allgemeinen Jaterie von Röschlaub, part I. 1804. § 324, 325 f.

§ XXX. Nothing happens in nature otherwise than in thoroughgoing limitation: nothing acts merely in general, but always as something determinate. So too there is no excitation in general, but each is one that is absolutely determinate. Nothing raises a factor of the organism in general, but always in a determinate manner. All original determinacy, however, lies only in the qualitative relation. Of this the quantitative relation is as certainly a mere accident as it is certain that existence follows from essence and not, conversely, essence from existence. The factors of the organism can never be one merely externally or in equilibrium, but are at all times internally one. Hence, too, it is never merely their external relation that can be affected, which is an accident of the internal one; rather, the action from without at all times immediately posits a determinate internal relation of both factors, and since this internal determinacy expresses itself as dimension, *every external action on the organism, in the whole and in the particular, immediately makes the demand* for a determinate dimension (e.g. of irritability or of reproduction), and this is the only mode of operation which external causes can exercise in general on an internally balanced, qualitatively articulated and self-enclosed whole, in a word an organic whole.

[p. 275] § XXXI. Such a whole is not merely externally movable, like a lever, but is absolutely movable only in itself, and is always actually in motion. Only the qualitative is immediately alterable here, the quantitative only mediately. This is a consequence of the general truth of reason that quantity can never be for itself, but only in and with quality. The degree of excitation (in the Brownian sense), however, expresses only the existence of the organism in abstraction from the essence, that is, only the quantity or energy of existence relative to external nature, not existence insofar as it is one with the essence and itself qualitative.

§ XXXII. But if external action can in general immediately affect only the dimensions of the organism, then every alteration of the relation of metamorphosis also occurs *without the* *mediation of excitation*, unless one were to understand by excitation precisely that evocation of the dimensions themselves, in which case, however, excitation coincides entirely with the immediately qualitative determination and is nothing distinct from it. But if one wishes to regard excitation as something still different from the qualitative affection, and to understand by it only that externally appearing degree of strength or weakness with which the organism maintains itself in its existence, then excitation is rather the appearance of the internal qualitative relation, and, far from determining it, is rather determined by it. For if that which acts upon the organism is, for example, of such a kind that it demands reproduction in particular from it, then, because reproduction designates the greatest preponderance of reality, there is thereby also posited, although even this only up to a certain limit, with respect to the whole organism a plus of the real factor, that is, a plus of energy. This too holds, as was said, only up to a certain limit. For the true strength of the organism rests on this, that each form of activity or dimension should emerge in a manner commensurate with its relation to the whole. The organism of the human being is not, like that [p. 276] of the plant, confined preponderantly to reproduction; irritability belongs just as essentially to the equilibrium of its life. If, then, the first dimension, in the particular or in the whole of the organism, e.g. in the irritable system itself, is raised to the detriment of the latter, the organism, as a human organism, is in a state of weakness on the side of irritability, e.g. in catalepsy and similar cases. In no case, therefore, can the degree of external vigor or weakness of life lead to the determination of the internal or essential state of the organism, and rather must the ground and the nature of the former itself be investigated in the latter.

§ XXXIII. With this we bid farewell to that merely formal construction of the states of life out of a reciprocally occurring rise and fall of receptivity and of the capacity to act (or however else one may express these factors); for in the organism we know no relation of the two factors in general, but only absolutely determinate relations of them, and it is only these that, in our conviction, are the immediately alterable and determinable, but by no means receptivity or the capacity to act as such. In the same way we shall briefly set out the remaining presuppositions of the theories hitherto held, and set over against them the views that in our opinion are more correct.

§ XXXIV. No external influence can immediately posit asthenia or hypersthenia in the organism, but only the more decided emergence of one dimension before the other, of irritability, e.g., before sensibility and reproduction, or conversely. Illness as such is an alteration of the dimensions of the organism, whereby it ceases to be a pure, untroubled reflex of the All; an originally and thoroughly qualitative affection. Thus the greatest alternation in the rise and fall of the relative strength and weakness of life, as well as of the external actions, can bring about no morbid alteration so long as the organism does not thereby step out of its dimensions; just as all so-called increase and decrease of excitation cannot make [p. 277] it healthy until it has re-entered them and found its way back into its qualitative relations and inner mobility.

§ XXXV. The division of illnesses into sthenic and asthenic is therefore wholly untenable; strength and weakness themselves always behave only as an accident of the qualitative state; every illness must be treated in accordance with this, without regard to so-called sthenia or asthenia, whose inessentiality in relation to it is already evident from what we cited above, that according to the pretension of the theory of excitation one and the same affection of the organism can appear, and must be treated, now as an asthenic, now as a sthenic illness. If there really are illnesses of this kind (e.g. peripneumonia), of which experience hitherto has shown that they did not in all cases permit the same treatment, but at one time required the so-called strengthening, at another the weakening plan of cure, it follows from this merely that neither of the two modes of treatment was the right one, but that there must be a third, which is exalted above this contradiction and which alone is true. According to this wholly identical view, involved in no opposition, illnesses must first be treated before one can speak of pronouncements of experience, which, if it is only really what it boasts of being, can never possibly find a contradiction in nature.

§ XXXVI. Of the same worth as the division of illnesses is that of the acting potencies, e.g. of medicines, into strengthening and weakening, and the dispute over positive and negative stimuli is therefore wholly empty. No action of any external principle can be determined according to its exciting property, but only according to its relations to the dimensions, and my principle in this respect is that like produces like and that no external principle acts through its opposition to the organic substance. Through the reciprocal opposition of the dimensions it happens that the same remedy which in one respect appears as exciting would, in another, on consistent [p. 278] consideration, have to be recognized as weakening. The so-called hydrogenous medicines, naphtha and so on, are accepted by the theory of excitation as strengthening; yet they by no means show themselves as such, but as evidently weakening in the most significant states of suffering reproduction, in dysenteries and the like. Here is the same contradiction as above (§ XXXV), where one and the same illness was supposed to be now of a sthenic, now of an asthenic nature. The truth is that naphtha in itself neither excites nor weakens; it seems to strengthen in the cases where it properly only evokes the positive principle of irritability; it seems to weaken when, in cases where reproduction should be demanded in a significant way, it evokes in its place irritability (the dimension with the preponderance of ideality).

§ XXXVII. Here one would like to raise the general question by what the theory of excitation judges the exciting property of a remedy, or from what it recognizes it. It necessarily lacks a ground a priori by which it would become comprehensible that *this* remedy in particular is an exciting one; supposing this property were grounded in its quality, it would have to acknowledge in the organism a corresponding qualitative relation in order to comprehend its *being-excited* by it. It can thus take up its mode of operation only as a fact of experience. But what does experience show it? Nothing but particulars, e.g. intensified, accelerated actions of individual systems, hence nothing but accidents and symptoms. What it therefore calls stronger excitation is in the end itself only a complex of symptoms; but how can it be permitted to infer from the complex what may not be inferred from the particular? From the symptom the illness is supposed not to be recognizable, but the efficacy of the medicine is supposed to be so from a complex of symptoms.
