For it might easily be recalled to this or that reader that the work of the Last Judgment was begun only after Raphael’s death. But Michel Angelo’s style was born with him, and accordingly also earlier in time than Raphael. Without giving the usual tales of the effect of the sight of Michel Angelo’s first Roman works upon the young Raphael more credence than they deserve, or deriving from this accident the fact that the latter, from an initially still more timid style, advanced to the boldness and grandeur of perfected art, it is nonetheless undeniable, not only that Michel Angelo’s style was a basis of Raphael’s art, but that through him art in general first won its way to complete freedom. — Of Correggio it should perhaps have been said less ambiguously: “Through him blooms the true golden age in art,” although no one will easily misunderstand what was said or fail to recognize what the author took to be the truly highest in modern painting.

After the appeasement of the first violence and of the vehement drive of birth, the spirit of nature is transfigured in soul, and grace is born. To this stage art attained, after Leonardo da Vinci, through Correggio, in whose works the sensuous soul is the working ground of beauty. This is visible not only in the soft contours of his figures; also in the forms, which are most similar to those of the purely sensuous natures in the works of antiquity. In him blooms the true golden age of art, which bestowed on the earth the gentle dominion of Kronos: here playful innocence, serene desire and childlike joy smile from open and cheerful faces, and here the Saturnalia of art are celebrated. The total expression of that sensuous soul is chiaroscuro, which Correggio developed more than any other. For what takes the place of matter for the painter is the dark; and this is the stuff to which he must fasten the fleeting appearance of light and of the soul. The more, then, the dark fuses with the bright, so that out of both only One being and [p. 320] as it were One body and One soul comes to be, the more the spiritual appears corporeal, the corporeal raised to the level of spirit.

After the barriers of nature have been overcome, the monstrous, the fruit of first freedom, has been driven out, form and figure are beautified by the foreboding of the soul: the heaven clears, the tempered earthly can join with the heavenly, this in turn with the gently human. Raphael takes possession of the serene Olympus, and leads us with him away from the earth into the assembly of the gods, of the abiding, blessed beings. The bloom of the most cultivated life, the fragrance of fantasy, together with the spice of spirit, breathe forth united from his works. He is no longer painter, he is philosopher, he is poet at once. Wisdom stands at the side of the might of his spirit, and as he represents things, so they are ordered in eternal necessity. In him art has reached its goal, and because the pure equilibrium of the divine and the human can be almost only in One point, the seal of uniqueness is impressed upon his works.

From here the painting, in order to fulfill every possibility grounded in it, could move further only toward One side, and whatever was undertaken in the later renewal of art and in whatever different directions it has made trial, it seems nonetheless that only One has succeeded in closing the circle of the great masters with a kind of necessity. As the new fable of Psyche closes the circle of the old stories of the gods: so painting, through the preponderance it gave to the soul, could still win a new, though not higher, stage of art. Toward this Guido Reni strove, and became the proper painter of the soul. Thither, it seems to us, his whole striving, often uncertain and in many a work losing itself in the indeterminate, must be taken to point, the elucidation of which, besides perhaps a few others, might be given by the masterpiece of his art which is set up, to general admiration, in the great collection of our King. In the figure of the Virgin raised toward heaven everything [p. 321] plastically harsh and severe is effaced to the last trace; indeed does not painting itself seem to soar in her, like the released Psyche freed from the hard forms, on its own wings to transfiguration? Here is no being that subsists outwardly with decided natural force; receptivity and quiet patience express everything in her, down to that easily perishable flesh, whose quality the Italian language designates by the name of *morbidezza*, wholly different from that with which Raphael clothes the Queen of Heaven descending, as she appears to the adoring Pope and a female saint. If the remark is well founded that the model of Guido’s female heads is the Niobe of antiquity, the ground of this resemblance certainly does not lie in a merely arbitrary imitation; perhaps an equal striving led to equal means. If the Florentine Niobe is an extreme for sculpture and the representation of the soul in it, so the image known to us is an extreme for painting, which here dares even to lay aside the need of shade and dark and to work almost with pure light.

If painting, on account of its particular constitution, may be granted a distinct preponderance in laying weight upon the soul, then instruction and teaching will nevertheless do best always to work toward that original center from which alone art can be ever newly generated, whereas on the stage last named it must of necessity stand still or degenerate into restricted mannerism. For even that higher suffering conflicts with the Idea of a perfectly vigorous being, whose image and reflected radiance art is called to show. The right sense will always rejoice to see a being formed worthily and, as far as possible, independently, even on its individual side; indeed, the Godhead would look down with pleasure upon a creature that, endowed with a pure soul, asserted the loftiness of its nature also vigorously outwardly and through its sensuously effective existence.

We have seen how, out of the depth of nature, the work<sup>64</sup> [p. 322] of art, growing up with determinateness and delimitation, begins, unfolds inner infinity and fullness, finally is [p. 323] transfigured into grace, and last of all arrives at the soul; but what in the creative act of art matured to ripeness is only one deed had to be represented as separated.

<sup>64</sup> This whole treatise demonstrates the basis of art, and therefore also of beauty, in the vitality of nature; what, however, is the doctrine of present-day philosophy is, as is well known, always better known to public critics than to its authors. Thus we learned recently, through the medium of a journal otherwise deservedly esteemed, from such a connoisseur that, according to the newest aesthetics and philosophy — (a far-reaching concept into which well-known half-connoisseurs from the common herd throw together everything displeasing, presumably so as to overthrow it the better) — there is only artistic beauty, but no natural beauty. We should like now to ask where the newest philosophy, and likewise aesthetics, has advanced such an assertion, did we not recall at this moment what concept judges of this kind are accustomed to connect with the word nature, especially in art. The critic cited, moreover, means no harm by that opinion itself; rather he seeks to come to its aid by a rigorous proof, in the idioms and forms of the newest philosophy. Let us listen to the excellent proof! “The beautiful is the appearance of the divine in the earthly, of the infinite in the finite. Nature is indeed also an appearance of the divine, but this nature — which has existed since the beginning of time and will endure to the end of days, as the wellinformed man expresses it more closely — does not appear to the human spirit, and only in its infinity is it beautiful.” — Take this infinity as we will, there is here the contradiction that beauty is the appearance of the infinite in the *finite*, and yet nature is supposed to be beautiful only in its infinity. Yet doubting himself, the connoisseur objects that every part of a beautiful work is surely also still beautiful, e.g. the hand or the foot of a *beautiful* statue. But (so he resolves the doubt) where do we have the hand or the foot of such a colossus (of nature, namely)? The philosophical connoisseur hereby makes known the worth and the sublimity of his concept of the infinity of nature. He finds it in the immeasurable extension. That a true, essential infinity is in every part of matter is an exaggeration to which the fairminded man certainly does not rise, though he speaks the language of the newest philosophy. And that man, for example, might well be something more than merely the hand and foot of nature — perhaps rather the eye —, and that hand and foot besides might well still be found — could not even be thought without extravagance. Accordingly the question itself seems not to have appeared annihilating enough to him, and the proper philosophical exertion only now begins. It is indeed true, says the excellent man, that everything individual in nature is an appearance of the eternal and divine — surely in this individual? — ; but the whole appears not *as divine*, but as earthly and perishable. — That is what one may call philosophical art! As at the command Apparais and Disparais the shadows in a shadow-play come and go, so the divine appears in the earthly, and also again does not appear, as the artist wills. But this is only the prelude to a following chain of inferences, whose links are worthy of special distinction. 1) “The individual, *as* *such*, presents nothing but an image of becoming and perishing — and indeed not the Idea of becoming and perishing, but an example of it, in that it becomes and perishes.” (One could say likewise of a *beautiful* painting that it presents an example of becoming and perishing, for this too only gradually begins to receive its coloration, then darkens and is attacked by smoke, dust, worms, or moths). 2) “Now, however, in nature there appears *nothing* but the individual” (a moment ago, however, everything individual was an appearance of the divine in the individual). 3) Thus nothing in nature can be beautiful, because the divine, which surely must appear enduringly and abidingly (in time, of course!), would have to appear enduringly and abidingly in the earthly in order that there be beauty, whereas in nature there is nothing but the individual, hence the perishable. Glorious proof! It suffers only from a few defects, of which only two shall be mentioned. The assertion no. 2, that in nature nothing appears but the individual; but before, there were, where now there is nothing but the individual, three things: A) the divine, B) the individual in which it appears, C) what has come to be in this combination, at once divine and earthly. Now, however, the modest man, who a moment before beheld his countenance in the mirror of the newest philosophy, forgets entirely how it was fashioned. He now sees of A, B, and C only B, of which it is of course easy to prove that it is not the beautiful, since by his own declaration only C was supposed to be that. He will not, on the contrary, wish to say that C does not *appear*; for he had already meant otherwise. For A (the divine) does not appear for itself, but only through the individual, B; hence in C. B, however, is at all only insofar as A appears in it, hence also only in C; C, then, is precisely the one thing that truly appears. — The second defect lies in the subordinate clause inserted in the conclusion, though only with half assurance, almost only as a query: that the divine, as such, must surely appear abidingly and enduringly! Evidently the well-oriented man has confounded the Idea of the eternal in itself, without all time, with the concept of what remains in time and endlessly endures, and demands the latter when he is to see the former. Well, if the divine can appear only in the endlessly continuing, let him see where he can prove an appearance of it in art, hence something artistically beautiful. — It cannot fail that this thoroughly instructed man at another time goes off and perhaps does not reproach others for the misuse of the newest philosophy without ground, through which sequence of potencies of ever better understanding the understanding, as one easily sees, must ever further thrive.

[p. 324] This spiritual generative power no doctrine or instruction can create. It is the pure gift of nature, which here closes for the second time, in that, wholly actualizing itself, it lays its creative power into the creature. But as in the great course of art those stages appeared one after another until on the highest they all became One, so too in the individual solid cultivation can spring forth only where it has lawfully risen from the germ and from the root up to the blossom.

The demand that art, like everything else living, must proceed from first beginnings and, in order to rejuvenate itself livingly, must ever anew return to them, may seem a hard doctrine in an age to which it has been said so variously how it can take the most cultivated beauty already finished from existing works of art and so, as if with a single step, attain the final goal. Do we not already have the excellent, the perfected, and how should we return to the primitive, the uncultivated? Had the great founders of modern art thought likewise, we should probably never have seen their wonders. Before them too there stood creations of the ancients, round sculptures and works in bas-relief, which they could have transferred directly into paintings. But this appropriation of what was<sup>65</sup> [p. 325] not acquired by themselves and therefore also of an uncomprehended beauty did not satisfy an artistic drive that went wholly to the original, and from which the beautiful was to generate itself anew, freely and with primal force. They did not therefore shrink from appearing simple, artless, dry beside those sublime ancients, and from nurturing art long in an inconspicuous bud until the time of grace had come. Whence comes it that we still now regard these works of older masters, from Giotto down to the teacher of Raphael, with a kind of devotion, indeed with a certain partiality, if not because the fidelity of their endeavor and the great earnestness of their quiet, voluntary restrictedness extort from us esteem and admiration? As these stood toward the [p. 326] ancients, so stands toward them the present generation. No living tradition, no bond of organically grown cultivation unites their time and ours: we must re-create art on its own path, but with a peculiar power of our own, in order to become equal to them. Even that late summer of art at the end of the sixteenth and the beginning of the seventeenth century could indeed call forth a few new blossoms on the old trunk, but no fruitful germs, still less plant a new trunk of art. To set aside the perfected works of art, however, and to seek out their still simple, plain beginnings in order to imitate them, as some have wished, this would be only a new and perhaps greater misunderstanding; they themselves would not have gone back to the original, the simplicity too would be affectation, and would become hypocritical semblance.

<sup>65</sup> That this, namely that monuments of ancient art stood before the founders of modern painting, cannot be asserted even of the first or oldest of them. For as the worthy *Fiorillo* expressly remarks in his history of the drawing arts, part I, p. 69, in the times of Cimabue and Giotto no ancient paintings and statues had yet been rediscovered; they lay neglected under the earth. “No one could therefore think of forming himself on the models which the ancients have left us, and the sole object of study for painters was nature. In the works of Giotto, the pupil of Cimabue, one notices that he had already consulted it diligently.” On this path, which could prepare for the antique and lead nearer to it, people went on after his example until, as the same historian remarks on p. 286, the house of Medici (namely with Cosmo) began to seek out monuments of ancient art. “Before that the artists had to content themselves with the beauties which nature offered them, yet this diligent observation had the advantage that a more scientific treatment of art was thereby prepared, and the philosophical artists who followed, a da Vinci and a Michelangelo, began to investigate the enduring laws underlying the appearances of nature.” — But even the rediscovery of the ancient works of art in the age of these masters and that of Raphael by no means had as its consequence the imitation of them in the sense that came up only later. Art remained true to the path once taken and perfected itself wholly out of itself; taking nothing from without into itself, but striving in its own manner toward the goal of those models, and coinciding with them only at the last point of perfection. Only with the times of the *Carraccis* did imitation of the antique, which means something quite different from the formation of one’s own sense after their spirit, become a formal principle, and passed especially through *Poussin* into the art theory of the French, who have for almost all higher things a merely literal understanding. Thereupon, through *Mengs* and through misunderstanding of the ideas of *Winkelmann*, the same became native with us too, and brought German art in the middle of the last century such a languor and spiritlessness, with such oblivion of the original sense, that even individual revolts against it were mostly again only misunderstood feeling, which led from one mania of imitation into another still worse. Who can deny that in the most recent times a far freer and more peculiar sense has again shown itself in German art, which, if everything concurred, afforded great hopes, and perhaps let one expect the spirit that would open in art the same higher and freer way that has been entered upon in poetry and the sciences, and on which alone an art could come to be that we could truly call *our own*, i.e. an art of the spirit and of the powers of *our* *people and our age*.

Yet what prospect would the present time offer for an art growing up from a fresh kernel and from the root? For this art is, after all, to a great extent dependent on the sense of its age, and who would promise such earnest beginnings the applause of the present, where those have on the one hand scarcely attained equal esteem with other instruments of prodigal luxuriance, and on the other artists and amateurs, with complete incapacity to grasp nature, praise and demand the ideal?

Art springs only from the lively movement of the innermost powers of heart and spirit, which we call inspiration. Everything that has grown from heavy or small beginnings to great power and height has become great through inspiration. So with empires and states, arts and sciences. But it is not the power of the individual that accomplishes it; only the spirit that spreads through the whole. For art in particular is dependent, like the more delicate plants on air and weather, so on public mood; it requires a general enthusiasm for sublimity and beauty, like that which in the Medicean age, like a warm breath of spring, called forth all the great spirits at once and on the spot, a constitution such as Pericles depicts for us in [p. 327] the praise of Athens, and which the mild rule of a paternal regent grants us more securely and more lastingly than popular government; where every power stirs freely, every talent shows itself with pleasure, because each is esteemed only according to its worthiness; where inactivity is a disgrace, vulgarity brings no praise, but an exalted, extraordinary goal is striven for. Only when public life is set in motion by the very same powers by which art rises, only then can art draw advantage from it; for it cannot, without giving up the nobility of its nature, direct itself toward anything external. Art and science can both move only about their own axis; the artist, like everyone who works spiritually, can only follow the law that God and nature have written in his heart, no other. No one can help him, he must help himself; so too he cannot be rewarded externally, since what he did not bring forth for its own sake would at once be void; for that very reason, too, no one can command him or prescribe the way he is to walk. If he is to be pitied when he has to struggle with his age, he deserves contempt when he is its slave. And how could he even manage this? Without great general enthusiasm there are only sects, no public opinion. Not an established taste, not the great concepts of a whole people, but the voices of individual, arbitrarily raised judges decide on merit, and art, which in its loftiness is self-sufficient, courts applause and becomes servile, when it ought to rule.

Different ages are granted a different inspiration. May we expect none for this age, since the new world now forming, as it already exists partly outwardly and partly inwardly and in the heart, can no longer be measured by any standards of previous opinion, but everything rather loudly demands greater ones and proclaims a complete renewal? Should not that sense to which nature and history have opened themselves more livingly again also give back to art its great subjects? To draw sparks from the ashes of what has sunk away, and to rekindle [p. 328] from them a general fire is a vain endeavor. But only a change that takes place in the Ideas themselves is capable of raising art out of its exhaustion; only a new knowing, a new faith is able to inspire it to the labor through which it would reveal, in a rejuvenated life, a splendor like the former. An art that in all determinations would be the same as that of earlier centuries, to be sure, will never come again; for nature never repeats itself. Such a Raphael will not be again, but another, who has attained the highest in art in an equally peculiar way. Only let that fundamental condition not fail, and the art coming to life again will, like the earlier, show in its first works the goal of its destiny: in the formation of the determinate characteristic already, it proceeds otherwise out of a fresh primal power, grace is present, though veiled, in both the soul is already predetermined. Works that originate in such a way are, even in initial imperfection, already necessary, eternal works.

We may confess it, in that hope of a new revival of a wholly peculiar art we have chiefly the fatherland in view. Already at the very time that reawakened art in Italy, there had sprung from native soil the full-grown growth of the art of our great Albrecht Dürer; how peculiarly German, and yet how akin to that one whose sweet fruits the milder sun of Italy brought to the highest ripeness. This people, from which the revolution of the way of thinking in modern Europe has gone forth, whose power of spirit the greatest inventions attest, which has given laws to the heavens and has explored the earth most deeply of all, in which nature has implanted an unperturbed sense for what is right and an inclination to the cognition of first causes more deeply than in any other, this people must end in a peculiar art.

If the fates of art depend on the general fates of the human spirit, with what hopes may we regard the nearest fatherland, where an exalted regent has given freedom to the [p. 329] human understanding, wings to the spirit, effectiveness to humane ideas, while solid peoples still preserve the living germs of old artistic endowment, and the renowned seats of old German art have been united with it. Indeed the arts and sciences themselves, were they otherwise banished everywhere, would seek a refuge under the protection of the throne on which mild wisdom wields the scepter, which grace as queen beautifies, hereditary love of art glorifies, through which also the young prince, whom in these days the loud jubilation of the grateful fatherland has received, has become the admiration of foreign nations. Here they would find the seeds of a future vigorous existence everywhere strewn, here the already proven common spirit and, fixed amid the change of times, at least the bond of One love and One general enthusiasm, for the fatherland and for the king, for Whose welfare and preservation to the furthest term of human years hotter wishes can rise in no temple than in this one which *He* has built for the sciences.

[p. 330]

[p. 331]

## Philosophische Untersuchungen über das Wesen der menschlichen Freiheit und die damit zusammenhängenden Gegenstände. — Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom and the Matters Connected Therewith

1809.

[p. 332]

[p. 333]

#### Vorbericht<sup>66</sup> — Preliminary Remarks<sup>66</sup>

<sup>66</sup> These remarks originally formed a part of the preface to Schelling’s *Philosophische Schriften*, first volume, Landshut 1809, where the treatise first appeared. The Editor.

Concerning the following treatise the author has only little to remark.

Since reason, thinking, and cognizing are reckoned first of all among the essence of spiritual nature, the opposition of nature and spirit was, quite fairly, considered first from this side. The firm belief in a merely human reason, the conviction of the complete subjectivity of all thinking and cognizing and of the utter reasonlessness and thoughtlessness of nature, together with the mechanical mode of representation prevailing everywhere, since even the dynamic, awakened anew by Kant, passed over once again into merely a higher form of the mechanical and was by no means recognized in its identity with the spiritual, sufficiently justify this course of consideration. That root of the opposition has now been torn out, and the consolidation of a more correct insight can calmly be left to the general progress toward better cognition.

It is time that the higher, or rather the proper, opposition should step forth, that of necessity and freedom, with which the innermost center of philosophy first comes into view.

Since the author, after the first general exposition of his system (in the *Zeitschrift für speculative Physik*), the continuation of which was unfortunately interrupted by external circumstances, confined himself solely to investigations in the [p. 334] philosophy of nature —and since, following the beginning made in the work *Philosophy and Religion*, which admittedly remained obscure through the fault of the presentation, the present treatise is the first in which the author sets forth his concept of the ideal part of philosophy with complete definiteness — he must, if that first exposition should have had any importance, place this treatise right beside it, which, already by the nature of its subject, must contain deeper disclosures about the whole of the system than all the more partial expositions.

Although the author had never before explained himself anywhere on the main points that are taken up in it, on freedom of the will, good and evil, personality, etc. (the single work *Philosophy and Religion* excepted), this has not prevented opinions about them, quite unsuited even to the content of this work — which, as it seems, has *not* been heeded at all — from being attributed to him at the pleasure of others. Unauthorized so-called followers, too, ostensibly according to the author’s principles, may have put forward much that is perverse about these matters as about others.

Followers in the proper sense, it seems, could indeed only have a finished, completed system. The author has never set up such a thing up to now, but has shown only individual sides of one (and even these often only in a single, e.g. polemical, relation); he has thus declared his writings fragments of a whole, whose coherence a finer gift of observation than is found among importunate adherents, and a better will than is usually found among opponents, was required to perceive. The one scientific exposition of his system, since it was not completed, has, in its proper tendency, been understood by no one, or by very few. Immediately after the appearance of this fragment there began slander and falsification on the one side, and on the other, elucidating, reworking, and translating, of which the translation into a supposedly more ingenious language (since at the same time a wholly unsteady poetic frenzy had taken possession of people’s heads) was the [p. 335] worst kind. Now a healthier time seems again to be setting in. What is faithful, diligent, and heartfelt is again being sought. People are beginning to recognize generally for what it is the emptiness of those who have strutted about with the maxims of the new philosophy like French stage heroes, or carried on like rope-dancers; at the same time the others, who sang off the newly snatched-up thing in all the marketplaces as to a barrel organ, have at last aroused such a general disgust that they will soon find no public any more; especially if, of every unintelligent rhapsody in which a few turns of phrase of a well-known writer have been put together, it is not said by otherwise well-meaning critics that it was composed according to his principles. Let them rather treat every such person as an original, which at bottom everyone wants to be, and which in a certain sense quite many also are.

May this treatise, then, serve to put down much prejudice on the one side, and much loose and idle chatter on the other.

Finally, we wish that those who have attacked the author from this side, openly or covertly, might now also set forth their opinion as frankly as it has been done here. If complete mastery over one’s subject makes possible its free and artful elaboration, still the artificial screw-windings of polemic cannot be the form of philosophy. But still more we wish that the spirit of a common striving may consolidate itself more and more, and that the sectarian spirit that only too often dominates the Germans may not hinder the attainment of a cognition and view whose perfect development has from of old seemed destined for the Germans, and which was perhaps never nearer to them than now.

Munich, March 31, 1809.

[p. 336] Philosophical investigations into the essence of human freedom can concern, on the one hand, the correct concept of it, inasmuch as the fact of freedom, however immediately the feeling of it is impressed upon everyone, nevertheless by no means lies so much on the surface that, in order even merely to express it in words, more than ordinary purity and depth of mind would not be required; on the other hand, they can concern the connection of this concept with the whole of a scientific view of the world. Since, however, no concept can be determined singly, and the demonstration of its connection with the whole first gives it its final scientific completion — which must be the case in an especial way with the concept of freedom, which, if it has reality at all, must be no merely subordinate or secondary concept, but one of the ruling centers of the system — these two sides of the investigation here, as everywhere, coincide. According to an old, yet by no means faded, saying, the concept of freedom is indeed supposed to be incompatible with system in general, and every philosophy laying claim to unity and totality is supposed to end in a denial of freedom. It is not easy to dispute against general assurances of this kind; for who knows what restrictive representations have already been bound up with the word *system*, so that the assertion states something very true, to be sure, but also something very common. Or is this the meaning, that the concept of system in general and in itself conflicts with the concept of freedom: then it is strange [p. 337] that, since the individual freedom in some way after all coheres with the world-whole (no matter whether this be thought realistically or idealistically), some system, at least in the divine understanding, must be present with which freedom coexists. To assert in general that this system can never attain to the insight of the human understanding is again to assert nothing; since, depending on how it is understood, the statement can be true or false. It depends on the determination of the principle with which man cognizes at all; and one would have to apply to the assumption of such a cognition what Sextus says with reference to Empedocles: the grammarian and the ignorant man may represent it as springing from boasting and from exaltation over other men, qualities which must be foreign to anyone who has even only a slight practice in philosophy; but whoever proceeds from physical theory and knows that it is a quite ancient doctrine that like is cognized by like (which is said to derive from Pythagoras, but is met with in Plato, though it was pronounced much earlier by Empedocles), will understand that the philosopher asserts such a (divine) cognition because he alone, keeping the understanding pure and undimmed by malice, comprehends the God outside himself with the God within himself . But<sup>67</sup> among those who are averse to science it is once for all customary to understand by it a cognition which, like that of ordinary geometry, is wholly abstracted and lifeless. Shorter or more decisive would be to deny the system also in the will or understanding of the primordial being; to say that there are only individual wills at all, each of which constitutes a center for itself, and, in Fichte’s expression, the I of each is the absolute substance. Yet reason, pressing for unity, like the feeling insisting on freedom and personality, will always be rejected only by a peremptory fiat, which holds out for a while and at last comes to grief. Thus the Fichtean doctrine [p. 338] had to attest its recognition of unity, if even in the meager shape of a moral world-order, whereby, however, it immediately fell into contradictions and untenabilities. It seems, therefore, that however much can be adduced for that assertion from the merely historical standpoint, namely from the systems hitherto — (grounds drawn from the essence of reason and cognition itself we have found nowhere) — the connection of the concept of freedom with the whole of the world-view will probably always remain the object of a necessary task, without whose resolution the concept of freedom itself would waver and philosophy would be wholly without value. For this great task alone is the unconscious and invisible mainspring of all striving after cognition from the lowest to the highest; without the contradiction of necessity and freedom not philosophy alone, but every higher willing of the spirit would sink into the death that is proper to those sciences in which it finds no application. To extricate oneself from the affair by abjuring reason, however, seems more like flight than victory. With the same right another could turn his back on freedom in order to throw himself into the arms of reason and necessity, without there being on the one side or the other a cause for triumph.

<sup>67</sup> Sext. Empir. adv. Grammaticos L. I, c. 13, p. 283. ed. Fabric.

Expressed more definitely, the same opinion was put in the proposition: the only possible system of reason is pantheism, but this unavoidably fatalism . It is undeniably an excel-<sup>68</sup> lent invention, this business of such general names, with which whole views are designated at once. Once one has found the right name for a system, the rest follows of itself, and one is relieved of the trouble of examining its peculiarity more closely. Even the ignorant man can, as soon as they are [p. 339] merely given to him, with their help pass judgment on the most profoundly thought things. Yet with so extraordinary an assertion everything depends on the more precise determination of the concept. For it can hardly be denied that, if pantheism meant nothing more than the doctrine of the immanence of things in God, every view of reason must in some sense be drawn to this doctrine. But precisely the sense makes the difference here. That the fatalistic sense can be combined with it is undeniable; but that it is not essentially combined with it is evident from the fact that so many were driven to that view precisely by the liveliest feeling of freedom. Most, if they were honest, would confess that, as their representations are constituted, individual freedom seems to them to be in contradiction with almost all the attributes of a supreme being, e.g. with omnipotence. Through freedom a power unconditioned in principle is asserted outside of and beside the divine, which according to those concepts is unthinkable. As the sun in the firmament extinguishes all the lights of heaven, so, and still much more, does infinite power extinguish every finite one. Absolute causality in one being leaves to all others only unconditioned passivity. To this is added the dependence of all beings of the world on God, and that even their continuance is only a constantly renewed creation, in which the finite being is yet produced not as something indeterminate and general, but as this determinate, individual one, with such and no other thoughts, strivings, and actions. To say that God holds back his omnipotence so that man may act, or that he permits freedom, explains nothing: if God withdrew his power for a moment, man would cease to be. Is there any other way out against this argumentation than to rescue man with his freedom, since it is unthinkable in opposition to omnipotence, into the divine essence itself, to say that man is not outside of God but in God, and that his activity itself belongs to the life of God? It is precisely from this point that mystics and religious hearts of all times have arrived at the belief in the unity of man with God, which seems to accord with the most inward feeling just [p. 340] as much or even more than with reason and speculation. Yes, Scripture itself finds in the very consciousness of freedom the seal and pledge of the belief that we live and are in God. How, then, can *that* doctrine necessarily conflict with freedom which so many have asserted with regard to man, precisely in order to rescue freedom?

<sup>68</sup> Earlier assertions of the kind are known. Whether the utterance of Fr. Schlegel in the work *Ueber die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier*, p. 141: “pantheism is the system of pure reason,” could perhaps have another sense, we leave undecided.

Another explanation of pantheism, one commonly believed to hit the mark more closely, is indeed this: that it consists in a complete identification of God with things, a commingling of the creature with the creator, from which a host of other harsh and intolerable assertions are derived. But a more total distinction of things from God than is found in Spinoza, accepted as the classic for that doctrine, can hardly be thought. God is that which is in itself and is comprehended solely from itself; the finite, however, is that which is necessarily in another, and can be comprehended only from this. Evidently, according to this distinction, things are not, as might indeed seem from the superficially regarded doctrine of the modifications, different from God merely in degree or through their limitations, but *toto genere*. Whatever may otherwise be their relation to God, they are absolutely separated from God by the fact that they can be only in and after an Other (namely Him), that their concept is a derived one, which would not be possible at all without the concept of God; whereas, on the contrary, He is the sole self-subsistent and original one, the sole self-affirming one, to which everything else can relate only as the affirmed, only as consequence to ground. Only under this presupposition do other properties of things hold, e.g. their eternity. God is eternal by his nature; things only with him and as consequence of his existence, i.e. in a derived way. Precisely because of this difference, all individual things together cannot, as is commonly alleged, make up God, since by no kind of summing up can that which is derived by its nature pass over into that which is original by its nature, any more than the individual points of [p. 341] a periphery, taken together, can make up the latter, since as a whole it necessarily precedes them according to the concept. Still more absurd is the inference that in Spinoza even the individual thing must be equal to God. For even if the strong expression, that every thing is a modified God, were found in him, the elements of the concept are so contradictory that it immediately dissolves again in the summing up. A modified, i.e. derived, God is not God in the proper, eminent sense; through this single addition the thing returns again to its place, through which it is eternally separated from God. The ground of such misinterpretations, which other systems too have experienced in abundant measure, lies in the general misunderstanding of the law of identity, or of the sense of the copula in the judgment. Though it is easy to make comprehensible even to a child that in no possible proposition which, according to the accepted explanation, asserts the identity of the subject with the predicate, is a sameness or even merely an unmediated connection of the two asserted — since, e.g., the proposition: this body is blue, does not have the sense that the body is also blue in that and through that in which and through which it is body, but only that the same thing which this body is is also blue, though not in the same respect — this presupposition, which betrays a complete ignorance of the essence of the copula, has nonetheless been made constantly in our time with regard to the higher application of the law of identity. Let the proposition, e.g., be set up: the perfect is the imperfect; then the sense is: the imperfect is not imperfect through the fact that and wherein it is imperfect, but through the perfect that is in it; but for our time it has this sense: the perfect and the imperfect are one and the same, everything is alike, the worst and the best, folly and wisdom. Or: the good is evil, which is as much as to say: evil has not the power to be through itself; that which is in it is (considered in and for itself) the good: this is then interpreted thus: the eternal difference between right and wrong, virtue and vice, is denied, [p. 342] both are logically the same, or if in another turn necessary and free are declared to be one, the sense of which is: the same thing (in the last instance) which is the essence of the ethical world is also the essence of nature, this is understood thus: the free is nothing but a natural force, a spring, which like every other is subject to mechanism. The same happens with the proposition that the soul is one with the body; which is interpreted thus: the soul is material, air, ether, nerve-fluid, and the like, whereas the converse, that the body is soul, or, in the previous proposition, that the apparently necessary is in itself a free thing, although it is just as well to be taken from the proposition, is carefully set aside. Such misunderstandings, which, if they are not intentional, presuppose a degree of dialectical immaturity beyond which Greek philosophy had already advanced almost in its first steps, make the recommendation of a thorough study of logic an urgent duty. The old, profound logic distinguished subject and predicate as the antecedent and the consequent (*antecedens et consequens*), and thereby expressed the real sense of the law of identity. Even in the tautological proposition, if it is not to be wholly senseless, this relation remains. Whoever says: the body is body, certainly thinks something other with the subject of the proposition than with the predicate; with the former, namely, the unity, with the latter the individual properties contained in the concept of body, which relate to it as antecedent to consequent. This is precisely the sense of another, older explanation, according to which subject and predicate were opposed as the enfolded and the unfolded (*implicitum et explicitum*) .<sup>69</sup>

<sup>69</sup> Mr. Reinhold, too, who wanted to remodel the whole of philosophy through logic, but who does not seem to know what Leibniz, in whose footsteps he imagines himself to walk, had already said on the occasion of the objections of Wissowatius (*Opp.* T. I ed. Dutens, p. 11) about the sense of the copula, still labors away at this error, by which he confuses identity with sameness. In a sheet lying before us stands the following passage originating from him: “According to the demand of Plato and Leibniz, the task of philosophy consists in demonstrating the subordination of the finite under the infinite, according to the demand of Xenophanes, Bruno, Spinoza, Schelling, in demonstrating the unconditioned unity of both”. Insofar as unity here, in keeping with the opposition, is evidently meant to denote equality, I assure Mr. Reinhold that he is in error, at least as concerns the last two. Where is a sharper expression for the subordination of the finite to the infinite to be found than the above one of Spinoza? The living must take up the cause of the no longer present against defamations, as we expect that in a like case those living after us will do in regard to ours. I speak only of Spinoza, and ask what one is to call this procedure: to assert, about systems, without knowing them thoroughly, offhand whatever one finds good, as though it were just a trifle to impute this or that to them? In ordinary ethical society it would be called *unconscionable*. — According to another passage in the same paper, the basic error of all more recent philosophy, just as of the older, lies for Mr. R. in the failure to distinguish (confusion, mix-up) unity (identity) from connection (nexus), and likewise diversity (diversitas) from distinction. It is not the first instance of Mr. R.’s finding in his opponents the very faults that he has brought along to them. It seems to be the way in which he applies the necessary Medicina mentis to himself; as one will have examples of persons of excitable imagination who have recovered through medicines that they let others take for them. For who commits this error of confusing — that which he calls unity, but which is sameness — with connection, in relation to older and newer philosophy, more definitely than Mr. R. himself, who construes the being-comprehended of things in God, in Spinoza, as asserted *equality* of both, and who generally takes non-diversity (according to substance or essence) for a non-distinction (according to form or logical concept). If Spinoza is really to be understood as Mr. Reinhold interprets him, then the well-known proposition that the thing and the concept of the thing are one would also have to be understood as if one could, e.g., defeat the enemy with the concept of an army instead of with an army, etc., consequences to which the earnest and thoughtful man himself certainly finds himself too good.

[p. 343] But, the defenders of the above assertion will now say, in pantheism it is not a question at all of God’s being everything (which, given the usual representation of his attributes, is hardly to be avoided), but of the fact that things are nothing, that this system cancels all individuality. It seems indeed that this new determination stands in contradiction with the previous one; for if things are nothing, how is it possible [p. 344] to mix God with them at all? There is then everywhere nothing but pure, untroubled Godhead. Or, if outside God (not merely extra, but also praeter Deum) nothing is, how can he be All otherwise than in mere word; so that the whole concept seems altogether to dissolve and to evaporate into nothing. Besides, it is questionable whether much is gained by the resurrection of such general names, which may indeed be held in honor in the history of heresy, but for productions of spirit, in which, as in the most delicate phenomena of nature, slight determinations cause essential changes, seem far too coarse handles. It might still be doubted whether even to Spinoza the determination last given is applicable. For if he recognizes outside (praeter) the substance nothing but the mere affections of it, as which he declares things, then this concept is indeed a purely negative one, which expresses nothing essential or positive. But it serves also merely to determine in the first instance the relation of things to God, not however what they may be when considered in themselves. From the lack of this determination, however, it cannot be concluded that they contain nothing positive at all (albeit always in a derivative way). Spinoza’s harshest expression is probably this: that the individual being is the substance itself, considered in one of its modifications, i.e. consequences. Let us now posit the infinite substance = A, the same considered in one of its consequences = A/a: then the positive in A/a is indeed A; but it does not follow that therefore A/a = A, i.e. that the infinite substance considered in its consequence is *the same* as the infinite substance considered absolutely; or in other words, it does not follow that A/a is not a particular substance of its own (albeit a consequence of A). This is of course not found in Spinoza; but first, the subject here is pantheism in general; and then the only question is whether the view given is in itself incompatible with Spinozism. One will hardly assert this, since it has been conceded [p. 345] that the monads of Leibniz, which are entirely what A/a is in the above expression, are no decisive means against Spinozism. Enigmatic, without a supplement of this kind, remain many utterances of Spinoza, e.g. that the essence of the human soul is a living concept of God, which is declared eternal (not transitory). If therefore the substance dwelt in its other consequences A/b, A/c . . . . only transitorily, it would nonetheless dwell eternally in that consequence, the human soul = a, and hence as A/a be separated in an eternal and imperishable way from itself as A.

If one wished to go further and declare the denial — not of individuality, but — of freedom to be the proper character of pantheism, then a multitude of systems that otherwise differ essentially from it would also fall under this concept. For until the discovery of Idealism the proper concept of freedom is lacking in all more recent systems, in the Leibnizian just as in the Spinozistic; and a freedom such as many among us have conceived, who moreover pride themselves on the liveliest feeling of it, according to which it consists, that is, in the mere dominion of the intelligent principle over the sensuous and the desires, such a freedom could be derived, not with difficulty but quite easily and even more definitely, from Spinoza as well. It seems, therefore, that the denial or assertion of freedom in general rests on something entirely different from the acceptance or non-acceptance of pantheism (of the immanence of things in God). For if it indeed seems at first glance as if freedom, which could not maintain itself in opposition to God, went under here in identity, one can nonetheless say that this semblance is only a consequence of the imperfect and empty representation of the law of identity. This principle expresses no unity which, revolving in the circle of sameness, would be non-progressive and for that reason itself insensate and lifeless. The unity of this law is an immediately [p. 346] creative one. Already in the relation of the subject to the predicate we have shown that of ground to consequence, and the law of ground is therefore as original as that of identity. The eternal must therefore immediately, and just as it is in itself, also be ground. That of which it is by its essence the ground is to that extent a dependent and, in the view of immanence, also something comprehended in it. But dependence does not cancel self-subsistence, does not even cancel freedom. It does not determine the essence, and says only that the dependent, whatever it may be, can be only as consequence of that on which it is dependent; it does not say what it is, and what it is not. Every organic individual, as something that has become, is only through another, and to that extent dependent in becoming, but by no means in being. It is not absurd, says Leibniz, that he who is God should at the same time be begotten, or conversely, just as it is no contradiction that he who is the son of a man should himself be man. On the contrary, were the dependent or consequent not self-subsistent, this would be rather contradictory. It would be a dependence without a dependent, a consequence without a consequent (Consequentia absque Consequente), and hence also no real consequence, i.e. the whole concept would cancel itself. The same holds of being-comprehended in another. The individual member, such as the eye, is possible only in the whole of an organism; none the less it has a life for itself, indeed a kind of freedom, which it evidently proves through the disease of which it is capable. Were that which is comprehended in another not itself alive, there would be a comprehendedness without anything comprehended, i.e. nothing would be comprehended. A far higher standpoint is afforded by the consideration of the divine essence itself, whose Idea would wholly contradict a consequence that is not begetting, i.e. positing of a self-subsistent being. God is not a God of the dead, but of the living. It is not to be seen how the most perfect being should find its pleasure even in the most perfect possible machine. However one may conceive the manner of the consequence of beings from God, it can never be a mechanical one, no mere effecting or placing [p. 347] there, whereby the effected is nothing for itself; nor, equally, emanation, whereby what flows out would remain the same as that from which it has flowed, hence nothing of its own, self-subsistent. The consequence of things from God is a self-revelation of God. But God can become revealed only in that which is similar to him, in free beings acting from themselves; for whose being there is no ground but God, but who are, even as God is. He speaks, and they are there. Were all world-beings even only thoughts of the divine heart, they would have to be alive for that very reason. Thus thoughts are indeed begotten by the soul; but the begotten thought is an independent power, continuing to work for itself, indeed, in the human soul, growing so that it subdues its own mother and subjects her to itself. But the divine imagination, which is the cause of the specification of the world-beings, is not like the human, in that it bestows on its creations merely ideal actuality. The representations of the Godhead can only be self-subsistent beings; for what is it that limits our representations other than that we see what is not self-subsistent? God beholds things in themselves. In itself is only the eternal, resting on itself, will, freedom. The concept of a derived absoluteness or divinity is so little contradictory that it is rather the middle concept of the whole of philosophy. Such a divinity belongs to nature. So little does immanence in God contradict freedom, that precisely only the free, and insofar as it is free, is in God, the unfree, and insofar as it is unfree, necessarily outside God.

However inadequate even for one who sees more deeply such a general deduction is in itself, so much nevertheless emerges from it, that the denial of formal freedom is not necessarily bound up with pantheism. We do not expect that Spinozism will be set against us. It takes no little heart to assert that the system, as it has come together in any man’s head, is the system of reason *κατ’ ἐξοχήν*, the eternal, unchangeable one. What does one understand then by Spinozism? Perhaps the whole doctrine as it lies before us in [p. 348] the writings of the man, hence e.g. also his mechanical physics? Or according to what principle does one wish to separate and divide here, where everything is supposed to be so full of extraordinary and unique consistency? It will always remain a striking phenomenon in the history of German intellectual development that at some time the assertion could be put forward: the system which mixes God with things, the creature with the creator (so it was understood) and subjects everything to a blind, thoughtless necessity, is the only one possible to reason — to be developed from pure reason! To comprehend it, one must call to mind the dominant spirit of an earlier age. At that time the mechanical way of thinking, which in French atheism climbed to the summit of its impiety, had by degrees taken hold of all heads; in Germany too one began to hold this way of seeing and explaining to be the proper and sole philosophy. Since however originally German heart could never reconcile the consequences of it with itself, there arose first the rift between head and heart, characteristic of the philosophical literature of recent times: one abhorred the consequences, without being able to free oneself from the ground of the way of thinking itself or to raise oneself to a better one. Yet one wanted to speak out these consequences; and since the German spirit could grasp mechanical philosophy only at its (supposed) highest expression, there was thus pronounced the dreadful truth: all philosophy, absolutely all, that is only purely rational, is or becomes Spinozism! Everyone was now warned against the abyss; it lay openly exposed before all eyes; the only means still seeming possible was seized; that bold word could bring on the crisis and frighten the Germans back from pernicious philosophy in general, lead them back to the heart, inner feeling, and faith. Today, when that way of thinking is long past, and the higher light of Idealism shines on us, the same assertion would neither be comprehensible in the same degree, nor promise the same consequences.<sup>70</sup>

<sup>70</sup> Mr. Fr. Schlegel’s advice, which in a review of Fichte’s more recent writings in the Heidelbergischen Jahrb. der Literatur (year 1, no. 6, p. 139) he gives to the latter, to hold in his polemical undertakings exclusively to Spinoza, because in him alone the system of pantheism, thoroughly complete according to form and consistency — which according to the utterance cited above would at the same time be the system of pure reason — is to be met with; this advice may indeed otherwise offer certain advantages, but nevertheless becomes odd in that Mr. Fichte is without doubt of the opinion that he has already refuted Spinozism (as Spinozism) through the Wissenschaftslehre, in which he is also quite right. — Or is Idealism perhaps no work of reason, and does the supposedly sad honor of being a system of reason really remain only with pantheism and Spinozism?

[p. 349] And here, then, once and for all our determinate opinion about Spinozism! This system is not fatalism because it lets things be comprehended in God; for, as we have shown, pantheism at least does not make formal freedom impossible; Spinoza must therefore be a fatalist on an entirely different ground, independent of that. The error of his system lies by no means in his placing things in *God*, but in this, that they are *things* — in the abstract concept of world-beings, indeed of the infinite substance itself, which for him too is a thing. Hence his arguments against freedom are entirely deterministic, in no way pantheistic. He treats the will too as a thing, and proves then very naturally that in every case of acting it must be determined by another thing, which again is determined by another, and so on ad infinitum. Hence the lifelessness of his system, the heartlessness of the form, the poverty of concepts and expressions, the unrelenting harshness of the determinations, which agrees admirably with the abstract way of consideration; hence also, quite consistently, his mechanical view of nature. Or does one doubt that through the dynamic representation of nature alone the fundamental views of Spinozism must be essentially altered? If the doctrine of the being-comprehended of all things in God is the ground of the whole system, it must at the least first be enlivened and wrested from abstraction before it can become the principle of a system of reason. How general are the expressions, that [p. 350] finite beings are modifications or consequences of God; what a gulf is here to be filled, what questions are to be answered! One could regard Spinozism in its rigidity as the statue of Pygmalion, which would have to be ensouled by the warm breath of love; but this comparison is imperfect, since it rather resembles a work sketched only in the outermost outlines, in which, if it were ensouled, one would first notice the many missing or unexecuted features. Rather would it be comparable to the oldest images of the deities, which appeared the more mysterious, the fewer individually living features spoke out of them. In one word, it is a one-sidedly realistic system, an expression which sounds less damning than pantheism, but nevertheless designates far more correctly what is peculiar to it, and is also not used now for the first time. It would be tiresome to repeat the many explanations to be found on this point in the first writings of the author. Reciprocal interpenetration of realism and Idealism was the avowed aim of his endeavors. The Spinozistic fundamental concept, spiritualized by the principle of Idealism (and altered in one essential point), received in the higher mode of regarding nature and the recognized unity of the dynamic with what belongs to the heart and to spirit a living basis, from which philosophy of nature grew, which as mere physics could indeed subsist for itself, but in relation to the whole of philosophy was always regarded only as the one, namely the real part of it, which only through the supplementation with the ideal, in which freedom rules, would become capable of elevation into the proper system of reason. In this (freedom), it was asserted, is found the last potentiating act, whereby the whole of nature is transfigured into sensation, into intelligence, finally into will. — There is in the last and highest instance no other being than willing. Willing is primal being, and to this alone all predicates of it apply: groundlessness, eternity, independence of time, self-affirmation. The whole of philosophy strives only to find this highest expression.

Up to this point philosophy in our time has been raised [p. 351] through Idealism: and only with this can we properly take up the investigation of our subject, since it could by no means be our intention to take into consideration all those difficulties that can be raised, and long since have been raised, out of the one-sidedly realistic or dogmatic system against the concept of freedom. But Idealism itself, however high we are placed by it in this respect, and however certain it is that we owe to it the first perfect concept of formal freedom, is nevertheless in itself anything but a completed system, and leaves us, as soon as we want to enter into the more exact and determinate, nevertheless helpless in the doctrine of freedom. In the first respect we remark that in Idealism developed into a system it by no means suffices to assert “that activity, life and freedom alone are what is truly actual,” with which even the subjective (self-misunderstanding) Idealism of Fichte can stand; rather it is required to show also conversely that everything actual (nature, the world of things) has activity, life and freedom for its ground, or, in the Fichtean expression, that not only is I-hood everything, but also conversely everything is I-hood. The thought of making freedom once for all the one and all of philosophy has set the human spirit in general, not merely in relation to itself, in freedom, and has given to science in all its parts a more vigorous impetus than any earlier revolution. The idealistic concept is the true consecration for the higher philosophy of our time and especially for its higher realism. Would that those who judge this or appropriate it would consider that freedom is its innermost presupposition; in how entirely different a light would they regard and grasp it! Only he who has tasted freedom can feel the desire to make everything analogous to it, to spread it over the whole universe. He who does not come to philosophy by this path merely follows and imitates what others do; without feeling why they do it. It will however always remain remarkable that Kant, after having first distinguished things in themselves [p. 352] from appearances only negatively, through independence of time, and afterwards in the metaphysical discussions of his Critique of Practical Reason having treated independence of time and freedom actually as correlative concepts, did not go on to the thought of transferring this only possible positive concept of the in-itself also to things, whereby he would have raised himself immediately to a higher standpoint of consideration and above the negativity that is the character of his theoretical philosophy. From the other side, however, if freedom is the positive concept of the in-itself in general, the inquiry into human freedom is thrown back again into the universal, in that the intelligible, on which alone it has been grounded, is also the essence of things in themselves. In order, therefore, to show the specific difference, i.e. precisely what is determinate in human freedom, mere Idealism does not suffice. Equally it would be an error to suppose that pantheism is canceled and annihilated by Idealism; an opinion that could arise only from confusion of it with one-sided realism. For whether it is individual things that are comprehended in one absolute substance, or just as many individual wills comprehended in a primal will, is for pantheism, as such, entirely the same. It is in the first case realistic, in the other idealistic, but the fundamental concept remains the same. From this it is already to be seen provisionally that the deepest difficulties which lie in the concept of freedom will be as little soluble through Idealism taken by itself as through any other partial system. Idealism gives, namely, on the one hand only the most general, on the other the merely formal concept of freedom. The real and living concept, however, is that it is a capacity for the good and for evil.

This is the point of deepest difficulty in the whole doctrine of freedom, which has been felt from time immemorial, and which affects not merely this or that system but, more or [p. 353] less, all : Most strikingly, to be sure, the concept of<sup>71</sup> immanence; for either a real evil is conceded, in which case it is unavoidable to posit evil in the infinite substance or the primal will itself, whereby the concept of a most perfect being is wholly destroyed; or else the reality of evil must in some way be denied, whereby at the same time the real concept of freedom vanishes. Not less, however, is the difficulty if even only the most remote connection is assumed between God and the world-beings; for if this is limited even to the mere so-called concursus, or to that necessary cooperation of God in the acting of the creature, which by virtue of the essential dependence of the latter on God must be assumed even if freedom is otherwise asserted: even so God appears undeniably as co-author of evil, since permitting in the case of an entirely dependent being is not much better than co-causing; or else the reality of evil must likewise in one way or another be denied. The proposition that everything positive in the creature comes from God must be asserted in this system as well. If it is now assumed that there is something positive in evil, then this positive too comes from God. Against this it can be objected: the positive of evil, insofar as it is positive, is good. With that evil does not vanish, though neither is it explained. For if the *existent* in evil is good, whence then is that *wherein* this existent is, the *basis*, which properly constitutes evil? Quite different from this assertion (though often, recently too, confounded with it) is that which says that in evil there is nothing positive at all, or, expressed otherwise, that it does not exist at all (not even with and on another positive), but all actions are more or less positive, and the difference between them a mere plus and minus of perfection, whereby no opposition is grounded, and hence evil altogether [p. 354] disappears. This would be the second possible assumption with regard to the proposition that everything positive comes from God. Then the force that shows itself in evil would indeed be comparatively more imperfect than that which shows itself in the good, but in itself, or considered apart from the comparison, still itself a perfection, which therefore, like every other, must be derived from God. What we call evil in it is only the lesser degree of perfection, which however appears as a deficiency only for our comparison, in nature is none. It cannot be denied that this is the true opinion of Spinoza. Someone might try to escape that dilemma by the answer: the positive that comes from God is freedom, which in itself is indifferent to evil and good. But if he thinks this indifference not merely negatively, but as a living positive capacity for the good and for evil, then it is not to be seen how from God, who is considered as pure goodness, a capacity for evil could follow. It becomes evident from this, to say in passing, that if freedom is really what it must be according to this concept (and it unfailingly is), then it would probably be the case with the derivation of freedom from God attempted above that it lacks validity; for if freedom is a capacity for evil, it must have a root independent of God. Driven by this one may be tempted to throw oneself into the arms of dualism. But this system, if it is really conceived as the doctrine of two absolutely different and mutually independent principles, is only a system of self-laceration and despair of reason. If, however, the evil basic being is in any sense conceived as dependent on the good, then the whole difficulty of the descent of evil from the good is indeed concentrated on one being, but thereby rather increased than diminished. Even if it is assumed that this second being was created good at first and fell away from the primordial being through its own guilt, the first capacity for a deed resisting God remains inexplicable [p. 355] in all previous systems. Hence, if one were even finally to cancel not only identity but every connection of the world-beings with God, and to regard their whole present existence and thus that of the world as a distancing from God, the difficulty would merely be pushed one point further, but not canceled. For in order to be able to flow out from God they must already have existed in some way, and least of all could therefore the doctrine of emanation be set against pantheism, since it presupposes an original existence of things in God and thus evidently presupposes the latter. For the explanation of that distancing, however, only the following could be assumed. It is either an involuntary one on the part of the things, but not on the part of God: then they are thrust by God into the state of unblessedness and wickedness, God therefore is author of this state. Or it is involuntary on both sides, caused perhaps by overflow of essence, as some express it: a wholly untenable representation. Or it is arbitrary on the part of the things, a tearing loose from God, therefore the consequence of a guilt, upon which an ever deeper sinking follows: then this first guilt is itself already evil, and so affords no explanation of its origin. Without this auxiliary thought, however, which, if it explains evil in the world, on the other hand extinguishes the good entirely, and instead of pantheism introduces a pandemonism, there vanishes precisely in the system of emanation every proper opposition of the good and evil; the first loses itself through infinitely many intermediate stages, by gradual attenuation, into that which has no semblance of the good any more, much as Plotinos subtly but<sup>72</sup> unsatisfactorily describes the transition of the original good into matter and evil. Namely, through a constant subordination and distancing a last thing comes forth, beyond which nothing more can come to be, and this very thing (that which is incapable of further producing) is evil. Or: if something exists after the first, there must also be a last, which has nothing more of the first in itself, and this is matter and the necessity of evil.

<sup>71</sup> Mr. Fr. Schlegel has the merit of having, in his work on India and in several places, asserted this difficulty especially against pantheism; whereby it is merely to be regretted that this acute scholar has not seen fit to communicate his own view of the origin of evil and its relation to the good.

<sup>72</sup> Ennead. I, L. VIII, c. 8.

[p. 356] In view of these considerations it seems hardly fair to throw the whole burden of this difficulty on one system alone, especially since the supposedly higher doctrine that is set against it satisfies so little. Nor can the generalities of idealism provide any help here. With such abstracted concepts of God as actus purissimus, of the kind the older philosophy put forward, or with those which the more recent philosophy, out of a solicitude to remove God as far as possible from all nature, keeps producing again and again, nothing whatever can be accomplished. God is something more real than a mere moral world-order, and has within himself quite different and more living motive forces than the meager subtlety of abstract idealists ascribes to him. The abhorrence of everything real, which supposes that the spiritual is contaminated by any contact with it, must naturally also make the eye blind to the origin of evil. Idealism, if it does not take a living realism as its basis, becomes a system just as empty and abstracted as that of Leibniz, or Spinoza, or any other dogmatic one. The whole of modern European philosophy since its beginning (with Descartes) has this common defect, that nature does not exist for it, and that it lacks a living ground. Spinoza’s realism is thereby just as abstract as the idealism of Leibniz. Idealism is the soul of philosophy; realism its body; only the two together make up a living whole. The latter can never furnish the principle, but it must be the ground and means in which the former realizes itself and takes on flesh and blood. If a philosophy lacks this living foundation, which is usually a sign that the ideal principle too was originally only weakly effective in it, then it loses itself in those systems whose abstracted concepts of aseity, modifications, etc., stand in the sharpest contrast to the life-force and fullness of actuality. But where the ideal principle does work powerfully to a high degree, yet cannot find the reconciling and mediating basis, there it generates a turbid and wild enthusiasm which breaks out in self-laceration, or, as with the priests of the Phrygian goddess, in [p. 357] self-castration, which in philosophy is accomplished by the surrender of reason and science.

It seemed necessary to begin this treatise with the rectification of essential concepts which have always, but especially of late, been thrown into confusion. The remarks so far are therefore to be regarded as a mere introduction to our proper inquiry. We have already declared: only from the principles of a true philosophy of nature can that view be developed which fully satisfies the task at hand. We do not deny, on that account, that this correct view has not long since been present in individual minds. But it was precisely these who, without fear of the terms of abuse that have always been customary against all real philosophy — materialism, pantheism, etc.— sought out the living ground of nature, and, in opposition to the dogmatists and abstract idealists, who expelled them as mystics, were philosophers of nature (in both senses).

The philosophy of nature of our time was the first to establish in science the distinction between essence insofar as it exists and essence insofar as it is merely ground of existence. This distinction is as old as the first scientific presentation of that philosophy . Although this is precisely the point<sup>73</sup> at which it diverges most decisively from the path of Spinoza, it could nevertheless be maintained in Germany up to the present time that its metaphysical principles are one and the same as those of Spinoza; and although it is precisely this distinction that at the same time brings about the most definite distinction of nature from God, this did not prevent people from accusing it of confusing God with nature. Since it is the same distinction on which the present inquiry is grounded, let the following be said here by way of elucidation.

<sup>73</sup> See the same in the Zeitschrift für spekulative Physik, vol. II, no. 2, § 54, Remark [IV, p. 146]; further Remark 1 to § 93 and the explanation p. 114. [= p. 203.]

Since nothing is before or outside God, he must have the ground of his existence in himself. All philosophies say this; [p. 358] but they speak of this ground as a mere concept, without making it into something real and actual. This ground of his existence, which God has in himself, is not God considered absolutely, that is, insofar as he exists; for it is only the ground of his existence, it is the *nature* — in God; an essence inseparable from him, to be sure, but yet distinct. By way of analogy this relation can be elucidated through that of gravity and light in nature. Gravity precedes light as its eternally dark ground, which is itself not actu, and flees into the night as the light (the existent) arises. Even light does not wholly loosen the seal under which gravity lies enclosed . It is for that very<sup>74</sup> reason neither the pure essence nor even the actual being of the absolute identity, but follows only from its nature ; or <sup>75</sup> *is* it, namely considered in the determinate potency: for otherwise even that which relatively to gravity appears as existing belongs in itself again to the ground, and nature in general is therefore everything that lies beyond the absolute being of the absolute identity . As for that preceding, it is to be<sup>76</sup> thought neither as a preceding in time nor as a priority of essence. In the circle out of which everything becomes, it is no contradiction that that through which the One is generated is itself in turn generated by it. Here there is no first and no last, because everything presupposes everything else reciprocally, none being the other and yet none being without the other. God has in himself an inner ground of his existence, which to that extent precedes him as existing; but just so God is in turn the prius of the ground, inasmuch as the ground, even as such, could not be if God did not exist actu.

<sup>74</sup> Loc. cit. pp. 59, 60. [= p. 163].

<sup>75</sup> Ibid. p. 41. [= p. 146].

<sup>76</sup> Ibid. p. 114. [= p. 203].

The consideration proceeding from things leads to the same distinction. First, the concept of immanence is to be set aside entirely, insofar as it is supposed to express a dead being-conceived of things in God. We recognize, rather, that [p. 359] the concept of becoming is the only one appropriate to the nature of things.
