But they cannot become in God, considered absolutely, since they are toto genere, or to speak more correctly, infinitely different from him. To be separated from God, they must become in a ground different from him. But since nothing can be outside God, this contradiction can be resolved only by the things having their ground in that which in God himself is not *He Himself* , that is, in that which is the<sup>77</sup> ground of his existence. If we wish to bring this essence closer to us in human terms, we can say: it is the longing which the eternal One feels to give birth to itself. It is not the One itself, but is nevertheless equally eternal with it. It wills to give birth to God, that is, the unfathomable unity, but to that extent the unity is not yet in it itself. Considered for itself, it is therefore also will; but a will in which there is no understanding, and therefore not an independent and perfect will, since understanding is properly the will in the will. Nevertheless it is a willing of the understanding, namely its longing and desire; not a conscious will, but a presaging one, whose presage is the understanding. We are speaking of the essence of longing considered in and for itself, which must indeed be kept in view, although it has long since been displaced by the higher that has risen out of it, and although we cannot grasp it sensibly, but only with the spirit and in thought. After the eternal act of self-revelation, namely, everything in the world as we now behold it is rule, order, and form; but the rule-less still always lies in the ground, as if it might break through again at some time, and nowhere does it seem as if order and form were the original, but as if an initially rule-less had been brought to [p. 360] order. This is in things the incomprehensible basis of reality, the remainder that never resolves, that which cannot be dissolved into understanding even with the greatest effort, but remains eternally in the ground. Out of this understanding-less the understanding is born in the proper sense. Without this preceding darkness there is no reality of the creature; gloom is its necessary inheritance. God alone — He Himself the existent — dwells in pure light, for he alone is of himself. Man’s self-conceit rebels against this origin from the ground, and even seeks out ethical grounds against it. And yet we would know of nothing that could spur man on more to strive with all his powers toward the light than the consciousness of the deep night out of which he has been raised into existence. The womanish complaints that in this way the understanding-less is made the root of the understanding, night the beginning of light, rest, to be sure, partly on a misunderstanding of the matter (in that one does not grasp how, with this view, the priority of understanding and essence can nevertheless subsist in respect of the concept); but they express the true system of present-day philosophers, who would gladly make fumum ex fulgore, for which, however, even the most violent Fichtean precipitation does not suffice. All birth is birth from darkness into light; the seed-corn must be sunk into the earth and die in the gloom, so that the more beautiful figure of light may rise and unfold in the sunbeam. Man is formed in the mother’s womb; and out of the darkness of the understanding-less (out of feeling, longing, the glorious mother of cognition) the luminous thoughts first grow. Thus, then, we must represent to ourselves the original longing, how it directs itself toward the understanding, which it does not yet recognize, as we in longing yearn for an unknown, nameless good, and moves in presage, like a surging, billowing sea, like the matter of Plato, according to a dark, uncertain law, unable to form anything lasting for itself. But corresponding to longing, which as the still dark ground is the first stirring of divine existence, there is generated in God himself an inner reflexive representation, through which, since it can [p. 361] have no other object than God, God beholds himself in an image of himself. This representation is the first in which God, considered absolutely, is realized, although only in himself; it is in the beginning with God, and is the God begotten *in* God himself. This representation is at the same time the understanding — the *Word* of that longing , and the eternal<sup>78</sup> spirit, who feels the Word within himself and at the same time the infinite longing, moved by the love which he himself is, utters the Word; so that the understanding now, together with longing, becomes freely creating and almighty will and forms in the initially rule-less nature as in its element or instrument. The first effect of the understanding in it is the separation of forces, since only thereby is it able to unfold the unity contained in it unconsciously, as in a seed, yet necessarily, just as in man the dark longing to create comes into light in that, in the chaotic medley of thoughts, which all cohere but each of which hinders the others from emerging, the thoughts separate and now the unity lying concealed in the ground, comprehending all under itself, arises; or as in the plant the dark bond of gravity loosens only in proportion to the unfolding and expansion of the forces, and the unity concealed in the separated matter is developed. For since this essence (of the original nature) is nothing other than the eternal ground for the existence of God, it must contain within itself, though enclosed, the essence of God, as it were, as a glance of life shining in the darkness of the depth. But longing, aroused by the understanding, now strives to retain the glance of life seized within it, and to shut itself up within itself, so that a ground may always remain. Since, then, the understanding, or the light set into the original nature, arouses the longing that strives back into itself to the separation of forces (to the abandonment of darkness), but in this very separation brings forth the unity enclosed in the separated, the concealed glance of light, there arises in this way first something comprehensible and individual, and indeed not [p. 362] through external representation, but through true *in-formation* (*Ein-Bildung*), in that what arises is formed into nature, or, more correctly still, through awakening, in that the understanding brings forth the unity or Idea concealed in the separated ground. The forces separated in this division (but not wholly asunder) are the matter out of which the body is afterwards configured; but the living bond arising in the separation, that is, out of the depth of the natural ground, as the center of the forces, is the soul. Because the original understanding brings forth the soul out of a ground independent of it as something inward, it remains for that very reason itself independent of it, as a particular essence subsisting for itself.

<sup>77</sup> This is the only right dualism, namely that which at the same time admits a unity. Above, mention was made of the modified dualism according to which the evil principle is not coordinate with the good but subordinate to it. It is hardly to be feared that anyone will confuse the relation set forth here with that dualism in which the subordinate is always an essentially evil principle and for that very reason remains wholly incomprehensible as to its descent from God.

<sup>78</sup> In the sense in which one says: the word of the riddle.

It is easy to see that, given the resistance of longing, which is necessary for perfect birth, the innermost bond of the forces loosens only in a gradual unfolding, and at each degree of the separation of forces a new essence arises out of nature, whose soul must be the more perfect the more it contains separated what in the others is still unseparated. To show how each successive process draws nearer to the essence of nature, until in the highest separation of forces the innermost center arises, is the task of a complete philosophy of nature. For the present purpose only the following is essential. Each of the beings that have arisen in nature in the manner indicated has a twofold principle in itself, which is nevertheless at bottom only one and the same, considered from the two possible sides. The first principle is that whereby they are separated from God, or whereby they are in the mere ground; but since between that which is in the ground and that which is prefigured in the understanding there is yet an original unity, and the process of creation goes only to an inner transmutation or transfiguration of the initially dark principle into light (because the understanding, or the light set into nature, in the ground properly seeks only the light akin to it and turned toward it): the principle that is dark by its nature is precisely that which at the same time is transfigured into light, and the [p. 363] two are, though only in a determinate degree, one in every natural being. The principle, insofar as it springs from the ground and is dark, is the self-will of the creature, which, however, insofar as it is not yet raised to perfect unity with the light (as principle of the understanding) (does not grasp it), is mere craving or desire, that is, blind will. Opposed to this self-will of the creature stands the understanding as universal will, which uses the former and subordinates itself as a mere instrument. But when at last, through progressive transformation and separation of all forces, the innermost and deepest point of the original darkness in a being is wholly transfigured into light, then the will of this being is, to be sure, insofar as it is an individual, likewise a particular will, but in itself, or as the center of all other particular wills, one with the primal will or the understanding, so that out of both there now becomes a single whole. This raising of the very deepest center into light occurs in none of the creatures visible to us except in man. In man is the whole power of the dark principle and, in the same man, at the same time the whole force of light. In him is the deepest abyss and the highest heaven, or both centers. The will of man is the germ, hidden in the eternal longing, of the God present as yet only in the ground; the divine glance of life enclosed in the depth, which God beheld when he conceived the will for nature. In him (in man) alone God loved the world; and it is just this image of God that longing seized in the center when it entered into opposition with the light. Man, by springing from the ground (being creaturely), has in himself a principle relatively independent of God; but because this very principle — without ceasing on that account to be dark in respect of the ground — is transfigured into light, there arises at the same time in him something higher, the *spirit*. For the eternal spirit utters the unity, or the Word, into nature. But the uttered (real) word is only in the unity of light and dark (vowel and consonant). Now in all things, to be sure, the two principles are present, but without perfect consonance because of the deficiency of what has been raised out of the [p. 364] ground. Only in man, then, is the word, still held back and incomplete in all other things, fully uttered. But in the uttered word spirit reveals itself, that is, God as existing actu. Since the soul is the living identity of both principles, it is spirit; and spirit is in God. Were the identity of both principles in the spirit of man just as indissoluble as in God, there would be no distinction, that is, God as spirit would not become manifest. That unity which is inseparable in God must therefore be separable in man, — and this is the possibility of good and of evil.

We say expressly: the possibility of evil, and seek in the first place only to make the separability of the principles comprehensible. The actuality of evil is the subject of an entirely different inquiry. The principle raised up out of the ground of nature, whereby man is separated from God, is the selfhood in him, which, however, through its unity with the ideal principle becomes spirit. Selfhood *as such* is spirit, or man is spirit as a selfish, particular being (separated from God), which connection precisely constitutes personality. But in that selfhood is spirit, it is at the same time lifted out of the creaturely into the supercreaturely, it is will that beholds itself in complete freedom, no longer an instrument of the universal will creating in nature, but above and outside all nature. Spirit is above light, just as in nature it raises itself above the unity of light and of the dark principle. Because it is spirit, then, selfhood is free from both principles. Now, however, this selfhood or self-will is spirit, and accordingly free, or above nature, only in that it is actually transformed into the primal will (the light), so that it indeed remains (as self-will) still in the ground (because there must always be a ground) — just as in the transparent body the matter raised to identity with light does not on that account cease to be matter (dark principle) — but only as bearer and, as it were, receptacle of the higher principle of light. But because it has the spirit (since the latter rules [p. 365] over light and darkness) — if, namely, it is not the spirit of eternal love — selfhood can separate itself from the light, or self-will can strive to be, as particular will, what it is only in identity with the universal will, to be also in the periphery or as creature what it only is insofar as it remains in the center (just as the quiet will in the still ground of nature is for that very reason also universal will, because it remains in the ground) (for the will of creatures is indeed outside the ground; but it is then also a mere particular will, not free, but bound). Thereby, then, there arises in the will of man a separation of the selfhood that has become spiritual (since spirit stands above light) from the light, that is, a dissolution of the principles indissoluble in God. If, on the contrary, the self-will of man remains in the ground as central will, so that the divine relation of the principles subsists (as the will in the center of nature never rises above the light, but remains beneath it as basis in the ground), and if, instead of the spirit of discord, which wants to divide the particular principle from the universal, the spirit of love holds sway in him, then the will is in divine manner and order. — That this very elevation of self-will is evil, is evident from what follows. The will that steps out of its supernaturalness in order to make itself, as universal will, at once particular and creaturely, strives to invert the relation of the principles, to raise the ground above the cause, to use the spirit, which it has received only for the center, outside it and against the creature, from which derangement ensues in it itself and outside it. The will of man is to be regarded as a bond of living forces; so long as it itself remains in its unity with the universal will, these forces too subsist in divine measure and equilibrium. But no sooner has self-will itself departed from the center as its proper place than the bond of forces too has departed; in its stead there rules a mere particular will, which can no longer unite the forces under itself, as the original will did, and which must therefore strive to form or compose out of the forces that have departed from one another, the rebellious host of [p. 366] appetites and desires (since each individual force is also a craving and desire), a life of its own and apart, which is possible insofar as even in evil the first bond of the forces, the ground of nature, still continues to subsist. But since it can yet be no true life, as such could subsist only in the original relation, there arises indeed a life of its own, but a false life, a life of falsehood, a growth of unrest and corruption. The most striking analogy is offered here by sickness, which, as the disorder that has entered nature through the misuse of freedom, is the true counter-image of evil or sin. Universal sickness never occurs without the concealed forces of the ground opening up: it arises when the irritable principle, which should rule in the stillness of the depth as the innermost bond of the forces, actuates itself, or the aroused Archeus leaves its quiet dwelling in the center and enters the circumference. Just as, on the other hand, all original healing consists in the restoration of the relation of periphery to center, and the transition from sickness to health can properly occur only through the opposite, namely the taking up again of the separated and individual life into the inner glance of light of the essence, from which the separation (crisis) again ensues. Particular sickness too arises only in that what has its freedom or its life only on condition that it remain in the whole strives to be for itself. As sickness, indeed, is nothing essential and properly only a semblance of life and a merely meteoric appearance of it — a wavering between being and nonbeing — and yet announces itself to feeling as something very real, so it is with evil.

This sole correct concept of evil, according to which it rests on a positive perversity or inversion of the principles, has in recent times been brought forward again especially by Franz Baader, and elucidated through profound physical analogies, namely that of disease .<sup>79</sup>

<sup>79</sup> In the essay “On the Assertion That No Bad Use of Reason Can Be,” in the Morgenblatt 1807, no. 197, and “On the Rigid and the Fluid,” in the Jahrbücher der Medicin als Wissenschaft, vol. III, no. 2. For comparison and further elucidation, let the relevant remark at the end of that essay, p. 203, also be set down here: “An instructive disclosure is given here by common fire (as wild, consuming, painful glow) in contrast to the so-called organic, beneficent glow of life, in that *here* fire and water enter together into one (growing) ground, or into conjunction, whereas *there* they step apart in discord. Now neither fire nor water was present as such, that is, as separated spheres in the organic process, but the former was present as center (mysterium), the latter as open or periphery in it, and precisely the unlocking, elevation, and kindling of the first together with the locking-up of the second gave disease and death. Thus, in general, I-hood, individuality is indeed the basis, the foundation or natural center of every creaturely life; but as soon as it ceases to be a serving center and enters ruling into the periphery, it burns in the latter as the tantalizing wrath of selfishness and egoism (of kindled I-hood). From ⊙ there now becomes O — that is: at one single place of the planetary system that dark center of nature is locked up, latent, and for that very reason serves as bearer of light for the entry of the higher system (ray of light or revelation of the ideal). For that very reason, then, this place is the open point (sun — heart — eye) in the system — and were the dark center of nature to rise or open there as well, the point of light would thereby be locked up, the light would turn into darkness in the system, or the sun would be extinguished!”

[p. 367] All other explanations of evil leave the understanding and the ethical consciousness equally unsatisfied. At bottom they all rest on the annihilation of evil as a positive opposite and on its reduction to the so-called malum metaphysicum, or to the negating concept of the imperfection of the creature. It was impossible, says Leibniz, for God to impart all perfection to man without making him God himself; the same holds of created beings in general; hence there had to be different degrees of perfection and all kinds of limitation of it. If one asks whence evil comes, the answer is: from the ideal nature of the creature, insofar as it depends on the eternal truths contained in the divine understanding, but not on the will of God. The region of the eternal truths is the ideal cause of evil and of the good, and must be put in the [p. 368] place of the matter of the ancients . There are, he says<sup>80</sup> in another passage, indeed two principles, but both in God, namely the understanding and the will. The understanding furnishes the principle of evil, though it does not thereby itself become evil; for it represents natures as they are according to the eternal truths; it contains within itself the ground of the permission of evil, but the will aims solely at the good .<sup>81</sup> This sole possibility God has not made, since the understanding is not its own cause . If this distinction of understanding<sup>82</sup> and will as two principles in God, whereby the first possibility of evil is made independent of the divine will, accords with the ingenious manner of this man, and if even the representation of the understanding (of the divine wisdom) as something in which God behaves rather passively than actively points to something deeper, then the evil that can descend merely from that purely ideal ground in turn amounts to something merely passive, to limitation, lack, privation, concepts that wholly contradict the proper nature of evil. For the simple reflection that it is man, the most perfect of all visible creatures, who alone is capable of evil, shows that the ground of evil can by no means lie in lack or privation. The devil, according to the Christian view, was not the most limited creature but rather the most unlimited .<sup>83</sup> [p. 369] Imperfections in the general metaphysical sense are not the usual character of evil, since it often shows itself united with an excellence of the individual powers that far more seldom accompanies the good. The ground of evil must therefore lie not merely in something positive in general, but rather in the highest positive that nature contains, as it indeed is on our view, since it lies in the revealed center, or primal will, of the first ground. Leibniz tries in every way to make comprehensible how evil can arise from a natural lack. The will, he says, strives for the good in general and must demand perfection, whose highest measure is in God; but if it remains entangled in the pleasures of the senses with the loss of higher goods, then precisely this lack of further striving is the privation in which evil consists. Otherwise, he thinks, evil requires a special principle as little as cold or darkness does. Whatever is affirming in evil comes into it only incidentally, as force and efficacy come into cold; freezing water bursts the strongest enclosing vessel, and yet cold consists properly in a diminution of motion . But since privation is in itself noth-<sup>84</sup> ing at all, and, even in order to become noticeable, requires something positive in which it appears, there arises the difficulty of explaining the positive that must nevertheless be assumed in evil. Since Leibniz can derive this only from God, he finds himself compelled to make God the cause of the material of sin, and to ascribe only its formal element to the original limitation of the creature. He seeks to elucidate this relation by the concept, found by Kepler, of the natural force of inertia of matter. This, he says, is the perfect image of an original (preceding all action) limitation of the creature. If two different bodies of unequal mass are moved with unequal [p. 370] velocities by the same impulse, then the ground of the slowness of the motion of the one lies not in the impulse, but in the propensity to inertia innate and peculiar to matter, that is, in the inner limitation or imperfection of matter .<sup>85</sup> Here, however, it is to be remarked that inertia itself cannot be thought as a mere privation, but is indeed something positive, namely the expression of the inner selfhood of the body, of the force by which it seeks to assert itself in independence. We do not deny that metaphysical finitude can be made comprehensible in this way; but we deny that finitude in itself is evil .<sup>86</sup>

<sup>80</sup> Tentam. theod. Opp. T. I, p. 136.

<sup>81</sup> Ibid. p. 240.

<sup>82</sup> Ibid. p. 387.

<sup>83</sup> It is striking in this connection that not only the Scholastics, but already several of the earlier Church Fathers, especially Augustine, posited evil as a mere privation. Particularly noteworthy is the passage contr. Jul. L. 1, C. III: Quaerunt ex nobis, unde sit malum? Respondemus ex bono, sed non summo, ex bonis igitur orta sunt mala. Mala enim omnia participant ex bono, merum enim et ex omni parte tale dari repugnat. — — Haud vero difficulter omnia expediet, qui conceptum mali semel recte formaverit, *eumque* *semper defectum aliquem involvere attenderit*, perfectionem autem omnimodam incommunicabiliter possidere Deum; neque magis possibile esse, creaturam illimitatam adeoque independentem creari, quam creari alium Deum.

<sup>84</sup> Tentam. theod. p. 242.

<sup>85</sup> Ibid. P. I. § 30.

<sup>86</sup> For the same reason every other explanation of finitude, e.g. from the concept of relations, must be insufficient to explain evil. Evil does not come from finitude in itself, but from finitude raised to selfhood.

This kind of explanation arises in general from the lifeless concept of the positive, according to which only privation can stand opposed to it. But there is still a middle concept, which forms a real opposition to it and stands far apart from the concept of the merely negated. This arises from the relation of the whole to the individual, of unity to multiplicity, or however one wishes to express it. The positive is always the whole or unity; what is opposed to it is the dismemberment of the whole, disharmony, ataxy, of the forces. In the dismembered whole there are the same elements that were in the unified whole; the material element is the same in both (from this side evil is no more limited or worse than the good), but the formal element in both is wholly different, and this formal element comes precisely from the essence or positive itself. Hence there must necessarily be in evil, as in the good, an essence, but in the former one opposed to the good, which perverts the temperature contained in it into distemperature. To cognize this essence is impossible for dogmatic philosophy, because it has no concept of personality, that is, of selfhood [p. 371] raised to spirituality, but only the abstracted concepts of the finite and the infinite. Should anyone therefore reply that disharmony is indeed itself a privation, namely a deprivation of unity, then, even if the general concept of deprivation contained that of the cancellation or dissolution of unity, the concept would nonetheless remain insufficient in itself. For it is not the separation of the forces in itself that is disharmony, but their false unity, which can be called a separation only relatively to the true one. If unity is wholly canceled, the conflict is thereby canceled too. Disease is ended by death, and no single tone for itself makes up a disharmony. But to explain that false unity there is need of something positive, which must accordingly necessarily be assumed in evil, but will remain inexplicable as long as a root of freedom in the independent ground of nature is not recognized.

Of the Platonic view, so far as we can judge it, there will be better occasion to speak in the question of the actuality of evil. The representations of our age, which on this point is far shallower and drives philanthropism to the denial of evil, stand in no way connected with such Ideas. According to them the sole ground of evil lies in sensibility, or in animality, or the earthly principle, in that they oppose to heaven, as would be fitting, not hell, but the earth. This representation is a natural consequence of the doctrine according to which freedom consists in the mere dominion of the intelligent principle over the sensuous desires and inclinations, and the good comes from pure reason, whereby, understandably, there is no freedom for evil (since the sensuous inclinations predominate here); or, to speak more correctly, evil is wholly canceled. For the weakness or ineffectiveness of the rational principle can indeed be a ground of the lack of good and virtuous actions, but not a ground of positively evil and vicious ones. But suppose that sensibility, or the passive relation to external [p. 372] impressions, produced evil actions with a kind of necessity; then man would in these actions himself be merely passive, that is, evil would have no significance with regard to him, hence subjectively, and since what follows from a determination of nature cannot objectively be evil either, it would have no significance at all. But to say that the rational principle is ineffective in evil is likewise no ground in itself. For why does it not exercise its power? If it wills to be ineffective, then the ground of evil lies in this will, and not in sensibility. Or if it cannot by any means overcome the resisting power of the latter, then there is here mere weakness and lack, but nowhere an evil. According to this explanation there is therefore only *one* will (if it can be so called), not a twofold one, and one could in this respect call the adherents of it, since the names of the Arians and others have already been successfully introduced into philosophical criticism, by a name likewise taken from church history, though in another sense: the Monothelites. But just as it is by no means the intelligent or light-principle in itself, but that connected with selfhood, that is, raised to spirit, which works in the good, so evil follows not from the principle of finitude for itself, but from the dark or selfish principle brought into intimacy with the center; and as there is an enthusiasm for the good, so there is an inspiration of evil. In the animal, as in every other natural being, that dark principle is indeed also active; but it is not yet born into the light in it, as in man, it is not spirit and understanding, but blind craving and desire; in short, no fall is possible here, no separation of the principles, where there is as yet no absolute or personal unity. The unconscious and the conscious are united in animal instinct only in a certain and determinate way, which for that very reason is unalterable. For precisely because they are only relative expressions of unity, they stand under it, and the force working in the ground preserves the unity of the principles that belongs to them in an always equal relation. The animal can never step out of the [p. 373] unity, whereas man can arbitrarily tear apart the eternal bond of the forces. Hence Fr. Baader rightly says that it would be desirable that the depravity in man went only as far as becoming animal; but, alas, man can stand only below or above the animal .<sup>87</sup>

<sup>87</sup> In the essay cited above, in the Morgenblatt 1807, p. 786.

We have sought to derive the concept and the possibility of evil from the first grounds and to uncover the general foundation of this doctrine, which lies in the distinction between the existing and that which is ground of existence . But pos-<sup>88</sup> sibility does not yet include actuality, and this, properly, is the greatest object of the question. And what is to be explained is not merely how evil becomes actual in the individual man, but its universal efficacy, or how it could have broken forth from creation as an unmistakably universal principle, everywhere in conflict with the good. Since it is undeniably actual, at least as a general opposition, there can indeed be no doubt in advance that it was necessary for the revelation of God; this follows also from what was said earlier. For if God as spirit is the inseparable unity of both principles, and this same unity is actual only in the spirit of man, then, were it just as indissoluble in the latter as in God, man would not be distinguished from God at all; he would be absorbed into God, and there would be no revelation and no mobility of love. For every being can become revealed only in its opposite, love only in hatred, unity in strife. Were there no separation of the [p. 374] principles, unity could not prove its omnipotence; were there no discord, love could not become actual. Man is placed on that summit where he has the source of self-movement toward the good and toward evil equally within himself: the bond of the principles in him is not a necessary but a free one. He stands at the point of parting; whatever he may choose, it will be his deed, but he cannot remain in indecision, because God must necessarily reveal himself, and because in creation generally nothing ambiguous can remain. Yet it seems that he also cannot step out of his indecision, precisely because it is this. There must therefore be a general ground of solicitation, of temptation to evil, were it only in order to make the two principles in him alive, that is, to make him conscious of them. Now the solicitation to evil itself seems able to come only from an evil primordial being, and the assumption of such a being seems nonetheless unavoidable, and that interpretation of the Platonic matter quite correct according to which it is an originally God-resisting and therefore in itself evil being. So long as this part of the Platonic doctrine lies in its present obscurity , a determinate judgment on the point<sup>89</sup> indicated is indeed impossible. In what sense, however, it can be said of the irrational principle that it resists the understanding, or unity and order, without on that account being assumed as an *evil* primordial being, is evident from the earlier considerations. So the Platonic saying too can well be explained, that evil comes from *the old nature*; for all evil strives back into chaos, that is, into that state where the original center was not yet subordinated to the light, and is an upwelling of the center, of the still understandingless longing. But we have proved once and for all that evil, as such, can arise only in the creature, since only in it can light and darkness, [p. 375] or the two principles, be united in a separable way. The original primordial being can never be evil in itself, since in it there is no duality of the principles. Nor can we suppose some created spirit who, himself fallen, solicited man to the fall; for how evil first arose in a creature is precisely the question here. Nothing is therefore given us for the explanation of evil except the two principles in God. God as spirit (the eternal bond of both) is the purest love, and in love there can never be a will to evil; just as little in the ideal principle. But God himself, in order to be, requires a ground, only that this ground is not outside him but in him, and he has in himself a *nature* which, although belonging to him himself, is yet distinct from him. The will of love and the will of the ground are two different wills, each of which is for itself; but the will of love cannot resist the will of the ground, nor cancel it, because otherwise it would have to resist itself. For the ground must work in order that love can be, and it must work independently of it, in order that it may exist really. If love now wished to break the will of the ground, it would be fighting against itself, would be at odds with itself, and would no longer be love. This letting-work of the ground is the only thinkable concept of permission, which in the usual reference to man is wholly untenable. Thus the will of the ground also cannot break love, nor does it demand this, although it often seems so; for, turned away from love, it must be a will of its own and particular, so that love, when it nevertheless breaks through it like the light through the darkness, may appear in its omnipotence. The ground is only a will to revelation, but precisely in order that this may be, it must call forth selfhood and opposition. The will of love and that of the ground thus become one precisely by being separated, and by each working for itself from the beginning. Hence the will of the ground already in the first creation co-excites the self-will of the creature, [p. 376] so that, when spirit now arises as the will of love, this may find something resisting in which it can realize itself.

<sup>88</sup> Augustine says against emanation: nothing can proceed from God’s substance but God; therefore the creature is created out of nothing, whence comes its corruptibility and defectiveness (de lib. arb. L. I, C. 2). That nothing has long been the cross of the understanding. A disclosure is given by the expression of Scripture: that man was created ἐκ τῶν μὴ ὄντων, out of that which is not, as also by the famous μὴ ὄν of the ancients, which, like the creation out of nothing, might first receive a positive significance through the above distinction.

<sup>89</sup> May the excellent interpreter of Plato, or even sooner the worthy Böckh, one day shed light on it; he has already given the best hopes for this by his remarks on the occasion of the Platonic harmonics he set forth and by the announcement of his edition of the Timaeus.

The sight of nature as a whole convinces us of this excitation that has taken place, through which all life first attained the final degree of sharpness and determinateness. The irrational and contingent, which shows itself joined with the necessary in the formation of beings, especially organic ones, proves that it is not merely a geometrical necessity that has been at work here, but that freedom, spirit, and self-will were also in play. To be sure, wherever there is pleasure and desire, there is already in itself a kind of freedom, and no one will believe that the desire that constitutes the ground of every particular life of nature, and the drive to preserve oneself not merely in general but in this determinate existence, was added only afterward to the already created creature, but rather that it was itself the creating agent. Even the concept of the basis, discovered through empirical means, which will take on a significant role for the whole of natural science, must, when scientifically appraised, lead to the concept of selfhood and I-hood. But there are in nature contingent determinations that can be explained only from an excitation of the irrational or dark principle of the creature that took place at the very first creation — only from activated selfhood. Whence, in nature, alongside the preformed ethical relations, the unmistakable portents of evil, if indeed its power was first aroused through man; whence phenomena that, even without regard to their danger to man, nonetheless arouse a general natural abhorrence [p. 377] . That all organic beings go toward dissolution<sup>90</sup> can by no means appear as an original necessity; the bond of the forces that make up life could, by its nature, just as well be indissoluble, and if anything, a creature that by its own forces restores again what has become defective in it seems destined to be a perpetuum mobile. Evil, meanwhile, announces itself in nature only through its effect; itself, in its immediate appearance, it can break forth only at the goal of nature. For just as in the original creation, which is nothing other than the birth of light, the darker principle had to be the ground, so that light could be raised out of it (as out of the mere potency to the actus): so there must be another ground for the birth of spirit, and hence a second principle of darkness, which must be as much higher as spirit is higher than light. This principle is precisely the spirit of evil, awakened in creation through the excitation of the dark ground of nature, that is, of the *disunion* of light and darkness, to which the spirit of love, as formerly light to the unruly motion of the original nature, now opposes a higher Ideal. For just as selfhood in evil has made light or the Word its own, and for that very reason appears as a higher ground of darkness: so the Word spoken into the world in opposition to evil must assume humanity or selfhood, and itself become personal. This happens only through revelation in the most determinate sense of the word, which must have the same stages as the first manifestation in nature, namely such that here too the highest summit of revelation, man, is the archetypal and divine man, he who was with God in the beginning, and in whom all other things and man himself were created. The birth of spirit is the realm of history, as the birth of light is [p. 378] the realm of nature. The same periods of creation, those that are in the one are also in the other; and the one is the likeness and explanation of the other. The same principle that was the ground in the first creation, only in a higher shape, is here too again the germ and seed from which a higher world is developed. For evil is nothing other than the primordial ground to existence, insofar as it strives toward actualization in the created being, and so in fact only the higher potency of the ground working in nature. But as this ground is eternally only ground, without itself being, so evil can never attain realization, and serves merely as ground, so that out of it the good, forming itself out through its own power, might be something independent of God through its ground and separated, in which God might have and cognize himself, and which as such (as something independent) might be in him. But as the undivided power of the original ground is first cognized in man as the inner (basis or center) of an individual, so too in history evil remains at first still hidden in the ground, and the age of guilt and sin is preceded by a time of innocence or of unconsciousness of sin. In the same way, namely, that the original ground of nature perhaps long before worked alone and, with the divine forces contained in it, attempted a creation for itself, which, however, again and again (because the bond of love was lacking) finally sank back into chaos (to which perhaps the series of generations that perished before the present creation and have not returned point), until the Word of love went forth, and with it the enduring creation began: so too in history the spirit of love did not at once reveal itself; rather, because God felt the will of the ground as the will to his revelation, and recognized by his foresight that a ground independent of him (as spirit) must be there for his existence, he let the ground work in its independence, or, to speak otherwise, he himself moved only according to his nature and not according to his heart or love. Because now the ground also contained in itself the whole divine essence, [p. 379] only not as unity, there could be only individual divine beings that held sway in this for-itself-working of the ground. This primeval age therefore begins with the golden age, of which only a faint memory has remained in legend to the present human race, a time of blessed indecision, where there was neither good nor evil; then followed the time of the ruling gods and heroes, or of the omnipotence of nature, in which the ground showed what it could do for itself. At that time understanding and wisdom came to men from the depths alone; the power of oracles springing from the earth guided and formed their life; all the divine forces of the ground ruled on earth, and sat as mighty princes on secure thrones. There appeared the time of the highest glorification of nature in the visible beauty of the gods and all the splendor of art and ingenious science, until the principle working in the ground finally emerged as a world-conquering principle, to subjugate everything to itself and to found a firm and enduring world empire. But because the essence of the ground by itself can never produce true and perfect unity, the time comes when all this glory dissolves, and, as through a terrible disease, the beautiful body of the previous world falls apart, and finally chaos returns. Even before this, and before the complete collapse has arrived, the powers holding sway in that whole assume the nature of evil spirits, just as the very forces that in the time of health were beneficent tutelary spirits of life become, as dissolution approaches, of a malignant and poisonous nature: belief in gods vanishes, and a false magic together with incantations and theurgic formulas strives to call back those who are fleeing, and to appease the evil spirits. More and more determinately the attraction of the ground shows itself, which, sensing in advance the coming light, already beforehand sets all forces out of indecision, in order to meet it in full conflict. As the thunderstorm is aroused mediately by the sun, but immediately by a counteracting force of the earth, so the spirit of evil (whose meteoric nature we have already explained earlier) is aroused by the approach of the good, not by virtue of a communication, but rather through a distribution of forces. Hence only with the [p. 380] decisive emergence of the good does evil too emerge wholly decisively and as such (not as if it first arose, but because only now is the opposition given in which alone it can appear wholly and as such); just as, conversely, the very moment when the earth becomes waste and void for the second time becomes the moment of the birth of the higher light of spirit, which was in the world from the beginning, but not comprehended by the darkness working for itself, and in a revelation still closed off and restricted; and indeed it appears, in order to confront the personal and spiritual evil, likewise in personal, human form and as mediator, in order to restore the rapport of creation with God at the highest stage. For only the personal can heal the personal, and God must become man, so that man may come again to God. With the restored relation of the ground to God, the possibility of healing (of salvation) is first given back. Its beginning is a state of clairvoyance, which by divine dispensation falls upon individual men (as organs chosen for this), a time of signs and wonders, in which divine forces counteract the demonic ones that emerge everywhere, the appeasing unity of the distribution of forces. Finally the crisis follows in the turba gentium, which flood over the ground of the old world, as once the waters of the beginning covered again the creations of the primeval age, in order to make a second creation possible — a new separation of peoples and tongues, a new realm, in which the living Word enters as a firm and enduring center in the struggle against chaos, and a declared strife of good and evil, continuing to the end of the present time, begins, in which God precisely as spirit, that is, as actu actual, reveals himself .<sup>91</sup>

<sup>90</sup> Thus the close connection in which the imagination of all peoples, especially all fables and religions of the Orient, places the serpent with evil is certainly not in vain. The complete development of the auxiliary organs, which has reached its highest degree in man, indicates namely already the independence of the will from the desires, or a relation of center and periphery which alone is truly healthy, in which the first has retreated into its freedom and self-possession, and has separated itself from the merely instrumental (peripheral). Where, on the other hand, the auxiliary organs are not developed or are wholly lacking, there the center has stepped into the periphery, or there is the centerless ring in the passage by Fr. Baader cited above (in the note).

<sup>91</sup> Compare with this whole section the author’s Lectures on the Method of Academic Study, Lecture VIII, on the historical construction of Christianity.

There is, therefore, a *general* evil, though not original but awakened only in God’s revelation from the beginning, [p. 381] through the reaction of the ground, which never comes to realization but constantly strives toward it. Only after cognition of general evil is it possible to comprehend good and evil in man as well. For if already in the first creation evil was aroused along with it and, through the for-itself-working of the ground, finally developed into the general principle, a natural propensity of man toward evil seems already explicable thereby, because the disorder of the forces, once entered through the awakening of self-will in the creature, is communicated to him already at birth. However, the ground continues to work incessantly also in the individual man and arouses selfhood and the particular will, precisely so that, in opposition to it, the will of love may arise. God’s will is to universalize everything, to raise it to unity with the light, or to maintain it therein; but the will of the ground is to particularize everything or to make it creaturely. It wills inequality alone, so that equality may become sensible to itself and to it. Therefore it reacts necessarily against freedom as the supracreaturely and arouses in it the desire for the creaturely, as, for one who is seized by vertigo on a high and steep summit, a secret voice seems to call that he should plunge down, or as, according to the old fable, irresistible siren song resounds from the depths, to draw the passing sailor down into the whirlpool. Already in itself the connection of the universal will with a particular will in man seems a contradiction, whose unification is difficult, if not impossible. The anxiety of life itself drives man out of the center in which he was created; for this, as the purest essence of all willing, is a consuming fire for every particular will; in order to live in it, man must die to all selfhood, which is why it is an almost necessary attempt to step out of it into the periphery, in order to seek there a repose for his selfhood. Hence the general necessity of sin and of death, as the actual dying away of selfhood, through which all human will must pass as through a fire, in order to [p. 382] be purified. In spite of this general necessity, evil remains always man’s *own* choice; evil, as such, the ground cannot make, and every creature falls through its *own* guilt. But precisely how in the individual man the decision for evil or good takes place, this is still wrapped in complete darkness, and seems to require a special investigation.

We have, on the whole, up to now considered the formal essence of freedom less, although insight into it seems to be bound up with no lesser difficulties than the explanation of its real concept.

For the common concept of freedom, according to which it is posited in a wholly indeterminate faculty of willing, of two contradictorily opposed things, without determining grounds, the one or the other, absolutely merely because it is willed, has indeed the original indecision of the human essence in the Idea on its side, but, applied to the individual action, leads to the greatest absurdities. To be able to decide without any moving grounds for A or −A would be, to tell the truth, only a prerogative of acting quite irrationally, and would distinguish man from the well-known animal of Buridan, which according to the opinion of the defenders of this concept of arbitrary choice would have to starve between two heaps of hay of equal distance, size, and quality (because, namely, it does not have that prerogative of arbitrary choice), not in the most excellent way. The only proof for this concept consists in an appeal to the fact, in that, for example, everyone has it in his power to draw in or stretch out his arm now, without further ground; for if one says he stretches it out precisely in order to prove his arbitrary choice, then he could just as well do so by drawing it in; the interest in proving the proposition could only determine him to do one of the two; here, then, the equilibrium is palpable, etc.; a thoroughly bad kind of proof, in that it infers from the not-knowing of the determining ground the non-existence of it, which here, however, would be applicable in just the reverse way; for precisely [p. 383] where not-knowing sets in, being determined takes place all the more certainly. The main point is that this concept introduces a complete contingency of individual actions and in this respect has very rightly been compared with the contingent swerving of the atoms, which Epicurus devised in physics with the same intention, namely, to escape fate. But contingency is impossible, conflicts with reason as with the necessary unity of the whole; and if freedom cannot be saved otherwise than with the complete contingency of actions, then it cannot be saved at all. Opposed to this system of the equilibrium of arbitrary choice, and quite rightly so, is determinism (or, according to Kant, predeterminism), in that it asserts the empirical necessity of all actions on the ground that each of them is determined by representations or other causes that lie in a past time, and which, at the time of the action itself, are no longer in our power. Both systems belong to the same standpoint; except that, if there were once no higher one, the latter would undeniably deserve the preference. Both are equally ignorant of that higher necessity, which is equally far removed from contingency as from compulsion or external determination, which is rather an inner necessity springing from the essence of the agent himself. All improvements, however, that were sought to be introduced in determinism, for example the Leibnizian one, that the moving causes only incline the will but do not determine it, help nothing in the main matter.

Idealism first of all raised the doctrine of freedom into that realm where alone it is intelligible. The intelligible essence of every thing, and especially of man, is, according to this, outside all causal connection, as outside or above all time. It can therefore never be determined by anything preceding, since it itself rather precedes everything else that is or becomes in it, not so much in time as in concept, as an absolute unity, which must always already be there whole and complete, so that the individual action or determination may [p. 384] be possible in it. We express the Kantian concept, namely, not exactly in his words, but nonetheless as we believe it must be expressed in order to be intelligible. But if this concept is accepted, the following also seems to be correctly inferred. The free action follows immediately from the intelligible of man. But it is necessarily a determinate action, for example, to cite the nearest case, a good or an evil one. From the absolutely undetermined to the determinate, however, there is no transition. That the intelligible essence should, out of pure, sheer indeterminateness, without any ground, determine itself, leads back to the above system of the indifference of arbitrary choice. In order to be able to determine itself, it would have to be already determined in itself, not from without, to be sure, which contradicts its nature, nor from within by some merely contingent or empirical necessity, since all this (the psychological as well as the physical) lies beneath it; but itself, as its essence, that is, its own nature, would have to be determination for it. It is, after all, not an undetermined universal, but determinately the intelligible essence of this man; of such a determinateness the saying: Determinatio est negatio, by no means holds, since it is one with the position and the concept of the essence itself, and so is properly the essence in the essence. The intelligible essence can therefore, as certainly as it acts absolutely free and absolute, as certainly act only in accordance with its own inner nature, or the action can follow from its inner being only according to the law of identity and with absolute necessity, which alone is also absolute freedom; for free is what acts only according to the laws of its own essence and is determined by nothing else, neither in nor outside it.

With this representation of the matter at least one thing is gained, that the absurdity of the contingency of the individual action is removed. This must stand firm, even in every higher view, that the individual action follows from the inner necessity of the free essence, and accordingly itself with necessity, which only must not be confused, as still always happens, with the empirical necessity based on compulsion (which [p. 385] is itself only veiled contingency). But what then is that inner necessity of the essence itself? Here lies the point at which necessity and freedom must be united, if they are at all compatible. Were that essence a dead being, and, in regard to man, one merely given to him, then, since the action can follow from it only with necessity, accountability and all freedom would be abolished. But precisely that inner necessity is itself freedom, the essence of man is essentially *his own deed*; necessity and freedom stand within one another, as one essence, which, considered only from different sides, appears as the one or the other, in itself freedom, formally necessity. The I, says Fichte, is its own deed; consciousness is self-positing — but the I is nothing different from this, but precisely the self-positing itself. This consciousness, however, insofar as it is thought merely as self-grasping or cognizing of the I, is not even the first, and, like all mere cognizing, already presupposes actual being. This being presupposed before cognizing is, however, no being, even though it is no cognizing; it is real self-positing, it is a *primal and ground willing*, which makes itself into something and is the ground and the basis of all essentiality.

But in a much more determinate sense than this general one, those truths hold in the immediate relation to man. Man in the original creation is, as shown, an undecided being — (which may be presented mythically as a state of innocence and original bliss preceding this life)—; only he himself can decide. But this decision cannot fall in time; it falls outside all time and therefore coincides with the first creation (though as a deed distinct from it). Man, though he is born in time, is nevertheless created into the beginning of creation (the center). The deed by which his life in time is determined belongs itself not to time, but to eternity: it does not precede life in [p. 386] time either, but goes through time (untouched by it) as a deed eternal by nature. Through it the life of man reaches to the beginning of creation; hence through it he is also, outside the created, free and himself eternal beginning. However inconceivable this Idea may seem to the common way of thinking, there is nevertheless in every man a feeling in agreement with it, as if he had been, what he is, from all eternity, and had by no means first become so in time. Hence, notwithstanding the undeniable necessity of all actions, and although everyone, if he is attentive to himself, must confess that he is by no means contingently or arbitrarily evil or good, the evil man, for example, nonetheless does not at all feel himself compelled (because compulsion can be felt only in becoming, not in being), but does his actions with will, not against his will. That Judas became a betrayer of Christ, neither he himself nor any creature could change, and yet he betrayed Christ not under compulsion, but willingly and with complete freedom . So too it is with the good man, that he is<sup>92</sup> namely not contingently or arbitrarily good, and nonetheless so little compelled that rather no compulsion, indeed even the gates of hell, would be able to overcome his disposition. In consciousness, insofar as it is mere self-grasping and only ideal, that free deed which becomes necessity cannot, to be sure, occur, since it precedes it, as it precedes the essence, and first *makes* it; but it is for that reason nonetheless no deed of which no consciousness has remained to man; for the one who, say, in order to excuse a wrong action, says: that is just how I am, is nonetheless well aware that he is so through his own guilt, however right he may be that it was impossible for him to act otherwise. How often it happens that a man from childhood on, at a time when we, considered empirically, can scarcely credit him with freedom and deliberation, shows a propensity [p. 387] to evil, of which it is to be foreseen that he will yield to no discipline and teaching, and who in the sequel really brings to maturity the bad fruits which we had foreseen in the germ; and that nonetheless no one doubts the accountability for them, and is as convinced of this man’s guilt as he could possibly be if every single action had been in his power. This general judgment of a propensity to evil, wholly unconscious in its origin and even irresistible, as an actus of freedom, points to a deed, and thus to a life before this life, only that it is not to be thought of as preceding in time, since the intelligible is altogether outside time. Because in creation there is the highest concord and nothing is so separated and successive as we must present it, but in the earlier the later also already cooperates and everything happens at once in one magical stroke, man, who here appears decided and determined, has in the first creation grasped himself in determinate shape, and is born as that which he is from eternity, in that through that deed even the kind and constitution of his corporization is determined. From of old the assumed contingency of human actions, in relation to the unity of the world-whole designed beforehand in the divine understanding, was the greatest stumbling block in the doctrine of freedom. Hence, since neither God’s prescience nor providence proper could be given up, the assumption of predestination. Its authors felt that the actions of man must be determined from eternity; but they sought this determination not in the eternal action, contemporaneous with creation, which constitutes the essence of man himself, but in an absolute, that is, wholly groundless, decree of God, by which the one was predestined to damnation, the other to bliss, and thereby they annulled the root of freedom. We too assert a predestination, but in a quite different sense, namely in this: as man acts here, so he has acted from eternity and already at the beginning of creation. [p. 388] His acting does not *become*, just as he himself as an ethical being does not *become*, but is eternal by nature. Thereby also falls away that oft-heard painful question: why is this man determined to act wickedly and impiously, that other, by contrast, piously and justly? for it presupposes that man is not already originally action and deed, and that as a spiritual being he has a being before and independent of his will, which, as has been shown, is impossible.

<sup>92</sup> So Luther in the treatise de servo arbitrio; rightly, even if he did not grasp in the right manner the union of such an unfailing necessity with the freedom of actions.

Once evil had been universally aroused in creation, through the reaction of the ground to revelation, man has grasped himself from eternity in self-hood and selfishness, and all who are born are born with the adhering dark principle of evil, even though this evil is raised to its self-consciousness only through the entry of opposition. Only out of this dark principle, as man now is, can the good be formed out as light, through divine transmutation. This original evil in man, which only one who has come to know man superficially, within himself and outside himself, can deny, is, although with respect to present empirical life wholly independent of freedom, nevertheless in its origin his own deed, and for that reason alone original sin, which cannot be said of that disorder of the forces, to be sure likewise undeniable, propagated as a contagion after the disruption had set in. For it is not the passions in themselves that are evil, nor do we have to contend merely with flesh and blood, but with an evil within and outside us which is spirit. Only that evil which is incurred through one’s own deed, yet from birth, can therefore be called radical evil; and it is noteworthy how Kant, who had not risen in theory to a transcendental deed determining all human being, was led, by mere faithful observation of the phenomena of ethical judgment, in later investigations to the acknowledgment of a ground of human actions which, as he expresses it, is subjective and precedes every deed falling within the senses, and which yet itself must in turn be an act of freedom; whereas Fichte, who had grasped in speculation [p. 389] the concept of such a deed, relapsed in his doctrine of morals into the reigning philanthropism and wanted to find that evil preceding all empirical action only in the sluggishness of human nature.

There seems to be only one objection that could be raised against this view: namely, that it cuts off all turning of man from evil to good, and conversely, at least for this life. Yet let it be that human or divine help — (man always needs help) — determines him to the transformation into the good, nevertheless the fact that he permits the good spirit that influence, that he does not positively close himself to it, likewise already lies in that original act through which he is this one and no other. Hence in the man in whom that transmutation has not yet taken place, but in whom the good principle too is not wholly dead, the inner voice of his own better essence — better in relation to him as he now is — never ceases to summon him to it, just as it is only through the actual and decisive turning that he finds peace in his own inner being and, as if the original Idea had only now been satisfied, finds himself reconciled with his guardian spirit. It is true in the strictest sense that, given how man is constituted, it is not he himself but either the good or the evil spirit that acts in him; and yet this does no injury to freedom. For precisely this letting-thegood-or-evil-principle-act-within-oneself is the consequence of the intelligible deed by which his essence and life are determined.

Having thus set forth the beginning and origin of evil up to its becoming actual in the individual man, nothing seems to remain but to describe its appearance in man.

The general possibility of evil consists, as has been shown, in this: that man can strive, instead of making his selfhood the basis, the organ, rather to raise it to the ruling element and to the universal will, and on the other hand to make the spiritual within himself a means. If in man the dark principle of selfhood and self-will is wholly permeated by light and one with [p. 390] it, then God, as the eternal love, or as actually existing, is the bond of forces in him. But if the two principles are in discord, another spirit takes the place where God ought to be; the inverted God, namely; that being aroused to actualization by God’s revelation, which can never reach the act from potency, which indeed never is but always wants to be, and which therefore, like the matter of the ancients, can be grasped (actualized) as actual not by perfect understanding but only through false imagination (λογισμῷ νόθῳ<sup>93</sup>) — which is precisely sin; for which reason it strives, through specular representations, borrowing, though itself not being, the semblance from true being, as the serpent borrows its colors from light, to bring man to the senselessness in which alone it can be received and comprehended by him. It is therefore rightly represented not only as an enemy of all creatures (because these subsist only through the bond of love) and especially of man, but also as his seducer, who lures him to false desire and to the admission of what is not into his imagination, in which it is supported by man’s own evil inclination, whose eye, unable to hold its ground while looking upon the splendor of the divine and of truth, always gazes at what is not. Thus the beginning of sin is that man passes over from true being into non-being, from truth into the lie, from light into darkness, in order to become a creating ground himself, and with the power of the center which he has within himself to rule over all things. For even in one who has departed from the center there always remains the feeling that he was all things, namely in and with God; therefore he strives toward it again, but for himself, not where he could be it, namely in God. Hence arises the hunger of selfishness, which, to the degree that it renounces the whole and unity, becomes ever more needy, poorer, but for that very reason more greedy, more hungry, more poisonous. It is in evil the [p. 391] self-consuming and ever self-annihilating contradiction that it strives to become creaturely precisely by annihilating the bond of creaturehood, and out of arrogance to be all falls into non-being. Moreover, manifest sin fills us not, like mere weakness and incapacity, with pity, but with terror and horror, a feeling explicable only by the fact that it strives to break the Word, to attack the ground of creation and to profane the mystery. Yet even this was to become manifest, for only in opposition to sin is revealed that innermost bond of the dependence of things and the essence of God, which is, as it were, prior to all existence (not yet mitigated by it), and for that reason terrible. For God himself clothes this principle in the creature and covers it with love, in that he makes it the ground and, as it were, the bearer of beings. Whoever now provokes it through misuse of the self-will raised to self-being, for him and against him it becomes actual. For since God cannot be disturbed in his existence, still less canceled, so, by the necessary correspondence that obtains between God and his basis, that very glance of life shining in the depth of darkness also in every individual man is inflamed into a consuming fire for the sinner, just as in the living organism the individual member or system, as soon as it has departed from the whole, feels the unity and conspiration itself, to which it has set itself in opposition, as fire (= fever) and is kindled by inner glow.

<sup>93</sup> The Platonic expression in the Timaeus, p. 349, vol. IX of the Zweibrücken edition; earlier in Tim. Locr. de an. mundi, ibid. p. 5.

We have seen how, through false imagination and a cognition directed to what is not, the spirit of man opens itself to the spirit of the lie and of falsehood, and, soon fascinated by it, loses its original freedom. From this it follows that, on the contrary, the true good can be brought about only through a divine magic, namely through the immediate presence of that which is in consciousness and cognition. An arbitrary good is as impossible as an arbitrary evil. True freedom is in accord with a holy necessity, such as we feel in essential cognition, [p. 392] where spirit and heart, bound only by their own law, freely affirm what is necessary. If evil consists in a discord of the two principles, then the good can consist only in their perfect concord, and the bond that unites them must be a divine one, since they are one not in a conditioned way but in a perfect and unconditioned way. The relation of the two cannot therefore be represented as an ethical life that is self-chosen or issued from self-determination. The latter concept presupposed that they are not one in themselves; but how are they to become one if they are not so? Moreover it leads back to the absurd system of the equilibrium of arbitrary choice. The relation of the two principles is that of a boundness of the dark principle (of selfhood) to the light. Let us be permitted to express this, according to the original meaning of the word, by religiosity. By this we do not understand what a sickly age so calls, idle brooding, devout-minded presentiment, or wanting-to-feel of the divine. For God is in us the clear cognition or the spiritual light itself, in which everything else first becomes clear, so far from its being itself unclear; and in whom this cognition is, it truly does not let him be idle or keep holiday. It is, where it is, something much more substantial than our philosophers of feeling suppose. We understand religiosity in the original, practical meaning of the word. It is conscientiousness, or that one act as one knows, and not contradict the light of cognition in one’s doing. A man to whom this is impossible not in a human, physical or psychological way, but in a divine way, is called religious, conscientious in the highest sense of the word. He is not conscientious who, in the case at hand, must still first hold the commandment of duty before himself in order to decide, through respect for it, to do what is right. Already by its verbal meaning religiosity admits no choice between opposites, no aequilibrium arbitrii (the plague of all morality), but only the highest decisiveness for what is right, without any choice. Conscientiousness does not appear necessarily and always as enthusiasm or as an extraordinary elevation above [p. 393] oneself, to which, when the conceit of self-chosen ethical life has been struck down, another and much worse spirit of arrogance would gladly make it too. It can appear wholly formal, in strict fulfillment of duty, where even the character of hardness and austerity is mixed into it, as in the soul of M. Cato, to whom an ancient ascribes that inner and almost divine necessity of acting, in saying that he was most like virtue, in that he never acted rightly in order to act so (out of respect for the commandment), but because he simply could not have acted otherwise. This severity of disposition is, like the severity of life in nature, the germ out of which true grace and divinity first emerge as blossom; but the supposedly more refined morality, which believes it may scorn this kernel, is like a barren blossom that bears no fruit . The highest is, pre-<sup>94</sup> cisely because it is the highest, not always the generally valid; and whoever has come to know the race of spiritual voluptuaries, to whom precisely the highest of science as of feeling must serve for the most unrestrained spiritual lewdness and for elevation above so-called common dutifulness, will think twice before pronouncing it as such. It is already foreseeable that on the path where everyone would rather be a beautiful soul than a rational one, and would rather be called noble than be just, the doctrine of morals will yet be traced back to the general concept of *taste*, according to which vice would then consist only in a bad or corrupted taste . When the<sup>95</sup> divine principle of earnest disposition, as such, breaks [p. 394] through, virtue appears as enthusiasm; as heroism (in the struggle against evil), as man’s beautiful free courage to act as God instructs him, and not to fall away in acting from what he has recognized in knowing; as faith, not in the sense of a holding-to-be-true that is even regarded as meritorious, or that lacks something of certainty — a meaning that has attached itself to this word through its use for common things —, but in its original meaning as trust, confidence in the divine, which excludes all choice. And when finally a ray of divine love descends into the unbreakable earnestness of disposition, which is always presupposed, there arises the highest transfiguration of ethical life in grace and divine beauty.

<sup>94</sup> Very accurate remarks on this moral genius of the age are contained in the review by Mr. Fr. Schlegel, cited several times, in the Heidelberger Jahrbücher, p. 154.

<sup>95</sup> A young man who, probably like so many others now, is too proud to walk the honest path of Kant, and yet unable to raise himself to something truly better, raves aesthetically, has already announced such a grounding of morality through aesthetics. With such progress the Kantian jest, to regard Euclid as a somewhat cumbersome introduction to drawing, may perhaps yet become earnest.

The origin of the opposition of good and evil, and how both work through one another in creation, we have now investigated as far as possible; but the highest question of this whole investigation still remains. God has until now been considered merely as a self-revealing being. But how does he then relate to this revelation as an ethical being? Is it an action that takes place with blind and unconscious necessity, or is it a free and conscious deed? And if it is the latter, how does God as an ethical being relate to evil, whose possibility and actuality depend on the self-revelation? Has he, in willing the latter, also willed evil, and how is this willing to be reconciled with the holiness and highest perfection in him, or, in the ordinary expression, how is God to be justified with regard to evil?

The preliminary question concerning God’s freedom in self-revelation seems indeed decided by what precedes. Were God for us a merely logical abstraction, then everything would have to follow from him with logical necessity; he himself would be, as it were, only the highest law from which everything flows, but without personality and consciousness of it. But we have explained God as the living unity of forces; and if personality, according to our earlier explanation, rests on the connection of something self-subsistent with a basis [p. 395] independent of it, so namely that these two wholly interpenetrate and are only one being, then God, through the connection of the ideal principle in him with the ground independent (relative to it), since basis and existing element in him necessarily unite into one absolute existence, is the highest personality; and also, if the living unity of the two is spirit, then God, as the absolute bond of them, is spirit in the eminent and absolute sense. So certain is it that only through God’s bond with nature is personality grounded in him, since on the contrary the God of pure idealism, as much as that of pure realism, is necessarily an impersonal being, of which the Fichtean and Spinozistic concepts are the clearest proofs. But because in God there is an independent ground of reality and therefore two equally eternal beginnings of self-revelation, God must also be considered with regard to his freedom in relation to both. The first beginning of creation is the longing of the One to give birth to itself, or the will of the ground. The second is the will of love, through which the Word is pronounced into nature, and through which God first makes himself personal. The will of the ground cannot therefore be free in the sense in which the will of love is. It is not a conscious will or one connected with reflection, though also not a wholly unconscious one that would move according to blind mechanical necessity, but of an intermediate nature, like desire or pleasure, and most nearly comparable to the beautiful impulse of a nature in becoming, which strives to unfold and whose inner movements are involuntary (cannot be omitted), without its yet feeling constrained in them. But absolutely free and conscious will is the will of love, precisely because it is such; the revelation following from it is action and deed. The whole of nature tells us that it exists by no means by virtue of a merely geometrical necessity; there is not pure sheer reason in it, but personality and spirit (as we distinguish the rational author from the spirited one); otherwise the geometrical understanding, which has ruled for so long, would long since have had to penetrate it and to confirm its idol of universal and eternal laws of nature more than has [p. 396] happened up to now , since it must rather recognize daily more the irrational relation of nature to itself. Creation is not an event but a deed.
