There are no consequences from universal laws, but God, that is, the person of God, is the universal law, and everything that happens happens by virtue of the personality of God; not according to an abstract necessity which we would not bear in acting, let alone God. In the Leibnizian philosophy, all too much dominated by the spirit of abstraction, the acknowledgment of the laws of nature as laws of ethical, not of geometrical necessity, and equally little of arbitrary ones, is one of the most gratifying aspects. “I have found,” says Leibniz, “that the laws actually demonstrable in nature are yet not absolutely demonstrable, which however is also not necessary. They can indeed be proved in different ways; but something must always be presupposed that is not wholly geometrically necessary. Hence these laws are the proof of a supreme, intelligent and free being against the system of absolute necessity. They are neither wholly necessary (in that abstract sense) nor wholly arbitrary, but stand in the middle as laws that derive from a wisdom perfect above all” .<sup>96</sup> The highest striving of the dynamic mode of explanation is none other than this reduction of the laws of nature to heart, spirit and will.

<sup>96</sup> Tentam. theod. Opp. T. I, p. 365, 366.

To determine, however, the relation of God as a moral being to the world, the general cognition of freedom in creation does not suffice; it must further be asked whether the deed of self-revelation was free in the sense that all its consequences were foreseen in God. This too must necessarily be affirmed; for the will to revelation would not itself be alive if it were not opposed by another will, going back to the interior of the essence; but in this holding-back-in-itself there arises a reflexive image of everything that is implicitly contained in the essence, in which God ideally actualizes himself, [p. 397] or, what is the same, previously cognizes himself in his actualization. So, then, since there is in God a tendency counteracting the will to revelation, love and goodness or the Communicativum sui must prevail, in order that there be a revelation; and this, the decision, first properly completes the concept of it as a conscious and ethically free deed.

Notwithstanding this concept, and although the action of revelation in God is necessary only ethically — or in relation to goodness and love — the notion of a deliberation of God with himself, or of a choice between several possible worlds, remains a groundless and untenable notion. On the contrary, as soon as the closer determination of an ethical necessity is added, the proposition is wholly undeniable: that from the divine nature everything follows with absolute necessity, that everything that is possible by virtue of it must also be actual, and what is not actual must also be ethically impossible. Spinozism errs by no means through the assertion of such an inviolable necessity in God, but in that it takes it as lifeless and impersonal. For since this system grasps of the Absolute only the one side — namely the real, or insofar as God works only in the ground — those propositions indeed lead to a blind and unintelligent necessity. But if God is essentially love and goodness, then what is ethically necessary in him also follows with a truly metaphysical necessity. Were choice in the strictest sense required for perfect freedom in God, one would have to go still further. For a perfect freedom of choice would have existed only if God could also have created a less perfect world than was possible under all conditions, as indeed, since nothing is so absurd that it has not once been put forward, some have actually and in earnest — not merely like the Castilian king Alphonso, whose well-known remark only struck the then-reigning Ptolemaic system — asserted: God, had he willed, could have created a better world than this. So too the grounds against the unity of possibility and [p. 398] actuality in God are taken from the wholly formal concept of possibility, that everything is possible that does not contradict itself; for example in the well-known objection that then all cleverly invented novels would have to be real events. Such a merely formal concept not even Spinoza had; all possibility holds for him only in relation to divine perfection, and Leibniz adopts this concept evidently merely in order to bring out a choice in God, and thereby to distance himself as far as possible from Spinoza. “God chooses,” he says, “between possibilities, and chooses therefore freely, without necessitation: only then would there be no choice, no freedom, if only One were possible.” If nothing further is lacking for freedom than such an empty possibility, it may be granted that formally, or without regard to the divine essentiality, the infinite was and still is possible; but this means wanting to assert divine freedom through a concept that is false in itself, and that is possible merely in our understanding but not in God, in whom an abstracting from his essence or his perfections surely cannot be thought. As for the plurality of possible worlds, something rule-less in itself, such as according to our explanation the original movement of the ground is, like a matter not yet formed but receptive of all forms, does indeed seem to offer an infinity of possibilities, and if the possibility of several worlds were perhaps to be grounded on that, it would only have to be remarked that no such possibility with regard to God would follow from it, since the ground is not to be called God, and God, according to his perfection, can will only One. But that rule-lessness too is by no means to be thought as if the archetype of the world alone possible according to the essence of God were not contained in the ground, which in actual creation is raised from potency to act only through separation, regulation of the forces, and exclusion of the rule-less that hinders or obscures it. In the divine understanding itself, however, as in primordial wisdom, in which God actualizes himself ideally or archetypally, there is, as there is only One God, so also only One possible world.

[p. 399] In the divine understanding there is a system, but God himself is not a system but a life, and therein alone lies the answer to the question for whose sake this was premised, concerning the possibility of evil in relation to God. All existence requires a condition in order that it become actual, that is, personal existence. God’s existence, too, could not be personal without such a condition, except that he has this condition *in himself*, not outside himself. He cannot cancel the condition, since otherwise he would have to cancel himself; he can only overcome it through love and subordinate it to his glorification. In God too there would be a ground of darkness, if he did not make the condition *his own*, did not unite himself with it as one and into absolute personality. Man never gets the condition into his power, although in evil he strives for it; it is one merely lent to him, independent of him; hence his personality and selfhood can never raise themselves to complete actus. This is the sadness clinging to all finite life, and even if in God there is a condition independent at least relatively, then in him too there is a source of sadness, which, however, never comes to actuality but serves only for the eternal joy of overcoming. Hence the veil of melancholy spread over the whole of nature, the deep indestructible melancholy of all life. Joy must have sorrow, sorrow be transfigured into joy. What therefore comes from the mere condition or the ground does not come from God, even if it is necessary to his existence. But neither can it be said that evil comes from the ground, or that the will of the ground is its author. For evil can only ever arise in the innermost will of one’s own heart, and is never accomplished without one’s own deed. The solicitation of the ground, or the reaction against the supercreaturely, awakens only the desire for the creaturely, or self-will, but it awakens it only so that an independent ground of the good may be there, and so that it may be overpowered and permeated by the good. For it is not the aroused selfhood in itself that is evil, but only insofar as it has torn itself away [p. 400] entirely from its opposite, the light or the universal will. But precisely this renunciation of the good is first sin. The activated selfhood is necessary for the sharpness of life; without it there would be complete death, a slumbering of the good; for where there is no struggle, there is no life. Only the awakening of life, then, is the will of the ground, not evil immediately and in itself. If the will of man encloses the activated selfhood within love and subordinates it to the light as the universal will, then there first arises from this actual goodness, made sensible through the sharpness found in it. In the good, then, the reaction of the ground is an effect toward the good, in evil an effect toward evil, as Scripture says: with the pious thou art pious, and with the perverse perverse. A good without effective selfhood is itself an ineffective good. The same thing that becomes evil through the will of the creature (when it tears itself entirely loose in order to be for itself) is in itself the good, so long, namely, as it remains swallowed up in the good and in the ground. Only the overcome selfhood, brought back from activity to potentiality, is the good, and in potency, as overpowered by the good, it also continues to subsist in the good forever. If there were not a root of cold in the body, warmth could not be felt. To think an attracting and a repelling force for themselves is impossible, for on what should the repelling force act, if the attracting does not make an object for it, or on what the attractive force, if it does not itself at the same time have something repulsive in it? Hence it is quite correctly said, dialectically, that good and evil are the same, only seen from different sides, or that evil is, in itself, that is, considered in the root of its identity, the good, just as the good, conversely, considered in its disunion or non-identity, is evil. For this reason that saying too is quite correct, that whoever has no matter nor forces for evil in himself is also unfit for the good, of which we have seen ample examples in our time. The passions, on which our negative morality wages war, are forces each of which has a common root with [p. 401] the virtue corresponding to it . The soul of all hatred is love, and in the most violent wrath there shows itself only the stillness attacked and provoked in its innermost center. In due measure and organic equilibrium they are the strength of virtue itself and its immediate instruments. “If the passions are members of dishonor,” says the excellent J. G. Hamann, “do they therefore cease to be weapons of manliness? Do you understand the letter of reason more cleverly than that allegorical chamberlain of the Alexandrian church understood that of Scripture, who made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven? — The greatest villains against themselves the prince of this aeon makes his favorites — — his (the devil’s) court fools are the worst enemies of fair nature, which indeed has Corybantes and Galli as belly-priests, but strong spirits as true worshippers.” Only let those whose philoso-<sup>97</sup> phy is made more for the gynaeceum than for the Academy or the palaestra of the Lyceum not bring those dialectical propositions before a public which, misunderstanding them just as they themselves do, sees in them an abolition of all difference between right and wrong, good and evil, and before which they no more belong than, say, the propositions of the old dialecticians, of Zeno and the other Eleatics, before the forum of shallow aesthetes.

<sup>97</sup> Kleeblatt hellenistischer Briefe II, p. 196.

The arousal of self-will occurs only so that love may find in man a matter or opposition in which to realize itself. Insofar as selfhood in its renunciation is the principle of evil, the ground does indeed arouse the possible principle of evil, but not evil itself, nor does it arouse to evil. But even this arousal does not occur according to the free will of God, who in the ground moves not according to this or his heart, but only according to its properties.

Whoever therefore asserted that God himself had willed evil would have to seek the ground of this assertion in the deed of self-revelation as creation, as has often been maintained [p. 402] elsewhere, namely, that whoever willed the world must also have willed evil. Yet in that God brought the disorderly births of chaos to order and expressed his eternal unity in nature, he thereby rather worked against the darkness, and set against the lawless motion of the understandingless principle the Word as a constant center and eternal light. The will to creation was thus immediately only a will to the birth of light, and thereby of the good; evil, however, did not come into consideration in this will, either as a means or even, as Leibniz says, as *conditio sine qua non* of the greatest possible perfection of the world. It was neither the object of a divine<sup>98</sup> decree, nor, still less, of a permission. The question, however, why God, since he necessarily foresaw that evil would follow, at least as a concomitant, from the self-revelation, did not prefer not to reveal himself at all, truly deserves no reply. For this would mean as much as: in order that there be no opposition to love, love itself is not to be, that is, the absolutely positive is to be sacrificed to that which has existence only as opposition, the eternal to the merely temporal. That the self-revelation in God must be considered not as an unconditionally arbitrary but as an ethically necessary act, in which love and goodness overcame absolute inwardness, we have already explained. Had God, then, not revealed himself for the sake of evil, evil would have triumphed over the good and over love. The Leibnizian concept of evil as *conditio sine qua non* can [p. 403] be applied only to the ground, namely in this sense, that the ground arouses the creaturely will (the possible principle of evil) as a condition under which alone the will of love can be realized. Why God now does not ward off the will of the ground or cancel it, we have likewise already shown. That would be as much as for God to cancel the condition of his existence, that is, his own personality. In order, then, that evil not be, God himself would have to not be.

<sup>98</sup> Tentam. theod. p. 139: Ex his concludendum est, Deum *antecedenter* velle omne *bonum* in se, velle consequenter optimum tanquam *finem*; indifferens et malum physicum tanquam *medium*; sed velle tantum *permittere* malum morale, tanquam *conditionem sine qua non* obtineretur optimum, ita nimirum, ut malum nonnisi titulo necessitatis hypotheticae, id ipsum cum optimo connectentis, admittatur“. — p. 292: Quod ad vitium attinet, superius ostensum est illud non esse objectum decreti divini, tanquam *medium*, sed tanquam *conditionem sine qua non* — et ideo duntaxat *permitti* — These two passages contain the core of the whole Leibnizian Theodicy.

Another objection, which, however, strikes not merely this view but every metaphysics, is this: that even if God did not will evil, he nevertheless continues to work in the sinner and gives him the power to accomplish evil. This is to be granted entirely and completely, with the proper distinction. The primordial ground of existence continues to work in evil too, as in sickness health still continues to work, and even the most deranged, most falsified life remains and moves still in God, insofar as he is ground of existence. But it feels him as consuming wrath, and is set, through the very attraction of the ground, into an ever higher tension against unity, up to selfannihilation and final crisis.

After all this the question still remains: does evil end, and how? Does creation have a final purpose at all, and if it does, why is this not attained immediately, why is the perfect not there from the beginning? There is no answer to this other than the one already given: because God is a life, not merely a being. But all life has a fate, and is subject to suffering and becoming. To this too, then, God has freely submitted himself, already when he first, in order to become personal, separated the world of light and the dark world. Being becomes sensible to itself only in becoming. In being, to be sure, there is no becoming; in it, rather, becoming is itself again posited as eternity; but in realization through opposition becoming is necessary. Without the concept of a humanly suffering God, which is common to all the mysteries and spiritual religions of antiquity, all of history remains incomprehensible; [p. 404] Scripture too distinguishes periods of revelation, and posits as a distant future the time when God will be all in all, that is, when he will be wholly realized. The first period of creation is, as shown earlier, the birth of light. Light, or the ideal principle, as an eternal opposite of the dark principle, is the creating Word, which redeems the life concealed in the ground from non-being, raises it from potency to actus. Above the Word the Spirit arises, and the Spirit is the first being which unites the dark world and the world of light and subordinates both principles to realization and personality. Against this unity, however, the ground reacts and asserts the original duality, but only to ever higher intensification and to the final separation of the good from evil. The will of the ground must remain in its freedom until everything is fulfilled, everything has become actual. Were it subjected earlier, the good would remain concealed in it together with evil. But the good is to be raised from darkness to actuality, in order to live imperishably with God; evil, however, separated from the good, in order to be cast out forever into non-being. For this is the final purpose of creation, that what could not be for itself *be* for itself, in that it is raised into existence out of darkness, as a ground independent of God. Hence the necessity of birth and of death. God gives the Ideas, which were in him without independent life, over into selfhood and into that which is not, so that, in being called out of this into life, they may be in him again as independently existing. The<sup>99</sup> ground thus brings about in its freedom the separation and the judgment (κρίσις), and precisely thereby the complete actualization of God. For evil, when it is entirely separated from the good, is also no longer evil. It could work only through the (misused) good that was in it, unconscious to itself. In life it still enjoyed the forces of external nature, with [p. 405] which it attempted to create, and still had mediate share in the goodness of God. In dying, however, it is separated from all good, and remains behind indeed as craving, as eternal hunger and thirst for actuality, but without being able to step out of potentiality. Its state is therefore a state of non-being, a state of constant consumption of the activity, or of that which strives to be active in it. Hence for the realization of the Idea of a final all-sided perfection there is by no means need of a restoration of evil to the good (the restoration of all things); for evil is evil only insofar as it goes beyond potentiality; reduced to non-being, however, or to the state of potency, it is what it was always meant to be, basis, the subjected, and as such no longer in contradiction with the holiness or the love of God. The end of revelation is therefore the expulsion of evil from the good, the declaration of it as entire unreality. By contrast, the good raised out of the ground is joined to eternal unity with the original good; those born out of darkness into light attach themselves to the ideal principle as members of its body, in which that principle is perfectly realized and is now wholly personal being. So long as the original duality lasted, the creating Word ruled in the ground, and this period of creation runs through all of them to the end. But when the duality is annihilated through the separation, the Word or ideal principle subordinates itself, and the real principle that has become one with it, jointly to the Spirit, and this, as the divine consciousness, lives in like manner in both principles; as Scripture says of Christ: He must reign, till he hath put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy that is canceled is death (for death was necessary only for the separation: the good must die in order to separate itself from evil, and evil in order to separate itself from the good). But when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all. For even the Spirit is not yet the [p. 406] highest; it is only the spirit, or the breath of love. But love is the highest. It is that which was before the ground and before the existing (as separate) were, but was not yet as love, but — how shall we designate it?

<sup>99</sup> Philosophie und Religion, (Tübingen, 1804) p. 73. [vol. IV, p. 63].

We come here at last upon the highest point of the whole investigation. We have long heard the question: to what end is that first distinction to serve, between essence insofar as it is ground and insofar as it exists? For either there is no common center for the two: then we must declare ourselves *for* absolute dualism. Or there is one: then both coincide again in the final consideration. We then have One essence for all oppositions, an absolute identity of light and darkness, good and evil, and all the absurd consequences into which every system of reason must fall, and which have long since been pointed out in this system too.

What we assume in the first respect we have already explained: there must be, *before* all ground and *before* all existing things, thus before all duality in general, an essence; how can we call it otherwise than the primordial ground or rather *unground*? Since it precedes all oppositions, these cannot be distinguishable in it nor be present in any way. It can therefore not be designated as the identity, it can only be designated as the absolute *indifference* of the two. Most people, when they reach the point of consideration where they must recognize a vanishing of all oppositions, forget that these have now really vanished, and predicate them again as such of the indifference, which yet arose for them precisely through a complete cessation of them. Indifference is not a product of the oppositions, nor are they implicitly contained in it, but it is an essence of its own, separated from all opposition, on which all oppositions break, which is nothing other than precisely the non-being of them, and which therefore has no predicate except that of predicatelessness, without being on that account a nothing or a non-thing. Either, then, they really posit in the unground preceding all ground the indifference: [p. 407] then they have neither good nor evil — (for that the elevation of the opposition of good and evil to this standpoint is altogether inadmissible, we leave aside for the time being) — and can predicate of it neither the one nor the other, nor yet both at once. Or they posit good and evil: then they also posit at once the duality and thus no longer the unground or the indifference. For the elucidation of the last, let the following be said! The real and the ideal, darkness and light, or however else we may wish to designate the two principles, can never be predicated of the unground as *oppositions*. But nothing prevents them from being predicated of it not as non-oppositions, that is, in disjunction and each *for itself*, whereby, however, precisely the duality (the actual twoness of the principles) is posited. In the unground itself there is nothing by which this would be prevented. For precisely because it relates itself to both as total indifference, it is indifferent toward both. Were it the absolute identity of both, it could only be both at once, that is, both would have to be predicated of it as *oppositions*, and would thereby themselves again be one. Immediately from the Neither — Nor, or the indifference, the duality therefore breaks forth (which is something quite other than opposition, even if we have hitherto, since we had not yet arrived at this point of the investigation, used the two as synonymous), and *without* indifference, that is, *without* an unground, there would be no twoness of the principles. Instead of this, therefore, canceling the distinction again, as was supposed, it rather posits and confirms it. Far from the distinction between the ground and the existing having been a merely logical one, or one summoned only as a makeshift and to be found spurious in the end, it showed itself rather as a very real distinction, which from the highest standpoint was first truly confirmed and fully comprehended.

After this dialectical discussion we can therefore explain ourselves quite definitely in the following manner. The essence of the ground, like that of the existing, can only be [p. 408] that which precedes all ground , thus the Absolute considered simply, the unground. But it can be this (as proved) only by going apart into two equally eternal beginnings, not in that it is both *at once*, but that it is in each *in like manner*, thus in each the whole, or an essence of its own. The unground, however, divides itself into the two equally eternal beginnings only so that the two, which in it, as unground, could not be at once or One, become one through love, that is, it divides itself only so that there be life and loving and personal existence. For love is neither in indifference, nor where opposites are bound that need the connection in order to be, but (to repeat a word already spoken) this is the mystery of love, that it binds such as each could be for itself and yet is not, and cannot be without the other. Therefore, as<sup>100</sup> soon as duality comes to be in the unground, love also comes to be, which binds the existing (the ideal) with the ground of existence. But the ground remains free and independent of the Word up to the final complete separation. Then it dissolves, as in man, when he passes over to clarity and grounds himself as an abiding being, the original longing dissolves, in that everything true and good in it is raised into bright consciousness, but everything else, the false, namely, and the impure, is shut up forever in darkness, to remain as the eternally dark ground of selfhood, as caput mortuum of his life-process, and as a potency that can never proceed to actus. Then everything is subordinated to the Spirit: in the Spirit the existing is one with the ground of existence; in it both are really at once, or it is the absolute identity of both. But above the Spirit is the original unground, which is no longer indifference (Gleichgültigkeit), and yet not identity of both principles, but the universal unity, equal toward all and yet seized by nothing, the beneficence free from all and yet working through all, in a word love, which is all in all.

<sup>100</sup> Aphorismen über die Naturphilosophie in den Jahrbüchern der Medicin als Wissenschaft. vol. I, no. 1. Aphor. 162. 163. [above p. 174].

[p. 409] Whoever, then, would say (as before) that in this system there is One principle for everything, that it is one and the same being that rules in the dark ground of nature and in eternal clarity, one and the same that effects the hardness and severance of things and the unity and gentleness, the very same that governs with the will of love in the good and with the will of wrath in evil — such a person, though he says all this quite correctly, would nevertheless have to remember this: that the One being, in its two modes of operation, really divides into two beings, that in the one it is *merely* ground of existence, in the other merely essence (and for that reason only ideal); and further, that God is, as spirit, the absolute identity of both principles, but only by this and insofar as, and to the extent that, both are *subordinated* to His personality. But whoever, moreover, at the highest standpoint of this view, were to find an absolute identity of good and evil, would show his complete ignorance, since evil and good form no original opposition at all, and least of all a duality. Duality exists where two beings really stand opposed to one another. But evil is not a being but a non-being, which is a reality only in opposition, not in itself. The absolute identity, the spirit of love, is also prior to evil for this very reason, because the latter can appear only in opposition to it. Hence it also cannot be comprehended by the absolute identity, but is eternally excluded and expelled from it .<sup>101</sup>

<sup>101</sup> From this it is evident how strange it is to demand that the opposition of good and evil be explained straightaway in the first principles. Whoever holds good and evil to be a real duality and dualism to be the most perfect system must of course speak thus.

Whoever, finally, because all oppositions disappear when considered in relation to the Absolute simply, would call this system pantheism, to him let this too be granted . We gladly<sup>102</sup> [p. 410] leave to everyone his own way of making the age, and what is in it, intelligible to himself. The name does not do it; it is the matter that counts. The vanity of a polemic from mere general concepts of philosophical systems against something determinate, which may well have many a point of contact in common with them and for that reason has already been confused with all of them, but which has its own peculiar determinations in each single point — the vanity of such a polemic we have already touched upon at the beginning of this treatise. Thus it is quick work to say that a system teaches the immanence of things in God; and yet, e.g., in relation to us nothing would thereby be said, although it could not be called outright untrue. For we have shown sufficiently that all natural beings have a mere being in the ground, or in the original longing that has not yet attained unity with the understanding, so that in relation to God they are merely [p. 411] peripheral beings. Only man is in God, and precisely through this being-in-God he is capable of freedom. He alone is a central being and for that reason ought also to remain in the center. In him all things are created, just as God accepts nature, too, and unites it with Himself only through man. Nature is the first or old testament, since things are still outside the center and hence under the law. Man is the beginning of the new covenant, through whom as mediator, since he himself is united with God, God (after the final separation) also accepts nature and makes it His own. Man is thus the redeemer of nature, at whom all its prefigurations aim. The word that is fulfilled in man is in nature as a dark, prophetic (not yet fully pronounced) word. Hence the presages, which have no interpretation in nature itself and are explained only through man. Hence the universal finality of causes, which likewise becomes intelligible only from this standpoint. Whoever now omits or overlooks all these intermediate determinations has an easy time refuting. Purely historical criticism, to be sure, is a comfortable business. One need set up nothing oneself, from one’s own resources, and can observe to perfection the Caute, per Deos! incede, latet ignis sub cinere doloso. But in doing so arbitrary and unproved presuppositions are unavoidable. So, in order to prove that there are only two ways of explaining evil — the dualistic, according to which an evil primordial being, no matter with what modifications, is assumed beneath or alongside the good, and the kabbalistic, according to which evil is explained by emanation and distancing — and that therefore every other system must cancel the distinction between good and evil: to prove this would require nothing less than the whole power of a profoundly conceived and thoroughly developed philosophy. In the system every concept has its determinate place, in which alone it is valid, and which also determines its meaning as well as its limitation. Whoever now does not enter into the interior, but merely lifts the most general concepts out of their context, how can he judge the whole correctly? Thus we [p. 412] have shown the determinate point of the system at which the concept of indifference is indeed the only one possible of the Absolute. If it is now taken universally, the whole is distorted, and it then follows also that this system cancels the personality of the highest being. We have remained silent about this oft-heard reproach, as about many another, up to now, but believe that in this treatise we have set forth the first clear concept of it. In the unground, or indifference, there is of course no personality; but is the starting point, then, the whole? Now we challenge those who have made that reproach so lightly to set before us, in opposition, according to their own views, even the slightest thing intelligible about this concept. Everywhere we find, rather, that they declare the personality of God to be incomprehensible and in no way to be made intelligible, in which they also do quite right, since they hold precisely those abstract systems in which all personality is altogether impossible to be the only ones in accordance with reason, which is presumably also the reason why they credit everyone with the same, who does not despise science and reason. We, on the contrary, are of the opinion that a clear rational insight must be possible precisely of the highest concepts, since only thereby can they become truly our own, be taken up into ourselves and be eternally grounded. Indeed, we go still further, and together with Lessing himself hold the development of revealed truths into truths of reason to be absolutely necessary, if the human race is to be helped thereby . We are likewise convinced that, in order to demonstrate<sup>103</sup> every possible error (in objects properly spiritual), reason is perfectly sufficient, and the heresy-judging mien in the assessment of philosophical systems is wholly dispensable . An<sup>104</sup> absolute dualism of good and evil transferred into history, according to which in all phenomena and works of the human spirit either the one or the other principle rules, according to [p. 413] which there are only two systems and two religions, one absolutely good and one downright evil; further, the opinion that everything began from the pure and unalloyed, and that all later developments (which were nevertheless necessary in order to reveal the partial sides contained in the first unity, and thereby the unity itself, completely) were only corruption and falsification: this whole view serves, to be sure, in criticism as a mighty sword of Alexander for cutting the Gordian knot in two everywhere without effort, but it introduces into history a thoroughly illiberal and highly restrictive point of view. There was a time that preceded that separation, and a view of the world and a religion which, though opposed to the absolute one, nevertheless sprang from its own ground, and not from a falsification of the first. The sanctuary is, historically speaking, as original as Christianity and, though only ground and basis of the higher, is yet derived from no other.

<sup>102</sup> No one can agree more than the author with the wish that Mr. Fr. Schlegel expresses in the Heidelberg *Jahrbücher*, no. 2, p. 242, that the unmanly pantheistic vertigo in Germany might cease, especially since Mr. S. adds to it also the aesthetic dreaminess and imagination, and to the extent that we may at the same time count the opinion of the exclusive rationality of Spinozism as part of that vertigo. It is indeed very easy, in Germany, where a philosophical system becomes the object of literary industry, and where so many on whom nature itself has denied the understanding even for everyday things believe themselves called to philosophize along, to arouse a false opinion, indeed even a vertigo. At least the consciousness can reassure one of never having favored it personally or encouraged it by one’s own helpful support, and of being able to say with Erasmus (little as one may otherwise have in common with him): semper solus esse volui nihilque pejus odi quam juratos et factiosos. The author has never wished, by founding a sect, to take from others, least of all from himself, the freedom of inquiry, in which he has still always declared himself to be engaged and probably always will. The course he has taken in the present treatise, where, even if the outward form of dialogue is lacking, everything nevertheless arises as though in conversation, he will also keep to in the future. Much could have been determined here more sharply and held less loosely, much guarded more expressly against misinterpretation. The author omitted to do so partly on purpose. Whoever cannot or will not take it from him in this way, let him take nothing at all from him; let him seek other sources. Perhaps, however, uncalledfor followers and opponents will grant to this treatise the regard which they showed to the earlier, related writing *Philosophie und Religion* through complete ignoring, to which the former were certainly moved less by the threatening words of the preface or the manner of presentation than by the content itself.

<sup>103</sup> *Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts*, § 76.

<sup>104</sup> Especially if, on the other side, one wants to speak only of *views* where one ought to speak of truths that alone bring salvation.

These considerations lead back to our starting point. A system that contradicts the holiest feelings, the heart and the ethical consciousness, can, in this character at least, never be called a system of reason, but only of unreason. On the other hand, a system in which reason really cognized itself would have to unite all the demands of the spirit as of the heart, of the most ethical feeling as of the strictest understanding. The polemic against reason and science permits, to be sure, a certain superior generality that avoids exact concepts, so that we can more easily guess its aims than its determinate sense. Yet we fear that, even if we were to fathom it, we should come upon nothing extraordinary. For however highly we place reason, we do not believe, e.g., that anyone is virtuous from pure reason, or a hero, or in general a great man; indeed not even, according to the well-known saying, that the human race is propagated by it. Only in personality is there life; and all personality rests on a dark ground, which therefore must certainly also be ground of cognition. But only the understanding [p. 414] is that which brings forth what is hidden in this ground and contained merely potentialiter, and raises it to the actus. This can happen only through separation, hence through science and dialectic, of which we are convinced that they alone will hold fast and bring to cognition forever that system which has been there more often than we think, but has always escaped again, which hovers before us all and has not yet been wholly grasped by anyone. As in life we really trust only a vigorous understanding, and miss every true delicacy of feeling most among those who are always parading their feeling before us, so too, where truth and cognition are at stake, selfhood that has got no further than feeling can win no trust from us. Feeling is glorious when it remains in the ground; but not when it comes to light, wants to make itself essence and to rule. If, according to the excellent views of Franz Baader, the drive to cognize has the greatest analogy with the procreative drive , then there is in cognition too<sup>105</sup> something analogous to chastity and modesty, and conversely also an un-chastity and shamelessness, a kind of faunish lust that dabbles in everything, without earnestness and without love, to form or shape something. The *bond* of our personality is *spirit*, and if only the productive union of both principles can become creative and generative, then enthusiasm in the proper sense is the effective principle of every generative and formative art or science. Every enthusiasm expresses itself in a determinate way; and so there is also one that expresses itself through dialectical artistic drive, a properly scientific enthusiasm. There is therefore also a dialectical philosophy, which as science is determinate, separated, e.g., from poetry and religion, and is something wholly self-subsistent, but not one with everything possible in turn, as those maintain who are now striving in so many writings to mix everything with everything. It is said that reflection is hostile to the Idea; but precisely this is the highest triumph of truth, that it nevertheless emerges victorious from the most extreme separation [p. 415] and division. Reason in man is what, according to the mystics, the Primum passivum in God, or primordial wisdom, is, in which all things are together and yet distinct, one and yet each free in its kind. It is not activity, like spirit, not the absolute identity of both principles of cognition, but indifference; the measure and, as it were, the universal place of truth, the quiet abode in which the original wisdom is received, looking to which, as to the archetype, the understanding is to form. Philosophy has its name partly from love, as the universally inspiring principle, partly from this original wisdom, which is its proper goal.

<sup>105</sup> See the treatise of the above content in the *Jahrbücher für Medicin*, vol. III, no. 1, p. 113.

If philosophy is deprived of the dialectical principle, that is, of the understanding that separates, but precisely for that reason orders and shapes organically, together with the archetype by which it is guided, so that it has in itself neither measure nor rule any longer: then nothing remains for it but to seek to orient itself historically, and to take *tradition*, to which reference was made earlier in the case of a like result, as source and plumb-line. Then it is time, as poetry among us was thought to be grounded by acquaintance with the poetry of all nations, to seek for philosophy too a historical norm and foundation. We have the greatest respect for the profundity of historical researches, and believe we have shown that the almost universal opinion, that man raised himself only gradually from the dullness of animal instinct to reason, is not ours. Yet we believe that the truth lies nearer to us, and that for the problems that have become astir in our time we should seek the solution first in ourselves and on our own soil, before we wander to such distant sources. The time of merely historical faith is past, when the possibility of immediate cognition is given. We have an older revelation than any written one, nature. This contains prefigurations which no man has yet interpreted, whereas those of the written one have long since received their fulfillment and interpretation. The only [p. 416] true system of religion and science would, if the understanding of that unwritten revelation were opened up, appear not in the meagerly assembled state of a few philosophical and critical concepts, but at once in the full splendor of truth and of nature. It is not the time to reawaken old oppositions, but to seek what lies outside and above all opposition.

The present treatise will be followed by a series of others, in which the whole of the ideal part of philosophy will be presented gradually.

[p. 417]

[p. 421] I.

To what extent is a system possible at all? Answer: there has long been a system, before human beings ever thought of making one — the system of the world. To find this, then, is the proper task. The true system cannot be *invented*; it can only be found as something already *at hand* in itself, namely in the divine understanding. Most philosophical systems are mere works of their authors — well or badly contrived — behaving almost like our historical novels (e.g. Leibnizianism). To want to assert a system in this sense as the only possible one is highly illiberal — a school system —. I assure you that I have had no wish to contribute anything to that.

Yet that true system, too, cannot be found in its *empirical* totality, for which the cognition of all the intermediate links, even the most particular, would be required.

If what is to be found is to be a system of the world, then it must 1) as a *system of the world* have a principle that bears itself, that subsists in and through itself, that reproduces itself in every part of the whole; 2) it must exclude nothing (e.g. nature), subordinate nothing one-sidedly or even suppress it; 3) it must have a method of development and progression by which one can be assured that no essential intermediate link can be skipped.

*What is the principle of my system*? — This principle has been expressed in various ways:

a) as the principle of absolute identity simply, to be carefully distinguished from absolute sameness; the identity [p. 422] meant here is an *organic* unity of all things. In every organism there is unity, without the parts of it being on that account held to be the same. Thus, for example, in the human body all differences of the organs and functions dissolve into one indivisible life, whose sensation, as that of an indivisible and harmonious life, is the sensation of well-being; but the parts and functions that make up this organic whole are not on that account the same; the stomach, for example, does not perform the functions of the brain, etc.

b) More precisely, this principle was expressed as absolute identity of the *real* and the *ideal*. The meaning here is not that the real and the ideal are numerically or logically the same; what is meant is an *essential* unity; one and the same thing is indeed posited in both forms, but in each of these forms it is a distinct being, and not the same one. If, for example, Jacob was also called Israel, it was always the very same individual, who was not individualized differently by the different names. But the identity of the real and the ideal is not like that. Suppose, for example, A / (B = C); here B and C are identical, because in essence they are A, but they are different from one another as forms, or considered in themselves; B can never become C, nor C B; likewise A in B and A in C is each a distinct being. Precisely because the same essence is in each, there is between them an *essential* (i.e. not merely formal, logical, or nominal) unity, but at the same time a real opposition or dualism, since they cannot cancel one another. For through the fact that A individualizes itself in B and in C, both acquire an equal right to existence.

Why, then, has the first principle been determined as identity of the real and the ideal? — First of all, precisely to indicate that neither the real nor the ideal as such is the first or the Absolute, but that both are only subordinate forms of the proper *primordial being*. But then it is also meant to state positively that in both there is the *same* essence. My principle [p. 423] is best explained in relation to Fichteanism. Fichte draws the inference: no existence *except for itself*. Now only the I exists for itself. Therefore etc. The minor premise I deny. For subject and object is the universal form in matter as much as in the I (in which, then, from the other side the difference may lie, this is of course to be shown only later): thus, for example, in the body the repulsive force is the objective, the attractive force, with respect to the body, is that which returns upon itself, hence the subjective force. To Fichte this dualism bound up with identity is foreign.

c) In a third expression the principle of my philosophy was called quite directly the *Absolute* or *God*. But the Absolute here is the principle of the *whole* of philosophy; this is only one whole, it lives and moves in God, whereas the dogmatic or Leibniz-Wolffian system, but also the Kantian, bring God in only *afterwards*. The difference between my philosophy, and philosophy in general, and theology, to which it is related, is this, that theology is more merely an abstract of philosophy; it takes God, in a manner, as a particular object, whereas philosophy regards God at the same time as the highest ground of explanation of all things, and therefore spreads the Idea of God also over other objects. The following is connected with this.

It is a common question: if philosophy makes God its ground, how do we arrive at the cognition of God or of the Absolute? — To this question there is no answer. The existence of the unconditioned cannot be proved as that of the conditioned can. The unconditioned is the element in which alone demonstration is possible. Just as the geometer, when he begins to prove his propositions, does not first prove the existence of a space but merely presupposes it, so philosophy does not prove the existence of God, but confesses that without an Absolute or God it would not be at hand at all. — Everything can be presented only in the Absolute; the unconditioned therefore does not precede the existence of philosophy either, [p. 424] but the whole of philosophy is concerned with this existence, the whole of philosophy is properly the continuing proof of the Absolute, which therefore may not be demanded at its beginning. If the universe can be nothing other than manifestation of the Absolute, and philosophy nothing other than the spiritual presentation of the universe, then the whole of philosophy too is only manifestation, i.e. the continuing demonstration of God.

We proceed now from the proposition: the primordial being is necessarily, and by its nature, absolute identity of the real and the ideal. With this proposition, however, nothing has yet been said: we have merely the concept of the primordial being, but we do not yet have it as an *actual*, real being. Thus, for example, if we say: the essence of the human being is an absolute identity of freedom and necessity — a free and a necessary principle are most intimately united in it —, we have thereby indeed a concept of the human being, but as yet no living, actual human being; for this (in order to have an actual human being) we must consider him insofar as these principles in him are really in opposition, engaged in struggle. — Expressed otherwise: the primordial being as absolute identity of the real and the ideal is itself again only subjectively posited, but we must grasp it just as well objectively: it must be absolute identity of the real and the ideal not only *in itself* but also *outside itself*, i.e. it must reveal itself as such, actualize itself — it must show itself also in existence as one that is in essence absolute identity of the real and the ideal. Now, however, everything can become manifest only in its opposite, hence identity in non-identity, in difference, in distinguishability of the principles. *How* this is possible in God, of that we do not yet speak here, but only of this, that a separation, a difference must be posited, if we wish, that is, to get from essence to existence.

This transition from identity to difference has very often been regarded as a *canceling of identity*; but this is by no means [p. 425] the case, as I shall show presently. It is rather only a doubling of the essence, hence an intensification of unity, which can again be made clear by analogy with ourselves. Consciousness arises through a separation of principles that were previously implicit in the human being, e.g. the rational and the irrational. Neither of the two is to be annihilated. Precisely in the strife and the reconciliation of the two our humanity is to prove itself. If we now become conscious — if light and darkness separate in us —, we do not thereby step *out of ourselves*; the two principles still remain in us as their unity. We lose nothing of our essence, but possess ourselves now only in a doubled shape, namely once in unity, and the other time in disunion. So with God.

Let us posit A = A as the state of being enfolded within itself; then in this A = A we already have three things to note: a) A as object, b) A as subject, c) the identity of the two; but all this really indistinguishable. Now difference of the principles is to be posited: so, since A as subject and A as object are distinguishable, A = A is transformed into A = B; but since nonetheless the unity of the essence persists, in place of A / (A = A) the expression of the difference is A / (A = B), i.e. one and two; A = B is the disunion, A the unity, the whole together the living, actual primordial being; A has in A = B an object, a mirror. Thus in itself the primordial being is always unity — *unity of opposition and of disunion*.

Only now do we ask: *how* is this separation in God possible? For since the bond of the principles in God is once and for all indissoluble, a separation seems in this respect wholly *impossible*, and yet it is necessary for revelation. How is this contradiction to be resolved?

If the primordial being in A and B is again the whole, then A and B can be separated without the absolute bond of the principles being annulled. We would therefore have to assume [p. 426] that the primordial being in each of the separated remained the whole, i.e. posited itself as whole in them, so that under B there would again be comprised B, i.e. the real, A, i.e. the spiritual, and the unity of both. Likewise under A. — But would a *real* distinctness thereby already be posited? By no means. In the formula A / (A = A) let the upper A be called the essence in itself. But since this same identity is also the copula in A=A (the form), let the identity, insofar as it is alive in the form, be called the essence in the form. We have, then, 1) essence in itself, 2) essence in the form. But the essence in the form, so long as this is A = A (the principles not being differentiated), is identical with the essence in itself and not distinguishable from it. Now distinguishability was to be posited by differentiation of the form into two subordinate forms; in the following way:

A = Essence in itself

A / (A = A) = Essence in the absolute form.

(A / (A = B))^A (A / (A = B))^B

But since in each of these forms the same bond lies again that lies in the absolute form, each of the two again resolves itself into *the essence of the absolute form*, and through this into the essence *in itself*.

We are thus back where we were before. *We now have,* *instead of the simple factors* A = B, the two unities, i.e. we have only a more highly developed unity, but no *difference*.

Yet this transformation of the absolute form into two subordinate forms, or, what is the same, this complete in-forming of the *whole* primordial being into the real and into the ideal, is the necessary way to the final actual differentiation.

On closer consideration it turns out, namely, that between the two unities there nevertheless obtains an actual difference, even if one not yet *posited as actual*. The real unity (that under the exponent of B) behaves as *being*, the ideal (that [p. 427] under the exponent of A) as *position of being*. Now being by itself is already position: hence the position of being is a position of position, i.e. a position of the *second potency*.

Here, then, the concept of potencies, so highly important for the whole, first arises for us. We have first a higher and a lower — a difference of dignity. The ideal is higher than the real in dignity. — Expressed in the formula this would be presented thus.

a) B, being, cannot be for itself. By virtue of the indissoluble bond neither B nor A can ever exist for itself. The *real* being is thus always only A in B, or under the exponent of B; we express this by

A = B = first potency.

b) A also cannot be for itself, but, as position of the first potency, must contain this ideally within itself; it is thus

A² = second potency.

Both unities or potencies are again one in the absolute unity, this, as the common position of the first and the second potency, is A³, and the fully developed expression of the original A = A is therefore

A³ / (A² = (A = B)).

With this, however, something more is given at the same time than a mere difference of dignity. The first potency must by its nature precede the second; between the two potencies there is thus a priority and a posteriority; the real is naturâ prius, the ideal posterius. The lower is, to be sure, thereby posited *before* the higher, but not according to dignity, which would indeed contain a contradiction, but according to *existence*.

Yet the priority of the first potency now developed is as yet only an ideal or logical priority of the real over the ideal, but not yet an actual one. We have merely shown that and [p. 428] how a differentiation is *possible*. But how do we now arrive at its actuality?

The ground of this actuality can admittedly lie only in the primordial being or God himself. The means, however, has already been given. The first potency, namely, as we have just seen, precedes the second in the Idea even in God considered absolutely — the one is naturâ prior, the other posterior. If the primordial being, then, wills the disunion of the potencies, it must posit this priority of the first potency as an actual one (transform that merely ideal or logical priority into an actual one), i.e. it must voluntarily *restrict itself to the first*, and cancel the simultaneity of the principles, as it originally is in it. This canceling of simultaneity, however, is neither a canceling of the inner (essential) unity, for this does not rest on simultaneity, nor is it a canceling of the *bond* of the potencies, because, as soon as the first potency is posited, the second and then the third must immediately be posited as well. If the priority of the first potency becomes an actual one, the identity of the potencies in the Absolute is not canceled; it is only transformed into a linkage or coherence of them. Before this the potencies lie in it in complete indifference or indistinguishability. Likewise the whole of time lies implicitly in it, as unity or as *eternity*. By God’s voluntarily restricting himself to the first potency — voluntarily being only *one* when he could be everything — he makes a beginning of time (NB. not in time). Through his withdrawing to the first potency a limitation is indeed first posited in him, but since this contradicts his essence, in that by his nature he is *all potencies*, there arises a progression from the first to the second, and with it a time. The potencies are now posited at the same time as periods of God’s self-revelation.

#### Allgemeine Anmerkungen hiezu. — General Remarks on This

⁠1) Passive restriction is admittedly imperfection, a relative [p. 429] lack of force; but to restrict oneself, to enclose oneself in one point, yet to hold fast to this with all one’s forces, not to desist until it has expanded into a world, this is the highest force and perfection. Goethe says:

Whoever wills great things must pull himself together, / In limitation the master first shows himself.

To enclose oneself in force: therein lies true originality, the root-force. In A = B it is precisely B itself that is the contracting principle, and when God restricts himself to the first potency, this is all the more to be called a contraction. But contraction is the beginning of all reality. Hence too it is not the expansive but the contractive human beings who are primal and fundamentally forceful natures. Meanwhile the beginning of creation is indeed a *condescension* of God; he properly condescends into the real, contracts himself wholly into it. But there is nothing in this unworthy of God. The very condescension of God is what is greatest in Christianity too. A metaphysically screwed-up God is fit neither for our head nor for our heart.

⁠2) This act of restriction or condescension on God’s part is voluntary. There is thus no ground of explanation for the world other than the freedom of God. Only God himself can break the absolute identity of his essence and thereby make room for a revelation. Now, to be sure, all true, that is, absolute freedom is again an absolute necessity. For of an action of absolute freedom no further ground can be given; it is so because it is so, that is, it is simply and to that extent necessary. Commonly one wants to see freedom only where a choice has taken place, a state of doubt has preceded, and finally the decision has followed. But whoever knows what he wills takes hold without choice. Whoever chooses does not know what he wills, and therefore does not will either. All choice is the consequence of an unenlightened will. If God acts ex ratione boni, he has precisely a very subordinate freedom. To go further and allow him to choose the best world out of infinitely many possible ones means leaving him precisely [p. 430] the lowest degree of freedom. Such an entirely absolute action is, in us, the one that grounds our character. Character too arises through a kind of contraction, whereby we give ourselves a determinateness; the more intensive this is, the more character. No one will claim that a human being has chosen his character; to that extent it is no work of freedom in the ordinary sense, and yet imputable. Here, then, we find such an identity of freedom and necessity.

⁠3) Through the self-restriction of God only a beginning *of* *time*, but not a beginning *in time*, is posited. God himself is therefore not posited in time.

Time is posited in the real; but the real is not God himself, though inseparably bound up with him. For the real in God is *being* or existence, the ideal is the existent, and that in which the real and the ideal are one is the actually existing, living God.

Time is posited in the real (the being of God). But the real itself, as a *whole*, is nevertheless not in time either. Only the individual restricted element in it advances and unfolds. “But then this time in the real would surely be posited for God, and God would thus be somehow mixed up with time?” Answer: in that the *difference* in the real, and with it time, is posited, there is posited in God also, again, the position of this difference = A², in which everything is contained at once and in an eternal manner that develops in A = B in a temporal manner. Since now again in God considered absolutely, that is, in God insofar as he is neither merely existence (the real) nor merely the existent (subject), so in God as A³, A² and A = B are in constant connection, A = B too in him as subject (A²), or in his consciousness, immediately dissolves again into the eternity of his essence.

A² (God as subject) is the focal point or the unity of time. A³, or God considered absolutely, is neither eternity nor time, but absolute identity of eternity and time. Everything that is [p. 431] in time is eternal in him as subject, and everything that is eternal in him as subject is temporal in him as object.

*Question* 1. Is that act of self-differentiation *in time*? Did it occur before an infinite or before a determinate time? Answer: neither of the two. It is not in time at all, it is *above* all time, it is by its nature eternal.

*Question* 2. Does the universe have a beginning or none? It has a beginning (because it is dependent), but not a beginning *in time*. All time is in it, none outside it.

Properly, *every* thing (not only the universe) has time in itself. There is no external, general time; all time is *subjective*, that is, an inner time, which every thing has in itself, not outside itself. But because every individual thing has other things before and outside itself, its time can then be compared with the time of other things, although it has only one subjective time of its own. Thus there arises the abstractum time, namely only through comparison, measurement. In itself, however, there is no time. What is real in time is merely the various restrictions through which a being passes. Philosophically, therefore, we can properly say only: a thing has passed through these and these restrictions, but not that it has lived *so and so long*. This determination of so and so long can arise only from comparison; but if I consider a being in comparison, I do not consider it *in itself*, that is, not philosophically. In the case of the universe all possibility of such an illusion now entirely falls away, because all things are in it, none outside it, because it therefore cannot be measured by the time of a thing that would be *before* or outside it.

#### II. — II.

Without doubt, some expressions, for example that of a contraction in God and the like, have struck *you* as strange. Allow me, then, a general explanation of them, which will cast a new light on the sense of my view itself.

[p. 432] If we want to form an idea of the primordial being, of its being and life, we really have only the choice between two views.

a) Either the primordial being is for us one that is finished all at once and unalterably present. This is the ordinary concept of God, that of so-called rational religion and of all abstract systems. But the more we screw this concept of God up, the more God loses in liveliness for us, the less is he to be grasped as an actual, personal being, living in the proper sense as we do. If we demand a God whom we can regard as a wholly living, personal being, then we must also regard him quite humanly; we must assume that his life has the greatest analogy with the human one, that in him, alongside eternal being, there is also an eternal becoming, that in a word he has everything in common with the human being, except dependence (a saying of Hippocrates).

This presupposed, I will now say to *you* in a generally human manner what has so far been said in more scientific expressions:

God is an actual being, who however has nothing before or outside himself. Everything he is, he is through himself; he proceeds from himself in order finally to end again, purely, in himself. Thus in a word: *God makes himself*, and as surely as he makes himself, so surely is he not something finished and present from the start; for otherwise he would not need to make himself. — So what, then, is the original state in which the primordial being, wholly merely in itself and having nothing outside itself, finds itself?

All living existence begins from unconsciousness, from a state in which everything is still together undivided that afterward evolves singly out of it; there is as yet no consciousness with separation and distinction. Just so the divine life too begins. It contains everything in itself, is infinite fullness not only of what is alike but of what is unlike, but in complete undividedness. God is as yet there only as a quiet musing on [p. 433] himself, without all utterance and revelation. This is the state that we have designated as the indifference of the potencies in him. It is in itself already absolute identity of the subjective and the objective, of the real and the ideal, but it is not so *for itself*, but would be so only for a third, looking on, of which, understandably, there is none. We can now say in advance that the whole process of the creation of the world, which is still always the life-process in nature and in history, that this is really nothing other than the process of the completed becoming-conscious, of the completed personalization of God. — I explain this striking claim as follows.

In us there are two principles, an unconscious, dark one and a conscious one. The process of our self-formation, whether we seek to form ourselves with regard to cognition and science, or ethically, or quite without restriction through life and for life, always consists in raising what is unconsciously present in us to consciousness, in raising the innate darkness in us into light, in a word in attaining clarity. The same in God. The darkness goes before him; clarity breaks forth only out of the night of his essence.

God has the same two principles in himself that we have in ourselves. From the moment that we become aware of the two principles in us, that we separate ourselves within ourselves, set ourselves against ourselves, raise ourselves with the better part of ourselves above the lower one — from that moment consciousness *begins*, but not yet full consciousness on that account. The whole of life is really only an ever higher becoming-conscious; most stand at the lowest degree, and those who do take pains still mostly do not come to clarity, and perhaps none in the present life to absolute clarity — a dark remainder always stays behind — (none attains the height of his good and the abyss of his evil).

The same holds now of God. The *beginning* of consciousness in him is that he separates himself from himself, sets himself against himself. For he has a higher and a lower in [p. 434] himself — which we designated precisely through the concept of the potencies. In the still unconscious state God has the two principles indeed in himself, but without positing himself as the one or the other, that is, without cognizing himself in the one or the other. With the beginning consciousness this cognition takes place, that is, God posits himself (in part) as first potency, as the unconscious, but he cannot contract himself as real without expanding himself as ideal, cannot posit himself as real, as *object*, without positing himself *at the same time* as subject (without thereby setting the ideal free); and both is *one act*, both absolutely *at the same* *time*; with his actual contraction as real his expansion as ideal is posited.

The higher in God as it were thrusts the lower away from itself, with which it was hitherto in indifference or mixture, and conversely, the lower by its contraction separates itself from the higher — and this, as in the human being so also in God, is the *beginning* of his consciousness, of his becoming personal.

But as the human being in the process of his self-formation or becoming self-conscious excludes from himself the dark, unconscious element in himself, sets it against himself, not in order to leave it forever in this exclusion, in this darkness, but in order gradually to raise this excluded element, this dark element itself, to clarity, to form it upward into his conscious, so also God excludes the lower of his essence from the higher and as it were thrusts it away from himself, but not in order to leave *it* now in this non-being, but in order to raise it out of it, in order to educe, form upward, create, out of the non-divine excluded from himself — out of that which is not *He himself*, and which he has for that very reason separated from himself — what is like and equal to him. Creation therefore consists in the calling forth of the higher, properly divine, in the excluded.

Only, naturally, this unconscious of God is an infinite like himself, hence not so soon exhausted, and hence the duration of the process of the creation of the world.

To open to you at once a further prospect: this subordinate [p. 435] being, this dark, unconscious element that God constantly seeks to thrust away from himself as essence, from his proper interior, to exclude, is *matter* (not, to be sure, matter already formed), and matter is thus nothing other than the unconscious part of God. But in that he seeks on the one side to exclude it from himself, he seeks on the other to draw it again to himself, to form it up to himself, to transfigure it — though subordinate — into his higher essence, to call forth the conscious out of this unconscious, out of matter. Hence the process of creation comes to a standstill only where, out of the unconscious, out of the depth of matter, consciousness is awakened and created, that is, in the human being; and although with the human being too an immense mass of unconsciousness is brought up to the higher level, which then in turn is decomposed and yields the material of new creations, God nevertheless first comes to rest in the human being; his chief purpose is attained in the human being.

It is indeed striking to the ordinary abstract way of viewing that in God there should be a principle that is not God, that is unconscious, that is less than He himself. Whoever thinks of God as an empty identity cannot, to be sure, grasp this. The proof of the necessity of this assumption lies in the *fundamental law of opposition*. Without opposition no life. In the human being and in every existence generally it is the same. In us too there is a rational and an irrational. Every thing, in order to manifest itself, needs something that is not *itself*, sensu stricto. (This conception is really directed only against the abstract concepts of God as ens realissimum — illimitatissimum; God is, to be sure, not limited toward the outside, but *in himself*, as surely as he is a determinate nature.)

To bring this togetherness of a higher and a lower in God still closer, the following serves.

The real, unconscious, is the being of God, purely *as such*. Now the being of God is not *one and the same* with God himself, but really different, as in the human being. Accordingly the ideal is the *being* God, or the existing God, or also God [p. 436] sensu eminenti. For by God in the strict sense we always understand the being God. Accordingly the two principles in God also relate as that which is and being. The ideal or *conscious* is the subject of being, the unconscious only the predicate of this subject, of that which is, and thus only for the sake of that which is.

If, then, God has separated himself within himself, he has separated himself *as that which is* from his *being*: which is also in the human being the highest moral act. Our being is only means, instrument for ourselves. The human being who cannot separate himself from his being (make himself independent of it, free himself), who is wholly grown together and remains one with his being, is the human being insofar as he is wholly sunk in his selfhood and unable to heighten himself in himself — morally and intellectually. For whoever does not separate himself from his being, being is what is essential, not his inner, higher, true essence. Likewise, if God remained grown together with his being, there would be no life, no heightening. Therefore he separates himself from his being, so that it is only an instrument for him.

A second expression of the relation of the two principles, following from the first, is that they relate as that which is and *that which is not*.

To investigate the essence of that which is not, precisely therein lies properly the hard part, the cross, of all philosophy. We grasp after it eternally and are not able to hold it fast.

From a misunderstanding of this concept the representation of a creation out of nothing has arisen. All finite beings are created out of that which is not, but not out of *nothing*. The οὐκ ὄν of the Greeks is as little as the μὴ φαινόμενα of the N. T. a *nothing*, it is only the not-subjective, that which is not, but for that very reason *being itself*. A not-being forces itself on us in many ways as something nevertheless in another respect again being. What is, for example, sickness? A state *against nature*; hence insofar a state that could not be and yet is, no reality at bottom and yet again an undeniably terrible [p. 437] reality. Evil is in the moral world what sickness is in the bodily one; it is the most decided non-essence considered from one side, and yet has a dreadful reality.

All that is not is only *relative*, namely in relation to a higher that is, but it has in itself nevertheless again something that is; B and A can therefore be separated in nothing.

So if B = the pure not-being, B could not be for itself; it has again an A in itself and is thus (A = B); but this *whole* (A = B) relates to a higher again as that which is not, as mere substrate, mere matter, mere organ or instrument; meanwhile it is *in itself* again a being. This now applied to what we have called being in God: this is, in relation to that which is in God, indeed a not-being, namely it relates to it originally merely as substrate, as that which is not itself, which merely is in order to serve the true being as basis. But yet it is again a being in itself.

In other words, and as I have otherwise also expressed it: there is nothing purely and merely *objective* in God, for that would be nothing; but that which is objective in relation to the higher in God is nevertheless in itself again also subjective and objective, not mere B, but A and B.

Yet from another side.

Also the mere being in God is no dead being, but again in itself a living one, which itself again encloses a being and a being-in-itself. God himself is *above* nature, nature his throne, his subordinate, but everything in him is so full of life that even this subordinate again breaks out into a life of its own, which considered purely for itself is a wholly perfect life, though in relation to the divine life a non-life. Thus Phidias depicted on the sole of the foot of his Jupiter the battles of the Lapiths and Centaurs. As here — perhaps led only by that [p. 438] wonderful instinct that is in all Greek works — the artist fills even the sole of the god’s foot with vigorous life, so the outermost and most remote from God is, as it were, still full, vigorous life in itself.

Through the theory of the two principles that are one in God we avoid two wrong paths on which one is apt to go astray in the doctrine of God. With regard to the Idea of God, namely, error is made on two sides. According to the dogmatic view, held to be orthodox, God is regarded as a particular, cut-off, individual being subsisting wholly for itself, whereby the creature is thus wholly excluded from him. The common pantheistic view, on the other hand, leaves God no particular, own, self-subsisting existence at all; it rather dissolves him into a universal substance, which is only the bearer of things. Now God is, however, both; he is first of all the essence of all essences, but as this he must nevertheless also himself exist, that is, as the essence of all essences he must have a hold, a foundation for himself. Thus: God is in his highest dignity the universal essence of all things, but this universal essence does not hover in the air, but is grounded and as it were borne by God as *individual* being — *the individual in God thus the basis or substrate of the universal*.

So there are also, according to this view, two principles in God. The first principle or the first primal force is that through which he is a particular, individual, individuated being. We can call this force the *selfhood*, the egoism in God. Were this force alone, then God would be only as an individual, cut-off, particular being, there would be no creature. There would be nothing but an eternal closedness and withdrawal into himself, and this proper force of God, because it would always be an infinite force, would be a consuming fire in which no creature could live. (We must think of it by analogy with the force of the heart as it manifests itself in a most reserved human being, who for that very reason is also called gloomy, to whom we ascribe a dark heart.)
