Answer: Darkness too has its light, as the existent has a non-existent in itself. Moreover, the highest opposite of clairvoyance [p. 478] is *madness*. Madness, then, is the state of hell. — One question is: what will memory be like? It will only not extend to everything possible, since a right-minded man would give much even here to be able to forget at the right time. There will be an oblivion, a Lethe, but with different effect: the good, having arrived there, will have oblivion of all evil, and hence also of all suffering and all pain, the evil by contrast the oblivion of all good. — Moreover, it will of course not be memory as it is here; for here we must first make everything *inward, there everything is* already inward. The designation memory is far too weak for it. Of a friend, a beloved, with whom one was one heart and one soul, one says that one remembers them, they live constantly in *us*, they do not come into our heart, they are in it, and so, then, will memory be there.

Through death the physical (so far as it is essential) and the spiritual are brought into one. Thus there the physical and the spiritual *together* will be the objective — the basis —, but the soul, though only among the blessed, will enter as the subjective, will become their proper subject, and this entails that they go to God, are united with God. Unblessedness consists precisely in this, that the soul cannot enter as subject because of the revolt of the spirit, hence separation from the soul and from God.

Because man is transposed into his own A², he is thereby transposed into the world of spirits. Here, then, the construction of the world of spirits finds its place. As there is a philosophy of nature, so there is also a philosophy of the world of spirits. On this only the following.

From the very beginning, when God separated the real and the ideal, he had to posit the ideal too as a world of its own. As, accordingly, in the real there was the real, the ideal, and the indifference of both, so also in the ideal, only everything under the potency of the ideal. Thus in the ideal of God there is again something that corresponds to nature, only that it is itself wholly ideal. The real in the ideal is, as we have just found on the occasion of man, the heart. In God too there is a [p. 479] heart, and this heart is in the spiritual of God again the real; it relates to the *spirit* in God, to the absolutely existent, again as first potency, as basis, as dark principle. The heart in God is therefore the matter of the world of spirits, as the properly real was the matter out of which the physical world, and out of which man, was created. Thus the pure spirits are created from the divine heart, and there is, as surely, a world of spirits, even independently of man, as there is a *world of* *nature*. *We* receive our heart from nature, the spirits from God himself.

Since in this way also in the pure spirits, created from the heart of God (which again is relatively independent of the spirit in God, that is, of the absolutely existent) — since, then, also in the pure spirits there is a relatively non-existent and an existent, *they* too are capable of freedom, hence also of good and evil. As it was God’s intention that through man, the highest creature of the world of nature, nature should receive a connection with the world of spirits, so it was probably also his intention that through the highest creature of the world of spirits the latter should receive the connection with nature. If now this creature also failed, then necessarily the same fall occurred in the world of spirits as in the visible world, and likewise a separation of the good and the evil spirits. Without doubt that highest creature of the world of spirits, which, as man was destined on the side of nature, so on the other side was destined to be lord of the world, wanted to be the *lord* of this world without God, by its own power, and so it fell. Naturally it had to be the highest interest of this highest created spirit to bring it about that this world should really become a world of its own, separated from God, because only then could he hope to rule it. Assuming, then, that his fall preceded that of man, his malice had to direct itself against man, because in him there was still the only possibility of how nature and the world of spirits could come together, hence the possibility that he might obtain a realm of his own, independent of God, as he indeed sought. Since now [p. 480] man before the fall still really stood in closer rapport with the world of spirits, that higher spirit could also really have an influence on man, more immediate than now; for now man, as he commonly is, is too bad even for the devil; the *bad* is the *mixed*; the pure evil is in its kind something pure. In this way, roughly, the Christian explanation of the fall could be made probable.

So much, then, for the original inhabitants of the world of spirits, that is, those created into it. But now the world of spirits is also a world in another respect, namely a system of objects, and indeed quite such a one as nature. For nature and the world of spirits are altogether no more different than — to use an example somewhat crass but nonetheless making the matter intuitive — the world of plastic art and the world of poetry, whose figures do not appear visibly, but must be generated anew in each person by his own activity, and are therefore intuitable only inwardly. The world of spirits is the poetry of God, nature his plastic art. In man there arises something intermediate, namely the visible drama, because it presents its spiritual creations at the same time in actuality. Hence history is best regarded as a great tragedy performed on the mournful stage of this world, which furnishes the mere boards, while the actors, that is, the persons represented upon it, are from a wholly different world. In that world everything that is in this one is only in a poetic, that is, spiritual manner, and can therefore be communicated much more perfectly, also in a spiritual way (the spirit wholly sight, wholly feeling). There are the archetypes, here the copies.

The immediate connection of nature with the world of spirits is indeed interrupted through man; yet for that reason they do not cease to be one world and to relate to one another at least from afar. A certain sympathy still remains between them, as between the strings of different instruments, where, when a tone is struck on one, the corresponding string of the other sympathetically resonates. Thus *this* relation of the world of spirits to nature continues forever; it is grounded in [p. 481] the essence of the universe itself , it was indissoluble. And as the world of spirits as a whole is bound with nature by a necessary consensus harmonicus, so also are the *individual* objects of the world of spirits and of the world of nature. So there must likewise be societies in the world of spirits that correspond to those in the world, only that there like comes altogether to like, whereas here the mixed is together. Hence that nation which has most removed itself from the mixture, that is, which has most excluded from itself either the evil or the good, thus either the most pious and virtuous or the most wicked and vicious, has the most power, because it is the most daemonic. Peoples among whom there still dwells freedom, innocence, purity of morals, poverty, that is, precisely separation from the things of this world, are in rapport with heaven and the good world of spirits; those among whom the opposite holds, with hell.

Likewise each individual man, according as either the good or the evil in him has come to higher purity, stands in relation either with the good or with the evil world of spirits. Through the ongoing life-process of the species, man becomes alternately receptive and unreceptive to the world of spirits in general. The man who has separated the good in himself purely from the evil would without doubt be capable of rapport with good spirits, who merely shun the mixture, and who, as the Bible says somewhere, constantly long to look into the mystery of outer nature, — where properly the greatest secret is being prepared, namely the complete incarnation of God, of which only the beginning has so far occurred. Likewise he who had the evil in himself purely separated from all good in himself would be in rapport with evil spirits. It is inconceivable how one could ever have doubted such a connection. We live under constant inspirations; whoever pays attention to himself finds it so. Especially in difficult cases these inspirations never fail man, and if he does not have them, it is his own fault. Man is never wholly forsaken, and amid the many sorrows that each one experiences he can [p. 482] nonetheless be certain that he has invisible friends, a heroic faith that makes one able to do much and also to suffer much.

As each man has a relation to the world of spirits, so also each thing of nature has, through its good side, a relation to heaven, through its evil side to the other side of the world of spirits. Hence man must be more cautious in nothing than in his intercourse with nature, but especially with other men. (Dietary precepts of the ancient philosophers.) The world of spirits cannot penetrate the present world only because of the mixture. But if one could wholly cover up, drive out, or overpower the good in a thing, e.g., then the evil spirits could work in it. This is the ground of *black* magic and of sorcery. — But let this suffice about the world of spirits, and perhaps it is already too much.

The world of spirits and nature must after all finally be united, the higher potency of the properly eternal and absolute life must still enter. Grounds for this are. 1) The highest *spiritual* blessedness is after all not yet the absolute. We wish to have something that is not *we ourselves*, as God has something in order to behold us in it as in a mirror. 2) Nature is subjected without guilt to the present state (Paul’s passage), it longs for the union; 3) so too God again for nature. He will not leave it standing eternally as a ruin. 4) All potencies must really be brought into one. So far there are only two periods: a) the present one, where indeed all potencies, but subordinated to the real; b) the life of spirits, where also all potencies, but subordinated to the ideal. There will therefore be a third, c) where all are subordinated to absolute identity — thus the spiritual or ideal does not exclude the physical and real; where both are subordinated in common and as of equal worth to the higher. This restoration, however, is impossible before the same separation takes place in nature. But in nature it comes about more slowly, because it has a much deeper life-force. Man is in this a sacrifice for nature, as it was first a sacrifice for him. He must wait with his perfect existence for its own [p. 483] to come. Finally the crisis of nature must come, by which the long sickness is decided. Every crisis is accompanied by an expulsion. This crisis is the last of nature, hence “the last judgment.” Every crisis, in the physical too, is a judgment. Through a truly alchemical process the good will be separated from the evil, the evil wholly expelled from the good, and out of this crisis a wholly sound, pure, clean, and innocent nature will emerge. Into this pure nature nothing will enter but the truly existent, which can be an existent only in its *right* relation; nature will thus be freed from the falselyexistent, the non-existent. In return the non-existent, which had raised itself in it to the existent, will be subordinated to *it* as basis, this non-existent or evil will be placed in the deepest depth *beneath* nature, and since this is already the mitigated divine egoism, it sinks into the consuming fire of the latter, that is, into hell. After this last catastrophe hell would thus be the foundation of nature, as nature is the foundation, the basis, of heaven, that is, of the divine presence. Evil is then no longer present in relation to God and the universe. Only in itself is it still present. It now has what it wanted, the complete being-in-itself, thus separation from the universal, the divine world. It is given over to the torments of its own egoism, to the hunger of selfishness.

Through the separation in nature each of its elements receives the nearest and most immediate rapport with the world of spirits. Hence the resurrection of the dead. The world of spirits enters into the actual one. The evil spirits receive their body also from the element of evil, the good from the element of the good — from that fifth element, the divine matter.

The highest final end of creation is now fulfilled, a) God wholly actualized, visibly corporeal, thus A³/(A² = (A = B)), b) the lowest has come to the highest (circuit) — the end in the [p. 484] beginning — only that now everything is explicit which was before implicit, c) especially the secret of *humanity*. In man the two outermost extremes are bound together. Therefore he is esteemed by God more highly than the angels. Man is from the lowest and the highest. Humanity, which was already deified through the God made man, is now universally deified, and through man, and with him also nature.

If we wish to be consistent, we must recognize also in the *third* period again periods or potencies. But these lie as far beyond our spiritual horizon as (to use a feeble image) the remotest nebula, resolvable by no telescope any more, lies beyond our bodily one. Thus if there are periods here still, they are to be placed in a successive rule: a) of the God made man (perhaps nonetheless still a particular rule of the world of nature and spirits, without separation however). b) Rule of the Spirit. c) Finally everything delivered up to the Father. Perhaps this then, when hell too is no more; and into these periods of eternity falls, then, the restoration also of evil, which we must believe. Sin is not eternal, hence neither is its consequence.

This last period in the last is that of the wholly perfect actualization — thus of the complete incarnation of God, where the infinite has become wholly finite without detriment to its infinity.

Then God is truly All in All, pantheism true.

[p. 485]

## Aufsätze und Recensionen aus der Jenaer und Erlanger Literaturzeitung und dem Morgenblatt — Essays and Reviews from the Jena and Erlangen Literary Gazettes and the Morgenblatt

[p. 486] From the Years 1807—1809.

[p. 487]

### Notiz von den neuen Versuchen über die Eigenschaften der Erz- und Wasserfühler und die damit zusammenhängenden Erscheinungen.<sup>108</sup> — Notice of the New Experiments on the Properties of Ore- and Water-Diviners and the Phenomena Connected Therewith.<sup>108</sup>

<sup>108</sup> From the Intelligenzblatt of the Jenaische Allgemeine Literaturzeitung, 1807, no. 36.

Of these remarkable experiments, which have been conducted in Munich since the end of last year, no literary journal has so far made any mention. Cotta’s Morgenblatt carried a popular report on them, which has stirred up considerable commotion here and there among scholars and the merely curious. It seems, however, that the matter has been taken up in earnest by only a few; that contradictions, inexplicable anomalies and phenomena have shown themselves in the experiments, which one no longer had the heart to trust. All these misgivings could now be remedied with a single bold word; but the present writer does not wish to be the first to pronounce it, since whoever does not find it for himself thereby already shows that he has not directed to the phenomena, any more than to himself, that attentiveness which may fairly be demanded.

The most recent history of the earnest revival of such experiments was, according to the account in the Morgenblatt, briefly this: Mr. Ritter received from a friend the news that at Guarignano on Lake Garda a young man possessed the same property by which Bleton, with whom Franklin, and Pennet, with whom Thouvenel and other Italian [p. 488] scholars had experimented, had become so well known , and that he had given manifold proofs of his feeling for water and metals under the earth throughout the whole region. Mr. Ritter’s wish to undertake calm investigations of this matter, so often rejected yet as often returned, was supported by the efforts of the profound Franz Baader, and the privy councillor von Schenk took it upon himself to lay it before the minister, Baron von Montgelas, who gave his approval with good will; and so Ritter was put in a position, and authorized, to undertake the journey. In a northern newspaper, where this undertaking is mentioned, the author of the article concerning it can hardly restrain his astonishment that a government should have been willing to spend money on the investigation of such a subject. Conceit of supposed science cannot well rise higher: governments are, it seems, to take the word of a few physicists, who have never concerned themselves thoroughly with these phenomena, that there is nothing in them! These very physicists, if they were so perfectly certain of their opinion, ought to be grateful to a government that gives them the opportunity finally to prove their opinion, which till now has been equal to a mere prejudice, and to ground it in actual experiments. Think of the fate of meteoric stones and similar phenomena, which were rejected with just as much impudence by similar investigators of nature and were at last verified through the zeal of true scholars and the support of large-minded governments. Praise and thanks, then, to the enlightened minister who held these phenomena important enough to favor a decisive examination of them even by external support!

After Mr. Ritter had carried out the preliminary exact experiments at the residence of the new ore- and water-diviner, which convinced him in general of the presence of that faculty in this individual, and after he had made the acquaintance in Milan, in the librarian of the Ambrosiana, Abbate Amoretti, of a scholar who had already penetrated deeply into this matter and from all sides by experiments, he took the [p. 489] young Campetti with him to Munich, in order to obtain, through continued investigations, such information as was not really yet available in the manifold but confused proceedings which, within the last twenty years, Pennet in particular had occasioned in Italy.

The most important moments of this new investigation seem to the present writer, according to what he had occasion to see for himself in Munich, to come down to the following chief points.

I. *The power of the human body in general to set other, so-called* *dead bodies, e.g. metals, into motion dynamically, without any* *intervention of mechanical influence.* — To this relate the experiments a) with the pendulum oscillations of Abbé *Fortis*. With these Ritter began his study of these phenomena: the article in the Morgenblatt contains the description of the manner<sup>109</sup> in which the experiment is to be conducted; and this is the one that has been repeated everywhere, with the varying success of which mention was already made above. It is undeniable that this experiment does not succeed with some persons; but just as undeniable that it succeeds with many. The former would be no stranger, even if no other ground contributed here, than that not all human beings possess equally great powers for magnetizing, or an equal capacity for being magnetized. More important, however, is that (as most at least imagine) a mechanical influence can hardly be excluded here, or at the very least that its absence cannot be established with full certainty, even for the most incredulous. Yet this is not entirely impossible, since the circular movements of the pendulum differ according to the difference of the bodies, of the metals e.g., with which the experimenting subject is in contact. Whoever, then, wished to convince himself of the reality of these experiments need only lay on the head, or under the sole of the foot, of a subject with whom the experiments succeed at all, now this, now that metal, without the subject himself [p. 490] being able to perceive it, in order to find that the movement with the same metal, all other circumstances being equal, is always the same, which, if some mechanical influence, even an unconscious one, were to intervene, could not possibly occur with such regularity. — These experiments can, namely, be set up in various ways: 1) so that the pendulum is held over a metal, over water, some other liquid, or a living part; 2) so that not the metal, but the experimenter, is in contact with such a body, or at least in its sphere of action; 3) also without any visible intervention of a third body, so that the power of the human body appears sufficient by itself to set the pendulum into circular movements. b) With the actual divining-rod or baguette, whose movements are only not whole but half rotations, and follow entirely the same laws as the pendulum movements, so that, like those, according to the nature of the metal with which the experimenter is in contact, they take place either from without inward or from within outward. c) With a rod or plate of metal (though also of sealing-wax and other non-conductors), which, balanced on the tip of a finger, begins after a few moments to move to the right or to the left, according to the nature of the third body with which the experimenter is in contact. For this experiment to succeed a high degree of power is already required, a higher one than for the movement of the baguette.

<sup>109</sup> This article is likewise by Schelling and is communicated in the Appendix as far as it serves to supplement what is said here. Ed.

II. *Differences and polarities of unanimated bodies, as of all* *parts of an animated one, which are found by means of those movements; and: the influence of general external potencies on the phenomenon.* Thus, e.g., the direction of the pendulum’s circlings is one over the north pole, another over the south pole of the magnet; one just as opposed over metals, which also in other, the galvanic, electrical and chemical experiments behave like the two poles of the magnet. A decided polarity shows itself at the opposite ends of a fresh egg, of a fruit, of a plant in general; [p. 491] further between the sexual parts of plants. Likewise a decided difference and polarity of all parts of the human body reveals itself, not only through the movement of the pendulum, but also through movements of the balanced rod and of the baguette. With the latter Amoretti has experimented through the whole surface of the human body, and has appended to a treatise which appears in the Scelta d’Opuscoli, published under his supervision, a drawing of the human figure with an indication of all the differences and poles on it. As for the influence of general external potencies on the phenomenon, there have so far been distinguished in particular as such: *sunlight*, which, oddly enough, exerts an effect that, according to the observation of several, the eye too can have, of strengthening, inhibiting or altering the direction of the movement; electricity, which not only has a determining influence on the experimenting subject, but, as already now seems proved partly by earlier experiments, partly by new ones made by Ritter, is able immediately and through itself to bring forth these very rotatory movements. This is only a proof of how much deeper the root of the electrical force still lies in nature than one was accustomed to imagine on the basis of the phenomena hitherto known.

III. *The faculty, in a certain way opposed to the power of movement which the human being dynamically exercises on other bodies,* *of being set in motion by these bodies, chiefly metals and water,* *inwardly, that is.* — It may for the present remain entirely undecided whether this is related to that perhaps as, in the animal body, the power of the nervous system to set the muscles, as external things, into motion is related to the capacity of receiving sensations from external things; and whether the former, accordingly, must be regarded only as a higher potency of the latter. Apart from the experiments which Mr. Ritter had already conducted in Italy with Campetti on this matter, and which all bore witness to the distinguished degree of strength and certainty of this particular capacity of sensation in him, no experiments on a large scale and in the open [p. 492] could so far be conducted in the harsher climate, which are therefore still to be expected when the better season has set in.

IV. *Connection of these phenomena with the other dynamical* *phenomena of nature.* — There is probably no one who would not at first glance be reminded of a relation of these phenomena to the galvanic and electrical ones. That they are, however, not so much explained by electricity as rather themselves first yield the true word for it, has already been remarked above. We add that this may well hold for all dynamical phenomena. Yet it is doubtful whether they will show themselves more important for the doctrine of electricity and what is connected with it, or for the physiology of the heavens, or for that of the human being and the medicine founded upon it. At least it is remarkable that the stimulus to these phenomena has occurred at the same time from different sides, and that the medical art laid claim to it even earlier than general physics. Connoisseurs may recall Wienholt’s endeavors; recently, in an article on animal magnetism in the<sup>110</sup> Jahrbücher der Medicin by Marcus and Schelling (vol. II, no. 2) the whole phenomenon, of metal-feeling as well as of moving, still independently of the most recent experiments, was brought into connection with the first-named phenomenon. Its relation to galvanism is presented there thus: “Galvanism, insofar as it lies midway between electricity and animal magnetism, we have hitherto cognized and grasped only from one of its two sides, namely from that where the inorganic plays the active, the organic the passive role, the former the communicating or tone-setting, the latter the receiving and subordinate one. But there is, it seems to me, still another side of it, in which everything stands precisely the reverse, where, namely, the organic is the communicating, the inorganic the receiving member.” Among the factual evidence for the actuality [p. 493] of such a relation an experiment is cited with the turning of a sword, whose guard is held in balance on a finger by two persons; an experiment which deserves to be added to those cited under no. I. as one all the less exposed to contradictions, since it is two different persons who hold the sword, and the experiment in this combination with others succeeds even with those who cannot accomplish it in another way. From what is mentioned there about the sensitivity of magnetized persons to the same bodies, metals and water, it appears that the peculiar faculty of the ore- and water-diviners can be regarded only as a lesser degree of somnambulism, and that, since the capacity to move foreign bodies too is present most strongly precisely in water- and metal-diviners, this whole phenomenon will resolve itself into that deeply misjudged, but soon no longer misjudgeable phenomenon, which for some decades has had such various fortunes under the name of animal magnetism.

<sup>110</sup> By Schelling’s brother, K. E. Schelling. Ed.

It is altogether strange that everything that is factual in this affair is not new; no experience has so far been made which is not recorded as a fact in many older, and even newer, books. Even the word concealed above is not merely on the tip of the writers’ tongues, but is clearly pronounced in most of the older works. But the sense is new in which the whole phenomenon is grasped and combined. The matter is at last treated with German earnestness and depth; under a happy constellation, where higher views of nature come to meet the experiment, and an experimenter such as Ritter finds an individual whose patience and childlike joy in the experiments holds out most faithfully, and who abhors the thought of the slightest deceit and would believe himself thereby to be robbing himself of his gift, which he values highly.

It cannot fail that very different judgments about the matter [p. 494] prevail; that sensible and senseless doubts, jocular and serious, are raised, even by those who have seen something, as well as something can be seen in distraction and without any prior knowledge of what matters; also by those who have not seen. But just such a stumbling-block in an age that deems itself wise, yet on the whole and in the large has gradually sunk to the deepest ignorance, must be welcome to the true friend of science.

Mr. von Aretin is occupied with writing a history of the divining-rod or baguette, which may become a very extensive work if he wishes to take up its traces everywhere, traces that of course reach far beyond the virgula divina of Cicero. — Mr. Ritter has so far made nothing public of his experiments. May he not hold back too long, and may the new, inestimably important service which he has rendered to the science of nature soon be added to his others!

#### Nachschrift an den Herrn Herausgeber der Jen. A. L. Z. — Postscript to the Editor of the Jen. A. L. Z.

As I am about to send off this notice, I receive your esteemed letter, in which you wish to obtain information about several other circumstances of these phenomena that have not been touched on in what precedes, e.g. how the power was discovered in Campetti. In reply to this: when Pennet at Guarignano, several years ago, was publicly conducting his experiments with the discovery of springs and describing his sensations in doing so, the then very young Campetti remarked that over flowing water he had quite the same feelings; whereupon Pennet, questioning him more closely, had to concede to him the same power as to himself. Further: in what do the peculiar sensations consist in feeling metals and water? So far as is already known from earlier statements of such individuals, the symptoms in the feeling of metals are chiefly: increased pulse, sensations of contractions in the lower region of the forehead toward the eyes, perhaps similar to the sensation of cobwebs in electrifying; further a taste on [p. 495] the tongue, now sour, now bitter, according to the nature of the metal present. Over rapidly flowing water a noticeable shock joins a part of these symptoms; in Pennet there appeared, over metals and water, even externally visible, involuntary twitchings, dilation of the pupil, etc. With regard to a third question I remark that the feeling extends to metal ores in the earth just as well as to native metal deliberately hidden in it. Campetti, when he is attentive, finds single coins of the size of a louis d’or by mere feeling, without any external indication. Coal also places itself in this respect entirely on a par with metal. Amoretti has obtained from the Italian government a piece of land, of which he had been informed through the feeling of a certain Anfossi, whom he uses as an instrument, that it was traversed by seams of coal, and has begun and thus far carried on its mining with no small profit.

*Appendix* : — — In order to connect the phenomenon, so<sup>111</sup> entirely individual in appearance, with a more generally diffused faculty and to make it more intelligible, Ritter, with the ingenuity peculiar to him, thought of the sulphur-pyrite pendulum of Abbé *Fortis*, whose oscillations had long since been suppressed again and rejected. He found only here that this experiment succeeds not merely for him but for nearly all who have so far undertaken it. In the space of a few weeks it has already been developed to the finest modifications and to most remarkable results; daily new phenomena show themselves.

<sup>111</sup> From the Morgenblatt, year 1807, no. 26.

I will now briefly indicate to you what it is about, and *how* *it is* to be done.

One takes a cube of sulphur pyrites or native sulphur or any metal (size and shape are indifferent; one can take, e.g., a gold ring for it), and hangs it horizontally on a twine thread, which may be ¼ or ½ ell long, and is best kept always somewhat moistened, by holding the thread with two fingers so steadily that the cube no longer moves mechanically back and forth.

[p. 496] So one holds it free and at not too great a distance over the center of a vessel with water or of any metal (a coin, a zinc or copper plate), and it will become alive and move in gently beginning, elongated ellipses describing, gradually rounding, regular oscillations.

Over the north pole of the magnet it will move: from the left to the right side.

Over the south pole: from the right to the left.

Over copper or silver: as over the south pole.

Over zinc and water: as over the north pole.

One must conduct the experiments uniformly, that is, so that one always approaches the object from above, or always from the side. From the side the relation changes in such a way that the kind of oscillation from the left to the right side, which is given above for the north pole, reverses and becomes as with the south pole, and vice versa.

It also makes a difference whether one operates with the right or the left hand, for between the right and the left side the opposition in some persons is developed to the most decided polarity.

Every supposition of deception that one might think up here will be refuted by one’s own definite feeling that the pendulum swings without any mechanical impulse. The regularity of the results will fully convince you. You can make all possible experiments on it, e.g. drive the cube mechanically around to the opposite side when it is already swinging: it will return to the first direction as soon as it has run out the mechanical impulse.

If one holds the cube over an orange, an apple, etc., it will swing over the fruit, there where it was attached to the stalk, as over the south pole of the magnet; if one turns the fruit to the opposite side, while continuing to hold the pendulum over it, the direction changes. Just such decided polarity shows itself at the two opposite ends of a fresh egg.

Most strikingly, however, the pendulum shows the polarity of the human organism.

The cube held over the head swings as over zinc. At the soles of the feet: as over copper.

At the forehead and eyes = north pole.

At the nose it turns = south pole.

At the mouth = south pole.

At the chin again as at the forehead.

In this manner the whole body can be experimented through. The inner and outer surfaces of the hand are opposed to each other. Over each fingertip the cube swings, and indeed over the fourth, or ring finger, alone toward the opposite [p. 497] side from the others. This finger is even able, when it is laid alone on the edge of the table where the experiment is made, to stop the oscillations or also to alter them.

The experiments on the polarity of the body were among those which the Abbate *Amoretti* had already undertaken with the baguette.

The baguette, in its efficacy, according to Ritter’s remark, is nothing other than a double pendulum, to set which in motion requires only a higher degree of the same power which produces those oscillations.

I have here indicated to you only in haste a few preliminary exercises, which you may cultivate further, and which will probably lead you to many of the results at which one has already arrived here. This faculty too wants practice. In *Ritter’s* hands the baguette at first did not incline, and it happened only when *Campetti* laid his hands on his shoulders. Now it happens to him and to several others. *Campetti’s* power seems to have something communicable about it. His immediate proximity suffices to disturb the regularity of the experiments made beside him; in him himself, on the other hand, the utmost regularity reveals itself in the experiments made with him, which are the purer since he is neither instructed how copper and zinc, e.g., act, and very often does not know which metal has been laid under his hand or at his foot while he holds the baguette, which likewise inclines inward or outward according to the difference of the metal; since he understands not a word of German, he also does not learn incidentally what effect is expected of him. He is a quite simple, selfcontented and vigorous man, who knows nothing except that God has bestowed this gift on him, and that he must preserve it through a temperate and pious life.

[p. 498]

### Die Weihnachtsfeier. Ein Gespräch. Von Friedrich Schleiermacher. Halle, 1806.<sup>112</sup> — The Christmas Celebration. A Conversation. By Friedrich Schleiermacher. Halle, 1806.<sup>112</sup>

<sup>112</sup> From the Jenaische Allgemeine Literaturzeitung, 1807, nos. 58. 59.

Holy Eve gathers a family of relatives and friends, children and adults. To all, from all, gifts are distributed in keeping with the custom of the festival; they are handed over to the “sensible and cheerful Ernestine,” who arranges them into an attractive, amiably symbolic impression and then opens the doors of the hall. — Little Sophie has received sheet music, religious compositions in the grand old church style; for only this does the wonderful child love and practice, and she at once strikes up the first notes of a higher celebration of the sociable evening; and so the conversation begins about her and the pious bent of her being. The unbelieving Leonhard senses in this something unnatural and dangerous, and fears for her a convent or a Herrnhut sisters’ house; but the more initiated recognize only the pure drive welling up from the depths, which does not now prevent Sophie from being an unaffected child, and which later will do no harm to her natural vocation but will only accompany her life with its holy fundamental tones. Then the conversation winds gracefully onward through the wreath of the confederates, touches delicately upon many a relation of life and of the religious disposition, preferring to dwell on the opposition of masculinity and femininity, and glorifying the first symbol of Christianity, [p. 499] which is indeed the mother with the child, and the child with the mother, in the inexhaustible loveliness of its turning. Now and then it is interrupted by musical chords, and at last it takes shape in three narratives, not so much of events as of situations from Christmas festivals past, in the mouths of the women, and three speeches on the part of the men, of which the first, by the unbelieving Leonhard, ironically praises the excellence of the festival and above all commends the fact that its service has been laid preferentially in the hands of women and children; the second has for its subject the beautiful joy of the festival in itself, and the third indicates a deeper sense of joy, in harmony with the universe. After the lighter conversation has thus drawn itself together somewhat stiffly, a friend arrives who was still expected by all, and helps it back into the open. “I have not come to give speeches,” he says, “but to rejoice with you. — The speechless object demands or produces in me a speechless joy as well; mine can, like a child, only smile or exult. — All human beings are children to me today and are for that very reason so dear to me. Let me see your splendors, and let us be cheerful and sing something pious and joyful.” —

Now after this celebration, just as everything happened and just as it was spoken, together with every little incident, has been artfully written down, it would not be impossible that a second conversation, less elegant to be sure, should be conducted about the first. Were someone, however, called upon to state his opinion on the whole, then, holding to the form, he could hardly do otherwise than admire the delicate work of art. But to speak about the content and foundation of the whole, he would have to take his standpoint outside it, and in order to enter into living interaction with the particular and inner aspects of the conversation, he would have to speak in particular from all the standpoints occurring in it, splitting himself and the whole into several.

Were someone now to attempt this in the manner indicated, he might address his speech to the men of the company approximately in the following words.

[p. 500] “Speaking first, then, about your whole conversation and about all of you together as one, I am compelled to assume a person who, far from being your adversary, nevertheless stands wholly outside your conversation hitherto. For though I recognize with praise how you have so magically adorned the hall with lights and flowers and delighted heart and eyes with an unusually harmonious sight, how you were at once so elegant and so spiritual, surrounded by pleasing prosperity and yet so homely; how your cheerfulness expressed itself so soberly and your sobriety again with such choice lightness; how music was not lacking, and you so rightly acknowledged that it is the best part of the matter and the proper element of devotion; how the narrations that the women wove in did not lack the picturesque quality of a finely cultivated imagination, and the speeches of the men bore witness that they have become familiar with the Plato who speaks in German tongue; yet forgive me, you excellent ones, if, leaving this renown undiminished to you, I nevertheless cannot congratulate Christianity that it is to be reborn in this way. For not to the wise and cultivated of this world has God revealed it, but to the simple and unlearned, i.e., to the common understanding and sense of human beings; and Christ the Lord himself thanked the Father that it is so. You show, to be sure, everywhere a laudable endeavor in your doings to betray nothing particular; not only in that there is “nothing formally religious at all in your circle, no prayer at set times, no special hours of devotion, but everything happens only when you feel so inclined,” but also in that you seek to glorify the festival through the most general and highest Ideas. Still I am in doubt whether I should not rather wish to see Christianity, together with what may seem to you perhaps a limitation but what might be precisely the truly universal, and the festival itself, celebrated in its thoughtless gaiety, than that your otherwise cultivated sociability now mirrors itself in it, and the magical light proceeding from the newborn one, which at its first appearance illumined the common, now [p. 501] serves to illuminate and explain the uncommon. Precisely in this, namely, that you join your thoroughly peculiar and distinguished being with the festival, universal in itself and belonging to all humanity, there arises something quite singularly particular, to whose special mixture I would by far prefer each of the two for itself, the festival in its old simplicity, and your cultivation too. Do not ascribe it to mere idiosyncrasy that I judge so. For if you wanted to keep your feeling and view to yourselves, you would already by that very fact be not Christian. For the first disposition of the Christian is love of the people; the anti-popular tendency, then, which you give to religion, is an obviously unchristian one! Or how can you in fairness still call Christianity that which links you only with your nearest friendship? But if you suppose that those, as you cherish them, will gradually be communicated to the world as well, then you cancel a relation that I must hold to be essential: a wholly objective foundation, freed from all peculiarity, to which one can return at any time, as one cannot to your views, and which, while connecting each with all, nevertheless leaves each free at the same time, as your manner likewise does not. That you, then, believe you have grasped the universal through an exaltation of spirit whose worth consists precisely in its particularity, and that, besides having the renown of the cultivated, you also still demand the goods of the simple — that you use old forms in which you display the wealth of your spirit, as surroundings of antique form adorn only the chambers of the rich: this, forgive my feeling, I censure, and it strikes me no differently than if you, substituting for the first and natural gifts, of wine and of bread, your late-born, subjective drink, tea (which you also made use of), had wanted to celebrate the glad, free, universal feast of the covenant. Also this seemed to me questionable, and indicative of the discord within yourselves, that at last, when your joy had become almost wholly formal, a freshly arriving friend had first to admonish you to give yourselves over to the right cheerfulness.”

[p. 502] “But to speak of Leonhard, the cultivated despiser, and indeed “as an advocate,” since you do not play along with him for the best, though he, as it seems, knows how to console himself about it: you let him appear among you only as what he is not, namely as an unchristian, but not as what he otherwise could still be, in which case he might easily carry within himself as much that is positive as you, something that would reconcile him with Christianity and make the negative vanish. Had he found room to present his aversion to your religiosity less from the usual side and merely as opposition, he might well, going further, have cited this very fact, that there is such an “evil principle” and a despiser like him for you, as a sign of the non-universality of your essence, and have maintained that there must be a point of cognition where you too in truth could comprehend him, and he in turn could gladly enter into the all-embracing circle. For even the irony peculiar to him seems to me the proper expression of a love of the universal, though one that has not come to clarity. He is excusable, then, in taking offense at you, already by the fact that you have taken offense at him, and that he would have to not only love and understand your way of viewing in its place but *appropriate* it to himself, so as not to be regarded as one who is outside. — That he nevertheless seems averse especially to your restoration of Christianity happens perhaps because he feels with a fresher sense that everything that has not sprung up and been generated from a powerful ground has neither duration nor truth at all. For not by the awakening of the dead is the living created, but the truly living is what can never be dead. But where the glow has collapsed into ashes, there blow on the sparks with as much fine will as you like, it will always be only like the revival of the old carved work and the artificial illumination of the house at Bethlehem which little Sophie arranged. And what will you answer if, on account of the opinion, unspoken to be sure but nonetheless betrayed, as if you had quietly to restore Christianity, he should find you [p. 503] yourselves guilty of unbelief, in that you assume that something could have become dead which is a word of eternal life? But even if he believed in the possibility of a general founding of your Christianity, still his manly disposition might reasonably come to doubt the durability of the same, just as *you* want to restore it. For you make it very plain, as he has already jestingly intimated, that everything masculine, and indeed the universally human, has among you passed over into the feminine. You appear, if it is permitted to say so, no longer to serve our dear Lady alone, but the women, which manifests itself not so much in that you meet them lovingly as Christ did, but in that you pay homage above all to their power of comprehension, their understanding, and their inclination. Or have you not given them the first place in the whole celebration, not in that you concede it to them, but in that they take it by themselves, as this is already foreshadowed in miniature by the relation between the large-minded child Sophie and the boy Anton? And not only to womanliness in general do you flatter, but more definitely: in that you seek to dissolve everything in music, yet not in the masculine, impelling, rhythmic, but in the soft, yearning, harmonic, so that Leonhard perhaps expressed himself most ironically in what he says to the idealistic enthusiasts: “You would be the heroines of this time with your contempt for the singular and actual, and one should regret that you do not have nothing but able, arms-bearing sons; you would have to be the proper Christian Spartan women.” For he can hardly hold that martial heroism should proceed from this disdain for the actual, since every state for which arms would after all be borne, were its constitution ever so idealistic, would yet at the same time have to carry the blemish of actuality, and one raised in this contempt would easily find it unworthy to defend it heroically. — But if you say that Leonhard shows himself averse not to Christianity but to religion in general, permit me here likewise to attempt a word of mitigation. For it has for some time become ever more general among us to proclaim [p. 504] a condition of the soul, which one calls religion, as the unconditionally highest thing in man. But the best, apart from the all-embracing, is one-sided and acts repellingly as soon as it wants to be something for itself. Thus most have grasped religion only as an inclination or attraction of the soul toward the divine, as devotion, adoration, presentiment; and even among you, although one can discern it more from the whole than infer it from individual utterances, it has to a greater or lesser degree taken on a similar aftertaste of subjectivity. But what will you hold higher: adoration, devotion, presentiment, in which the soul always persists as something situated outside God, to which he hovers before it as an object, or the unity of the whole essence of the soul with God? Christ too sets this as the highest, that we should become like God. This is true religion, the genuine service of God, that each one, as an organ of God, in inward unity with the being living and operative in all, fulfill vigorously and joyfully the place he has in the whole of things, without stepping out of it, just as the eternal too does not step out of itself, but, blessed and constant, remains within itself. It is not contemplation that I reject; for precisely the sinking of the soul into the All with all its powers I call contemplation, from which doing and living are then not different, but which is itself being and acting. As the single tone is not to depart from the melody and reflect apart about the whole, but to sound full and pure in its place, so man. There is therefore a state of the soul in which religion too, in that sense, vanishes as a one-sidedness, so that even someone other than Leonhard might seem not unjustly to resist it in this way. And had you already found this right and great melody, this true church style, you could have no more despisers, neither cultivated nor uncultivated. Everyone would willingly be in your community, because everyone would want to express and proclaim God in his own way.”

“Having now, not without love, mindful that even in [p. 505] heaven there is more joy over one sinner who turns to the good than over ninety-nine righteous, spoken a word for the unchristian, I turn to the Christian-minded, of whom the first, Ernst, expressed himself and you in a manner perfectly clear to me when he said: “We ourselves begin in discord and attain concord only through redemption, which is nothing other than the cancellation of those oppositions, and which therefore can proceed only from him for whom they did not first need to be canceled” (the immediate Son of God). In this I agree with him, however, when he soon afterwards gives as the most general Idea of the festival, persisting independently of everything historical, the necessary Idea of the redeemer. I even hold this very Idea of redemption to be the birth of Christianity itself; but also only its birth. For all redemption is only liberation from an existing evil or a barrier, and thus only the negative beginning of a new world; for he who redeems, redeems not that nothing else may come to be, but that something may come to be. And after this other, this positive, which was to follow upon the beginning of Christianity, redemption, and which is first the actual Christianity itself, we ask. For if there were no consequence of redemption, and it might not, after Christ proclaimed it, be assumed as having happened in deed for all and forever, then it would still always be only the beginning and not Christianity itself, and you could then really only adorn the child Jesus, each time anew, with flowers and golden clasps. But if the redeemer has once been born, and redemption, as it had occurred from eternity, has been revealed and realized in time, then it is not the case that, beginning in discord, we first attain redemption, but rather that, beginning from redemption, we live immediately and first of all in eternity. Assume, then, once and for all, that we *are* redeemed, and renounce the old faintheartedness and care, and rejoice in the freedom with which Christ has set you free. Show “the life and the joy of the original nature, in which those oppositions do not obtain at all between appearance and essence, time [p. 506] and eternity,” and say no further “that it is *not our* life”; for by that very saying you say that we are not redeemed through Christ. For the contradiction of essence and appearance, of eternity and time, gives birth to death and sin and hell; but Christ, you say yourselves, has overcome death, taken away sin, carried off the triumph over hell. And has not He himself promised us the positive, when he promised to send the Paraclete, the spirit encouraging, impelling, cheering, who was to lead you into all truth, well knowing that he did not complete the work through redemption, as he himself says: “I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that one, the Spirit of truth, shall come, he will tell it to you.” — Do not suppose, therefore, that the merely repeated celebration of the birth of the world-redeeming child will bring the Lord back. He must come again by his own might, and he will come again, through the mouth not of mere celebrants but of called prophets, and he who was a child, and led the work of his teaching only up to his birth, will present it in full manhood and fill the new world with the glory of his kingdom.”

“Deeper now penetrates the thought, and mystically, as he himself announces to us beforehand, yet at the same time moving the object of the festival out into the freedom of a more universal intuition, indeed befriending *man in himself* with the spirit of the earth, the last speech, Eduard’s, emerges, so that, as he opens this leaf, one here too, like Faust, might joyfully say: You, spirit of the earth, are nearer to me — but soon, and after the apparition has transformed and drawn itself together in an almost magical way, with averted face cry out like him: Woe, I cannot endure you! For you others, to be sure, who heard the speech spoken, it may have seemed that your thoughts simply could not keep pace with the rapid sequence of connections by which the spirit, to whom before the earth was temple and body, all that lives an organ, draws itself together into the narrow walls and dull halls of the [p. 507] church; but to me, who have this sequence in writing before me and could follow it at leisure, it has seemed almost strange through its lightness and nimbleness, so that it was certainly a spirit that appeared here, even if not the spirit of the earth. First of all, however, in order to enter into this manner of mystical interpretation, would it not well accord with the festival and a more general interpretation to make *ourselves* alone, as we all are, or the human race, egoistically the object of it, without thinking of the virginal, ever-blooming mother, nature, who yet always and inseparably appears with the one born? — The spirit of the earth then, as he is eternally man *in himself*, is to *become* in the individual also as this one, namely to recognize itself again as the in-itself of man in the individual, which is so expressed that he is to become as the *thought* of man and as the thought of a communal life. “Only when the individual,” said the speaker, “beholds and recognizes humanity as a living community of individuals, bears its spirit and consciousness within himself, and in it loses and refinds his separated existence, only then does he have the higher life and the peace of God in himself — this community, however,” he continued, “through which man inhimself is thus presented or restored, is the church.” Is that now also your opinion, you other speakers, that the work of the spirit of the earth finally closes with the work of man, the church? For some are wont to do this: they first let a word be granted them only as poetic or in another and higher meaning than the usual, but afterwards make a thoroughly unpoetic use of it, and attach to it again everything that was otherwise connected with it. Now I greatly fear whether something similar has befallen you with the word church; as when, though it was brought about first only as a birth of the spirit of the earth *in thought*, then as a community *through disposition*, the speaker nevertheless immediately afterwards says that it can be denied only *outwardly* by those who possess science — where it has therefore already become something external, and indeed again one that the cultivated deny; further, that [p. 508] the women, because the higher consciousness is with them in feeling, cling for that reason the more intimately and *exclusively* to the church, all of which indicates that it is a restriction and separation, if not in your thoughts, yet in those of the speaker, hence also a human institution, and erected by human hands. — But if he wished to say: the church, even so taken, as an institution namely, is nevertheless a necessary and eternal Idea, he seems to me thereby to contradict his own first utterances. For the spirit of the earth is to *become*, or to recognize itself, also in the individual as the in-itself of humanity; but how would this be possible, except through a leading back of the general consciousness of humanity to what it already is in deed and truth from eternity; I mean to the perfect freedom and unity of existence, in which there is no barrier, no exclusion, and hence also no church.”

“Also this has seemed to me incomprehensible and almost contradictory, that, since the speaker — not without reference to his predecessor, as it seemed to me — said of man in himself that there is no corruption and no fall and no need of redemption in him, he would have to say the same of what he calls the church, namely the community through which man in himself is presented, that is, that through the existence of the church all that must be regarded as already canceled, wiped away and effaced, as if it had never been, yet nevertheless afterwards it is spoken of as a *means* of rebirth, and it is said that we (the individuals) are reborn *through* the spirit of the church. Thus the church is not the presentation and celebration of the original unity already restored, but only the means to its restoration, and presupposes corruption and fall: means of healing and atonement are its retinue; far from presenting the original health of pure nature free from all opposition, it is entangled in frailty and sinfulness, and is no longer an eternal Idea but a temporal means. — But if you now, in return, called me to account for what I myself could want [p. 509] instead of the church, I would say: the public, universal religion living in the spirit and heart of a people, from which to wish to be separated would be as foolish as to be separated from the nation itself, or to wish to flee the universally enlivening air that encloses us all. For precisely by your separating religion and what you call church entirely from what otherwise unites a people as a whole, indeed by your setting it in opposition to it, you transform it into something particular and resistant to the common, contrary to the sense of him who designated his community with the same word (ἐκκλησία) with which the visible community of a people, presenting itself as visible, was otherwise expressed, as he who was well master of the language and knew the meaning of the words rendered it into German not by church but by community. In that you now set this community against the public association, you not only concede that for him who separates himself from the latter there is still another life in and with his people, through the other community, and thereby make apostasy possible for him, but you also give to yourselves, to your own community, a relation of strife, and transform the *Ecclesia triumphans*, which, great through itself, disdained to fight against unbelievers and thereby to acknowledge them (since rather whoever is not wholly null will of himself live in it), into the Ecclesia militans, from which, because the wrong is on its side, there at last rightly becomes the oppressa. — But if it is the spirit of the earth, or the universal spirit of things, unconscious to them, that is to become manifest through humanity, then this conscious community, which expresses itself in public religion, must unite human beings as freely as that original community of the universe united things, so that no peculiarity is suppressed by that of another, no innermost feeling has to bristle against that of another, which is the fundamental defect of your church. The community should, as you yourselves must admit if you do not wish to turn arbitrarily away from this Idea, be such that it is not subject that has to agree with subject, which is unholy and begets hatred, but [p. 510] each with the common bond, which bears and sustains all and is for that very reason love. This seems also to have been the thought of the divine teacher and of the heralds who followed, who, beholding humanity as truly one and canceling every partition wall, foretold that the time would come when you will worship God in spirit and in truth, when there will be no more ordinances, no priests and Levites, but Christ, that is, the living God as All in all.”

Having now sought in this manner to enliven the whole, the speaker remarks how from the various standpoints he has nevertheless always come at last upon One thing, from which arises the belief that everything else was only play, but this was the true. Yet he does not believe thereby to have spoken against the author of the work; for who knows what thoughts he harbors who does not himself appear, and who, if he had the intention of presenting the determinate and actual religious views of individuals of our time with their oppositions and peculiarities, has proved most strongly the power of objective presentation precisely through the pure expression of subjective ways of thinking. And stepping back again to the viewpoint of the artistic unity of the whole, elaborated with utmost delicacy, he gives it back to the author untouched, and with the greater admiration in that the author of the *Reden* *über die Religion* thereby attests that both the graceful measure and the strength are at his command.

[p. 511]

### Der Streit des Philanthropinismus und Humanismus in der Theorie des Erziehungsunterrichts unserer Zeit dargestellt von Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer. Jena, 1808.<sup>113</sup> — The Dispute of Philanthropinism and Humanism in the Theory of Instruction in Education of Our Time, presented by Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer. Jena, 1808.<sup>113</sup>

<sup>113</sup> From the Jenaische Allgemeine Literaturzeitung 1809, nos. 13, 14, 15.

The present work will, we do not doubt, already be in the *hands* of all for whom education and instruction are important *subjects*. This notice has not been written to make it known or to begin spreading it; and other journals have anticipated us in general praise of it. But the thoroughness of its execution and the dialectical nature of the inquiry itself invite us, instead of confining ourselves to the mere announcement, to say a scientific word about it, and to take the work precisely from that side by which it distinguishes itself from the ordinary pedagogical writings.

First, something about its historical relation and its interest for the age. About thirty years ago, when a restless spirit of change, an indefinite weariness with what existed, began to show itself, and, for want of strength to improve things from the ground up, everything was being tried in detail, the salvation of the world was to be brought about all at once by an overthrow of the previous manner of education and instruction. To be sure, the spirit of the public institutions was not so easy and quick to drive out as the reformers wished; they therefore had to confine themselves to private undertakings, and set up institutions on their own account which, in keeping [p. 512] with the sentimental activity of the age, received the name of Philanthropines, a name that would have fitted just as well poorhouses and reformatories, or institutions for the infirm and the feeble-minded. Meanwhile the new pedagogy had been born into the world with these; the old, which is called humanism in the work above, had been set at open war with the new, or with philanthropinism; by a hundred entrances the latter first penetrated into domestic education; in public education it at least produced a condition of unrest and vacillation. Only later, when no one any longer expected it, it appeared in a state whose mighty advances toward improvement had long since aroused general attention, in a new shape and developed into a public system of instruction: a phenomenon that seemed incomprehensible to many. Given the unequal progress of culture in the different parts of Germany, it was indeed nothing unusual that what had long since been given up in one part was only beginning to take firm root and to flourish in another. But precisely through this later revival philanthropinism coincided with the general philosophical movement, which, where monkdom and priestcraft had indeed been quickly and easily removed as to their matter, while their form and the whole stamp of spirit which they imparted adhered all the more indelibly, had to produce a new scholasticism of its own kind, one all the more barbarous as the study of classical antiquity had there lain prostrate since time immemorial and had never risen to its true purpose. Through the combination of these two circumstances philanthropinism had to take on a shape far more dangerous for public education, for the freedom of the spirit, and for the true progress of culture. We believed we had to remark thus much on a phenomenon that, under the given circumstances, had almost inevitably to appear, and which it was far better to comprehend as a necessary one than to invent intentions that were not present at all.

Apart from every particular relation, however, the dispute between the two systems of instruction has a general interest [p. 513] and a purely scientific significance. Far from its having already been settled in this sense, we should rather say that it has not yet really begun. A multitude of principles that belong, mediately or immediately, to philanthropinism have crept into the opposed systems. How many who had otherwise opposed that so-called Enlightenment — a true *dis-spiriting* of the nation, in the author’s phrase (p. 18) — have not escaped its influence themselves, and show themselves now, in their ultimate heartfelt opinion, at one with it! Where everything is so impure and mixed, the true dispute cannot yet have begun. The great process of separation of the good from the bad begins only now; also in the important matter of the theory of educational instruction it has been truly initiated only by the present work.

Or is the old simply to be restored unconditionally, a means to which lack of self-creating power and faintheartedness, after so many failures, now generally resorts? Only someone who, banished wholly within the confines of his school, had never cast a free glance at the conditions of the world, could be of the opinion that, while all the conditions of life have so mightily changed, the demands of the world upon us have become so entirely different, and all relations are renewed or in the course of renewal, instruction and education alone have no need of transformation. A simpler system of education, for that very reason a more vigorous one, built on greater principles, is a pressing need. The guilt for what has happened, for the weakness of the generation now acting and its aberrations, if one is once willing to go back to education as a source of them, surely cannot be borne by the attempts at innovation alone; where, then, has the old school formed the practically great men whom the age required? While those strove after a shallow utility, has not this school, on the contrary, withdrawn ever more from life, and narrow-heartedly renounced the world and universal human activity? But most intolerable of all seems it when that which did not [p. 514] even oppose those weak attempts with success, which showed itself impotent to save the slightest thing, is to be offered anew to our age as a medicine, or even forced upon it. At the base even of the darkest striving for change there usually lies a correct instinct, though not a comprehended one. Thus the indefinite longing for something new mentioned above was a premonition of the coming events, which, better understood, could have given these themselves another turn. Such a dark feeling has also guided the endeavors, calling themselves philanthropinist, to transform educational instruction. Our task now is to make it clear and to raise it to consciousness. Thus this feeling showed itself as a striving for the useful for the common good without insight into what the truly useful consists in. This should now have become clear to us. The older system had at its base from the start more clear insight and even scientific knowledge; but has not the original sense been lost from it, as from so many other systems? The thought, then, of conducting the dispute between the two systems of instruction in such a way that the relatively true of each, mutually correcting itself, yields the perfectly-true as product, is entirely timely and worthy of a scientific execution.

In every investigation of a dispute that aims in particular at a reconciliation, the finding of the fundamental opposition is the most important thing. The one found for the present dispute might well be nearly the one found for the dispute of the whole age. The author busies himself with this task in the second section, which therefore bears the heading: Scientific Foundation of the Investigation. The right word for it the author at first thinks, to be sure, to have found in the concepts of animality and rationality, which are supposed to coexist in man; and in fact the opposition is wide enough for a great deal to be traced back to it. But the later remark (p. 67), that nowhere in man can a point be shown where pure animality begins, that (p. 68) this has, in man, through its [p. 515] connection with reason not only (negatively) ceased to be animality but become something positively other and itself sanctified (p. 40), seems to prove that for man generally this opposition may have been chosen too wide. If animality in man is already permeated by spirituality, the body, as the author says, a temple of the Holy Spirit, then the opposition is already resolved by the essence of man as such; a higher and different one must emerge. We believe, therefore, that we must take these expressions not in a strictly scientific sense but roughly as we take the others, of earth and heaven, to designate the real and the ideal. Perhaps they are to be ascribed to a concession to what is current, which, given the aim of general intelligibility, deserves no censure. As is well known, the antithesis of animality and spirituality has attained a certain popularity in our literature, in that it must serve partly as a polemical means (although the times of the Encyclopedists are long past), partly is indispensable because otherwise certain systems would lack an explanatory ground of evil and of the corruption of human nature, which one, where it really is, either cannot or will not see. In the same way we explain it also when the terms reason and understanding-for-ends are used as parallel expressions to those two. For the esoteric opinion of the author, who everywhere determines sharply and distinguishes exactly, cannot be that the understanding of art is common to us with the animals; something that completely confuses the concepts of humanity and animality. The art that is practiced by the animal is, in respect of itself, an altogether blind one, bound up with no consciousness of an end; in it something other than itself acts. Understanding presupposes personality, and at a time when, alas, so little superfluous understanding has been shown by men, it is truly not necessary to let the animals have it liberally. We believe, therefore, in order not to miss the true sense of the author, that we had better hold to the freer expressions of the opposition in the following turns of phrase. “To the one system man [p. 516] is pure spirit, life in the ideal his only true vocation. According to the other, spiritual life has no independence, and creating and working in the world of the senses is the only sure vocation of man. The former scorns all education for external ends, all effort for the means necessary for the realization of the Ideas in the outer world; the other has as its ultimate aim not at all the education of the spirit in itself, but that for merely external ends, for the future calling and advancement in the world.” But only in what those means, or, to speak more exactly, in what that — surely likewise positive — principle consists, by whose power man realizes Ideas in the outer world — on this we should have wished a definite explanation from the author. For if perhaps by this again only *items of knowledge* are understood, e.g. the so-called knowledge of the world, of man, of positive institutions, etc. (p. 42), then the opposition is unawares lost to us again; we remain thereby only in the sphere of the spiritual.

Should the true opposition, to be sought here alone, not be the following? — To reason, which, as the apprehending and the universal in respect of man, has more the character of repose and devotion, can be opposed only the active, the self-effecting, in one word *personality*. The former, reason, determines in man everywhere only his generic concept, his universal essential character; the latter, personality, is that by which we esteem the particular capability and excellence of man, so that, e.g., to be called a rational man (the most universal thing that can be said of a human being) is a praise almost as ambiguous as the other, to be called a good man, whereas personality in and for itself and without further addition receives praise. In fact we comprehend under this name all the virtues and qualities which man shows in vigorous realization of Ideas. Besides, it is also not to be denied that the whole striving of modern humanism went wholly toward the cultivation and disproportionate elevation of those impersonal qualities, while the personal ones were left aside as something bad and [p. 517] little to be esteemed. It is as if one Fate had determined the outer events and the inner directions of the spirit, as if all selfhood and I-hood, after the nation had long since lost its personality, were to be uprooted, root and branch, in the individual too. Whence else in the interior of our nation that deliberate and conscious raging against prominent individuality, and indeed as such — whence the suppression of all peculiarity by the uniformization of instruction, against which the author (p. 198 ff.) speaks such pertinent words, and through which the dissolution into the universal has at last reached among us the most substanceless transparency; not that of the diamond, which coexists with the greatest determinateness and hardness of individuality, but of the unsubstantial air? Whence, without assuming such a fate, would it be comprehensible that a philosophy which, more vigorously than any before it, had exalted personality, indeed made it the universal center, became in the hands of its originator something wholly other, which does not know how to condemn vigorously enough every self-effecting, every activity of man of his own? Whence, without this complete giving up of all personality, the faintheartedness which opens the door to a pietistic unreason, to a new sentimentality, all the more repulsive because philosophical, all the more pernicious because practical, and finally means renouncing all thinking of one’s own, as long since willing of one’s own, and seeking the source of wisdom in doing nothing or — in the Church Fathers? Whence, finally, the general disparagement of the learned with respect to world and life, as of this decided impersonality coupled with supposedly high education, all-sided humanity, indeed even the extolling of antiquity, whose models excite our admiration precisely through the union of the highest and most universal education with the most determinate personality? — Be it that no philanthropinist conceived the opposition thus (the most perverse means for healing the evil they have in any case seized upon); yet the true word of the opposition can be only this, for the objection that the awakening and education [p. 518] of personality falls to moral education, and therefore does not come into consideration in the question of the highest end of instruction, we are unwilling to credit to anyone. Our opinion too is that without freedom of the will in the proper and literal sense personality is a nonentity, but if independence and creative — what is not, *bringing-forth* — power is the universal character of personality, if decisiveness, certainty, presence of mind in the particular case are its most determinate marks, then it is evident that only self-created concepts, only that certainty of principles which springs from a fully formed view of the world, to which each can attain and be led from every point, together with freedom from prejudices (by which are here understood all limiting opinions), give true personality and determine the manner as well as the matter of its expression. For this very reason it may be doubted whether instruction can ever be spoken of by itself, since it is an essential part of education, and both taken together first constitute the true art of the formation of man.

After the cognition and determination of the opposition, the most important thing is to find the principle of decision or reconciliation.
