The right principle for the present case we believe we find in the author already in the first (historical) section, in the words (p. 33): “Another spirit, to which that of the Enlightenment as mere forerunner has made way, has appeared among us with the reawakening of genuine philosophical thinking. — The same remarkable reform which has called forth the ideal again to the honor of being reality is visible in the whole compass of our culture, in science and art, philosophy and religion, in all branches of doing and of life. — The ideality of truth and the truth of the ideal is ever more generally and loudly acknowledged, the voice of those who mock that conviction ever more furtive and weaker.” Are we mistaken, or would clarity have been gained if the author had held fast to this point of view also at the beginning of the second [p. 519] section? For if there the fundamental fault of both systems is placed in *one-sidedness*, in that “humanism has had in view, of the two sides of human nature, only the spiritual, philanthropinism only the animal, then the right would have to emerge already by both sides being regarded only at once or united, which the author (p. 67) expressly denies, and which also conflicts with the spirit of his whole view. But if the dispute is not to be decided by combination, then the ground of the evil also does not lie in the one-sidedness of reflection — in the seeing of the one without the other side —, but rather in this, that two sides were seen, an opposition sought where there was none — in the assumption that there is a spiritual activity which is not at the same time real, and a real one which would not at the same time be spiritual. This fundamental fault both systems have *in common*, and the one-sidedness stated by the author is only a consequence of it. The author, who everywhere proceeds with logical exactness, will not construe this remark, important for the clarity of the decision, as hair-splitting over syllables. That he expressed himself in the manner stated, is without doubt solely the fault of the chosen designation of the opposition. For between rationality and animality as such there is indeed a perfect opposition. Where the latter is, the former cannot be, for that very reason, and conversely where the former is — understood, as personal rationality, not as the universal, which of course is in every stone and animal — the latter, animality, must have ceased, and be transfigured into something higher. That humanism, the degenerate kind namely, as the author depicts it in several places, made this opposition so, is indeed undeniable; but if it sought to disparage and weaken the animal, as the supposedly evil principle, and to exalt the other in contrast, then the fault lay not in this one-sidedness, on the contrary praiseworthy according to the presupposition, but in the assumption that in man, where evidently a higher struggle begins, spirituality has its opposition in animality. The old and genuine humanism by no means knew this modern polemic against animalism, and knew how to take the latter [p. 520] altogether with more freedom of spirit, as the well-provident foundations for the bodily nourishment and necessities of students prove — so many monuments of the old pedagogy, of which philanthropinism, notwithstanding its name, has none to show, it having served only to enrich its administrators —, as further the care for the formation of bodily strength and dexterity at our universities proves, where since the oldest times masters in all bodily exercises have been appointed, which only a pedantry of a newer and gloomier kind has made a show of banishing. We apply the above remark at once to the decision of the most general points of dispute about the *end* of educational instruction, with which the author deals at the beginning of the third section. The first is whether that end consists in the education of the spirit in itself, or in education and preparation for the future calling? The fault of both systems lies here too not in a one-sidedness of reflection upon the one or the other of the activities corresponding to those two ends, but in the one-sidedness of the *concept* of each; in the assumption that spiritual activity and the activity of a calling are generally really distinguishable. For that was the wisdom put forward with triumph, that the highest intellectual education is useless for actual life, and that truly practical activity is one wholly independent of the ideal. This opinion too both parties again had *in common*. Though it was a product of modern enlightenmentism, the great mass of the humanists nevertheless willingly chimed in. Who confessed more loudly than they themselves the unfruitfulness of Ideas for life and the uselessness of all speculation? An assertion which they soon made true. For precisely in that they drew science more and more down to the need of everyday use, or transformed it into a wholly unfruitful erudition, the Ideas went out of it, and with them all practical power, so that life had soon grown over its head. The few who still felt in themselves that pure and unconditional love of science for science’s sake, of Ideas for the sake of Ideas, which had exalted [p. 521] the earlier ages, withdrew voluntarily or under compulsion from world and life. The genuine disciples of those masters, however, were either truly and thoroughly spoiled for practical life, or were indeed educated enough in a shallow, useful sort of way, but through their lack of Ideas incapable of intervening independently in the age, which was too great for them. To complete the confusion, this finally universally felt lack of practical power was ascribed to genuine humanism, and an attempt was made to remedy the evil by a still more perfect and extended carrying-out of philanthropinism. The opinion of the genuine, of course already ancient, humanism was: science and spiritual education are the salt of the earth; a people hastens toward decline when either the salt turns foolish, i.e. the wise become unable to govern, or conversely it is salted with foolishness, i.e. the unwise govern.

To lead ours back to this conviction, which was the strength of former centuries, is what the present work strives for with dignity and earnestness. It decides unconditionally for (rightly understood) humanism, evidently only on the presupposition stated. The asserted identity is, namely, not to be understood as *equality* — concepts which every exact usage of language, every logic teaches us to distinguish —; the sense is that the positive of both activities is one and the same, the nerve of practical activity itself being the spiritual. Every opposition in which it is found that the one (rightly understood) comprehends the other, this therefore being the comprehended of that, must be decided according to the principle of subordination. This is just what the author throughout assumes. No wonder, then, that humanism everywhere decisively remains in the right, and for that reason no assurance of impartiality (p. 74) was needed. — “He who is educated for the unconditioned, says the author p. 101, is alone properly educated, and brings education also to the conditioned. He who has learned to know a reality other than that of the earth, and to believe in a higher vocation of his life, for him life has *an entirely different seriousness* than that of necessity. Only the latter makes one petty and common, the other elevates [p. 522] man.” — “For the glance that has been practiced on objects of the inner world it will be far more possible to see through the things of the outer world than for him who has busied himself with ever so many things, i.e. externalities.” — Nor, for this very reason, can the order be reversed; for the moving force of the outer lies itself in the inner. “What is worth seeing on earth — also in the events of the world, we add — is itself the invisible.” Whoever would now set against this the present shape of the world, the confusion and entanglements of the structures of state, etc., would forget that this shape itself is the consequence of that separation of life from the one animating principle. That in the question of what ought to be, the living state is reckoned upon, not the dead, goes without saying, surely. — How was it possible, then, that in the Roman republic the same man could perform the services of war in youth, the office of judge at the onset of manhood, that of a manager of public revenues in riper years, finally steer the helm of the whole state in peace and war, the same man at once be head of the commonwealth at home and victorious commander at the head of the armies, and lastly in old age still live for the Muses and philosophy? It is a necessary Idea (see p. 95) that the activity of a calling (by which is understood real *activity*, not servile or merely mechanical labor) be a continued exercise of humanity, a continuing education and heightening of spiritual power on the resisting matter of actuality; an Idea which, if only for a short time, has yet shown itself realized in individual fortunate states, more often in the public life of great men dominating their age. Those who have always regarded the state only as a mechanism, to whom its positive concept, to be the most comprehensive presentation of the Ideas in actuality, has never become clear, may look down contemptuously upon every activity of a calling. But if in human affairs too only Ideas are the guiding, ordering, and truly creative principle, then spiritual education, without prejudice to its universality, must be [p. 523] immediately education for life, and rather than draw away from it must awaken its highest power and the effective principium of its ennoblement.

Another opposition mentioned by the author is that the acquisition of specific kinds of knowledge appears to some as the exercise of the spirit in itself, to others as the chief end. Of a true opposition there can here be no question at all, since spirit and knowledge are related as soul and body; the only question can be which is higher and which subordinate, which is end and which is means. Even philanthropinism can hardly be supposed so blind as to esteem the force by which everything is moved less than the mass to be moved. Rather has modern humanism, through the excessive value it has placed on knowledge as such, brought erudition and extensive learning into ill repute, since indeed an understanding of languages and the most exact knowledge of world events, drawn from all the history books, could not, without a fortified heart and an independent spirit, protect against the falsest judgments and the grossest blunders. Usually, however, that opposition is determined more closely, so that Ideas and practically useful or generally beneficial knowledge, exercise of the contemplative force, which generates Ideas, on spiritual objects and exercise of material activity on merely material things stand opposed to one another. Let us not condemn the demand for utility too unconditionally! Whoever can benefit human beings surely fulfills the purpose of nature, since we may agree with that humane thought: what would be the point of all the apparatus of solar systems, Milky Ways, and nebulae, if in the end some rational being or other did not rejoice in existence! But since the human race is created for unity, and the individual can find his true advantage in life only as a member of a smaller or larger whole, then, when utility is in question, everything is ultimately to be referred to the whole, and only that is truly to be called generally beneficial which benefits not individuals, however many, but the state, the people as such. Quite to the contrary, the most recent age has called generally beneficial precisely what profits [p. 524] only the individual. Thus, to stay with one of the nearest examples, the invention of vaccination saves many an individual life and spares individual fathers and individual mothers grief and pain; but what has the state as such gained from it? That the population is thereby increased is doubtful, as long as one does not know whether death does not fetch its prey in another way, since this one has been cut off from him; that increased population is unconditionally desirable for every state is likewise only a shallow assertion of more recent times; but granting both, the state does not consist in population, nor through it, and without morals and religion every vaccinated people will go to ruin, if along with these the unvaccinated maintains its freedom and wholeness. The state itself is a spiritual Idea, and so only spiritual Ideas too can be called generally beneficial; everything else is only means and has value only if it serves as an instrument of Ideas. Accordingly, Ideas and what is generally beneficial cannot be set in opposition at all, and those who do so (as is still done by the majority) neither know nor understand what “generally beneficial” means. But if the dispute was from the outset only about private utility, then the question which stands higher, this or Ideas, deserves no answer whatever. Whoever asks so might as well doubt that for the German people, for example, a great lawgiver, a Solon, a Lycurgus, even a Moses, humanly speaking, would have been far more salutary than all the inventors of economy stoves, spinning machines, or beet sugar. — In the other opposition, between exercise of the contemplative force on purely spiritual things and exercise of the material force on purely material objects, if by the latter the *materially cognizing* force is meant, then this opposition reverts to the previous one; there is no doubt which is the more important, indeed which is the unconditionally important one, namely that which is able to grasp a whole as a whole, the force of Ideas and of totality. But if by material force the *acting* force is to be understood, and the talk is of the human being, in the author’s expression, being not merely awakened to reason but also enabled to present it outwardly in work [p. 525] and deed , then, since all enabling can only be personal, we again come upon the fundamental opposition between formation toward reason and formation toward personality. But everything that forms the spirit, that makes it truly free and elevates it, also forms and elevates personality. By nothing is it more surely depressed than by dark, confused concepts, by an excess of disordered knowledge; hence it is nothing rare to see the man of few concepts show more presence of mind and decisiveness in action than the man who, with much knowledge, has still reached neither clarity nor unity of view. One seems, therefore, in the case of those who are one day to be realizers of Ideas in the proper sense, to have only the choice of leading them either to the highest of formation, to a vigorous overview of the whole, joined with determinate cognition of the particular, or of equipping them, after the manner of the philanthropinists, with a few concepts lying close at hand and entirely sober. For what lies in the middle — the formation not carried through, the clarity not fully won about points that otherwise would better have been left at rest — precisely that, which our modern education and teaching usually delivers, is utterly useless and pernicious. Only those principles and concepts which have attained irresistible clarity for the understanding also take possession of our personality, and cease to be general concepts and principles, by becoming our own and individual ones; but without this becoming-personal the highest principles of reason, the most sublime Ideas of the understanding, are only sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. From this it follows that a vigorous and thoroughly carried-out theoretical formation — not as the only thing, but as first and foremost and as the foundation of every other — is the one right remedy for our nation. Formerly religious faith, which has vanished, was its inner bond; one cannot go back, once the path of free cognition has been entered upon; only if carried through can the deed begun give back unity, steadfastness, certainty, faith. Praise [p. 526] and thanks are therefore due to the author, who so manfully champions purely spiritual formation, who rescues religious instruction for the people, whose only time of formation is school, who strives to ward off occupation with the so-called useful, through which the child is already to feel in advance the burden and heat of coming life, but who seeks to preserve the independence of a free and purely spiritual formation for those whom inner vocation consecrates as future representatives and administrators of humanity.

We believe we have, through what has gone before, brought out the governing idea and fundamental tendency of this work, which is the essential duty of a review. We can be briefer on the more special points of dispute, and restrict ourselves almost to a mere excerpt. The first concerns the *objects* of instruction, and indeed first of all their *number*. The newer method of instruction in particular wanted to extend it, as if everything possible had to be known by everyone, as if what is the task of the whole species, or what only a few chosen ones may reach out their hand for, had to be attained by each individual. “Formation (general, public formation) may be compared to the fragrance of a garden, which streams forth from the quiet life of the most various single flowers and returns to each single one as heightened refreshment. Whence, then, is formation to come, if we all flee quiet, distinctive life, deem individual being and working unworthy of ourselves, and hold the dispersion and dissolution of our force into the indeterminate and general to be our true vocation?” — If it is not training for a profession, if it is the formation of the human being in itself that is the immediate end, then in general surely no great extension of the objects of instruction is required; what is unconditionally necessary for all, even in material respect, is only the knowledge of Ideas, especially the religious and ethical; for those who can devote a longer time to free formation the extension is of course greater; but precisely these are to be held sacred above all; everything that serves merely arbitrary ends is to be excluded from instruction proper to education, which, because it is this, stands opposed to every special instruction, including professional [p. 527] instruction. — As to the *kind* of objects, philanthropinism (and perhaps modern humanism too) has of the spiritual in general merely negative concepts. For it the spiritual is what is opposed to the spatial, the corporeal — the spirit has nothing peculiar, nothing positive; its best things are concepts, that is, abstractions of the corporeal, whence the cry for intuition, and likewise the fact that under the (barbarously so-called) Realien only corporeal things are meant. Is not spirit, at the very least, likewise a real, and does it not have, besides the corporeal world, itself as object, and with that concepts of a purely spiritual kind, and above both still that in which nature and spirit have their common root, the Absolute, whose concept designates the highest circle of spiritual objects? What, then, does philanthropinism oppose to this? It wants to place dead external intuitions beside the empty formulas of inner abstractions, and thinks to remedy one one-sidedness by the other. Far from it; rather, in both domains — that of Ideas and that of things — concept and intuition are to interpenetrate; and since with regard to Ideas this unity can be presented only through word and speech, especially insofar as it is art, language and speech are also in and for themselves a truly spiritual object of instruction. The enemies of language knew of spiritual objects no other presentation than that of a definition correct by the schoolbook, not the immediate appearance that stirs life. “Language is the form of appearance of the spirit, its immediate body; in it the spirit presents, for itself and others, not only itself but also what is higher and lower than itself. Through the word the bodiless Idea is embodied and fixed, the spiritless thing is spiritualized and made mobile.” Instruction, therefore, is not only necessarily tied to the word, even where the thing cannot be shown, but the word itself and its form, raised to an object of instruction, is so little mere verbiage that one may rather maintain that the worst instruction in language still stirs up more spirit than mere instruction in things. — It is undeniable that nature itself, through variously apportioned talent, [p. 528] implanted inclination, etc., with respect to the spiritual and the material seems to have made a separation of individuals, that the one seems created more for objects of the first, the other more for objects of the other kind. This diversity of inner vocation — but also only this, not the arbitrarily assumed external one — can then also make a division of instruction permissible, indeed necessary, so that the more spiritual talent is not tormented with material objects (as the complaint resounds from the philanthropinist institutions that the most talented pupils must spend their time counting and fingering stones, herbs, and the rest of the raw stuff), nor the more material talent (as perhaps in the humanist schools) with merely spiritual things. This formal division will be far better than the newer attempt to mix everything, and to make of each individual a microcosm of all knowledge and perfections, whereby all determinateness of individuality must necessarily be effaced. (Excellent remarks, already mentioned above, on this suppression of individual peculiarity are interwoven here. — Individuality is indeed not personality itself, but yet its basis and, as it were, its organ. The possible ideal of formation in an individual is attained when, with a hearty view of the world (in whatever way it may have arrived at it) and clarified, assured reason, it combines the decided development of that particular talent, of that determinate spiritual or material disposition, which lies in its individuality. Everything else is useless or of the evil one.) — Only let material occupation then not be pursued merely atomistically and mechanically-dissectingly, as hitherto, nor let one believe that one can make the *beginning* with this, as the easier, even with those who are really created for it. For either the occupation is really made easy, namely through superficiality: then it is mere play; or it is no mere going to and fro on the surface, but a penetration into the inner nature: then it is truly easier to grasp the spiritual, what is in itself living, spiritually, than the [p. 529] seemingly dead. For “the Ideas that present themselves *in* things are properly what makes up the object of instruction when it occupies itself with things.” Only after the spiritual eye has been strengthened by purely spiritual exercises, and the talent has at the same time had time to decide, may the division proceed, yet in such a way that the connection of both spheres and the organic unity of all formation are never lost from view. This division is unnecessary for those who can receive only the necessary formation of the human being; only let one not oppose the latter, as popular formation, to the free formation as scholarly formation. The difference between the two is only that the former restricts itself to the awakening of the essential, distinctive forces of the human being, the latter has in view the ideal of humanity, that is, the all-sided and harmonious development of all dispositions. There is to be no education of scholars. Every vocational formation is unfree; in this humanism has erred, untrue to its principles, that it set in the place of the unrestricted and purposeless spiritual formation the purposeful and restricted formation toward the scholar. In a special appendix to this division the author speaks still more fully of the high value of the study of language and of classical philology. The contentions of the moderns are refuted with the thoroughness one can expect given the mode of thought shown so far, and ingenious remarks (such as that on p. 228 about the study of the ancient languages as a surrogate for the mathematical) alternate with inspiring presentations, such as that of the high sense of speech, p. 222 ff., which we regret that for reasons of space we cannot excerpt.

If Ideas become objective first of all *through* the form of their presentation, then in instruction too regard must be paid to the latter. This reflection leads the author to the dispute over the archetypal character of classical antiquity for all branches of our culture and for all kinds of presentation. Here we would wish only that one chief proof be dropped, which the author draws, for the importance of antiquity, from the present state of taste and the wantonness of reading; a proof [p. 530] which cannot, after all, be valid for all times, and which has therefore probably been advanced by the author only with the intention of also giving his voice on the factions in literature; yet there would still be much to say about the presupposed relation of classical literature to our own. Until now it was evidently more a negative and restrictive one than a positively inspiring one. A distinctive formation would first have to be more widely spread in order to be allowed to presuppose the true feeling for antiquity. Is it, then, so reprehensible if the nation is no longer satisfied by the hollow classicism of many works, if it seeks to return again to its own original essence, as it speaks to it out of the works of authentically German vigor, past which only smooth ignorance, whose whole knowledge of the past derives from the common prattle of our compendia, passes with disgust and an air of distinction? — Hellenes we cannot become, after all; our own distinctive color we must keep, we must remain ourselves. To which of us does Shakespeare not stand infinitely high above all imitators or re-formers of Greek tragedy? — Heartening is the author’s remark that for the formation of national taste (and truly not of this alone) something else remains for us to do, namely to make the native works of the spirit national. From mouth to mouth, from generation to generation, what is excellent must be passed on. — Only let what is truly national be chosen for this, what is born of the heart and spirit of the nation; for never, one may well say, never has that passed into the nation, become its heart and soul, which now meets, to be sure, with almost general disdain, of which the author speaks (p. 236), and on the contrary what is truly national, like Faust and the like, has surely come not merely to a *second* reading (p. 236). — Let, for example, the Song of the Nibelungs become our German Homer, the national song which, read in the schools, imbibed by the young, and transformed into sap and blood, still inspires old age; it will steel the descendants differently than the false strength or the trifling of the poets from the celebrated age. Only the original force newly won through renewed contact with the ancestral [p. 531] soil will also open to us the positive sense for antiquity. Recognizing our own divinity, we shall no longer *dally* with the foreign gods (it was never more than that, after all); more vigorous, as ourselves vigorous, we shall recognize them, not look upon the old models merely for the form, in order to fetch from them an empty, frosty elegance, and to form Griechlein (*Graeculos*), not Greeks — not chase after their so-called beauties, but feel the eternal and indivisible beauty of their works, and imbibe from them the kindred heroic spirit.

With regard to the method of instruction the following points are brought up. The recommended facilitation and sweetening of learning. — On the whole, one should not let work depend on pleasure. Industriousness is a virtue of the will, a second nature through practice, etc. — Untimely universalizing of instruction, under the pretext of accustoming the pupil at once to an overview of the objects in their reciprocal connection. — Harder is the habituation to concentration on One object, and this is the formal chief task of instruction; the spirit is all too diffusible anyway. Accumulation precisely makes one timid, if the pupil notices no proper progress in any single part. Only against the abuse of the method of isolation do the usual proofs hold. — Untimely systematizing. — This trait seems to belong almost only to the latest philanthropinism. — The system is the product of a manifoldly heightened formation; sad if, as happens almost as a rule, those reach for it first who have not yet traversed the lowest steps; still sadder and more perverse if this blunder is carried over into public instruction. The author shows that precisely such a procedure multiplies that wretched species of empty heads who cover the most pitiful ignorance with parroted, uncomprehended formulas about the Absolute and the like, and who by their foolish conduct disgrace science itself. — The universal cannot be given; it cannot be learned, only found; the teacher can only arouse [p. 532] and guide toward finding for oneself. — Perverse development of the powers of the spirit, dispute as to which is to be exercised earlier and preferably, memory or the power of judgment. — Both methods, chosen exclusively for the whole range of instruction, would be faulty. But to awaken the slumbering force too early is still more harmful than to retard the awakening one. The so-called exercises of the understanding consist in a mere analyzing in advance, in which the pupil remains inactive, whereas in memory tasks he must help himself, must himself invent methods. The best exercise of the powers is their application, without further reflection on them; special exercises of judgment presuppose that otherwise there would be no exercise. In the natural sequence of the spiritual activities analyzing by no means comes first: the first is the apprehension of the particular. This, called intuition, must be the beginning, from intuition, that is, the child must learn before it reasons. But the necessary first, that is, the spiritual objects. Exercise of the intuiting of spiritual objects is for the earliest time precisely exercise of memory. The exercise of judgment too must be begun with the spiritual; equal thoroughness on natural objects would exceed the child’s capacity. Intuition of the external world in aesthetic respect is to be combined with the exercises in the arts, which the modern system has rightly reclaimed as a part of free formation.

The fourth section of the work makes the application of the general principles to the various kinds of instruction in education. — Only briefly does the author touch here on an important question which forces itself upon us through what precedes. If the future external vocation makes no difference, is the pupil’s future relation to the world then not to be taken into account at all? There always remains, after all, the double side of the individual, since it is on the one hand a self-whole and independent, but then also only a complementary part of a higher whole, of the universe, of humanity, of its people. “Who, then, measures,” says the author, “the relation which the individual has to the unsurveyable whole? Who can say: for this it is destined, for nothing else? But if so determinate a [p. 533] point cannot be found, then no firm direction can be given to instruction in education either.” But One determinate point can nevertheless be specified, namely that it shall be a member of this people and of no other. The question of a national education could have come up here; on the admissibility or conceivability of such a thing we would gladly have heard the author. Is everything perhaps to be built on the attachment to national literature demanded above, as many in Germany now think? — The chief kinds of instruction are given, first, by the difference of the sexes (here an extensive treatment of the instruction in education of women), second, by the difference in kind among individuals of the same sex, already determined above (whereby the restrictions and closer determinations that have already occurred are repeated). Among those called to free formation, however, those who are to be educated for Ideas of the spirit constitute the proper estate of the *scholars* in the highest and in the widest sense, since all state officials also belong to it. Not to have grasped this or that knowledge suffices for this estate, but the coherent overview of the system of knowledge and a universal acquaintance with what is most worth knowing of all times. The state which exempts the scholarly estate from this universality, or perhaps even gives the formation of it a direction exclusively toward the bread-and-butter or professional sciences, sooner or later loses its place in the rank of cultivated nations, and ceases to be an active member in the spiritual empire of the world, upon which the loss also of its external independence necessarily follows.

We conclude with a general remark. — An elaborated ideal of public instruction in education the author has not wanted to set forth. The elaboration restricts itself to that period which is consecrated purely and without any other aim to the development of humanity as such; the period of school, then of so-called gymnasium instruction. Nor is it an unconditioned ideal; for that, a great deal else would have had to be determined beforehand. Much can therefore hold only conditionally. The author has had before his eyes the condition [p. 534] of a given time and culture, but for this he also sets forth what is true, what alone is right. Yet we believe we have shown our respect for the meritorious work better through the sympathetic, detailed review than we could by any praise, which it also does not need. May it have the most beneficial consequences everywhere! May it work especially for the good of the vigorous, distinctive people, in whose formation the influence on public education gives the author a significant share! May this people, past whom so much false wisdom, which time has meanwhile annihilated, has happily gone by, now that it has entered into the place long ordained for it by nature among the peoples of Germany, be granted the benefit of a system of public education in which it need not repeat the experiences of other peoples in itself, which is formed not according to some restricted view, old or new, but according to the eternal and all-valid canon of free and beautiful humanity, and stands equally far from the gloom of earlier times and the conceit of a half-enlightenment, barbarous in its whole essence and therefore leading back thither.

[p. 535]

### Ehrenpforte und Triumphbogen für den Theaterpräsidenten von Kotzebue bei seiner Rückkehr ins Vaterland. Mit Musik. Gedruckt zu Anfang des neuen Jahrhunderts. Ohne Druckort.<sup>114</sup> — Gate of Honor and Triumphal Arch for the Theater President Kotzebue on His Return to the Fatherland. With Music. Printed at the Beginning of the New Century. No Place of Printing.<sup>114</sup>

<sup>114</sup> From the Erlanger Literaturzeitung 1801, no. 35.

*Kotzebue’s* fate, to be stopped at the Russian frontier and himself transplanted to Siberia, the scene of one of his most popular plays — as well as the pardon that followed and the return to Petersburg, with the well-known circumstances by which the story ended like a genuinely Kotzebuesque drama — has no doubt produced various witty ideas in many who heard of it — but something of the kind that the Arch of Honor and Triumph named above is, is no mere idea; it is an enduring and self-subsistent whole of witty inventions of every kind, which always take delight at once in the most peculiar thoughts and the most peculiar forms, and unite into a monument which, erected not merely for the moment, will still be named as a model and pattern even when the object to which it is dedicated has long been forgotten along with its fate. Those who find it necessary may resort to the usual expedient of impotence, and lament or condemn the wicked heart and the malice of wit that shine through this work. We shall be permitted to regard it from the higher standpoint of art, and to contribute in our part to its true appreciation, since [p. 536] through its own inner vigor, the victorious wit with which it rises above its object, it will without doubt make its own way, of itself, through the German reading public. We regard the whole as a phenomenon entirely new in German literature, significant in many respects, but above all from the side of art and poetry.

The beginning is made by sonnets of a kind that until now one has had to read from only a single poet — and in which the art of the author himself seems to have raised itself to a new potency. One is in doubt what to attend to first: whether to the perfection of the sonnet in this peculiar form, the burlesque, which announces itself now through the most exquisitely chosen rhymes (in part rime strucciole, which have a fine effect especially in the first sonnet), now through a deliberate distortion of the meter, e.g. in the sixth sonnet

You no longer shy from the Literatur-Zeitung,

now (and almost always) through the most delightful puns, through assonances, and whatever else of such play the language may offer; or to the art with which all possible circumstances of the object at hand and of its history (which, to be sure, now appear in hindsight as very favorable to the poet) have been used to produce the most amusing effect possible. We give, in place of all the others, the first sonnet as a specimen. Of lewd tears there are now holidays, And no one impregnates our stage’s Muses: The national theater of the Tungus Goes to be formed by Kotzebue in Siberia. Apostle, you, from England to Hesperia, Of naive humanity in fallen bosoms! Soon, as parterre-petrifying Medusas, You bring us Kamchadal materials, Second Benyowsky! Bayard without reproach! Beyond the Boreas now come to know The land of [p. 537] which you prophesied as seer. Russia’s monarch grants you higher nobility: Donkey you were made by birth and stars, But Hyperborean by the kibitka.

The second sonnet is composed in two languages, German and English, and contains an appeal to the English to come to the aid of their poet Kotzebue. We pass over the following ones in order to quote something from the eighth. It contains a witty comparison of the effect of Kotzebuesque plays with the galvanic frog experiments. But you understand the organism

Better than any physicist of our day, And all your plays, one may say, Are only experiments with galvanism. The silver thaler of current magnanimity Together with the light plates of your zinc-like wit, You know how to apply to armed (better: bared) nerves. And oh, what a wonderful effect it has! You force, with the sensation of a flash, The public, the great frog, to twitch.

After the sonnets follow *epigrams*, and a *Catalogue raisonné* of K.’s plays. After the strong pepper of the preceding poems, these are indeed a weaker, yet still agreeable, seasoning. — The center of the whole is made by: *Kotzebue’s Rescue, or the* *Virtuous Exile, a sentimental-romantic play in two acts.* — It would be an unreasonable demand that this little piece should be something perfected from the side of art. As the object, so the parody. We can therefore say in its praise only this much, that all the motifs which the story as well as Kotzebue’s dramatic inventions offered have been exhausted in this piece and used to the full.

There follows next *Festival Song of the German Actresses on* [p. 538] *K.’s Return* — a masterpiece of a sarcastic parody, and a fine pendant to Goethe’s Muses and Graces in the Mark. Here are the first three stanzas, since space forbids communicating the whole: Dearest Kotzebue! Had we no peace, Since they took you from us, Until you finally came back. Ah, we were very distressed, For we are in love with you; Now welcome, dearest you, Kotzebue! Kotzebue! Bubu — bubu — bubu — bu! We forsaken ones, were you gone, Would have a woeful gain: Shakspeare, Goethe, Schiller playing With inhuman feelings, And the iambs’ hard distress, Which we hate unto death. From this only you rescue us, Kotzebue! Kotzebue! Bubu — bubu — bubu — bu! You are our heart’s own man, Who can guess us right. Speeches, tears you can write, As we carry them on at home, So that by the lamp’s light We believe ourselves wholly to be ourselves. That no one can do like you, Kotzebue! Kotzebue! Bubu — bubu — bubu — bu! This festival song, delivered in the appended music only indifferently, must shake the most desiccated midriff! Next comes an ode<sup>115</sup> [p. 539] in which Kotzebue is hailed in each stanza alternately as sans-culotte and as aristocrat, and of which one would like to say that it cuts to the marrow. We would gladly linger yet over the romance that describes K.’s journey through the Siberian steppes, did we not wish to devote the space remaining to the poem, unique in its kind: *Kotzebue’s Travel Account*, in tercets. This poem is so poetically conceived and invented, and composed with such art, that it will retain a truly imperishable worth in German literature. The invention rests on this, that K.’s journey through the Mongolian peoples is presented as an allegory of his reputation spread among the various peoples of Germany, for which purpose the names of the former have been altered in an ingenious way. We cannot refrain from preserving at least in part, in our own Yearbooks, something that deserves to remain eternally in literature. First on the workaday fields

<sup>115</sup> According to a letter in existence, the author protests against the expression “the most desiccated midriff” as used by him. Ed.

I found the naturalistic Klozaks, Who scorn all art, like wise savages. Thereupon I came to the Zotiaks, Who tore themselves apart over my Bahrdt, And the Schmutzkens even sat upon my heels. So I fled to the Zähregisses, Who bear a bosom full of humanity, And weep more than other peoples piss. Next to them dwell then the Tugendusen; A noble people; how could I move them both Through the lyings-in of my tender Muses! They have the Quergisses and Plattkirs As allies, against the fantasts, Who write poetry merely for beauty, to wage war. Who believes it? the Quergisses’ casket Of the brain stood much farther back to the left: They twisted the [p. 540] hand when they grasped something. The Plattkir let his slanting eye blink, Pressing me with a flattened nose in friendly fashion, So that in fervor I thought I would sink down. How was it with me, the friend of man, blissful, To exchange my heart there with each and all! No applause ever was so enrapturing to me. Much kindness did the Dummojeds do me, Unassuming, and without boasting of it, The Wischwash too praised my speeches. More witty, however, are the Lahmschädals, They felt the fine point of my jests, Then I saw their broad cheeks beaming. They have widened their mouth with a great slit, In order to laugh to the full, So far goes the fondness for wit. But we must break off here, and add only the solution of the riddle.

Germany harbors the countless nations, Whom you visit, in their home territory; Here is Kotzbuzkoi, and here you shall dwell.

To set out the geniality of the whole invention might well be good for those who themselves belong to one or another of the nations depicted above. Connoisseurs will find of themselves that this work has opened a new region of poetry, hardly known until now in Germany, which seems quite especially and preeminently the author’s own, and which certainly cannot please the false humanity that agrees amicably with everything that is dissolute and bad, that slackens morals and corrupts the imagination, and protects it, and finds only the strictness of demands in art and science intolerable, because it claims for itself the same leniency. Thus that inventive whole [p. 541] will not only maintain, for the greater part, an independent existence, but will also endure through its effect. The sonnet, and likewise the tercet, has become in the hands of the author a vigorous organ of great capacity, of which it cannot be measured how far it will yet develop. Meter, even the most artificial, stands at his command for every purpose and every content as it does for no German poet before. Where such advantages unite, the effect cannot fail.

The reviewer notes yet expressly that he has no personal ground for finding a satire on Kotzebue and kindred spirits good. He would, even if he belonged among them, and held Kotzebue for something quite other than he can hold him in conviction, nevertheless have to accord that work unconditional applause from the side of poetry and art. Those who may continue to find good a cause whose badness has been uncovered in so manifold and unmistakable a way, one cannot of course prevent; but should they be inclined to defend it, they will do well first to take to heart the last stanza of the *paean* with which the whole closes: The Bahrdt that you have shorn, Is thrown into your beard. To shear you were lost labor, Like washing at the Moor, For forever stand the ears Long and rough-haired on you, That lies in your nature. O were you never born! How one tugs your beard! You wanted to bore asses, But you will be overbored. These are the Hyperboreans, Who chose for themselves to their delight, To bore through the heads, Which, as yours is eared, With laurels are wreathed, O were you never born! How you will be overbored!

[p. 542]

### Einiges über die Schädellehre.<sup>116</sup> — Some Remarks on Skull Doctrine<sup>116</sup>

<sup>116</sup> From the Morgenblatt 1807, no. 74.

The main proposition of *Gall’s* doctrine, that namely the brain forms the skull after itself, is already very definitely indicated in *Lavater’s* physiognomic fragments, among other places in the second part, p. 161, in the following words:

“The brain-case, hard as it is, is at first and for a long time so soft and pliable that furrows, grooves, unevennesses arise on the inside of the brain-case from the constant pressure of the blood, the veins, even of the brain itself, against it. — The hollowing of the brain-case is governed, as one can plainly observe, by the contained mass of the large and small brain and its growth through all stages of age, so that the outer shape of this inner organ appears perfectly expressed on the inner surface of the brain-case; and who doubts that *just so the* *outline of its outer surface* is determined thereby?”

The present writer thinks much of physiognomy, especially of the total expression of the whole human being; he goes so far as to believe that the soul builds its house more or less itself, and indeed furnishes it according to its pleasure and comfort, more than according to rules of architectural beauty. Most, even of the beautiful souls, practice only civil architecture, in which some proceed clumsily, others, following the finest turns of spirit and mood, though without proportion, [p. 543] make the dwelling prettily habitable; still others do not trouble themselves at all about where and how they live, any hut is good enough for them; but one sees this in them, and does not let oneself be misled about them. Very few indeed are in a position to erect palaces, where beauty, proportion and comfort meet. A German poet lives in whom this is the case. Another, who lives no more, looked like a sublime tower. — In the special determinations of Mr. *Gall*, the writer has always found it merely droll that so many able and capital faculties find no rightful lodging there, while others, subordinate and derivative, sit themselves down quite broadly; at times these have even had to yield, and their superiors have been quartered in their stead. Also the examples are such that doubts against them might be raised by many odd people, and other specimens called for. What a Babylonian confusion could arise, e.g., if the organ of the poet were first found in *Alxinger*, or the field-marshal organ in General Mack, and then sought afterward in, say, *Schiller* and *Massena*; one would then have to look around for quite different skull-heights. We keep believing that, up to now, Mr. *Gall* understands the structure of the brain better than the faculties that dwell in it. Why does he also pursue the penitentiaries, the thieving and brawling sense, more than the noble capacities? He ought, in fairness, to try his hand once at an academy of sciences, and sort out there the mathematicians, philosophers, physicists, philologists, poets, historians, etc. But to make the experiment perfect, he would have to be led among them in the dark, or better, blindfolded, so that nothing be betrayed to the sense of sight by other indications, which the sense lodged in the five feelers of the hand must be able to make out by itself alone. It would then become a pretty game of blindman’s buff, in which it would matter just whether he succeeded in catching this one and that one out of the assembly.

[p. 544]

### Bild vom Zinsgroschen.<sup>117</sup> — Picture of the Tribute Penny<sup>117</sup>

<sup>117</sup> From the Morgenblatt 1807, no. 269.

The task that was to be solved here is not among the easy ones; the subject not even among the favorable ones, if one will take the well-known principles of the Propyläen as the measure; there is in it no action to be represented, but a mere word, which cannot well speak itself. Nevertheless it is expressed here with great distinctness, and the picture has succeeded so eloquently and dramatically as it could, without touching the line where art passes over into the theatrical. On a quiet walk through the streets Jesus appears to have been stopped by the tempters; of his own people only John is with him. He himself stands turned imperceptibly to the side, hardly checked in his stride, as if he had instantly understood, answered, and were going on, to leave the group. The beautiful countenance is filled with untroubled calm, clear and conscious of every sublimity; the head, with the neck and the light-brown, gently curled hair that surrounds it, makes a broad, splendid oval, whose *outline* is of a particular strength and graciousness at once. One must wish to see this head executed once in life size. The spokesmen-questioners stand to the left of Christ; toward their side he has turned his head only a little, so that it still appears quite en face, and as he returns the coin to them with a gentle bending of the left arm, he points with the right toward heaven, thus through the [p. 545] twofold, yet calm movement of both arms rendering the decision sensible: “Render unto Caesar what is Caesar’s, and unto God what is God’s.” The raised arm is a beauty in itself through drawing and roundness; the wide sleeve falls back somewhat, and lets the well-formed hand be seen from the wrist on. Since the artist wished to treat the task on a larger scale than most are wont to do (as *Titian*, e.g., merely with three figures), gradations of character and passion were necessary. The spokesmen are two white-bearded old men, and this double specimen is excellently nuanced: the cunning of the one is of that kind which hides under a certain imbecile outward appearance of good intention, that of the other more lively and talkative, yet the word dies on the tongue of him who had just wanted to speak, and he cannot ward off dismay, which is visible in the whole figure, even in the cast of the folds. The garment of sallow, ambiguous color is of one piece with the rest of the expression. The first, who receives back the coin, goes on by contrast speaking and signifying, in the hope of still changing the judgment. Opposite these two on the right side, thus somewhat behind Christ’s back, stands the powerful figure of a man who shows his resentment at the failed plot with unconcealed passion; grasping hard at his breast with the left hand, clenching the right sideways, as if he would tear himself apart inwardly. The rage rages quite openly in his face as far as the beard bristling forward. A double counterweight is given him; a pictorial one in the tender and mildly gracious head of John appearing beside him; a more characteristic one in the head of a quite calm old man, who bears in his face not only the deadness of age but that of a much-experienced cunning, and seems to have foreseen that the plot would fail. Between John and Christ, finally, a younger head looks forth merely curious. Opposed to John, on the left side, seems to stand a young Israelite of a face indeed beautiful but not benevolent, and, as in agitated water the [p. 546] circles grow weaker toward the periphery and the movement finally vanishes entirely, so the picture closes on the one (the right) side with a figure that is recognized as male almost only by its beard, but otherwise in its whole habitus and the kind of its curiosity has much in common with an old woman, on the other with a head whose immobility and lack of outwardly visible sympathy springs from complete inner obduracy and hardening.

The background is made by buildings with colonnades; from there above a group of male and female heads eavesdrops on the scene; the one woman has grasped what it is to signify; behind her raised hand she whispers it to her neighbor, a girl with a lovely, innocently watching face. On a balustrade on the right farther into the distance a few Roman soldiers are indicated, thereby at once the condition of the people and the significance of the question. Beside it opens the view into the open.

This is the manner in which the story is presented, simple, without proper episode, without sought-out motifs. Distance from everything conventional, indeed from all existing pictorial devices that do not lie immediately in the matter itself, that is what distinguishes this painting as a whole and in all its parts. The studies which may have been made for it from nature by no means show through announcing themselves; but the ever more attractive thoroughness of it lets one surmise them. The execution is held thoroughly definite, without hardness; but above all the treatment of the garments is worthy of the greatest praise. They are not only faultlessly correctly cast, according to material and figure, but of a grand, unaffected character. Where they, as with the various old men in the picture, more enwrap than set forth the limbs, the outline of the whole figure is nevertheless always suited to the posture and expression of the head, and the true body that fits it. In the passionate one the figure is not covered by the clothing, and is of the most excellent drawing; both from the side of the picturesque and of the characteristic it is well considered [p. 547] that precisely this one shows itself more unveiled. The figure of Christ becomes visible more than all others *through* and by means of the garment.

The light in the painting is a gentle daylight that illuminates almost all heads equally. These even stand fairly on the same line; on the other hand they are separated from one another in coloring by the faintest and truest gradations, as generally the color has been treated with uncommon correctness, and from this its further freshness and delicacy proceed.

If, now, as the peculiarity of the whole work, the complete freedom from all mannerism, both as to the presentation of the story and the pictorial execution, can be stated, so that one could hardly name the artist whose manner it recalls: it deserves further to be mentioned as especially gratifying that this truth, solidity and purity of art, in its effect on the formation of younger artists, lets us expect further fine fruits, since Mr. *Langer* is designated director of the Academy of Formative Arts in Munich. One might be vexed to see him, since his absence from Düsseldorf, unemployed as a teacher, did he not meanwhile teach by the deed, and had we not to thank this leisure, among other things, for this painting, which does not flatter the senses through a superficial and specious beauty, but penetrates to the understanding, and, artistically satisfying, at the same time rouses the thinking powers of the spirit. Nothing can be more salutary to the present art-zealous youth than the lesson, confirmed by example, that art, in order to be seriously effective, must proceed above all from exact and correct thinking. We have yet to expect a Holy Family, as a counterpart to it, from Mr. Langer.

Mr. Langer the son has likewise completed a series of drawings, which he intends shortly to etch: a Raising of Lazarus; Christ as he teaches in the Temple; Paul before Festus, and others; all distinguished by genuine fullness of content, significance and invention in composition. They ought properly all to be executed on a large scale and in colors, [p. 548] as will also be done with the Lazarus. To be sure, artists must choose the shortest and nearest means of communicating themselves. Who commissions large paintings? One must be glad if, since artists are no longer employed through public life, at least individual private persons do not withdraw their means from art. Mr. Langer the younger is just now occupied with a Phocion (an oil painting), destined for Mr. Moritz *Bethmann* in Frankfurt. May this one awaken many [p. 549] emulators!

### Notiz über ein merkwürdiges Bildniß von Herrn Direktor Langer in München.<sup>118</sup> — Note on a Remarkable Portrait by Director Langer of Munich.<sup>118</sup>

<sup>118</sup> From the Morgenblatt 1808, no. 181.

— I cannot refrain from giving you news of a new work from the master hand of our worthy director of the Academy, Mr. *Langer*, which is just now arousing a twofold interest, that of the art and that of the subject. It is a portrait of Frau von *Montgelas*, wife of the first royal minister of state, full-length, seated, and life-size. Fortunate the artist to whom there falls, as here, the task of representing not only an outstanding beauty, imposing in figure and features, but in these at the same time a thoroughly animating significance! On the other hand, such a beauty also demands such a painter, whose peculiar spirit it is to wed the beautiful with the characteristic — for surely distant ages too will still delight in this painting.

To express its manner and style in a single word, it is a historical picture, which would remain significant and beautiful in itself even if it were not a portrait. The very choice of the moment marks an artist practiced in the delicate grasp of the individual. A representative pose would perhaps have been advantageous for expressing the dignity of the whole figure, but would not have suited this speaking countenance. Not leaning listlessly into the armchair, but sitting on it sideways, [p. 550] and upright of her own accord, the left arm propped on the tastefully designed reading-table, the right laid in indescribably charming foreshortening over the not high back of the chair, the lively image seems truly to breathe; the head is turned somewhat to the side, whereby the beautiful profile becomes clearer; the expression in it and in the half enthusiastic, half penetrating gaze is a light tension between clear composure and lively looking, which is just what occasions the extremely deceptive effect of life, and yet does not disturb the beholder by the restlessness of a portrait set in perpetual action. Through this light bearing and arrangement everything straight is at the same time interrupted, the mass broadened, and the black velvet dress (cut in the now customary, only more richly pleated fashion) and a red shawl, which flows down from the left arm round the lower part of the figure, are motivated into the most judiciously understood passages of drapery. Through the turn of the head a part of the neck, with the setting of the shoulder, is placed in a halfshadow softened by reflection, which has turned out so clear and transparent that it seems itself woven only of light, as this holds also of the arm foreshortened by half-shadows. In contrast, the beautiful bosom, enclosed by a lace collar standing up somewhat at the back, is rounded in full light and without noticeable shadow with wondrous delicacy; a difficult task of painting, which since *Titian* few have even undertaken to solve. The masterly treatment of the velvet must be mentioned all the more since it does not veil the limbs heavily, but marks them gracefully by its folds and creases, as is the case especially over the left knee and with beautiful effect. Light in its contours, the beautiful picture nevertheless appears in full vigor and steadiness like the pictures of earlier masters, without the frivolity by which in superficial portraits the shallow mind is otherwise bribed. By means of the nuancing of the background, which with some conventional liberties suggests a room into which the light falls through a narrow window opening that at the same time shows a landscape view, the bright keeping of the whole is pleasantly concluded; the colors [p. 551] are separated, but well in accord; of superfluous ornament and finery there is nothing to be found; the browncurled hair is to be adorned only with pearls, and the whiteness of the neck interrupted by a large string of pearls; the shawl is bordered with a golden embroidery. The likeness of the portrait goes without saying, for all this, and must be conceded at first glance. Though it is, as said, treated in the historical style, still no beautification can be demonstrated in it, either in detail or in the impression of the whole.

I would note further that Mr. *Langer* the elder, besides several portraits begun, has completed a Holy Family, in which Mary, Elizabeth, the two children, and Joseph come together in a landscape at a well, a painting which, by an uncommon loveliness, expressed especially in the quite peculiarly pure features and contours of the Madonna, offers a true softening counterpart to the sterner characterization in the Tribute Penny by the same master.

Only briefly do I mention some excellent drawings by Mr. *Langer* the younger, since they are destined to be etched and thus to become generally known: *Paul*, who defends himself before *Festus*, and the risen Lazarus. A pure and truly rare taste, an uncommon skill remote from all affectation, reveals itself in the first, in the treatment of the garments, the naturalness of the postures, the noble apostolic expression in *Paul*, the fitting sort of emptiness in *Festus*, in the excellently posed and drawn Roman behind *Festus*. The latter sits in the middle, seen from the side in too negligent a posture, *Paul* stands before him at one end of the picture, between him and *Festus* some wicked Jewish individuals, whose faces are to be praised only relatively, but their garments unconditionally; behind *Festus* too there stand several men listening not without partisan interest, so that from the judicial calm in the middle the movement proceeds to both sides. The scene is composed [p. 552] without solemnity, but speakingly, and it is not possible to see a more beautifully executed drawing, of which the etched sheet will give ocular proof. In inwardness of composition and variety of movement it is, however, still surpassed by the Lazarus, as indeed the subject itself brings with it.

[p. 553]

### Ueber die Verfassung der neuen königlichen Akademie der bildenden Künste in München.<sup>119</sup> — On the Constitution of the New Royal Academy of the Formative Arts in Munich.<sup>119</sup>

<sup>119</sup> From the Morgenblatt 1808, nos. 171–174.

The establishment of a royal Academy of the formative arts in Munich, a city where so much combines for the flourishing of such an institution, must rightly arouse the joyful expectations of all friends of art and artists.

Whatever has ever been objected, with more or less semblance, against academies of the arts rests partly on presuppositions to which most academies hitherto perhaps gave ground enough, but which are by no means necessarily bound up with the concept of an academy; partly it contains rather the indictment of the present general condition of art, which requires special institutions for the preservation of the arts, after the sense for them and their use has vanished from public life.

In the latter respect blame could fall on academies only if, instead of procuring for art, wherever possible, a free life again, they narrow-heartedly pushed it back and shut it off from what is common. In the former respect, however, much will depend on the constitution which a new institution of this kind receives, and still more on that which it gives itself.

When artists of truly free and great mind declare themselves with vivacity against academies, they might, it seems, well spare themselves this polemic; for were it true that academies, [p. 554] instead of favoring the free and self-reliant impulse of art, constitute themselves hothouses of art, instead of the healthy growth raise the sickly plant of an art that is itself artificial; that they put convention in the place of truth, propriety in the place of nature, and in place of style a limited manner clinging, as it were, to the soil of the place: then this will always be the case only where no great independent spirits devote themselves to art and produce works whose genuine, solid and original splendor extinguishes those shadow-and semblance-images of art. Never does the school as such, but always and everywhere, wherever it appears genuinely, genius give the rule, the standard of judgment and of the general and public feeling for the beauty of art. The truly powerful spirit has no school or academy to fear. As for those, however, who would only give themselves the semblance of such a spirit, and reject academies especially because they are painfully reminded by them of the neglected or despised foundations, they deserve no consideration. Do we not experience elsewhere too, in science for example, that those rebel most loudly against the school who could have attained some excellence only through strict discipline.

The constitution of the new Academy of the Arts in Munich, as it was made known in the Bavarian Government Gazette of the first of June, bears the traces of mature deliberation and of regard for previous experience, as well as for the proposals of insightful men for a better arrangement of such institutions. The statutes of the foremost academies appear to have been compared in the process, namely those of the Academy of Art at Vienna (of the year 1800), which have recently become more generally known through their reprinting in the *Prometheus*, and which in fact breathe a far more liberal spirit than the *Regulations for the Academy of the* *Formative Arts and Mechanical Sciences at Berlin* (Berlin, Unger, 1790).

With pleasure one will see several proposals of the essay in the *Propyläen on Institutions of Instruction in Favor of the* [p. 555] *Formative Arts* realized here by royal ordinances, and will not withhold the just homage from the spirit of a government which always takes the most advancing and most vigorous into its plans for the ennobling of its people.

Above all, the weight is gratifying which the constitution of the Bavarian Academy lays on *instruction* as the chief purpose of the institution. In a time or in a realm where excellent artists are present in great number, where the love of art is great enough to put every renowned master in a position to occupy a number of pupils with his works, the need for public institutions of instruction established by the state will be felt less, or not at all. There academies would be more like corporations or sodalities, which the already formed artists erect among themselves, as was the case with the oldest of all academies, the Florentine. Where, on the other hand, those circumstances do not obtain, where the artist is not sufficiently honored and employed by the general inclination to art to raise pupils and apprentices on his own account as a respectable master, there the state, which does not lack the means, if it does not otherwise want art to die out, must step in, and both appoint skilled artists to give public instruction and facilitate the acquisition of the manifold foundations of artistic formation through generally accessible institutions. Such a condition then also requires that the institution of teaching and instruction be the basis of an academy of art; through that and out of it the latter would first have to generate itself as a free union and society of art. Otherwise the so-called academy would soon degenerate into an empty game, where under the semblance of great busyness nothing would at bottom be done, and in place of living progress a dead standstill would set in.

The Bavarian Academy of the Arts is indeed to combine both purposes; it is to regard itself at once as an institution of teaching or instruction and as a free society of art, but the first purpose is always to be treated as the foremost and most important.

No academy in the world will create a *Raphael*, a *Titian*, or [p. 556] similar artists in the proper sense. But every innate talent requires sustained practice and acquired knowledge in order to show and move itself with freedom. What painful feelings spirits arouse in us who were destined to present great Ideas sensibly, but, deserted by the more exact knowledge of the human figure and other foundations, feel hemmed in in the execution and attain only a wavering, imperfect efficacy! But how hard it is for the artist to arrive by himself at a thorough and well-worked understanding of the human figure! What difficulties our climate, habit, and the limited means of the individual set against the study from nature! The masterworks of art too are with us less than even in Italy, incomparably less than in antiquity, public property; antiques and their casts, as well as exemplary paintings, are put under lock and key, and, unless the state opens the entrance, are not granted to the artist for continued, undisturbed use. The more abundantly, then, an academy provides for these aids to the acquisition of the first knowledge, the more surely will it train the artists whom it forms, though not to be all great, which depends on no human arrangements, yet to be capable masters, sure of their art, who are able to present what they have conceived with correctness, truth and propriety.

In the constitution of the Bavarian Academy a special teacher has been appointed for anatomy, among other subjects; for the benefit of anatomical study can hardly be fully attained for the pupil of art without instruction specially calculated for his needs and given to him under the eyes of his teachers. Elsewhere the study from nature and from the nude is mostly restricted to the winter, and suffers besides from many other inconveniences; at the Bavarian Academy, however, the evenings in winter are to be devoted to drawing and modeling from nature, in summer to drawing, painting and modeling from nature and from the draped figure. The study [p. 557] from works of art is treated with the greatest liberality. The collection of antiques and casts is an immediate attribute of the Academy; but all the other collections, notoriously so rich and excellent, of paintings, engravings, hand drawings, are also to stand constantly open to the artist for the most convenient use possible.

As the painter and sculptor, so the architect too requires certain fundamental knowledge, which is more theoretical and has a scientific character. The sequel will have to show whether, given the seriousness with which architecture has been treated in the Bavarian Academy, a special instruction measured for artists in geometry and the other mathematical sciences is not necessary, so that a whole of doctrine and instruction may arise.

The manifold various kinds of knowledge and skill which the one art of painting comprises make some difficulty in the distribution of the branches of instruction. Several teachers are necessary; shall each now teach the whole of art, so that they alternate, as at the Academy at Vienna among others, and each on the day when he appears at the Academy gives guidance and instruction to all classes of pupils? or shall these be divided into classes, and a special teacher set over each class? Both arrangements may have their disadvantages; the first, however, evidently the most. With the other, which has been chosen for the Academy in Munich, it will depend on not observing the division into classes too strictly in practice, but leaving each pupil the freedom to turn to all the teachers alike, and to those in whom he has conceived a particular confidence, without regard to the division into classes.

It is to be regarded as a significant advantage of the arrangement made in Munich that the pupils are not kept year by year in certain classes or studies, but at any time, according to the progress made, may pass from one class into another, and also that the classes are generally not kept so separate, but, for example, in the study from nature the pupils may all attend together.

[p. 558] As to the scope of instruction, every insightful person will find it praiseworthy that the merely mechanical arts are excluded from it. All too easily these, where they are admitted, raise themselves to the essential, and spread the common spirit of the craftsman, which is the true antipode of free art.

Once the artist has acquired those fundamental knowledges and skills, to be attained only through diligence, assiduous practice and thorough transmission by perfect masters, he then enters a higher domain, where he must be left more to his freedom; where the intuition and explanation of what exists of the exemplary, where counsel given in passing and the improving judgment of the teacher in particulars initiate him best into the secrets of composition. For this stage of instruction, therefore, the conversations of the teacher of the third class, prescribed by law, will be of evident use, in that once a week he accompanies his pupils to the art collections, explains to them the works of great masters, compares them with one another, and makes the peculiarity of each noticeable.

For the same stage lectures on the theory of the arts, and on archaeology as well, have been established elsewhere, for example at the Berlin Academy. If these keep to the generality customary hitherto, it is hardly to be seen what they are to profit the artist: unless the wretched chatter about art, which belongs to the tone of the age, should take possession of the artist too, against which the constitution of the Bavarian Academy has already taken precaution in the first instruction. “No half-artists are to be trained, who are able only to reason about art, but not to execute anything.” Should theoretical lectures, however, engage in the specifics of art, as for example the treatises of *Mengs* do — should they treat in particular the secrets of composition, of grouping, of the distribution of shadow and light, of contrast, and so on, then here too the immediate practical instruction, given out of the fullness of experience on single occasions, will be of far greater importance. The artist must accustom himself early, with all the [p. 559] general formation he may fairly acquire, nevertheless, as soon as he has to present and produce, to act altogether specifically. Only then will he more or less hit upon the one thing right, so as not to become monotonous and run the risk of constantly repeating, as it were, one basic scheme. Lectures on antiquities, if they are filled with erudition, draw the artist into a domain that is not his own; if he is nevertheless seized by it, learned artists result; if he takes it more lightly, the whole preparation was unnecessary, and he could have acquired what he needed of antiquarian knowledge, by use and through instruction in the particular case, more easily and more briefly.

The only lectures of this kind that are to be given at the Bavarian Academy are lectures on *mythology*. It might indeed seem that the budding artist could draw his knowledge of mythology from the sources just as well through his own reading, especially of the poets; and a collection of classical poets, ancient and modern, to be lent to the students, is listed among the endowments of the Bavarian Academy. Yet the study of mythology has, without doubt, a higher end still than that of historical knowledge. A deeper initiation into its spirit is perhaps the most powerful means of raising the artist from the historical and the merely moral characterization (which is always bound up with the former) to the symbolic and to the characterization of nature; for he must by all means be raised to the standpoint from which he sees what is highest in art, just as not everyone arrives of himself at the highest standpoint of the contemplation of the world, but must be raised to it. This seems especially necessary in art, since most are so glad to content themselves with the attainment of lesser ends. As soon as he can begin to use art freely as a means of representation, he must learn that the historical is never to be represented solely for its own sake, but as the veil of an Idea, and that only in the measure in which it is permeated by this does there arise that single highest thing, the beautiful and pleasing [p. 560] that is, without any further end, beautiful in itself. It will therefore be necessary to immerse the pupil early in the spirit of genuine symbolism, which can by no means be done by merely retelling mythological fictions, but only by presenting and treating mythology as a whole of living artistic ideals.

A principal objection to the founding of academies of the arts is this too, that a multitude of artists are trained who afterwards lack employment, and whose heads and hands might better have been used for other ends. This remark is only too well founded in a state where neither the dignity of art in itself and its significance for the spirit of the whole nation, nor its influence extending even to everyday life, is recognized. There academies may appear as decorations, which exist only so that nothing be missed that one demands, once and for all, of the larger state; or, should even this sacrifice made to opinion seem too great, they may be degraded to ends of mechanical utility. Here too the Bavarian government is different. Drawing is regarded as a branch of *general* public instruction; through schools of drawing, which no town of note will be without, taste and a feeling for art are to be spread into the workshop of the craftsman and even into the domestic life of the citizen. Three admirably chosen cities of the kingdom, *Nuremberg*, the cradle, *Augsburg*, the old nursery of German art, and *Innsbruck*, the capital of a land whose inhabitants have from of old shown a particular aptitude for art, are to receive schools of art of their own. Of these, to be sure, the constitution of the Academy mentions only the provision that they are to be nurseries for it; yet it is to be expected that at their founding, on which the new Academy is to give its opinion, they will receive, besides that end, a more independent destination as well.
