If such a connection is established between the schools of art and of drawing and the Academy that these different institutions are directed, each in its own way, by One spirit, then Bavaria is the state in which [p. 561] something is first done for art according to a thoroughgoing coherence. State institutions that do not in the end react upon the nation, and have as their basis the great mass of the people, from which new, refreshing forces must always come again to the arts and sciences, hover without support, and retain something foreign, not engaging with the whole, in the midst of the state. If the Bavarian Academy of the Arts were merely to send out capable teachers into the schools of art, as these in turn into the schools of drawing, an honorable effect would thereby be achieved. Since the subordinate institutions are immediately useful for the ends of general life, the Academy can pursue the higher, indeed the highest ends all the more freely; and all the more undisturbed if the following true word of the *Propyläen* is kept in view (vol. 2, no. 2, p. 7): “All those good influences (on comfort, grace and enjoyment of life, on the ennobling even of the common implements of life through the power of the arts) increase or decrease unfailingly in the measure in which their primal source, high art, flows more abundantly or diminishes and dries up. With the decline of taste the beautiful form soon vanishes; what had been simple and graceful becomes overloaded, interest disappears, and in a short time only the necessary is left; constraint now does the work, need and no longer love, every innovation is merely a further straying from the good and the beautiful.”

But more still, the decree on the founding of the Academy contains the following truly royal word: “We will that at least the public buildings remain consecrated to art, and that under Our government hardly any of some significance arise in which, besides architecture, sculpture and painting too have not their share.” — In general the whole organization rests on the right view that the most powerful means of promoting art consists not in pensions, which are consumed idly and without use for the whole, but in ample employment and fitting payment for individual outstanding works. This view has determined even the provision concerning the prizes, which deserves special mention.

[p. 562] There is a threefold awarding of prizes: an annual one for the pupils, one recurring every three years for those of the higher classes, and finally one that recurs every four years. In the second, the prize for the native artist consists in the commission to execute a painting, a statue or a bust, for which he receives a studio, the materials and models free; since he carries out his work under the eyes of the teachers, this must bring him a considerable step forward in art, and since these works are to be used for the adornment of public buildings, he at the same time does not miss the fair profit otherwise attached to winning a prize. The choice of subjects is to be made with this in view, so far as is feasible, — so no patriotic paintings of the kind that were demanded in another state some ten years ago, representing acts of war and the like in modern soldiers’ costume and barbarous soldiers’ cut! — In the third competition, held every four years, the prize for native sculptors, painters and architects consists in an ample support, with which they are sent to Italy for *three* years; the engraver receives support for two years. These provisions are so far unique in Germany; in the highest degree purposeful and worthy of praise.

In the second competition, held every three years, foreigners are to compete as well, as indeed in all the arrangements the right principle shines forth that art and science, in order to be promoted in a single state, must be promoted in the large and in the whole as the common possession of mankind. Like the native, every foreigner too has free access to the instruction, which is to be without charge for all pupils. He may enter as a beginner at the age of thirteen or fourteen, or, if he is already further advanced, in order to complete his studies. Indeed, what German city could at this moment have more attraction for the young artist than the Bavarian royal city! Separated from Italy only by the mountains, to which [p. 563] the friend of nature is drawn by high and wondrous beauties, it encloses a rare collection of the most important art treasures of every kind, which are increased daily; and what is more than this, a lively and vigorous striving meets the stranger here from all sides. Though the state of becoming has its imperfections, these are nevertheless not to be compared with the influences that the sight of deadness and stagnation has on the young, striving heart. The same height is not the same when it is taken on the line of ascent and when it is taken on that of descent. — We will not mention the favor which the personal love of art of the Bavarian reigning house promises to the arts, which has revived with new strength in the excellent Crown Prince. We are convinced that the artists near and far who are at this moment employed by him cannot have heard of the founding of an academy of art in Munich without sympathy. — Bavaria is the first state to extend its awarding of prizes in the field of the arts to outsiders as well; but in general foreigners are to be invited at every art exhibition to send in their works, even those made without regard to competition for a prize; the costs of sending them there and back are reimbursed by the Academy for all that are at all significant, the Academy which, as the charter expressly says, “will moreover take it to heart to requite with tokens of respect and honor the sympathy shown to it by cultivated artists.” It would thus depend only on the German artists themselves to form in Munich a center for the art of the whole fatherland. They have often complained of the lack of such a thing; and it would arise better through voluntary agreement than through external power. They will be all the more inclined to make use of this proffered point of union, since here there is talk of *reciprocal action* in the true sense, and not of some authority to be exercised at some time or other. To the artist from abroad not merely reward and encouragement are offered, but at the same time the advantage is acknowledged which native art draws from intercourse [p. 564] with art abroad. “Our Academy (these are the very words of the charter) is to enter into reciprocal action with the contemporary endeavors in art, and to work upon the age, in order in turn to be furthered by it, and so most surely to *forestall any one-sidedness or narrow nationality* that might show itself in instruction or in practice .”<sup>120</sup>

<sup>120</sup> In the Berlin regulations the teacher of *landscape painting* is even instructed to visit with his pupils, in order to show them how they must imitate nature correctly and with taste, *the best localities lying in the country*. Such zeal was shown there in granting to art only patriotic subjects!

The constitution of the Academy as an *art society* is wholly designed to keep alive in it the spirit of freedom and of progress. The Academy is an independent institution, directly dependent only on the Ministry of the Interior; nor is it an appendage of another institution, as the French Academy of the Arts is the fourth class of the National Institute. To be sure, the latter has in return a greater extension, in that musicians and actors too are members of it; yet it is surprising that one did not then straightway make only two classes in general, one of the arts and one of the sciences, and did not throw the different sciences together in the latter no more than the different arts in the former. The government has appointed only the basis of the academic personnel, and has reserved to itself only the appointment of these, whereby the Academy is left free to complete itself and to join to itself, for the common end, every distinguished talent of the country. The permanent personnel consists of the director, the secretary-general and the teachers of the four schools of art, of painting, sculpture, architecture and engraving. On the other hand every artist admitted by the Academy as an ordinary member attends the sessions with full right to vote, if the Academy is willing to grant him this. This arrangement will have the consequence that the Academy will never be burdened with useless ordinary assessors, and yet every deserving artist can be sure of finding the place due to him.

[p. 565] In a state where the mechanism of the conduct of business counts for the highest, the so-called men of business will easily crowd even into institutions of liberal ends and soon stifle with their formalism all life of the actual members . Another evil in academies of the arts can spring from the<sup>121</sup> crowding in of scholars, who, if they gain a preponderance, [p. 566] easily turn the institution toward ends quite other than its own and original ones. Even in the Vienna Academy it might not be advantageous to the purity of the end that the academic council is composed half of scholars. Yet an academy of the arts really needs scholarly cooperation in many cases, and if it is to stand in contact with the age, this is hardly possible by any other means than by the general one of literature. In this respect the expedient adopted at the Bavarian Academy is perhaps the simplest, since the direction of all literary affairs of the Academy, and of the business that results from its concept as an art society, is entrusted to a scholar who holds the post of permanent secretary-general.

<sup>121</sup> The limitation of posts at the Bavarian Academy of the Arts will be found especially estimable in comparison with the accumulation of them at other academies. In the personnel roster of the Berlin Academy there is found first of all a *curator* in the person of a minister of his own, who himself *presides* at the weekly sessions, and without whose foreknowledge the director and the academic senate may settle no matter of importance; then a consultant and *Justitiarius*; a *Kassencurator*, who is at the same time reporting councillor and conducts the dispatches; finally a director, after him a *Vicedirektor*, and an academic senate, from which the Academy itself is still distinct; at the senate there are, as *ordinary assessors*, several councillors of the Oberschulcollegium, several members of the Oberhofbauamt, a chemist, on account of the constituents of the colors, the opera decorator and director of the porcelain manufactory — last the *professors* of the schools of art. After this long procession there follow only then the artists, who are *members* of the Academy, and whose number in turn is exceeded by that of the *honorary members and assessors* (all non-artists). Finally there closes the series a special economy-inspectorate with an economy-inspector and a *treasurer* of the academic fund. How much might still fall to the poor artist under such an arrangement; and how he must have felt in a crowd of persons, so many of whom understood nothing of actual art, and yet made themselves the spokesmen and vote-leaders! The honor that the assemblies are presided over by a minister of state would hardly count here: it must rather be most detrimental to the free expression of opinions and views if the chief, who reports to the regent and determines the highest decision, at the same time conducts the debates of the society. What consequences and what spirit this union of the *curator* and president in One person has drawn after it, artists of that time can give the best account, and it may be inferred from the facts in *Carstens’s Life by Fernow* alone. Far more advantageous and honorable it certainly is if the curatorship of the Academy, as in Bavaria, is in the hands of that minister to whom the direction of all internal affairs is entrusted, and if the members are quite free in the expression of their opinions and disturbed by no alien presence.

In the great general competition, which takes place every three years, the reasoned judgments are to be made known through a special program of the Academy; on the one hand all suspicion of partiality is thereby met, and on the other these programs will serve as yearbooks of the arts in Bavaria. Exemplary are the provisions concerning the admission of ordinary members (on whom, after the model of Italian academies, the title of professors of the Bavarian Academy may also be conferred), honorary members and correspondents. *Ordinary members* are to be only *practicing artists*, who have either delivered a piece for admission, or enter into a regular connection with the Academy and send in works from time to time to its art exhibitions. In the elections the procedure is to be strict and according to the most exact impartiality, “so that the Academy may not render its tokens of honor worthless by profusion, and may assure itself of public approval more through the qualities of its members than through their number.”

The regulations on the deliberations and the order at the sessions agree almost entirely with those of the Vienna Academy. By these all arbitrariness and caprice is forestalled; the members appear in fact as members, between whom a free [p. 567] reciprocal expression and liberal communication of opinions takes place, and among whom, for that very reason, a firm common view must soon form on the main points. In general the constitution fulfills what is promised in the declaration on the ends of the Academy: “A point of union is to be secured to the artists of the kingdom, a distinction for which they strive, and whose conferment includes the public declaration of real mastery. That noble emulation, so salutary to the arts, is to be maintained also among the teachers and the already trained artists, and the individual, after attaining maturity in art, is to find in union with men of like cultivation the means of ever more raising and extending his scientific concepts of art.” Not only the outer rights and privileges of a learned society are granted to the Academy, but its inner freedom and liveliness too are preserved to it. — It is, further, a real public authority in matters of the arts, “which through its deliberations is to promote the growth of the arts, and to put into effect the means to be applied by the government to their good.” It is to be heard in an advisory capacity not merely in its own affairs, in the filling of posts or the granting of pensions, but in the execution of public works and the appraisal of native or foreign inventions. The establishment of a special *committee for the administration of the art treasures*, standing in closest connection with the Academy, opens to it a great, beautiful and extremely useful sphere of action; the connection, finally, in which it is placed with the schools of art and of drawing of the kingdom, gives it the means to be active on a scale such as is, proportionately, possible to no other academy.

In general it deserves mention as a characteristic trait of the whole constitution that it throughout acknowledges the relation of the arts to public life, and grounds art in the essence of the nation itself, rather than presenting it as something external, wholly remote from life and from the common good. Among other things the beautiful wish is expressed in it [p. 568] to bring back those times when handicraft stood nearer to art, and capable artists emerged from the midst of it. To this end the Academy is granted the right to confer the title of academic artist also on native craftsmen whose works are receptive of beautiful forms; a useful provision, which is contained also in the constitution of the Berlin Academy.

The fulfillment of all the beautiful hopes which this constitution awakens for art in Bavaria and — we may say so — for German art in general, will depend partly on the continuing, active support of the government, which has created this institution; yet still more on the zeal of the members, and the judicious conduct of the whole institution — especially on this, that, never going after show, it always remains clearly aware of its end, and, esteeming lasting fame higher than the quickly spread, wishes to raise the beautiful plant whose care is entrusted to it only slowly, but to a durable flowering.
